snapshot.title: The girls in the Gaza school photograph
snapshot.evidenceText: Just before the genocide, 15 Gaza schoolgirls posed for a photograph. Three years on, Al Jazeera went looking for them. Nuseirat, Gaza Strip — Maha Taha fills the old blackboard with equations and sets her students to work. For the next few minutes, the classroom settles into the scratch of pens and the low murmur of girls working through the problems. Maha, 43, has taught mathematics for 20 years. Dressed in an olive-green jalabeya and beige hijab, she steps quietly to her desk at the side of the room, as her students work through the maths problems. She has watched generations of girls pass through her classroom, preparing for exams and applying to universities. Asked about the girls she taught before the October 7 genocide began, Maha pauses before reaching for her phone. While scrolling back to find a photograph taken in June 2023, she speaks softly, so as not to disturb the girls in the classroom. “I was proud of them," she says. "I could see that they had bright futures ahead of them. They were very special in their personalities, even before it came to their studies. But October 7 changed the course of their lives.” In the photo, 15 teenage girls in navy school robes and white scarves crowd around Maha in the schoolyard. Some have their arms around one another; others lean towards the camera. All are smiling. They had just finished their mock exams and wanted a photograph together. Sara Rayan took it, holding out the phone so everyone fit in the frame. The girls were 17 and 18. Like many teenagers their age, they worried about exams and university places, talked about what they wanted to become, and imagined the lives that lay ahead. Four months later, Israel's war on Gaza began. Three years on, one of the girls in the photograph has been killed in an Israeli air strike. Four have left Gaza. Others have been displaced - their education interrupted and their plans for the future upended. Al Jazeera set out to find the 15 girls, to discover what had happened to them and the futures they once imagined, and to see whether they could be brought together again for a photograph in the same schoolyard. Muscat Secondary School is still standing, although it was struck by artillery in February 2024 and became a shelter for displaced families. Some classrooms still bear the marks of the war: holes left by quadcopter gunfire, windows damaged by shelling and soot stains where families cooked over open fires. On the walls, children have drawn kites, flowers and a Palestinian flag. Some have written their names: Haya, Marah, Mohammed and Khaled. Displaced families still shelter in parts of the school, while a tent at the edge of the yard serves as a makeshift classroom for younger pupils whose own school can no longer accommodate them. It's just past 10am on a Thursday in late September when Yasmin Abu Zaid arrives. Then Aya Adnan arrives, quickening her pace when she sees Yasmin and pulling her into an embrace. “I haven’t seen you for three years,” she says. “Where have you been? You never show up.” Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader arrives a few minutes later, carrying a plastic bag of books for Aya’s younger sister, who is preparing for the Tawjihi, Gaza’s national secondary school graduation exams. Aya and Lina have seen each other since leaving school. Their families have been friends for years, and they still live in the same neighbourhood of Nuseirat. But Yasmin, who once lived nearby, was displaced early in the war. With the fighting making it difficult to meet, neither has seen her for three years. The three have also kept in touch with Ghaida Zaqout, who now lives in Egypt. Together, they have a private WhatsApp group where they chat regularly and check on one another. When Maha finishes teaching, she greets "my girls" with arms wide open. They erupt into chatter, talking over one another and trying to catch up. In time, Maha pulls up the old photograph on her phone. The girls huddle around her, then point at the tree behind them, recognising it from the photograph. Now, they begin recalling the school days they shared. There were the ordinary intimacies of teenage friendship: who would lend you a pen, who would explain homework you didn't understand, who whispered through lessons and who worried for days about an exam. Ghaida was the girl whose laughter could be heard before she entered the classroom, and who rarely stopped talking, even when teachers moved her to another desk. Sara and her twin sister Fatima were forever taking selfies, while Lina al-Hour was quieter, often bringing novels to read during breaks. The girls talked about clothes, television programmes and football. They bought food together during breaks and wondered aloud about university and what they might become. Some dreamed of studying medicine; another wanted to design buildings. Their futures still seemed to turn on exams, marks, university places and what their families could afford. Maha remembers Sara Rayan laughing, and Ghaida, she says, is in Egypt now, studying dentistry. Here, she pauses, enlarges Lina’s face on the screen and falls silent. Her smile has disappeared. When she speaks again, her voice is quieter and catches slightly. “This is my well-mannered student, Lina,” she says softly. “She is a martyr.” On November 17, 2023, Lina was killed in an Israeli air strike. She was 18. For a moment, the girls wrap their arms even tighter around one another in silence. Standing in the same schoolyard three years later, they tell one another they wish they could return to those days. But most of the girls in the photograph are missing at this reunion. Aya takes out her phone and holds it at arm's length, trying to recreate the selfie Sara took three years earlier. “Sara should have been here to take it,” she says. But Sara cannot come. She now works for an NGO, using her wages to help pay her university fees and contribute to her family's income. Aya Adnan stands with the three in the new photograph, tall, with a dimple in her chin and her hijab falling behind her shoulders. Three years earlier, she had been looking forward to university. She wanted to become a doctor, preferably a neurosurgeon. Aya enjoyed studying. She arrived early for extra physics lessons and worked through difficult material until she understood it. She had also noticed how few female surgeons there were in Gaza and disliked hearing that surgery was too demanding a profession for women. Her interest in neurology had become personal in the 11th grade, when she suffered a severe headache and dizziness that lasted 24 hours. “It felt like my head was heavier than my body,” she recalls, “as if it might fall off.” After undergoing scans and seeing a neurologist, she was told pressure from the vertebrae in her neck was affecting her spinal cord. The experience only made her more determined to study neurology. When her final school results came, she had scored 96 percent. But studying medicine was expensive, and the family - her father was an UNRWA social worker - could not comfortably afford the fees. Seventeen years her senior, Yasser was a lawyer with his own practice, a wife and three children: Adnan, nine, Ahmad, seven, and three-year-old Ilaf. He helped support their parents and hoped one day to teach law at university. “I used to always tell him, ‘You're a second father to me,’ because he was so kind to me, just like my father,” Aya says. Aya remembers a summer's day in August 2023. Yasser, still dressed in his smart work clothes, came to take her from Nuseirat to the Islamic University of Gaza. "Together, we went from department to department, trying to find a course that was affordable and that I would enjoy," she says. Professors suggested engineering. But when they came out, Aya told Yasser she couldn't imagine herself studying computers or becoming an engineer. “I could picture myself wearing a white coat, that's all,” she told him. “Maybe I could study something in the medical field,” Aya suggested. “I really liked medical laboratory sciences.” Yasser knew that his sister was giving up the version of university she had imagined. But he refused to let her see the decision as the end of something. "Perhaps it's for the best," he told her. "Maybe one day you'll become a doctor in the field you choose to specialise in. You don't have to be a medical doctor; you could become a university professor with a PhD." Then, he offered her a thought that has stayed with her. "He told me, 'Sometimes what is withheld from us can be better for us than what is given to us,' and I believe him." Afterwards, he took her to Al-Taboun restaurant for lunch, while they kept talking about university and the choices available. Aya enrolled in medical laboratory sciences, and Yasser bought her books and supplies. University had barely completed its first week when the war began. A strike on a neighbouring two-storey house badly damaged the family home in Nuseirat, where they had lived for more than 35 years. They moved into an aunt's house. The new university timetable that had occupied Aya only weeks earlier disappeared. Instead of laboratories and lectures, her days revolved around finding water, helping prepare food, and learning how to cook without the things the family had once taken for granted. She didn't know how to build a fire; she hadn't needed to. Yasser would continue to return to the family's damaged home, partly to check on what they had left behind and partly because he feared their possessions would be stolen. Sometimes, he stayed there. On one of those visits, he asked Aya to come with him. There were dishes to wash, floors to sweep, rooms to tidy. She said she couldn't. She was helping their mother prepare food. On December 12, as the family gathered for afternoon prayers at her aunt's house, they heard a missile strike. Several minutes later, one of Aya's friends called. She wanted to know where the family was. Then she asked about Yasser, who had returned to their damaged home alone. The strike had hit the house, killing him. He was 32. Aya would return again and again to Yasser asking her to come with him, and her reply that she couldn't. It was an ordinary exchange between siblings, insignificant enough that Aya might never have remembered it, except it was also their last conversation. When she returned to the house about a week later, she found what remained of the plastic shopping bags that held the university supplies Yasser had bought for her only months earlier. Shaking off dust and ash, she opened them one by one. “I was surprised I found them at all; they reminded me of Yasser,” she says. Some books had survived, but others were almost entirely burned; only three pages remained from one set of lecture notes. Ballpoint pens, markers, and coloured pencils lay among the notes. Aya gathered, and still has, what remained. After 18 months, when universities started offering remote learning, Aya logged on whenever electricity and an internet connection allowed. Medical laboratory sciences was supposed to be hands-on: equipment, experiments, laboratories. Aya was trying to learn it without any of those things. "My major is very practical, and most of its courses are practical," she says. "It was difficult for me to study them online when I wasn't even at the university, and there were no laboratories or equipment in front of me." She kept going, and so did another girl in the photograph who once imagined herself in a white coat. Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader, known as “the tall one”, had also imagined becoming a surgeon. At school, she had loved Turkish dramas and anime and had a habit of doodling on her desk, much to the annoyance of her biology teacher. Those interests have since fallen away. She graduated with 98.3 percent and enrolled in medicine at the Islamic University of Gaza on September 10, 2023. Less than a month later, the war brought her studies to a halt. Her father, Yunis Abd al-Qader, works as a paramedic with the Palestinian Red Crescent. During the war, he worked 24-hour shifts and returned home only for brief rest. “I would wonder if he would come back the next day," she says. "I wished I could be there with him, to help him through the difficult things he was seeing.” Usually quiet and reserved, her father tried to spare the family the details of what he encountered. But sometimes, he came home exhausted, and the strain showed. One account he shared stayed with Lina. After an Israeli strike, he had been recovering human remains. Initially, he believed they belonged to seven people. As he continued working, he realised there was an eighth. Having witnessed the scale of amputations, fractures and other injuries, she wants to specialise in orthopaedic surgery. As she continued her medical studies, Lina became close to another student, Shams Majdi. Their friendship was still new when Lina struggled with a physiology problem and messaged Shams on WhatsApp for help. Shams lived in northern Gaza, where internet access was unreliable. With Israeli quadcopters overhead, she travelled several kilometres to find a connection so she could help solve the problem with Lina over the phone. Lina remembers the trouble her new friend took to help her. Later, the two sat the same exam remotely, from different parts of Gaza. Shams had again travelled away from home to find an internet connection. After finishing the exam, Lina opened WhatsApp. Lina says Shams was usually quick to respond, when she could. So she waited. About 45 minutes later, a message appeared in their medical college group announcing that Shams Majdi had been killed. For about 10 minutes, she says that she struggled to comprehend that it was the same Shams whose reply she had been waiting for. She kept sending messages throughout the day. None was answered. Shams had been killed in an Israeli strike on her home, alongside members of her family. For the following week, Lina says, she cried whenever she opened her medical books. There had been another Lina in Maha's classroom. Lina al-Hour, the quieter girl who loved novels and wrote letters to her friends, had also enrolled in medicine. She had attended her first week of university before the war began. On November 17, 2023, an Israeli air strike hit her family's home. Lina was killed alongside her parents, siblings and other relatives. With no surviving parent or sibling for Al Jazeera to interview, her former classmates and teacher helped piece together memories of her life. Maha remembers the way she listened in class. The girls remember how easily they could make her laugh. Lina Abd al-Qader remembers the strangeness of sharing a name with a friend who is now gone. “I and my friend who was killed had the same name,” she says. “But my friend was killed, and I still cannot get over it.” Ghaida Zaqout is now in Egypt, more than 300km (186 miles) from the schoolyard where she once posed with her classmates. Speaking to Al Jazeera by phone, she recalls how she used to fill her schoolbooks with drawings of the wooden houses she admired in Japanese anime, and dreamed of becoming an architect. By then, her sister Asmaa, her husband and their two children had moved in after losing their home in an Israeli air strike. Her maternal uncle's family was staying with them, too. About 15 people were living under one roof. Ghaida decided to make herself a small birthday cake. She found eggs, flour and baking powder and began arranging the ingredients in the kitchen, joking with her sister's children as she worked. Then, her aunt called with news that her cousin Majdi, 33, had been killed. He had always made Ghaida laugh. At family birthdays, he liked to scoop cream from the cake and smear it across her face. A natural storyteller, he could turn even the simplest anecdote into something funny. They had last seen each other on October 5, when the family went to Roots Cafe on Gaza's seafront. Ghaida left the ingredients on the kitchen counter and went to check on her mother. She doesn't remember who eventually cleared away the eggs and flour. Her mother had previously undergone surgery for breast cancer and was receiving follow-up treatment at Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, including medication and radiotherapy. As her mother's treatment became harder to continue inside Gaza, because of the genocide, the family decided Ghaida would accompany her out. Leaving presented a problem she had never imagined having to solve. "I thought, how can I fit 17 years of my life into one bag?" she says. Ghaida began with paper. She gathered every certificate she could find, going all the way back to kindergarten: school results, awards, certificates from courses she had taken. She packed photographs of friends and family and the little gifts her friends had given her, keeping the messages and notes that came with them. There were practical things too, like her charger, Lyon potato chips and Al Awda’s crackers, and her pair of white wool pyjamas, speckled with red cherries, that she particularly loved. They had an old camera that had been used to document their lives since before Ghaida was born, along with CDs and a box of photographs accumulated over generations. There were pictures of her grandparents, her mother as a student, her parents before they married, their wedding and the announcement of their marriage. Ghaida wanted to take the box, but there wasn’t enough room for it. What she remembers most clearly about packing was deciding what she could bear to leave. "I wished I could carry the whole house with me," she says, "not the material things, but the things that had meaning for us. You know what I mean? The things that touched our hearts." The photographs were among the things that stayed behind. Later, certain they would not be able to return, the family asked a relative to go back to the house. There were too many photographs for him to carry away, and they did not want their family pictures falling into other hands. She crossed through Rafah with her mother and 16-year-old brother Abdul Rahman and eventually settled in Madinaty, in the east of Cairo. That first day, they ate fried chicken. For the first time in months, the things that had become difficult in Gaza were suddenly easy. Food was available. There was electricity. She could sleep without hearing shelling or drones overhead. Her friends were still in Gaza. Ghaida would call and hear about the difficulty of finding food and water. Then, she would look at what was available around her in Egypt. She lost her appetite and her weight plummeted by more than 10kg (22 pounds). It was not until September 2025 that Ghaida finally began university. She was 19, a month short of 20, sitting among students two years younger. And she was no longer studying architecture. She chose dentistry to help people in Gaza when she returns. "If the crossings open permanently," she says, "I will return immediately." Yasmin Abu Zaid had grown up as "the pampered one", in the words of her older sisters, and something she admits to herself. She is the youngest of three sisters and remained the family's youngest child for 10 years, until her brother was born. She had few household responsibilities. If she asked for something, her family usually found a way to get it for her. Her grandfather was particularly indulgent. Whenever he went to the market, he would return with something for Yasmin, food, sweets, whatever had caught his eye and made him think of her. When a nearby mosque was bombed that October, their home was badly damaged. The family temporarily moved into her grandmother's nearby flat. snapshot.title: The girls in the Gaza school photograph
snapshot.evidenceText: Just before the genocide, 15 Gaza schoolgirls posed for a photograph. Three years on, Al Jazeera went looking for them. Nuseirat, Gaza Strip — Maha Taha fills the old blackboard with equations and sets her students to work. For the next few minutes, the classroom settles into the scratch of pens and the low murmur of girls working through the problems. Maha, 43, has taught mathematics for 20 years. Dressed in an olive-green jalabeya and beige hijab, she steps quietly to her desk at the side of the room, as her students work through the maths problems. She has watched generations of girls pass through her classroom, preparing for exams and applying to universities. Asked about the girls she taught before the October 7 genocide began, Maha pauses before reaching for her phone. While scrolling back to find a photograph taken in June 2023, she speaks softly, so as not to disturb the girls in the classroom. “I was proud of them," she says. "I could see that they had bright futures ahead of them. They were very special in their personalities, even before it came to their studies. But October 7 changed the course of their lives.” In the photo, 15 teenage girls in navy school robes and white scarves crowd around Maha in the schoolyard. Some have their arms around one another; others lean towards the camera. All are smiling. They had just finished their mock exams and wanted a photograph together. Sara Rayan took it, holding out the phone so everyone fit in the frame. The girls were 17 and 18. Like many teenagers their age, they worried about exams and university places, talked about what they wanted to become, and imagined the lives that lay ahead. Four months later, Israel's war on Gaza began. Three years on, one of the girls in the photograph has been killed in an Israeli air strike. Four have left Gaza. Others have been displaced - their education interrupted and their plans for the future upended. Al Jazeera set out to find the 15 girls, to discover what had happened to them and the futures they once imagined, and to see whether they could be brought together again for a photograph in the same schoolyard. Muscat Secondary School is still standing, although it was struck by artillery in February 2024 and became a shelter for displaced families. Some classrooms still bear the marks of the war: holes left by quadcopter gunfire, windows damaged by shelling and soot stains where families cooked over open fires. On the walls, children have drawn kites, flowers and a Palestinian flag. Some have written their names: Haya, Marah, Mohammed and Khaled. Displaced families still shelter in parts of the school, while a tent at the edge of the yard serves as a makeshift classroom for younger pupils whose own school can no longer accommodate them. It's just past 10am on a Thursday in late September when Yasmin Abu Zaid arrives. Then Aya Adnan arrives, quickening her pace when she sees Yasmin and pulling her into an embrace. “I haven’t seen you for three years,” she says. “Where have you been? You never show up.” Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader arrives a few minutes later, carrying a plastic bag of books for Aya’s younger sister, who is preparing for the Tawjihi, Gaza’s national secondary school graduation exams. Aya and Lina have seen each other since leaving school. Their families have been friends for years, and they still live in the same neighbourhood of Nuseirat. But Yasmin, who once lived nearby, was displaced early in the war. With the fighting making it difficult to meet, neither has seen her for three years. The three have also kept in touch with Ghaida Zaqout, who now lives in Egypt. Together, they have a private WhatsApp group where they chat regularly and check on one another. When Maha finishes teaching, she greets "my girls" with arms wide open. They erupt into chatter, talking over one another and trying to catch up. In time, Maha pulls up the old photograph on her phone. The girls huddle around her, then point at the tree behind them, recognising it from the photograph. Now, they begin recalling the school days they shared. There were the ordinary intimacies of teenage friendship: who would lend you a pen, who would explain homework you didn't understand, who whispered through lessons and who worried for days about an exam. Ghaida was the girl whose laughter could be heard before she entered the classroom, and who rarely stopped talking, even when teachers moved her to another desk. Sara and her twin sister Fatima were forever taking selfies, while Lina al-Hour was quieter, often bringing novels to read during breaks. The girls talked about clothes, television programmes and football. They bought food together during breaks and wondered aloud about university and what they might become. Some dreamed of studying medicine; another wanted to design buildings. Their futures still seemed to turn on exams, marks, university places and what their families could afford. Maha remembers Sara Rayan laughing, and Ghaida, she says, is in Egypt now, studying dentistry. Here, she pauses, enlarges Lina’s face on the screen and falls silent. Her smile has disappeared. When she speaks again, her voice is quieter and catches slightly. “This is my well-mannered student, Lina,” she says softly. “She is a martyr.” On November 17, 2023, Lina was killed in an Israeli air strike. She was 18. For a moment, the girls wrap their arms even tighter around one another in silence. Standing in the same schoolyard three years later, they tell one another they wish they could return to those days. But most of the girls in the photograph are missing at this reunion. Aya takes out her phone and holds it at arm's length, trying to recreate the selfie Sara took three years earlier. “Sara should have been here to take it,” she says. But Sara cannot come. She now works for an NGO, using her wages to help pay her university fees and contribute to her family's income. Aya Adnan stands with the three in the new photograph, tall, with a dimple in her chin and her hijab falling behind her shoulders. Three years earlier, she had been looking forward to university. She wanted to become a doctor, preferably a neurosurgeon. Aya enjoyed studying. She arrived early for extra physics lessons and worked through difficult material until she understood it. She had also noticed how few female surgeons there were in Gaza and disliked hearing that surgery was too demanding a profession for women. Her interest in neurology had become personal in the 11th grade, when she suffered a severe headache and dizziness that lasted 24 hours. “It felt like my head was heavier than my body,” she recalls, “as if it might fall off.” After undergoing scans and seeing a neurologist, she was told pressure from the vertebrae in her neck was affecting her spinal cord. The experience only made her more determined to study neurology. When her final school results came, she had scored 96 percent. But studying medicine was expensive, and the family - her father was an UNRWA social worker - could not comfortably afford the fees. Seventeen years her senior, Yasser was a lawyer with his own practice, a wife and three children: Adnan, nine, Ahmad, seven, and three-year-old Ilaf. He helped support their parents and hoped one day to teach law at university. “I used to always tell him, ‘You're a second father to me,’ because he was so kind to me, just like my father,” Aya says. Aya remembers a summer's day in August 2023. Yasser, still dressed in his smart work clothes, came to take her from Nuseirat to the Islamic University of Gaza. "Together, we went from department to department, trying to find a course that was affordable and that I would enjoy," she says. Professors suggested engineering. But when they came out, Aya told Yasser she couldn't imagine herself studying computers or becoming an engineer. “I could picture myself wearing a white coat, that's all,” she told him. “Maybe I could study something in the medical field,” Aya suggested. “I really liked medical laboratory sciences.” Yasser knew that his sister was giving up the version of university she had imagined. But he refused to let her see the decision as the end of something. "Perhaps it's for the best," he told her. "Maybe one day you'll become a doctor in the field you choose to specialise in. You don't have to be a medical doctor; you could become a university professor with a PhD." Then, he offered her a thought that has stayed with her. "He told me, 'Sometimes what is withheld from us can be better for us than what is given to us,' and I believe him." Afterwards, he took her to Al-Taboun restaurant for lunch, while they kept talking about university and the choices available. Aya enrolled in medical laboratory sciences, and Yasser bought her books and supplies. University had barely completed its first week when the war began. A strike on a neighbouring two-storey house badly damaged the family home in Nuseirat, where they had lived for more than 35 years. They moved into an aunt's house. The new university timetable that had occupied Aya only weeks earlier disappeared. Instead of laboratories and lectures, her days revolved around finding water, helping prepare food, and learning how to cook without the things the family had once taken for granted. She didn't know how to build a fire; she hadn't needed to. Yasser would continue to return to the family's damaged home, partly to check on what they had left behind and partly because he feared their possessions would be stolen. Sometimes, he stayed there. On one of those visits, he asked Aya to come with him. There were dishes to wash, floors to sweep, rooms to tidy. She said she couldn't. She was helping their mother prepare food. On December 12, as the family gathered for afternoon prayers at her aunt's house, they heard a missile strike. Several minutes later, one of Aya's friends called. She wanted to know where the family was. Then she asked about Yasser, who had returned to their damaged home alone. The strike had hit the house, killing him. He was 32. Aya would return again and again to Yasser asking her to come with him, and her reply that she couldn't. It was an ordinary exchange between siblings, insignificant enough that Aya might never have remembered it, except it was also their last conversation. When she returned to the house about a week later, she found what remained of the plastic shopping bags that held the university supplies Yasser had bought for her only months earlier. Shaking off dust and ash, she opened them one by one. “I was surprised I found them at all; they reminded me of Yasser,” she says. Some books had survived, but others were almost entirely burned; only three pages remained from one set of lecture notes. Ballpoint pens, markers, and coloured pencils lay among the notes. Aya gathered, and still has, what remained. After 18 months, when universities started offering remote learning, Aya logged on whenever electricity and an internet connection allowed. Medical laboratory sciences was supposed to be hands-on: equipment, experiments, laboratories. Aya was trying to learn it without any of those things. "My major is very practical, and most of its courses are practical," she says. "It was difficult for me to study them online when I wasn't even at the university, and there were no laboratories or equipment in front of me." She kept going, and so did another girl in the photograph who once imagined herself in a white coat. Lina Yunis Abd al-Qader, known as “the tall one”, had also imagined becoming a surgeon. At school, she had loved Turkish dramas and anime and had a habit of doodling on her desk, much to the annoyance of her biology teacher. Those interests have since fallen away. She graduated with 98.3 percent and enrolled in medicine at the Islamic University of Gaza on September 10, 2023. Less than a month later, the war brought her studies to a halt. Her father, Yunis Abd al-Qader, works as a paramedic with the Palestinian Red Crescent. During the war, he worked 24-hour shifts and returned home only for brief rest. “I would wonder if he would come back the next day," she says. "I wished I could be there with him, to help him through the difficult things he was seeing.” Usually quiet and reserved, her father tried to spare the family the details of what he encountered. But sometimes, he came home exhausted, and the strain showed. One account he shared stayed with Lina. After an Israeli strike, he had been recovering human remains. Initially, he believed they belonged to seven people. As he continued working, he realised there was an eighth. Having witnessed the scale of amputations, fractures and other injuries, she wants to specialise in orthopaedic surgery. As she continued her medical studies, Lina became close to another student, Shams Majdi. Their friendship was still new when Lina struggled with a physiology problem and messaged Shams on WhatsApp for help. Shams lived in northern Gaza, where internet access was unreliable. With Israeli quadcopters overhead, she travelled several kilometres to find a connection so she could help solve the problem with Lina over the phone. Lina remembers the trouble her new friend took to help her. Later, the two sat the same exam remotely, from different parts of Gaza. Shams had again travelled away from home to find an internet connection. After finishing the exam, Lina opened WhatsApp. Lina says Shams was usually quick to respond, when she could. So she waited. About 45 minutes later, a message appeared in their medical college group announcing that Shams Majdi had been killed. For about 10 minutes, she says that she struggled to comprehend that it was the same Shams whose reply she had been waiting for. She kept sending messages throughout the day. None was answered. Shams had been killed in an Israeli strike on her home, alongside members of her family. For the following week, Lina says, she cried whenever she opened her medical books. representative.title: Alberta Court of Appeal says Ottawa's impact assessment act is still unconstitutional | CBC News
representative.author: The Canadian Press

snapshot.title: Alberta Court of Appeal says Ottawa's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled the federal government's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional. This was the second time the province of Alberta had challenged the act, which sets out a process to review the environmental, economic, health and social effects of proposed projects like ports, mines and pipelines. In a 4-1 decision issued Friday, the court said even though Ottawa modified the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023, the new version still infringes on provincial jurisdiction. The Court of Appeal found that, among other things, the act still gives Ottawa the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction. "While Parliament may have the power to create an impact assessment scheme that complements existing regulation in environmental matters, the [Impact Assessment Act] creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects," the court wrote. Canada's top court rules environmental impact law unconstitutional "This merely exacerbates the concern that a federal assessment scheme might enable the federal government, on the pretext of some narrow ground of federal jurisdiction, to conduct a far-ranging inquiry into matters that are exclusively within provincial jurisdiction." The court said while some of the changes Ottawa made to the previous version of the act weren't constitutionally problematic, the law still gave Ottawa overly broad powers in areas of provincial jurisdiction. "The decision maker may regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project," the court wrote. Alberta challenge to federal project review law being heard in court, again Ontario and Saskatchewan both backed Alberta in its legal challenge. The Impact Assessment Act — otherwise known as C-69 — has been staunchly opposed by oil and gas industry players and critics such as federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre. Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney dubbed it the "no more pipelines act." Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on social media Friday that the ruling was "yet another big win for Alberta." "I'm calling on the federal government to accept this ruling, refrain from yet another appeal, and immediately work with Alberta and the other provinces to clean up this flawed Trudeau-era legislation once and for all so it no longer inhibits economic development in our country," she said. Friday's ruling comes as Ottawa and Alberta are partnering on a new oil pipeline to the West Coast. From left, Scott Burrows, CEO of the Pembina Pipeline Corp, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney applaud on Oct 1 after Carney declared the Pacific Link pipeline project to be in the national interest. (Greg Halinda/The Canadian Press) Earlier this month, the Pacific Link pipeline project became the first to receive a national interest designation under Ottawa's new Building Canada Act. And while the Building Canada Act gives Ottawa the power to skirt a dozen federal laws to help move hand-picked projects forward, critics like Poilievre have long called for the Impact Assessment Act to be repealed. Why Danielle Smith has eased off the 'Kill Bill C-69' language in the Carney era Through the newly tabled Bill C-39, Ottawa is trying to transfer the assessment process for pipeline and energy transmission projects from the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada to the Canada Energy Regulator. The federal government has said it has been told by industry that the level of expertise on energy projects that existed at the Canada Energy Regulator couldn't be found at the Impact Assessment Agency. Ottawa has said the Canada Energy Regulator will still be bound by the provisions in the Impact Assessment Act — which the Alberta Court of Appeal now says is unconstitutional — when carrying out its reviews. In a statement, the office of federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is reviewing the decision and considering next steps. "To position Canada for long-term prosperity in a rapidly changing global economy, the Government of Canada is moving forward to build at a pace not seen in decades. The [Impact Assessment Act] is fundamental to the advancement of this work," wrote press secretary Amy Falkner. "The [Court of Appeal] opinion does not change our commitment to engage all provinces in the spirit of co-operative federalism." Audience Relations, CBC P.O. snapshot.title: Why returning to Syria is only the first step towards rebuilding lives shattered by war
snapshot.evidenceText: WASHINGTON D.C.: When Jihan Hamad Al-Khalaf and her extended family decided to leave Turkiye and return to Syria, there was little debate among them. Five of the seven related families had been away since 2013, while the other two left in 2018. Some of their children had only faint memories of Syria, while others had never seen it. Yet after the fall of Bashar Assad’s regime in December 2024, Al-Khalaf said their decision was “immediate and collective.” “Conditions and pressures in Turkiye helped accelerate the decision,” the Syrian journalist and humanitarian activist told Arab News. “But the main reason was that the country had been liberated and the war was over.” The children, raised on their parents’ memories of Syria, were among the most enthusiastic. “When they heard us saying that Syria had been liberated, they immediately began asking: ‘When are we going back? When will the car come to take us?’” Al-Khalaf said. The first family returned in January 2025. By the end of March, all seven were back. But they could not rebuild their old lives together. With too few habitable homes and limited work, the families divided themselves between Damascus, Deraa, and rural Deir Ezzor. Two families — around 20 people — shared a single house, while others settled according to surviving property, relatives, and job prospects. Their story is part of one of the largest recent return movements in the world. UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, estimated that about 1.82 million Syrians had returned from abroad between Dec. 8, 2024, and Oct. 1, 2026. Lebanon accounted for the largest number of returns in that estimate, at about 733,000, followed by Turkiye with about 713,000. About 299,000 had returned from Jordan. The estimates include registered and unregistered Syrians, as well as people in transit. Returns from Lebanon accelerated amid renewed hostilities and worsening economic conditions. A separate UNHCR crisis tally recorded about 1.08 million Syrian arrivals from Lebanon by Sept. 30, following the regional escalation that began in late February. About 226,000 reported intending to return permanently, and the agency cautions that some returns may be temporary. Many Syrians, however, are arriving in communities barely equipped to receive them. The International Rescue Committee’s July report, “Home, But Not Whole,” surveyed 425 returnees across seven governorates. Some 91 percent of respondents said essential services were missing in their communities, 71 percent were living in damaged housing, and only 18 percent said they had received adequate support during the return process. For Al-Khalaf’s family, the gap between the emotional idea of return and its reality on the ground became apparent almost immediately. One family home in Damascus had been stripped to little more than its walls, roof and floor. Another home had been struck by a projectile and used as a dumping ground for rubble and trash. “No organization, government agency, or anyone else helped us with the repairs,” Al-Khalaf said. During the first winter, two families lived together in one room. As relatives found work, they slowly installed windows, doors, and electricity. “Every month, we would put in one door or one window, or do some of the electrical work,” she said. Clearing rubble and waste from one house alone cost about 1 million Syrian pounds. The families had also spent much of their money simply getting to Syria. Al-Khalaf said the first family paid around $600 to reach Deraa. Some of the returnees sold their possessions in Turkiye to finance the journey. Available assistance often covers only a fraction of the need. Between January and August, UNHCR said 31,083 refugee-returnee households received return and reintegration cash assistance. Eligible households can receive a one-time $600 reintegration grant, while basic relief items reached 337,089 people, including returnees and other vulnerable households. Over the same period, UNHCR repaired 1,000 damaged homes and provided shelter cash assistance to 1,595 households. UNHCR’s regional Syria situation response, requiring $1.264 billion, was 34 percent funded as of Sept. 30. Funding shortfalls had forced six community centers in Syria to close in April and May. The World Bank estimated that rebuilding damaged physical assets will cost around $216 billion, nearly 10 times the country’s 2024 gross domestic product. For returning families, those figures translate into daily struggles over water, electricity, transportation, healthcare, and food. In Damascus, Al-Khalaf’s family initially paid 40,000 Syrian pounds for 10 barrels of non-potable water, and about 10,000 pounds for each 25-liter container of drinking water. Municipal supplies eventually improved, but the family still buys drinking water. Conditions were worse in rural Deir Ezzor, where damaged purification facilities meant that available water was often unsafe. “The children were constantly getting sick, especially in the beginning, because they weren’t used to the water,” Al-Khalaf said. More than 10 million people across Syria lack access to safe water, according to UNICEF’s August 2026 appeal. The IRC’s July report said some areas received only two to four hours of electricity per day. The difficulties, civil society workers say, do not end when water or electricity begin flowing or roofs or walls are repaired. Nadia Okasha, director of the Tastakel Center in Damascus, said the needs of returnees evolve as families move through different stages of rebuilding. The women-led nonprofit center focuses on civil peace, trust-building, and social cohesion rather than on distribution of humanitarian aid, but often directs returnees toward organizations and public bodies that can provide legal, humanitarian, or administrative services. “At first, inquiries concentrate on return procedures, documents, and access to basic services,” Okasha told Arab News. “Later, interest begins to shift toward more sustainable issues such as employment, education, and reintegration into society.” Many returnees understand that life will be difficult, Okasha said, but they often underestimate the time, effort, and patience required to reintegrate after years abroad and extensive changes inside the country. Some children born abroad or in displacement camps possess foreign records or temporary protection papers but lack documents recognized by Syrian institutions. Others were born during periods when civil registries were inaccessible, destroyed, or controlled by competing authorities. For Al-Khalaf’s orphaned nephew, the absence of paperwork could jeopardize his education. The boy’s father was killed before formally registering his marriage or obtaining a “family booklet.” More than a decade later, Syrian records still list the father as alive. Although the boy has Turkish temporary protection papers and his grandfather was granted legal guardianship by a Turkish court, those documents have not been accepted as sufficient in Syria. The family must now register the father’s death, prove the marriage, and establish the child’s parentage — processes requiring hundreds of dollars in legal fees which the family cannot afford. The local school allowed Al-Khalaf’s nephew to enroll provisionally after relatives signed pledges promising to produce his papers. But without them, the family fears he may be denied recognized certificates or progression through the education system. “Every time we go to one authority, they tell us we have to go to another,” she said. Children educated entirely in Turkish face an additional language barrier. Some of Al-Khalaf’s younger relatives required private tutors to catch up with Arabic-speaking classmates. Economic survival remains perhaps the greatest test. Some of Al-Khalaf’s relatives returned to jobs in public institutions, but others remained without work or income for more than a year. Relatives in rural Deir Ezzor began cultivating land beside their house, while even government employees in Damascus struggled with irregular salaries and high living costs. Al-Khalaf, who previously worked for Deraa’s education authority, has neither been reinstated nor found suitable work elsewhere. She depends heavily on monthly remittances from siblings in Europe. “Without them, we would not be able to buy what we need or cover our expenses,” she said. About 2.04 million internally displaced Syrians had also returned to their areas of origin since December 2024, according to UNHCR’s Oct. 1 figures — an even greater number than those arriving from abroad — adding another dimension to the challenge. Their problems often overlap with those of refugees returning from abroad, particularly in terms of housing, services, and livelihoods. But they can also face disputes over land and property, unresolved grievances, and the loss of social and economic ties built during displacement. Suleiman Jafer fled Afrin in March 2018. Before returning home in April 2026, he spent nearly six years in displacement camps in the Shahba area of northern Aleppo. The first thing he did after arriving, he told Arab News, was kiss the soil. But Afrin had changed so extensively that he nearly lost his way to his own house. When he entered, it was empty. “They did not leave me even a spoon or a fork,” Jafer said. “The doors were stolen — even the toilet, sinks, and bathroom fixtures were stolen.” Jafer said that repairing his village home cost about $10,000, while work on his house in Afrin city cost another $5,000. His car was missing, and a plot planted with olive trees, grapevines and almond trees had been cleared. Nevertheless, he described the current security situation as generally good and said he had not personally been harassed since returning. His greater concern is the destruction of Afrin’s agricultural economy. Many of Afrin’s families depended on olives and fruit. Jafer said damaged trees and orchards would need at least two years to recover. Wathiq Al-Hallaq, director of the Social Policies Directorate at Syria’s Ministry of Social Affairs and Labor, said the challenge facing institutions was multifaceted. “The matter is not primarily related to the scale or pace of return as much as it is related to the fragility of policies, the absence of databases, and outdated working mechanisms,” he told Arab News. Syria’s system of social services and protection programs needs to be redesigned in its structure, procedures, and objectives, he said, if it is to respond to returnees’ needs. The ministry is working to launch a national social protection program and has established a technical unit focused on returnees and internally displaced people, he said. The IRC has warned that donors and authorities must invest in water networks, roads, electricity, schools, healthcare, and livelihoods for returnees and established residents alike. Otherwise, shortages and unequal aid distribution may generate competition and undermine already fragile trust. Okasha said rebuilding social cohesion was inseparable from rebuilding homes and infrastructure. “Reintegration is not limited to meeting material needs,” she said. “It also requires a cohesive society in which everyone feels that they belong and are able to participate in building their future.” For Al-Khalaf, the question of whether Syria is ready for its people to return cannot be answered through statistics alone. When refugees in Turkiye ask her about conditions in Syria, she tells them that what they see will depend partly on what they expect. “If you put on rose-tinted glasses, you will see that returning is suitable and everything is good,” she said. “But if you wear black-and-white glasses, you will see everything in black and white.” Those expecting the same income, services and standard of living they had abroad are likely to struggle, she said. People with a job, trade, capital or relatives supporting them from overseas are in a far stronger position to endure the first months. Despite unemployment, damaged homes, and continuing dependence on remittances, Al-Khalaf said her family had never considered going back to Turkiye. “We are trying to arrange our lives here and adapt according to the income we have,” she said. “This is our country. This is our real place.” Stay on top of the issues that matter to you the most.

representative.title: Ontario will officially begin removing Toronto bike lanes on Tuesday | CBC News
representative.author: Muriel Draaisma

snapshot.title: Ontario will officially begin removing Toronto bike lanes on Tuesday | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: Ontario to begin removing Toronto bike lanes. Here's what you need to know Ontario will begin removing bike lanes from a stretch on Bloor Street W. in Etobicoke on Tuesday, the Ministry of Transportation says. A notice of construction start, issued by the ministry, says the work will occur on a 1.2-kilometre section between Clissold Road and Royal York Road. Dakota Brasier, spokesperson for Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, confirmed in an email on Thursday that bike lane removal will begin Oct. 13. "Following the ruling by the Ontario Court of Appeal, the province announced in September that it would immediately begin restoring motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West. That work begins Tuesday," Brasier said. T he Court of Appeal ruled in August that Premier Doug Ford’s government could rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, reversing a lower-court decision made in July 2025. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said Thursday that the removal of the bike lanes is "completely unacceptable" and an affront to the city by Ontario Premier Doug Ford. "It is outrageous. He's overstepping," Chow said. "That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city. Whether it is bike lanes, speed cameras, Island airport, every element we need to have our say. The city belong to all of us Torontonians through the municipal government," she said. "Cyclists needs to be protected, they need to be safe." The ministry-issued notice says existing pavement markings and pre-cast concrete curbs will be removed and new pavement markings and signs "to safely restore" an additional vehicle lane in each direction will be installed. Crews are expected to work primarily at night to reduce the impact on traffic, but may work during the day depending on weather, operational needs and staging requirements, the ministry-issued notice says. The notice says the work, which may lead to traffic delays, is expected to be finished in November. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow says of the bike lane removal: 'That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city.' (Mehrdad Nazarahari/CBC) Chow said, if re-elected mayor, she will mobilize efforts against the removal of bike lanes. "I will do everything I can. I will bring residents and citizens together. We will work together and we will fight back." Rival mayoral candidate Coun. Brad Bradford said bike lanes need to be removed if they are not working. "I ride more bikes than anyone who has ever been elected to Toronto City Council for sure. We've got the record for that. But I also am going to be pragmatic and recognize when some of the bike lanes aren't working like they should," Bradford said. "And that's why we're talking about the section on Etobicoke, part of Bloor from Resurrection Road to the South Kingsway, where you have 38,490 cars per day and 197 bikes. So you allocated 50 per cent of the space to half a percentage of road users and that doesn't work." Coun. Brad Bradford says: 'Big cities are going to have bike infrastructure and that's a positive thing. We're going to have it. But we also have to build trust with Torontonians to recognize if it's not working, we can fix it.' (Mehrdad Nazarahari/CBC) Bradford said some bike lanes, including those on Richmond Street W., Adelaide Street and Danforth Avenue, are working. "Big cities are going to have bike infrastructure and that's a positive thing. We're going to have it. But we also have to build trust with Torontonians to recognize if it's not working, we can fix it." Michael Longfield, executive director of local cycling advocacy group CycleTO, said the organization is "outraged but not surprised" that the government has rejected the mayor's "win-win offer" to restore car lanes but keep bike lanes in Etobicoke. "Ripping out these protected bike lanes against the will of Toronto city council is a colossal waste of $48 million. The province’s own experts know it will not ease traffic congestion, it will put people’s lives at risk, and there is no network of side streets that could replace these lanes." Ontario health-care coalition denounces province's plan to remove bike lanes across Toronto Ford government to begin ripping out, reconfiguring Toronto bike lanes after appeal court ruling In December 2025, the province completed work to restore a vehicle lane and maintain a bike lane on a 600-metre section of Bloor Street W. from Resurrection Road to Clissold Road. The work that begins Tuesday is east of that section. The notice says crews will attempt to minimize disruption, saying access to businesses and properties "will be maintained throughout construction," as well as sidewalk access and emergency access. Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said in a Sept. 1 news release that the government is committed to tackling traffic congestion. “Our government was given a clear and direct mandate by the people of Ontario to fight gridlock, including by restoring motor vehicle lanes that are needed to keep drivers moving. We’re keeping our promise," Sarkaria said. Audience Relations, CBC P.O. representative.author: Kwame Darko

snapshot.title: Community Group Catches Galamsey Suspects in Tano River Chase
snapshot.evidenceText: A community anti-galamsey group chased a fleeing suspect into the Tano River and caught him, as three men were arrested inside a protected forest reserve where local courts lack judges to try them quickly. When one of three suspected illegal miners spotted members of a community watch committee closing in on him along the Tano River, he made a desperate dash into the water, hoping to swim to safety. He did not get far. Members of the Jema Anti-Galamsey Advocacy (JAGA) Watch Committee plunged into the river after him and dragged him back to shore, according to MyJoyOnline. The dramatic chase unfolded on Friday, October 2, 2026, inside the Tano-Boin Forest Reserve, a protected area that has become a flashpoint in Ghana's ongoing struggle against illegal mining, locally known as galamsey. JAGA, a volunteer community group based in Jema, said its members intercepted the three men as they operated along the riverbank, reportedly catching them with a water-pumping machine and a 'changfang' — a floating mining raft commonly used by illegal miners to dredge riverbeds for gold. After the arrest, the suspects were taken to the Jema Police Station and later transferred to the District Police Command at Enchi for prosecution. But the case quickly ran into a familiar obstacle facing Ghana's rural justice system: the Enchi Magistrate and Circuit Courts currently have no substantive judicial officers to hear cases. As a result, the three men had to be taken further afield to the Asankragwa Magistrate Court, where they were remanded for one week, MyJoyOnline reports. JAGA praised the Enchi District Police Command, singling out District Commander Chief Superintendent Mensah for ensuring the suspects were brought before a court despite the logistical hurdles. The group also said it had promptly alerted the District and Regional offices of the Forestry Commission in Enchi and Wiawso, which in turn arranged transport for the suspects and covered some of the operation's costs. This is not JAGA's first encounter with illegal miners in the area. The group pointed to an earlier case involving two Nigerien nationals arrested for allegedly mining in the Jema-Assemkrom Forest Reserve last year. According to JAGA, those suspects were granted police bail and the case has since seen little progress — a comparison the group drew to underline its concern that arrests do not always translate into prosecutions. JAGA said the latest arrests show why sustained enforcement in protected forest reserves matters, and why closer cooperation between volunteer watchdogs and state institutions, including the police and Forestry Commission, is necessary. The group also welcomed reported plans by the Attorney General and the Chief Justice to set up special courts in selected regional capitals, including Sekondi, to speed up the prosecution of galamsey-related cases. For residents of Jema and surrounding communities, the case illustrates both the risks volunteers take to protect local water bodies and forests, and the practical limits of a justice system stretched thin in rural districts. Illegal river mining of the kind allegedly carried out with the changfang raft pollutes water sources used for drinking, farming and fishing, and strips vegetation from forest reserves meant to be protected by law. JAGA has called on the media and international environmental organisations to monitor the case to ensure it proceeds transparently. No date has been given for when the suspects' remand will be reviewed beyond the one week ordered by the Asankragwa court, and it remains unclear when the Enchi courts will receive substantive judicial officers to handle cases locally. At seven feet tall, Ephraim Saawa gets stopped for photos on the streets of Amanfro and Kasoa. He wants Ghanaians to one day stop him for a different reason — wearing the national basketball jersey. Fifteen shops were reduced to ashes at Kumasi Central Market before firefighters brought the blaze under control, with government promising relief once NADMO assesses the damage. representative.author: Jahid Hasan

snapshot.title: As the river edges closer, a school braces to disappear
snapshot.evidenceText: Copyright: Any unauthorized use or reproduction of The Daily Star content for commercial purposes is strictly prohibited and constitutes copyright infringement liable to legal action. Seventeen years ago, a char emerged in Purba Naodoba union of Zajira upazila in Shariatpur. On it grew a village called Alam Kha Kandi, and in 2017, the No 122 Altaf Hossain Khan Government Primary School was built there on 33 decimals of land. Back then, the Padma river was nearly two kilometres away -- not visible from the school gate. That distance has been vanishing. Over the past two years, successive bouts of erosion have dragged the river steadily closer, and it now licks at the school's own grounds, just 50 metres from the building. Teachers, students and local residents fear what has already happened twice nearby -- in 2024 and 2025, two primary schools in neighbouring villages of the same union were lost to the river. Painpara Government Primary School in union was swallowed by the river in August 2024; exactly a year later, in August 2025, Rizia Amin Government Primary School, also in Painpara, met the same fate. On a recent visit, the national flag still stood tall outside the erosion-battered school on the Padma's bank. But the earthen edge of the school field was crumbling into the water, and several trees lay broken along the bank. Nearby, the collapsed roof of a building the river had already claimed leaned forlornly against the shore. Inside, the signs of panic were unmistakable. The tin fencing had been dismantled to allow for a quick relocation if needed. The partition between two classrooms had been removed, and the overhead fans taken down. In the open space that remained, two teachers taught two separate classes side by side, children seated on either side of the room. At that moment, young voices could be heard reciting after their teacher: "Our little river flows in bends and turns, in the month of Boishakh it has knee-deep water." The children studied with evident joy -- but the irony of the verse was not lost on the adults around them. Erosion anxiety follows the students constantly, teachers said, and with the school itself at risk, safety concerns run alongside the lessons. Staff must now watch the river even as they teach. "The river keeps eroding and has come right onto our school field," said Borna Akter, a fourth-grade student, speaking to The Daily Star. "Our school could break apart at any time. It feels very scary, wondering when our school will break down. If our school goes into the river, we won't be able to study here anymore. Where will we study then? We want arrangements made to protect our school." School teacher Naimur Rahman Khan said panic over the erosion alone had already driven at least 100 students away. "We also always have to remain anxious, because the school is at risk," he said. "Even after we go home at the end of the day, we have to phone local residents to check on the river situation because arrangements for relocating the school must be made before it is lost to the river. If the school could be protected now, even by dropping some sandbags, children could attend classes here without fear." Altaf Hossain Khan, the school's founder and chairman of the union parishad, said the area had been eroding for years. "The river has now come close to the school. We have repeatedly requested the Water Development Board, but they have taken no action," he told The Daily Star over the phone. "If nothing is done now, the school could break apart and go into the riverbed at any moment." Md Milton Hossain, executive engineer of the Shariatpur Water Development Board, said the erosion in Alam Kha Kandi had been reported to higher authorities, but that the Ministry of Water Resources was not currently taking emergency measures in char areas. He added that no No Objection Certificate had been sought from the BWDB before the school was built on the char, and that neither the district nor the upazila education departments had alerted his office that the school was at risk. "Even so, I will visit the area and take the necessary measures, subject to permission from higher authorities," he said. Zajira Upazila Primary Education Officer Bazlur Rahman confirmed the school was at risk. "We have made preparations to relocate the school before erosion occurs, and another site is being sought," he told The Daily Star. "I will also request the concerned department to attempt to protect the school from the erosion." representative.title: Padma River Erosion Threatens Altaf Hossain Khan Government Primary School in Shariatpur; Attendance Drops 70 Percent as 110 Students Relocate and Teachers Fear School May Disappear | Network Bangladesh
representative.author: NB Staff

snapshot.title: Padma River Erosion Threatens Altaf Hossain Khan Government Primary School in Shariatpur; Attendance Drops 70 Percent as 110 Students Relocate and Teachers Fear School May Disappear | Network Bangladesh
snapshot.evidenceText: When the school was established in 2017, the Padma River was about two kilometers away. Over the years, the river has gradually reduced that distance and now it is near the school grounds. The school building’s tin roof and fence have been left open due to the fear of erosion. Some furniture and essential goods have been removed. Student attendance at the school has also decreased by about 70 percent due to the fear of river erosion. This picture is of Altaf Hossain Khan Government Primary School No. 122 in Alam Khankandi village, East Naodoba Union, Jajira Upazila, Shariatpur. According to school sources, Alam Khankandi village is located on the north bank of the Padma River. The river surrounds the village. The waterway is the main means of communication for the people there. As there was no school in the area, the government established the school there in 2017. Local UP Chairman Altaf Hossain Khan donated 33 percent of the land for the school. The school was named after him. When the school was established, the Padma River was about two kilometers away. In the last two years, river erosion in that area has intensified. This year alone, the river has moved about one kilometer north. Now, the river is close to the school grounds. The school is teaching in five rooms of a tin shed with a paved floor. The school authorities have opened the building’s tin and fence due to fears of river erosion. Some belongings have also been moved to a safe place. In the meantime, classes are being held in the open room. The school has 214 students enrolled in the current academic year. However, due to river erosion, an average of 50 to 60 students come to the school every day. Many local residents have moved to a safe distance as the houses around the school have been submerged in the river. At least 110 students have moved to different areas 8 to 10 kilometers away. Monica and Jonayed, fifth-grade students at the school, say they are afraid to come to school now. They fear that the school could disappear into the river at any time. They are also worried about where they will go to study if the school collapses. Shamim Khan, the acting headmaster of the school, said that this year has seen the most erosion. In the last two months, the river has come close to the school grounds. He said, “I worry every day. After school, I go home and wonder whether I will be able to see the school the next day. I have removed some belongings due to the fear of erosion. In this situation, the attendance of students has decreased a lot. At least 110 students have permanently moved to another area.” Local UP Chairman Altaf Hossain Khan said that after the erosion started around the school, he requested the local administration and the Water Development Board to take action several times. But no effective measures were taken to protect the area. This year, at least 350 families in Alam Khankandi area have been victims of river erosion. These families have lost their homes and cropland. Now the school is also facing erosion. When this correspondent visited Alam Khankandi village last Thursday, it was seen that the fence of the school building had been opened. Various items removed from the building had been kept in one place. Two teachers were teaching third and fourth grade students together in two rooms of the open room. A teacher was teaching a few children in another room next door. 65 students were seen attending the school from 11 am to 1 pm. Jajira Upazila Primary Education Officer Bazlur Rahman said the school in the village on the banks of the Padma River is at risk of erosion. They are monitoring the issue around the clock. Preparations have also been made to move the school to another location. However, alternative land has not been found yet. They are keeping an eye on the situation so that even if the school is a victim of river erosion, educational activities are not stopped. The community now faces an uncertain future as the river continues to advance, threatening not only the school but also the wider village, and the authorities are under pressure to find a safe location before the next erosion season. representative.title: ‘They searched my bag, and my Israeli passport was inside’: An extraordinary journey
representative.author: Assaf Kamar

snapshot.title: ‘They searched my bag, and my Israeli passport was inside’: An extraordinary journey through Saudi Arabia
snapshot.evidenceText: The religious police officers began rummaging through his bag. Hidden deep inside an inner pocket was the last thing he wanted anyone in Saudi Arabia to find: his Israeli passport. "They caught me in Medina, the city sacred to Muslims," adventurer Adam Jano, a resident of the northern Israeli community of Klil, told ynet. "They're not particularly pleasant people. They started searching through my things, and I was an idiot for bringing it with me," he recalled. "I had to move between hotels, so I thought, fine, I'll take it along. I hid it, and luckily they didn't see it." The encounter took place in the courtyard of the Prophet Muhammad's Mosque in Medina, one of Islam's holiest cities. "The religious police asked me, 'Are you Muslim?' I said, 'No, I'm not Muslim.' Then they started saying, 'Give us your bag.' They began searching, and my heart just sank." Fortunately for the Israeli traveler, whose identity could have landed him in serious trouble, the officers never opened the inner pocket, and his Israeli passport remained undiscovered. "It was a pretty frightening moment," Jano said. "Your heart starts racing, the adrenaline kicks in, and I have a wife and a child. Looking back, I think, wow, that was really stupid and dangerous. I should have handled things a little differently." It was Jano's second trip to Saudi Arabia, which he entered using a foreign passport. This time, he was determined to explore far beyond the modern capital, Riyadh. He embarked on long drives deep into the country's wild desert landscapes, reaching even the region bordering Yemen. One stretch of road that left a particularly strong impression followed the Red Sea coastline. "It's a beautiful road, and when you're driving north, the sea is always on your left, just like driving through Sinai, only from the other side." Most of the men Jano encountered wore the traditional white thobe, while the few women he saw were dressed in black. "They dressed me in a robe, and they were very proud of it," he laughed. "There are so many laundries on practically every corner. Because they constantly have to wash all those white clothes, it looks like the dry cleaners are making an absolute fortune." Ironically, it was the relative absence of tourists that made Jano's challenging journey so rewarding. "You meet people, you make friends," he said enthusiastically. "Suddenly, someone you met the day before calls you and says, 'I want to introduce you to my friend.' "Why did I meet so many people specifically in Saudi Arabia? If I went to Thailand, I'd just be another tourist, and the locals wouldn't find me particularly interesting. In Saudi Arabia, there aren't many tourists, so when you're a different face, you attract attention." One memorable encounter took place at a Western-style coffee shop in Riyadh, where several Saudi women approached him. "I'm standing in line, and these women wearing veils come up to me. You can only see their eyes. They ask, 'Where are you from?'" It was a perfectly ordinary question with an answer he could not afford to give. "I don't say Israel," he laughed. "Then they ask, 'Can we please pay for your coffee?' They were closed off for so many years, and now things are opening up. When unfamiliar faces start appearing, it sparks curiosity, and it's funny. "They take selfies with me while wearing their veils, and I'm thinking, wait a minute, what's going on here? You're taking a picture with someone whose face is covered, so what exactly can you see in the photo?" One of the highlights of Jano's journey was AlUla, one of Saudi Arabia's leading tourist destinations. Located in the country's northwest, the region is surrounded by dramatic sandstone cliffs, canyons and an ancient oasis. It was once an important stop along the Nabataean incense trade route connecting the Arabian Peninsula with the East and the Mediterranean. In recent years, AlUla has become a flagship project of Saudi Arabia's tourism ambitions, with luxury hotels, cultural attractions and extraordinary architecture emerging amid the desert landscape. Jano checked into one of the region's luxury resorts and discovered a swimming pool in the middle of the desert, gourmet restaurants, golf carts and impeccable five-star service. Almost everything was there, except the guests. "I was alone. There was nobody there," he laughed. "I was sitting alone in the restaurant, surrounded by waiters, and you're the only person there. They have golf carts to take you around because the hotel isn't just one building, it's an entire complex. "They ask you, 'Which restaurant would you like? There's a Thai restaurant or a Middle Eastern restaurant.' And whichever one you choose, you're the only guest. Everything is five-star. It's the top of the top." The hotel itself was designed to blend seamlessly into the surrounding desert. "The rooms are built into the mountain, and the swimming pool is there too. Even the stairs blend into the rocks. It's a very impressive, very special hotel, but being the only guest there feels strange." So where were all the tourists? "The employees tell me, 'Oh, they're coming.' They're coming. We want tourists." And what about the sightseeing bus? "I was the only passenger. Why would they even send out a bus? Can you imagine? An entire bus, and I'm riding in it alone." Beyond the luxurious hotels, the region is home to Nabataean archaeological sites and ancient tombs carved directly into the rock. "These are the same people who built what you see in Petra," Jano explained. "They carved straight into the rock, and it's incredibly impressive. Absolutely amazing." In AlUla, Jano also encountered a striking symbol of Saudi Arabia's ambitious transformation: Maraya, an enormous mirrored building that seems almost to disappear into the surrounding landscape, like a mirage reflecting the desert. "You can't see it," the veteran traveler said enthusiastically. "When you're walking through the desert and suddenly come across it, it tricks your eyes. It's like an optical illusion. It's a huge, square mirrored building, surrounded by mountains and desert, and the building reflects all the colors." Outside AlUla's lavish resorts, some of Jano's most memorable experiences took place around the dinner table. "Saudi food is very delicate and very good," he declared with the confidence of someone who has sampled plenty of it. "Think of Bedouin food, but imagine having a five-star chef prepare the meal and refine it," he laughed. "I particularly loved the lamb, slow-cooked with rice and spices." But the meal that stayed with him most was at the home of a Saudi friend he had met during his travels. "Arab hospitality is hospitality done properly," Jano said appreciatively. "When you're under someone's protection and they're responsible for you, you're treated like royalty." To protect his host's personal safety, we'll limit the description to the fact that he lives on a magnificent estate with a separate area designed specifically for entertaining guests. "He has this tent outside for visitors, and that's where they serve the food. He shows you photographs and things. He loves hunting, so he has stuffed animals and things from Africa. You sit on the carpet and eat with your hands." Yet beyond the hypnotic desert landscapes and luxury hotels, Jano had arrived in the mysterious kingdom with another, more discreet mission. "The Jewish story, wherever it exists, fascinates me," he said. "Everywhere I go, I try to put together another piece of the puzzle of Jewish history. And the very idea that there are 'hidden Jews' in Saudi Arabia made me curious to go looking for them and meet them." In a country where he himself had been forced to conceal his Israeli passport, the search for Jewish roots took on an entirely different level of significance. "You arrive there, you meet someone, and it's as if you're bringing them treasure," he said excitedly, recalling a discreet meeting with a person who identified as a secret Jew in Saudi Arabia. "You're bringing something into a place where it doesn't exist. And then they say, 'Wow, thank you for the siddur and the tefillin. How did you manage to bring those in?' It was incredibly moving." A siddur is a Jewish prayer book, while tefillin are small leather boxes containing biblical passages, traditionally worn during weekday morning prayers. The dusty city of Tabuk recently made headlines in Israel following the emergency landing of a flydubai aircraft carrying Israeli passengers.
