Hidden deep inside an inner pocket was the last thing he wanted anyone in Saudi Arabia to find: his Israeli passport. "They caught me in Medina, the city sacred to Muslims," adventurer Adam Jano, a resident of the northern Israeli community of Klil, told ynet. "They're not particularly pleasant people. They started searching through my things, and I was an idiot for bringing it with me," he recalled. "I had to move between hotels, so I thought, fine, I'll take it along. I hid it, and luckily they didn't see it." The encounter took place in the courtyard of the Prophet Muhammad's Mosque in Medina, one of Islam's holiest cities. "The religious police asked me, 'Are you Muslim?' I said, 'No, I'm not Muslim.' Then they started saying, 'Give us your bag.' They began searching, and my heart just sank." Fortunately for the Israeli traveler, whose identity could have landed him in serious trouble, the officers never opened the inner pocket, and his Israeli passport remained undiscovered. "It was a pretty frightening moment," Jano said. "Your heart starts racing, the adrenaline kicks in, and I have a wife and a child. Looking back, I think, wow, that was really stupid and dangerous. I should have handled things a little differently." It was Jano's second trip to Saudi Arabia, which he entered using a foreign passport. This time, he was determined to explore far beyond the modern capital, Riyadh. He embarked on long drives deep into the country's wild desert landscapes, reaching even the region bordering Yemen. One stretch of road that left a particularly strong impression followed the Red Sea coastline. "It's a beautiful road, and when you're driving north, the sea is always on your left, just like driving through Sinai, only from the other side." Most of the men Jano encountered wore the traditional white thobe, while the few women he saw were dressed in black. "They dressed me in a robe, and they were very proud of it," he laughed. "There are so many laundries on practically every corner. Because they constantly have to wash all those white clothes, it looks like the dry cleaners are making an absolute fortune." Ironically, it was the relative absence of tourists that made Jano's challenging journey so rewarding. "You meet people, you make friends," he said enthusiastically. "Suddenly, someone you met the day before calls you and says, 'I want to introduce you to my friend.' "Why did I meet so many people specifically in Saudi Arabia? If I went to Thailand, I'd just be another tourist, and the locals wouldn't find me particularly interesting. In Saudi Arabia, there aren't many tourists, so when you're a different face, you attract attention." One memorable encounter took place at a Western-style coffee shop in Riyadh, where several Saudi women approached him. "I'm standing in line, and these women wearing veils come up to me. You can only see their eyes. They ask, 'Where are you from?'" It was a perfectly ordinary question with an answer he could not afford to give. "I don't say Israel," he laughed. "Then they ask, 'Can we please pay for your coffee?' They were closed off for so many years, and now things are opening up. When unfamiliar faces start appearing, it sparks curiosity, and it's funny. "They take selfies with me while wearing their veils, and I'm thinking, wait a minute, what's going on here? You're taking a picture with someone whose face is covered, so what exactly can you see in the photo?" One of the highlights of Jano's journey was AlUla, one of Saudi Arabia's leading tourist destinations. Jano checked into one of the region's luxury resorts and discovered a swimming pool in the middle of the desert, gourmet restaurants, golf carts and impeccable five-star service. Almost everything was there, except the guests. "I was alone. There was nobody there," he laughed. "I was sitting alone in the restaurant, surrounded by waiters, and you're the only person there. They have golf carts to take you around because the hotel isn't just one building, it's an entire complex. "They ask you, 'Which restaurant would you like? There's a Thai restaurant or a Middle Eastern restaurant.' And whichever one you choose, you're the only guest. Everything is five-star. It's the top of the top." The hotel itself was designed to blend seamlessly into the surrounding desert. "The rooms are built into the mountain, and the swimming pool is there too. Even the stairs blend into the rocks. It's a very impressive, very special hotel, but being the only guest there feels strange." So where were all the tourists? "The employees tell me, 'Oh, they're coming.' They're coming. We want tourists." And what about the sightseeing bus? "I was the only passenger. Why would they even send out a bus? Can you imagine? An entire bus, and I'm riding in it alone." snapshot.title: Attack on Riyadh airport leaves 12 dead, more than 300 injured
snapshot.evidenceText: At least 12 people were killed and 309 others injured in an attack on Saudi Arabia's King Khalid International airport in Riyadh as Iran-backed Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom. The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said in a statement on Sunday that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack on late Saturday. The authority said some of the injured were in critical condition and that all were receiving medical care at several hospitals. Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter told Reuters. Jordan's foreign ministry said in a statement on Saturday that two injured Jordanians were discharged from hospital while two others were still receiving treatment. One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport. An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a departure gate collapsed. Saturday's attack, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, occurred without warning, with no alert issued by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. This week's two previous attacks on the airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac. All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. The Iran-backed group, which is yet to claim responsibility for the latest attack, has aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there – except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina – is a target. The attack on the airport comes amid escalating fighting between Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces and Houthis. Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, spokesman for the government forces, said more than 1,900 operations carried out in the past 24 hours targeted weapons and ammunition depots, camps and military positions, reinforcements and other “military objectives deep within areas controlled” by the Houthis. The coalition called the attack a 'war crime' and said it will respond firmly to the attack on the airport, Reuters reported. Flight-tracking site flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point. Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences, including the World Petroleum Conference. Organisers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, according to Reuters. In an advisory issued earlier on Saturday, King Khalid airport urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and check their flight status before heading to the airport amid reports of disruptions to air traffic, without specifying the cause of the disruptions. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also instructed Saudi citizens travelling to the kingdom to contact local embassies if their travel itineraries have been disrupted following the attack. At the same time, foreign embassies in Riyadh, including those of the US, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Canada, issued advisories on social media to their citizens in Saudi Arabia. The US embassy in Saudi Arabia urged Americans to avoid the airport and surrounding areas. In a statement released on Sunday, the US Mission said US government employees working in the kingdom required special authorisation to use the King Khalid airport, as well as airports in Jeddah and Dammam. It said US government employees are not to travel within 20 miles (32km) of the Yemeni border due to safety risks, and need special authorisation for travel to the provinces of Jazan, Asir, Najran, and the cities of Qatif, Yanbu and Taif. The UK and Irish embassies advised their nationals about “a serious incident” at the airport. Canada’s embassy advised citizens in Riyadh to avoid all travel to the airport, noting “ongoing military activity”. Following reports of the latest attack, United States President Donald Trump was asked by reporters outside the White House whether Washington planned to join the Saudi strikes on the Houthis. “We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the ⁠⁠⁠⁠recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said. “I think it’s terrible. The Saudis are good fighters but I think the attack was a terrible thing,” the US president said. Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman about it. He said the US had communication with the Houthis and added that “what they did was very bad”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the United States strongly condemns recent attacks on Saudi Arabia. He said an American citizen was killed in the strikes. "These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now," Rubio wrote on X. The attack was widely condemned, with Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs calling it “a direct threat to the security of the region”. Qatar’s former prime minister says today’s attack on King Khalid airport shows that it is “more urgent than ever” to stand with Saudi Arabia in a “practical and decisive” manner. “It has now become clear that Iran is our primary adversary”, Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani said in a post on X, adding that the Gulf Cooperation Council today confronts “several hostile plots and conspiracies” that require “unity and profound foresight”. He said it has become “more urgent and evident” that Qatar stands with Saudi Arabia against the “threat from within Yemen” that is being “plotted and directed from outside [Yemen]”. The situation “necessitates setting aside all peripheral disputes” among Gulf Cooperation Council members and “demonstrating unity” instead, he said. Japan’s embassy also “strongly” condemned Houthi attacks on airports and other Saudi civilian facilities. Kuwait Airways said it was cancelling flights because the airport had closed due to a “security situation”. Egypt's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Egypt expressed its “profound denunciation of these blatant attacks”, their “flagrant violation” of international law, and the “disregard” for the safety of citizens that they entail. Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces. The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict. That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

snapshot.title: Coalition Forces vow firm response over Riyadh airport strike, Trump says Houthi attack ‘not acceptable’
snapshot.evidenceText: RIYADH: The Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen has vowed a firm response to a Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 12 people and injured 309 others, as US President Donald Trump condemned the strike as “not acceptable.” Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki, spokesman for the coalition forces, said the attack on a passenger terminal at the airport on Saturday constituted a war crime under international humanitarian law. “The attack on King Khalid International Airport is a terrorist act and will be met with a firm response,” Al-Maliki said in a statement released on X and carried by the Saudi Press Agency (SPA). He described the attack by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia as a “full-fledged war crime” under international humanitarian law and its customary rules, condemning it as an act that violated fundamental principles and values. “The Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will respond to this terrorist attack firmly and in accordance with international humanitarian law and its customary rules,” he said. US president to speak with Saudi crown prince Trump, speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in the United States on Saturday, condemned the attack and said he would speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is also the Kingdom’s prime minister. “What happened in Saudi Arabia’s not acceptable,” Trump said, according to AFP. ‘Attacks a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life’ US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also strongly condemned the recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying an American citizen had been killed in the strikes. “These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now,” Rubio wrote on X on Saturday. Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said early Sunday that 12 people had been killed and 309 injured in Saturday’s attack on King Khalid International Airport. The dead included four Saudi citizens and nationals of Bangladesh, Palestine, the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan. Some of the injured were in critical condition. GACA said airport operations had been temporarily suspended while authorities assessed the damage. The attack was the latest in a series of Houthi strikes targeting the Kingdom’s civilian aviation infrastructure. Hours after the Riyadh attack, Al-Maliki announced on X that a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in the Kingdom’s Eastern Province. He did not provide further details about the incident. Al-Maliki later posted social media that a drone targeting the Kingdom’s eastern region was intercepted and destroyed. The coalition also announced that a Houthi ballistic missile had been intercepted in Al-Kharj governorate, according to a separate statement carried by SPA. The incidents have heightened concerns about the growing threat to Saudi Arabia’s airports and air travel as the regional conflict continues. King Fahd International Airport, one of the Kingdom’s busiest transport hubs, had not previously been reported as a target since the Iran war erupted on Feb. 28. At least 291 flights at Riyadh’s airport were canceled over a 24-hour period, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. Several international airlines, including Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines, had also suspended flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, citing the Houthis’ ability to strike targets deeper inside the Kingdom and an increased focus on aviation infrastructure. It warned that missile and drone attacks, as well as interception efforts, increased the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. The attacks have also prompted diplomatic action over the wider threat posed by the Houthis. Yemen’s internationally recognized government submitted a letter to the United Nations and the Security Council concerning a Houthi attack on Aden airport early Wednesday, according to SPA. The letter, addressed by Yemen’s Permanent Representative to the UN, Ambassador Abdullah Al-Saadi, to Secretary-General António Guterres and the Security Council president for October, Greece’s Ambassador Aglaia Balta, called for condemnation of the attack, accountability for those responsible and full implementation of the arms embargo imposed on the militia. The Yemeni government said confronting the threat required addressing its underlying causes, particularly the continued control of parts of the country by armed militias and their possession of capabilities used against civilians, civilian infrastructure and international navigation, SPA reported. Saudi Arabia has repeatedly warned against the use of Yemeni territory as a launchpad for attacks on the Kingdom and threats to regional security and maritime navigation. Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences, including the World Petroleum Conference. Organisers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned, according to Reuters. In an advisory issued earlier on Saturday, King Khalid airport urged passengers to contact their airlines directly and check their flight status before heading to the airport amid reports of disruptions to air traffic, without specifying the cause of the disruptions. Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also instructed Saudi citizens travelling to the kingdom to contact local embassies if their travel itineraries have been disrupted following the attack. At the same time, foreign embassies in Riyadh, including those of the US, the United Kingdom, Ireland and Canada, issued advisories on social media to their citizens in Saudi Arabia. The US embassy in Saudi Arabia urged Americans to avoid the airport and surrounding areas. In a statement released on Sunday, the US Mission said US government employees working in the kingdom required special authorisation to use the King Khalid airport, as well as airports in Jeddah and Dammam. It said US government employees are not to travel within 20 miles (32km) of the Yemeni border due to safety risks, and need special authorisation for travel to the provinces of Jazan, Asir, Najran, and the cities of Qatif, Yanbu and Taif. The UK and Irish embassies advised their nationals about “a serious incident” at the airport. Canada’s embassy advised citizens in Riyadh to avoid all travel to the airport, noting “ongoing military activity”. Following reports of the latest attack, United States President Donald Trump was asked by reporters outside the White House whether Washington planned to join the Saudi strikes on the Houthis. “We may. We’re going to look at it. We just found out about the ⁠⁠⁠⁠recent attack, so we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly,” he said. “I think it’s terrible. The Saudis are good fighters but I think the attack was a terrible thing,” the US president said. Trump said he planned to speak to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman about it. He said the US had communication with the Houthis and added that “what they did was very bad”. "These reprehensible attacks demonstrate a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life. They must stop now," Rubio wrote on X. The attack was widely condemned, with Qatar’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs calling it “a direct threat to the security of the region”. Qatar’s former prime minister says today’s attack on King Khalid airport shows that it is “more urgent than ever” to stand with Saudi Arabia in a “practical and decisive” manner. “It has now become clear that Iran is our primary adversary”, Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani said in a post on X, adding that the Gulf Cooperation Council today confronts “several hostile plots and conspiracies” that require “unity and profound foresight”. He said it has become “more urgent and evident” that Qatar stands with Saudi Arabia against the “threat from within Yemen” that is being “plotted and directed from outside [Yemen]”. The situation “necessitates setting aside all peripheral disputes” among Gulf Cooperation Council members and “demonstrating unity” instead, he said. Kuwait Airways said it was cancelling flights because the airport had closed due to a “security situation”. Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces. The war was fought to a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict. That ceasefire unravelled over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far made slow gains, even as the Houthis put the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

representative.title: Mass Protests in Hasakah Under ‘Friday of the Syrian Flag’ Banner
representative.author: Asharq Al Awsat

snapshot.title: Mass Protests in Hasakah Under ‘Friday of the Syrian Flag’ Banner
snapshot.evidenceText: Mass Protests in Hasakah Under ‘Friday of the Syrian Flag’ Banner Thousands of residents of Syria’s Hasakah province rallied after Friday prayers to demand state authority across the province and the release of detainees and people forcibly disappeared in prisons run by the dissolved Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). In scenes described as the “greatest celebration” and the “Hasakah flood,” protesters gathered in Freedom Square in the city center under the slogan “Friday of the Syrian Flag.” They called for state sovereignty and a stronger presence for its institutions, a day after the national flag was raised on the square’s tallest flagpole before a large gathering of residents and officials. The protests capped a week of rapid developments in Hasakah over the implementation of a Jan. 29, 2026, agreement between the Syrian government and the SDF. The deal called for the former Kurdish Autonomous Administration’s civilian, security and military institutions to be integrated into state structures. Arabs, who make up the province’s population majority, have complained that the SDF remains dominant despite its announced dissolution in late August. Residents began arriving early in the morning from Hasakah’s al-Aziziya, al-Kallasa and al-Nashwa neighborhoods and from other towns, including al-Shaddadi, Markada, al-Hol and al-Arisha. They gathered outside Abu Bakr al-Siddiq Mosque in Ghweiran before marching after Friday prayers to the city’s main square, known as Liberation Square, carrying Syrian national flags. Government internal security forces reinforced their presence across the city from midnight Thursday to protect protesters, residents and public and private property. The deployment followed indiscriminate gunfire by “outlaw” gunmen in several neighborhoods. Activists accused a Kurdish group referred to as “Revolutionary Popular” of stirring tensions to impose a curfew and block the demonstrations. Internal security forces restored calm that night, Syria’s Al-Ikhbariya television channel reported. Protesters carried national flags, photographs of SDF detainees and pictures of “martyrs of the Syrian revolution.” They chanted, “One, one ... the Syrian people are one,” seeking to reassure the province’s Arab, Kurdish and Christian communities that all were subject to the law and equal in rights and duties. Their demands included extending state sovereignty and authority across Hasakah, restoring state institutions and making them operational, releasing detainees forcibly disappeared in SDF prisons, and allowing their sons to join the internal security forces. They also called for an end to the province’s dual authorities and the presence of Revolutionary Youth. Videos posted on social media showed protesters removing Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and SDF flags and banners from streets and buildings. Sohaib al-Yaarubi, an activist from the province’s Arab tribes and one of those who called for the protests, said the message was clear: the overwhelming majority in Hasakah supported the Syrian state, wanted its sovereignty extended across the province and wanted only the flag of the Syrian Arab Republic flown there. Yaarubi told Asharq Al-Awsat the demonstrations were “successful” and the demands “patriotic and legitimate.” He said there were no tensions or provocations apart from one incident involving Revolutionary Youth members, which protesters defused. Ibrahim al-Halabi, another activist from the province’s Arab tribes, described the crowds in Liberation Square as “awe-inspiring, beautiful and truly wonderful.” The peaceful demonstrations lasted about two hours. He said the raising of the national flag brought overwhelming joy, stirring emotions that recalled the early days of the Syrian revolution against the former government in 2011. “Some described the demonstrations and the crowds in Liberation Square as the greatest celebration in Hasakah, a city denied the chance to celebrate the victory achieved when the ousted government fell nearly two years ago,” Halabi said. Delegations from other provinces, including Deir Ezzor, joined the Hasakah protests. Similar demonstrations took place in several provinces in support of its residents’ demands. The Friday rallies followed Thursday’s raising of the national flag on the tallest flagpole in central Hasakah before a large gathering of residents and officials. Government officials also inspected the courthouse to “create suitable conditions for making the judicial system operational.” Internal security forces had deployed around the courthouse after members of the dissolved SDF vacated their positions there, while the government strengthened its security presence across the city. On Tuesday, the SDF’s counterterrorism forces had handed over their positions to internal security forces. Maj. Gen. Abdul Qader Tahhan, head of Syria’s General Intelligence Service, and Brig. Gen. Abdul Rahman al-Dabbagh, head of foreign intelligence, subsequently arrived in Hasakah with a large security delegation. The developments followed mass peaceful protests after prayers the previous Friday in several towns and cities across Hasakah province, demanding state authority and a stronger presence for its institutions throughout the province. Judicial Source: Lebanon Arrests 2 Suspected Hezbollah Members over Explosives Lebanese authorities arrested two suspected Hezbollah members accused of secretly transporting half-a-ton of explosives, a judicial source told AFP on Saturday. According to the source, who spoke on condition of anonymity, the two men were caught Thursday afternoon at a security checkpoint in Dahr al-Baidar in Lebanon's east, near a road linking the country with Syria. After searching the vehicle, security forces seized "250 kilograms of TNT-type explosives and 250 kilograms of C4-type, a highly explosive substance,” the source said. Based on initial investigations, one of the suspects is the son of a Hezbollah official and the other is also a member of the group, according to the source. The explosives' destination remains unknown, the source added. Lebanese authorities have not confirmed the source's information. But Justice Minister Adel Nassar vowed on X Saturday that "the investigation into the seized explosives, and everything that follows from it, will continue to the very end.” He insisted that work toward "disarming illegal groups, combating terrorism and prosecuting all outlaws is... irreversible and speeding up.” Lebanon approved a plan to disarm Hezbollah in 2025, following a ceasefire the previous November that ended a devastating war between the group and Israel. However, the conflict flared back to life in March this year when Hezbollah attacked Israel in support of Iran in the Middle East war. Israel invaded in response and now occupies a band of territory in Lebanon's south. A new ceasefire was struck in June, and Israel and Lebanon have agreed to a framework deal that involves Hezbollah's disarmament, a gradual Israeli withdrawal and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the region. MSF: Houthi Escalation Leaves Thousands of Yemenis Without Shelter The ordeal is far from over for the thousands of Yemenis who have fled the Houthi escalation in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah. Reaching safer areas did not mark the end of their struggle, as many families found themselves without shelter after traveling long distances on foot under intense heat, only to face hunger, disease, and a shortage of clean water amid growing risks of malnutrition and cholera. Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) has warned of deteriorating health and living conditions among displaced people in the governorates of Lahj and Aden, noting that those fleeing the escalation are experiencing high rates of severe acute malnutrition, cholera, acute watery diarrhea, measles, and other infectious diseases. At the same time, their ability to secure food, clean water, and medical care continues to decline. According to MSF, the latest wave of escalation has displaced families from areas along Yemen’s western coast that have come under Houthi control, leaving them once again facing harsh conditions after abandoning their homes, possessions, and livelihoods in search of safety. Conditions documented by mobile medical teams reveal the extent of the displaced population’s suffering. Many have traveled long distances across desert terrain in extreme heat, with no guarantee of access to food, water, or shelter from the harsh weather. “Displaced people who cannot find shelter in host communities, and formal or informal camps have been seen by our teams on the road or sleeping under the shade of trees,” MSF said. Those who have settled around Lahj governorate “are in critical need of medical and humanitarian support, including water and sanitation services in the informal places where they settle, such as schools and mosques. The risk of waterborne diseases, like cholera, is increasing rapidly in the current conditions.” The consequences of displacement extend far beyond the loss of homes and the hardships of the journey. Women and children face growing health risks amid worsening food insecurity, the loss of income and livelihoods, and the struggle to meet basic needs, making daily survival a constant challenge for families forced to flee. “In the many camps across Lahj and Aden governorates, 70 percent of the patients treated by MSF mobile clinics are women and children. People present with skin infections, fever, diarrhea, and communicable diseases,” MSF said. “The long walks have caused foot injuries and ear and eye infections,” it added. The risks are even greater for children suffering from malnutrition, as their chances of obtaining adequate nutrition and regular healthcare continue to decline due to poverty, displacement, and limited access to medical services. MSF teams have identified cases of severe acute malnutrition among children requiring specialized medical intervention. Food insecurity and declining sources of income, coupled with a rise in cholera cases, are further exacerbating the health challenges faced by displaced people. Many are struggling to access medical facilities or obtain the referrals needed for essential treatment. “In response to the needs of displaced people, we sent mobile clinics across Aden and Lahj governorates, with 775 total consultations since 15 September. Twenty children were diagnosed with severe acute malnutrition,” said MSF. For families that have traveled long distances in search of safety, the struggle does not end once they leave conflict zones behind. Instead, a new battle begins: securing food, drinking water, and shelter to protect their children from heat and disease. As needs continue to grow, the urgency of providing shelter, food, healthcare, and clean water for displaced people becomes increasingly evident. These are families who have been forced to abandon their homes and start over under extremely harsh conditions. Lebanon Welcomes Trump's Move to Lift 41-year US Flight Ban Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said on Saturday that President Donald Trump's decision to revoke flight restrictions between Lebanon and the US that were imposed four decades ago was an indication of American confidence in steps taken by Lebanon to address civil aviation safety. Direct flights between the US and Lebanon were suspended in 1985 by the Reagan administration following the hijacking of TWA Flight 847. Trump made the surprise announcement that he would allow American carriers to resume direct flights to Lebanon during a visit by Aoun to Washington in July. While he ordered the lifting of the restrictions nearly two weeks ago, the decision was publicly announced on Saturday. انشئ حساباً خاصاً بك لتحصل على أخبار مخصصة لك ولتتمتع بخاصية حفظ المقالات وتتلقى نشراتنا البريدية المتنوعة

representative.title: India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief : NPR
representative.author: The Associated Press

snapshot.title: India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
snapshot.evidenceText: A protester shout slogans as they are detained and taken in a police vehicle during a protest demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi, India, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Manish Swarup/AP hide caption NEW DELHI — Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India's youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities. Police moved to break up the demonstration before it could begin, intercepting demonstrators on their way to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders, opposition lawmakers and student activists were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start. The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators. Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters. Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late. Sambit Patra, a spokesperson for Modi's party, dismissed the demonstrators as "anarchic elements." "Their flop show has been completely demolished," Patra said. The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July. Policemen detain protesters during a youth demonstration demanding the resignation of the country's election chief Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Vipin/AP hide caption Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men. "The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement. Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas, with police briefly detaining some of them. Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained. "We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights," said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?" The police response marked an extraordinary show of force in a capital where Modi's government has repeatedly sought to contain public dissent in the past. Under Modi, authorities have often used arrests and restrictions on public gatherings to contain demonstrations, raising questions about the space for protests in the world's largest democracy. The latest crackdown renewed criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent. "Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press. Brittas was later detained by police. Security personnel detain a protester during a demonstration by the Cockroach Janta Party demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi, India, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Manish Swarup/AP hide caption The protests center on India's Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far. The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries. The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. Saturday's planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police. Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi's party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists. The commission and the government deny the allegations. For the "Cockroach" movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign. The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years. For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi's home state, will test the party's standing. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July. Policemen detain protesters during a youth demonstration demanding the resignation of the country's election chief Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Vipin/AP hide caption Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men. "The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement. Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas, with police briefly detaining some of them. Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained. "We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights," said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?" Under Modi, authorities have often used arrests and restrictions on public gatherings to contain demonstrations, raising questions about the space for protests in the world's largest democracy. The latest crackdown renewed criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent. "Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press. Brittas was later detained by police. Security personnel detain a protester during a demonstration by the Cockroach Janta Party demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in New Delhi, India, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far. The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries. The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists. representative.title: ICE has quietly used this warehouse as a detention facility all summer, neighbors say : NPR
representative.author: Jasmine Garsd

snapshot.title: ICE has quietly used this warehouse as a detention facility all summer, neighbors say
snapshot.evidenceText: A Roxbury, N.J., warehouse was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants. José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR hide caption ROXBURY, N.J. — On a warm morning on Sept. 4, masked immigration agents rolled into Dover, N.J. Footage of the raids rippled across social media, sent people into hiding and reignited rumors that had been circulating for months: Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were taking people to a nearby warehouse. The warehouse in Roxbury was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants as part of President Trump's mass deportation efforts. That plan to convert warehouses into detention centers faced fierce backlash and legal challenges from residents and immigrant advocates. It was largely abandoned, and in several sites, including Roxbury, the government is legally forbidden by a court order from converting them to a detention facility, pending environmental assessments. But an NPR investigation has found signs that the New Jersey facility is being used. And the state's Office of the Attorney General says it is looking into similar reports. In early 2026, Homeland Security bought 11 warehouses to turn into ICE detention facilities. They spent about a billion dollars on these. NPR spoke to an official at a government contractor whose company was approached to convert several of the warehouses into ICE facilities. He spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation from the government. "No one that we spoke to at DHS was for this idea whatsoever. The deputy director told us point-blank that they had pushed back very hard on it. Everybody knew warehouses are horrible places to put people," he says. At a meeting with a deputy director at DHS, he says, his company proposed an alternative: FEMA-style camps in Texas that would be more humane. He says that idea was swiftly shot down. While White House adviser Stephen Miller was not at the meeting, they were told that this was not what Miller wanted. The contractor says his understanding from that meeting was that "Miller did not want the facilities that were comfortable. He did not want facilities that were humane. We were told point-blank that that was not what the administration wanted." "Steve Miller certainly seemed to make that point to everyone that he wanted it to be cruel. This was what Miller had stated to the DHS at that time, to the DHS director and deputy director. What surprised me was just how adamant the people were that it was going to happen. Damn the consequences. I would say in 25 years of working with the U.S. government, I've never been in that position before." In a statement to NPR, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the contractor's comments were "false hearsay allegation(s) from someone who has never even met or talked with Stephen Miller." Bis also said that Miller "has never made any remarks to anyone about wanting illegal aliens to have worse detention facility conditions. It simply isn't true and this is defamatory." The White House did not respond to repeated requests to speak to Miller directly. Early on, the warehouse plan was met with protests in both conservative and liberal towns. Several state attorneys general filed lawsuits to halt construction, based on environmental concerns. "It very quickly became an absolute boondoggle," says Michael Wriston, a former military intelligence analyst who co-founded Project SaltBox, a watchdog group that tracks ICE's expansion. "It was really about the optics of people being kept in these cages and these large warehouses. They wanted a lot of what they called B-roll to play on social media, but they didn't do any due diligence of making sure that they conformed with environmental policy or that the construction wouldn't disturb local water tables." A DHS official who served during Trump's first term, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared government retaliation, says that while they were not in the meeting the contractor described to NPR, they had often heard higher-ups in the administration wanting to make a point of showcasing difficult conditions immigrants were being held in. Then, with the departure of DHS Secretary Kristi Noem in March, there was a shift: Her replacement, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, sought to do less showy immigration crackdowns. Today, Homeland Security is selling several of the warehouses. But they're still holding on to a few, including in Hagerstown, Md. , Surprise, Ariz., and Roxbury, N.J. " These locations are very critical to ICE's deportation agenda," says Wriston, "because they fill in the gap in places where ICE does not have a robust detention network. They don't have a lot of jails there." They are also located in areas where there are no partnerships with the police who can house detainees in local jails. In Maryland , Arizona and New Jersey , following lawsuits from each of the state attorneys general, DHS has either agreed or been ordered by a judge to halt the conversion of the warehouses into detention centers, pending environmental impact assessments. But throughout the summer, in the towns surrounding the Roxbury warehouse, rumors started to bubble. Over the summer, there was a historic surge in ICE arrests: around 100,000 people in July and August. In New Jersey, the rumor mill started churning. The Roxbury warehouse is located in a wooded area, on a road right off Route 46. Project NINJA (No ICE in North Jersey Alliance), a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, says several neighbors reported vehicles, often in a caravan, speeding up the road. Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner in Dover, N.J., on Sept. 17. José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR hide caption "They're holding people in that warehouse," one woman says in a WhatsApp group in the town of Dover, which is about 15 minutes from Roxbury. "I have a co-worker who was taken there. They hold them there and at night they take them somewhere else." The message was forwarded to NPR by Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner. "But, you know, it's like third- and fourth-hand accounts," says Wittner. "It just didn't seem probable at the time because of the court order. But it kind of made you scratch your head a little bit." A woman says she was driving to work when she saw a raid taking place in Dover. She decided to follow the car carrying people who were detained. "I just needed to know, is he going to Roxbury?" She took video as she trailed them up Route 46. She asked that NPR not use her name because what happened next made her fearful of what the government might do. She says the car she was following turned onto the woodsy road that leads to the warehouse. She says she waited to see if there was any more movement. "And then maybe five minutes after that, a white Dodge Durango started kind of circling around me," she says. "And then on his last loop, he started filming me. He had a yellow case on his cellphone. After that, a black Tahoe started doing the same thing. I was on a public sidewalk, and it was intimidating. It was really intimidating. I'm scared. But I am more scared for our community." Councilwoman Wittner says she strongly suspects ICE is using the Roxbury warehouse: "The immigration enforcement activity happened in Dover between 7 a.m. and 8 a.m." Wittner points to the woman who was able to follow the vehicle up Route 46: "The last vehicle entered the warehouse road at 8:25 a.m." Meanwhile, footage of the raid started circulating on social media. Back in Dover, another woman says she saw the videos as she got her kids ready for school. NPR viewed the videos and confirmed their authenticity. In one of them, a worker is cornered against a wall by two masked agents. She says she was thunderstruck. She asked that we not use her name because she fears being targeted. At 8:25 a.m., she says, she got a call from her father. He's 59, she says, and he sounded disoriented. He told her he was handcuffed in some kind of jail. She found it strange, she says, because the Roxbury warehouse would be the only place he could have been taken in that short a time span. She also discovered a friend of hers had been picked up. She hasn't been able to speak to her father since then, and neither has NPR. But NPR located her friend in Honduras, where he's been deported. He requested anonymity, because he fears repercussions for his loved ones who are still in the U.S. "I was picked up on my way to work, on Friday, Sept. 4. The agents loaded me into a van. They took us to Roxbury," he said. He says he and the other people detained were handcuffed and held in the parking lot for several hours. He counted nine other men with him. "I just went into a state of shock," he says. "I signed my deportation papers. The next morning I regretted it. But I was scared. Eventually, they transferred us to a real facility." In a statement to NPR, DHS did not respond to a question about whether it was holding people at the Roxbury location. But it did give NPR a statement it has previously sent about ICE detention, saying DHS upholds strict standards and that immigrants can choose to leave detention by being deported. A member of Project NINJA, a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, in Roxbury on Sept. 17. José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR hide caption The activists at NINJA say ICE's actions violate the legal order. The order lists several actions ICE can take with the site — mainly upkeep — but nowhere on that list is detention an acceptable action, they say. Harvard professor Andrew Mergen, a former attorney with the U.S. Department of Justice Environment & Natural Resources Division, says ICE may technically not be violating the court order, which stipulated it would not convert the place into a detention center pending an environmental assessment. Ultimately, Mergen says, the situation shows the limitations of using environmental claims. "The community is acting here to prevent people from being detained," says Mergen. "And the administration seems to have cleverly elided that intention, by sort of saying, 'Well, we're not going to build this facility, but we're going to use this space in furtherance of detention.'" He says he understands the frustration: "It's just infuriating if what you are trying to do is say 'No. Not here. Not here.' " Wittner says since the raid, she's heard from other close relatives or close friends of two men who were picked up that day, who say they were inside the Roxbury warehouse. She says the situation is unacceptable: "We need our Congress members to conduct an oversight visit yesterday, quite honestly. We need our state to aggressively pursue this investigation and demand to get inside." She says DHS has had time "to go in and clean up their mess if they, in fact, got caught doing something that they shouldn't have." Meanwhile, in Dover, the streets where the raid happened remain deserted. At an empty diner at lunchtime, a waitress who did not want to be named because of the climate of fear in town says one of the workers who was taken used to come here for a bite. Then she leans over and asks: "Do you know where they took those men?" The warehouse in Roxbury. José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR hide caption NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

representative.title: New Liberal major projects bill clears first vote, heads to special committee | CBC News
representative.author: David Baxter

snapshot.title: New Liberal major projects bill clears first vote, heads to special committee | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: A key piece of the Carney government's economic agenda, Bill C-39, passed its first vote in the House of Commons on Thursday, with Conservatives and the majority Liberals sending the bill for study by a special committee. The 243-page bill proposes to extend the government's approach to major infrastructure projects to other projects across the country. The government wants those projects to undergo one review instead of several reviews, and to have that single review completed within one year. The legislation is a core part of the Liberals' plans to pivot the economy away from reliance on the United States and present Canada as a reliable trading partner to overseas markets. Before the vote, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party would support sending the legislation to committee in order to propose amendments to what he called a "weak, watered-down, long-delayed" bill. Poilievre told reporters he wants the government to speed up the decision timeline on projects to between six months and a year, and to add measures to protect workers' rights. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says his party will be proposing amendments to Bill C-39. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press) He also said Conservatives would seek to eliminate the industrial carbon price and create "shovel-ready zones" with pre-permitting for developments. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government will use a special committee formed to study the sweeping legislation. The 11-member committee includes MPs from the Liberals, Conservatives and Bloc Québécois, with the Liberals holding a majority of seats. It doesn't include representation from the NDP, which does not have official party status in the House of Commons, a requirement for automatic inclusion on standing committees. NDP House leader Don Davies said he asked the government to allow his party to participate in the committee but Government House leader Steven MacKinnon turned him down, a move Davies called "fundamentally undemocratic." Carney government to study new major projects bill with tool last used in Harper era Green Party Leader Elizabeth May said she also asked for committee standing but was denied. She said the bill is the "omnibus of omnibuses" and threatens to trample the environment in order to build things quickly. "What is currently happening, this Prime Minister's Office is more contemptuous of Parliament and less concerned about transparency and accountability than any previous PMO," May said, in a scrum with reporters before question period. Critics warn Bill C-39 puts environment at risk At a news conference Thursday with labour and First Nations leaders, Davies and NDP Leader Avi Lewis said the legislation must not pass as written because of what it does to labour and treaty rights. Lewis said the bill "must be scrapped" because of the massive changes it would unleash and because the government failed to consult adequately with Indigenous communities and other affected groups. He compared it to omnibus bills tabled during the Stephen Harper era. On Tuesday, B.C. Liberal MP Patrick Weiler took some shots at his own government's bill during debate in the House of Commons. Critics accuse Carney government of proposing 'sacrifice zones' for the environment Liberals table bill to speed up major project approvals, avert labour disruptions Weiler said while he agrees with the overall direction of the bill, he's not comfortable with C-39 giving cabinet the power to fast-track project timelines. He also warned the one-year project timelines under the bill could undermine the government's duty to consult with Indigenous communities. Lewis said Weiler took a "courageous stand" and he's heard similar concerns from Liberal voters. Carney faces climate, labour pushback over new nation-building bill "There are people in the progressive Liberal universe who are dismayed by this legislation and I encourage more of them to speak up before it's too late," Lewis said. Poilievre was asked how he would enforce the tight timelines he proposes while giving Indigenous communities and other stakeholders enough time to consider the proposals. He said Indigenous people have already given their consent to an aggressive infrastructure agenda. "Indigenous people want to build, and I believe that Indigenous Canadians can be the richest people anywhere on earth if we unblock our resources, get the government out of the way and get building," Poilievre said. Also on Thursday, Cold Lake First Nations filed in Federal Court for a judicial review of Ottawa's decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline a project in the national interest. The First Nation accuses the government of failing to adequately consult with them on the project. Chief Shelly Moore-Frappier, of the Teme Augama Anishinabek nation, told Thursday's news conference with Lewis that her community is not anti-development but this legislation must not pass as written. She said she wants to see the bill amended to compel the government to obtain Indigenous consent for developments, eliminate the legislation's deadlines on consultation and require companies to clean up former industrial sites. "Last year I told the Senate that Bill C-5 was economic coercion. Ottawa used the threat of tariffs to push First Nations into line, and we got painted as the problem," Moore-Frappier said, referring to the Carney government's initial major projects law. "We were told the fast-track was temporary. C-39 takes it and makes it permanent." She said her community is home to deposits of copper, cobalt, platinum and other critical minerals — along with inactive mines that have been left unremediated. The government insists it will uphold its duty to consult with Indigenous groups on projects and argues the legislation does not threaten the right to strike. Bill C-39 proposes new rules on when the jobs minister can intervene in a labour dispute affecting a federally regulated sector. Any new restrictions on right to strike are 'unacceptable': Canadian Labour Congress Bea Bruske, president of the Canadian Labour Congress, called C-39 an attack on workers' rights at a news conference on Thursday. Bruske said changes to clarify a minister's power to scuttle a work stoppage when the "national interest" is at stake completely undermine unions' ability to use the threat of a strike to extract gains at the bargaining table. Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has said the federal government will not compromise workers' rights to strike, but she did not answer directly when asked at the Senate earlier this week whether the bill could impose limits on that right. The Liberals argue changes proposed to the Canada Labour Code in the bill will put "guardrails" around the minister's ability to intervene in a labour dispute. Poilievre said the Conservatives will also introduce amendments at committee to protect workers' rights but offered no specifics. David Baxter is a reporter with The Canadian Press Audience Relations, CBC P.O. Box 500 Station A Toronto, ON Canada, M5W 1E6 It is a priority for CBC to create products that are accessible to all in Canada including people with visual, hearing, motor and cognitive challenges. Before the vote, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party would support sending the legislation to committee in order to propose amendments to what he called a "weak, watered-down, long-delayed" bill. Poilievre told reporters he wants the government to speed up the decision timeline on projects to between six months and a year, and to add measures to protect workers' rights. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says his party will be proposing amendments to Bill C-39. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press) He also said Conservatives would seek to eliminate the industrial carbon price and create "shovel-ready zones" with pre-permitting for developments. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government will use a special committee formed to study the sweeping legislation. The 11-member committee includes MPs from the Liberals, Conservatives and Bloc Québécois, with the Liberals holding a majority of seats. It doesn't include representation from the NDP, which does not have official party status in the House of Commons, a requirement for automatic inclusion on standing committees. NDP House leader Don Davies said he asked the government to allow his party to participate in the committee but Government House leader Steven MacKinnon turned him down, a move Davies called "fundamentally undemocratic." Carney government to study new major projects bill with tool last used in Harper era Green Party Leader Elizabeth May said she also asked for committee standing but was denied. She said the bill is the "omnibus of omnibuses" and threatens to trample the environment in order to build things quickly. "What is currently happening, this Prime Minister's Office is more contemptuous of Parliament and less concerned about transparency and accountability than any previous PMO," May said, in a scrum with reporters before question period. Critics warn Bill C-39 puts environment at risk At a news conference Thursday with labour and First Nations leaders, Davies and NDP Leader Avi Lewis said the legislation must not pass as written because of what it does to labour and treaty rights. Lewis said the bill "must be scrapped" because of the massive changes it would unleash and because the government failed to consult adequately with Indigenous communities and other affected groups. He compared it to omnibus bills tabled during the Stephen Harper era. On Tuesday, B.C. Liberal MP Patrick Weiler took some shots at his own government's bill during debate in the House of Commons. Critics accuse Carney government of proposing 'sacrifice zones' for the environment Liberals table bill to speed up major project approvals, avert labour disruptions Weiler said while he agrees with the overall direction of the bill, he's not comfortable with C-39 giving cabinet the power to fast-track project timelines. He also warned the one-year project timelines under the bill could undermine the government's duty to consult with Indigenous communities. Lewis said Weiler took a "courageous stand" and he's heard similar concerns from Liberal voters. Carney faces climate, labour pushback over new nation-building bill "There are people in the progressive Liberal universe who are dismayed by this legislation and I encourage more of them to speak up before it's too late," Lewis said. Poilievre was asked how he would enforce the tight timelines he proposes while giving Indigenous communities and other stakeholders enough time to consider the proposals. He said Indigenous people have already given their consent to an aggressive infrastructure agenda. "Indigenous people want to build, and I believe that Indigenous Canadians can be the richest people anywhere on earth if we unblock our resources, get the government out of the way and get building," Poilievre said. Also on Thursday, Cold Lake First Nations filed in Federal Court for a judicial review of Ottawa's decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline a project in the national interest. The First Nation accuses the government of failing to adequately consult with them on the project. Chief Shelly Moore-Frappier, of the Teme Augama Anishinabek nation, told Thursday's news conference with Lewis that her community is not anti-development but this legislation must not pass as written. She said she wants to see the bill amended to compel the government to obtain Indigenous consent for developments, eliminate the legislation's deadlines on consultation and require companies to clean up former industrial sites. "Last year I told the Senate that Bill C-5 was economic coercion. Ottawa used the threat of tariffs to push First Nations into line, and we got painted as the problem," Moore-Frappier said, referring to the Carney government's initial major projects law. "We were told the fast-track was temporary. C-39 takes it and makes it permanent." She said her community is home to deposits of copper, cobalt, platinum and other critical minerals — along with inactive mines that have been left unremediated. The government insists it will uphold its duty to consult with Indigenous groups on projects and argues the legislation does not threaten the right to strike. Bill C-39 proposes new rules on when the jobs minister can intervene in a labour dispute affecting a federally regulated sector. Bruske said changes to clarify a minister's power to scuttle a work stoppage when the "national interest" is at stake completely undermine unions' ability to use the threat of a strike to extract gains at the bargaining table. Jobs Minister Patty Hajdu has said the federal government will not compromise workers' rights to strike, but she did not answer directly when asked at the Senate earlier this week whether the bill could impose limits on that right. The Liberals argue changes proposed to the Canada Labour Code in the bill will put "guardrails" around the minister's ability to intervene in a labour dispute. Poilievre said the Conservatives will also introduce amendments at committee to protect workers' rights but offered no specifics.
