representative.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft | Longform | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Aatif Ammad

snapshot.title: High silver prices threaten Lucknow’s famed bridal nagra craft
snapshot.evidenceText: Lucknow brides can no longer afford traditional silver nagras In Lucknow, the capital of Uttar Pradesh and a city known for its Nawabi heritage and artisanship, 55-year-old Azhar Hussain sits at the bench where he has spent years making decorative footwear. His tools are still there, but the customers are not. Amid soaring silver prices over the past year, demand for his work has plummeted. The small workshop sits beside Chowk Bazaar, one of Old Lucknow’s oldest and busiest markets, a famed hub for wedding shopping full of silver jewellery and handcrafts. For three decades, Hussain has been one of the bazaar’s busiest craftsmen, making a distinctive form of silver slip-on shoes, known locally as nagras. He starts by cutting a thin silver sheet into the outline of a nagra, then sketches floral and leaf motifs onto the metal. Hussain then rests the sheet on heated lac, a soft natural resin that cushions the metal while he uses a hammer and engraving tool to tap intricate designs into place. Hussain then bends the silver around a foot-shaped furma, or mould, before fitting it over a base of cardboard, rubber and velvet, soldering the pieces together and polishing the pair. Craftsmen have used this process to make silver nagras since the 1600s. Originally, the decorative shoes were made for daily use by the Nawabi, Muslim rulers of the former kingdom of Awadh. “Silver nagras used to be the most important part of a nawab’s attire,” said 68-year-old Nawab Masud Abdullah, an eighth-generation descendant of Nawab Muhammad Ali Shah, the ninth Nawab of Awadh, who ruled from 1837 until he died in 1842. “They were not just footwear; they represented our culture and heritage,” he added. Once reserved exclusively for Nawabs, silver nagras have become a cherished wedding tradition over the last century, embraced by Lucknow’s middle and upper classes alike. “Our forefathers wore silver nagras every day. Later, they became reserved for celebrations and eventually only for special occasions,” Abdullah explained. “The good thing was that the tradition spread beyond the Nawabs. People, particularly brides across Lucknow, embrace it as their own and now a bride is considered incomplete without a nagra.” Hussain and his family of craftsmen have seen this transformation firsthand. “In the past, only Nawabs could afford these shoes because they symbolised wealth, power and status,” he said. “But over the last seven or eight decades, they became popular among middle-class and wealthy families too, especially for weddings and special occasions.” There are two types of silver nagras — open-toed chappals and closed-toed jutis, and customers can choose different patterns, ornamentation and designs. Hussain’s family has been making nagras since the early 1900s and the trade has provided a comfortable living. Before each wedding season, he has typically made about 10 pairs a month, he says, with each priced between $105 and $230 (10,000 and 22,000 rupees). “We lived with dignity,” he said quietly. “We earned enough to feed our family, educate our children and save a little every month. We never imagined that one day we would struggle even to run our household.” Over the past year, however, the orders have vanished with the rise in silver prices. The metal was already costing a bit more before the U.S.-Iran war launched in February, owing to tight supplies and growing investor demand. But the conflict added another jolt, as uncertainty in global markets drove investors towards silver and put the metal — and the nagras — out of reach for many Lucknow shoppers. Prices for precious metals actually began rising with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine back in early 2022, but economists say prices surged significantly with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran. In 2023, silver prices in India largely fluctuated between $725 (70,000 rupees) and $830 (80,000 rupees) per kilogramme, rising to around $985 (98,000 rupees) in 2024. But this year, amid the conflict with Iran, silver prices briefly soared as high as $4,670 (450,000 rupees) per kg before easing after the ceasefire. Even now, after some decline, prices are hovering around $2,600 (250,000 rupees) per kg, more than three times their levels just a few years ago. Dr. Salahuddin Ayyub, an economist and international trade expert with India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry, said geopolitical conflicts have triggered unprecedented volatility in global commodity markets. “When stock markets become volatile, investors move their money into safer assets, such as gold and silver,” Ayyub explained. “This sudden surge in demand pushes the prices of precious metals sharply upwards.” The consequences have been particularly severe in India, he said, because gold and silver remain deeply intertwined with weddings, other cultural traditions and family savings. As prices continue to rise, many households are increasingly opting for lower-cost alternatives, such as artificial jewellery. He warned that while consumers may find substitutes, those whose livelihoods depend on the precious metals industry, including artisans, silversmiths, jewellery shopkeepers and traditional craftsmen, have far fewer options. “The impact extends well beyond consumers,” Ayyub said. “Entire communities whose incomes depend on these metals are now facing shrinking demand and growing economic uncertainty.” The surge in silver prices has had another consequence that is often overlooked by the government and policymakers. According to Ayyub, when a country witnesses a sharp rise in demand for imported precious metals, governments often intervene to curb imports and protect their foreign exchange reserves. “India depends heavily on imported silver. A sudden spike in imports puts pressure on the country’s foreign exchange reserves, so the government tries to discourage excessive imports through tariffs and other restrictions,” Ayyub said. These import duties are eventually passed on to consumers. “As tariffs increase, the landed cost of silver rises. That is one of the reasons why silver prices in India are currently trading above global prices,” he said. Globally, silver currently costs $2,100 (201,000 rupees) per kg, but in India, it’s more than 20 percent higher because of heavy government import taxes and strict licensing that chokes off supply. India depends on imports to meet more than 80% of its domestic silver demand and its purchases account for over 20 percent of the global trade in refined silver. India more than doubled its effective import taxes on gold and silver in May. That saw silver imports plunge by 87 percent to just $75.6 million that month, down from $566.2 million the previous year, the country’s lowest level in over three years. High silver prices are now forcing Lucknow’s brides to make tough, sometimes devastating, decisions. For 28-year-old Lucknow resident Uzma Siddique, who is set to marry in December, owning and wearing a pair of silver nagras on her big day has always topped her wedding wishlist. “My mother wore silver nagras at her wedding in 1992. So did my grandmother and so did my great-grandmother,” Siddique said. “I always imagined myself wearing them and taking my wedding photographs in them and posting them on Instagram. It was never just footwear; it was an emotion and a family tradition.” But when she visited the market with plans to order a pair, the prices stunned her. “A pair that cost around $156 to $208 (15,000 to 20,000 rupees) just a few years ago is now selling for nearly $673 (65,000 rupees),” she said. Determined to have a pair, she decided to give up on other wedding luxuries instead. “I had to cut back on many other wedding expenses. I bought a lighter lehenga (long skirt), reduced the number of suits I planned to purchase, and trimmed my budget in several places, just so I could afford these nagras.” Despite the financial strain, she says giving up the footwear tradition was never an option. “They have become incredibly expensive, but our emotions are attached to them. That’s why I still bought them,” she said. But many of her friends have had to go without. “Some had dreamed of wearing silver nagras on their wedding day, but they had to let go of that dream because they simply couldn’t afford them. They are deeply hurt by it,” she said. Not far from Siddique’s home lives her friend, 25-year-old Safiya Khan, who is also getting married in December. Unlike Siddique, Safiya has not been able to buy silver nagras for her wedding. From a lower middle-class family, she says soaring prices put upholding that tradition out of reach. “My entire wedding shopping budget is around $1,250 (120,000 rupees). I simply cannot spend more than half of it on a pair of shoes,” Khan said, noting that she was sad to end the family tradition. “I think this tradition will end with my generation,” she said. “My mother had a pair of silver nagras, but she had to sell them last year because of financial difficulties. We always believed we would buy another pair for my wedding. Had we known silver prices would rise so dramatically, we would never have sold them.” She has been shocked by how a distant war has so negatively affected this beloved local tradition. “I know the recent conflicts have pushed silver prices higher, but I never imagined that a war thousands of km away could take away a tradition so close to my heart,” she said. “I had always dreamed of taking my wedding photographs in silver nagras. Now that dream will never come true.” Naseem Jahan, a Lucknow resident in her late seventies, still treasures the pair of silver chappals her mother gave her for her wedding in 1972. “I remember my mother paid around $2.50 (250 rupees) for this pair,” Jahan recalled. “We had to wait nearly seven months after placing the order before it was finally ready. Those were beautiful days.” More than five decades later, the silver slippers remain one of her most cherished possessions. She has them polished every three years and proudly wears them to weddings and other important family gatherings, as do many of the older women in Lucknow. “Every time I wear them, people come to admire them and praise their beauty. That makes me so happy,” she said with a smile. But Jahan fears the tradition may not continue into the next generation. “Today, very few people can afford such footwear,” she said. When she recently visited the market to buy a similar pair for her granddaughter, the soaring price of silver made it unaffordable. Still, she wants her granddaughter to have traditional bridal footwear, so she has made a tough decision. “I have decided to gift her my own pair,” she said. “Let these slippers adorn her feet now. I want them to continue their journey.” As the only precious keepsake she has preserved from her wedding, Jahan knows how connected brides feel to the shoes. “I have developed an emotional bond with them. They remind me of my mother, my wedding day and the Lucknow I grew up in. I only wish silver prices would come down again so that more people could experience this tradition.” Jahan’s decision to part with her silver nagras will keep a pair in her family, but it will not bring new work to the craftsmen who once made the footwear for Lucknow’s brides. In Chowk Bazaar, dwindling demand has left many artisans facing the prospect of a trade that may not survive long enough to serve the next generation. Jabbar Hussain, 48, a fourth-generation craftsman and shopkeeper who makes nagras and sells them in his shop, sits in his empty store in Lucknow’s Chowk Bazaar, struggling to understand what has happened to a business that once flourished. Between June and September, Hussain’s shop would normally be crowded with customers placing orders for nagras. But over the past three months, Hussain says, he has not sold a single pair. He blames the unprecedented rise in silver prices for making the handmade footwear a luxury few can now afford. “A pair that once sold for around $125 (12,000 rupees) now costs between $622 and $778 (60,000 and 75,000 rupees) because silver has become so expensive,” he said. “People still walk into the shop, admire the craftsmanship and ask about the price. But the moment they hear it, they quietly leave. Every customer who walks away feels like another piece of our family's future disappearing.” Hussain, like others before him, now fears he will be forced to close his shop. “There were nearly 30 of us not long ago,” he said. “Most have already abandoned the profession because silver has become too expensive and orders have dried up. Those who are still here are also thinking of leaving.” He is now thinking of taking a loan to open a cafe, which he hopes will provide a steady income. “I need to find another way to earn,” he said. Hussain had hoped to teach the craft to his sons so they could carry forward the family’s legacy, but now he is advising them to pursue other professions. He no longer sees a future in the silver nagras trade and blames the war in the Middle East. “We have nothing to do with this war, yet we are paying the price,” he said, frustrated at how a conflict so far away has threatened his livelihood. “I don’t know what our future looks like anymore. Sometimes I think about what will happen to this craft and I cry. This wasn’t just our profession; it was our identity, our heritage and everything we were known for.” Still, Hussain clings to the hope that silver prices will decline and orders will return. Economists and market analysts are less optimistic. Ayyub said silver prices are expected to remain above $2,085 per (200,000 rupees) kg for the foreseeable future because once precious metal prices rise sharply, they rarely fall significantly enough to return to their previous levels. Historically, the same has been the case with gold. “Even if prices decline, they are unlikely to return to their earlier levels,” Ayyub said. Not far from Hussain’s workshop, 40-year-old former silver nagras maker Kuldeep Gautam now spends his days behind the counter of a jewellery shop. Known for his intricate workmanship, Gautam once earned between $415 and $518 (40,000 and 50,000 rupees) a month making the ornate footwear. But he has not received a single order since January, he says. As orders disappeared and his savings dwindled, Gautam was forced to abandon the craft and take up a job as a salesman. “I left the craft because I had no other choice,” he said. “Whenever I pass my old workshop, I don’t even look at it. It hurts too much.” Beyond the loss of income, Kuldeep says he mourns the loss of the identity his craft had given him. “People knew me for my work and appreciated my craftsmanship. It gave me dignity. Today, I earn only $155 (15,000 rupees) a month, and I struggle to pay my children’s school fees. I never imagined my life would come to this.” “I still yearn to make nagras, but there are no buyers anymore. The war has destroyed our lives.” Back in his shop, Azhar Hussain also faces the prospect of abandoning a craft that has carried his family for more than a century. His plan, he says, is to secure a bank loan to buy an electric rickshaw so he can start earning again. “At least an e-rickshaw will earn me $5 to $7 (500 to 700 rupees) a day,” he said. “I don’t want to leave this craft, but I have no choice.”

Every customer who walks away feels like another piece of our family's future disappearing.” Hussain, like others before him, now fears he will be forced to close his shop. “There were nearly 30 of us not long ago,” he said. “Most have already abandoned the profession because silver has become too expensive and orders have dried up. Those who are still here are also thinking of leaving.” He is now thinking of taking a loan to open a cafe, which he hopes will provide a steady income. “I need to find another way to earn,” he said. Hussain had hoped to teach the craft to his sons so they could carry forward the family’s legacy, but now he is advising them to pursue other professions. He no longer sees a future in the silver nagras trade and blames the war in the Middle East. “We have nothing to do with this war, yet we are paying the price,” he said, frustrated at how a conflict so far away has threatened his livelihood. “I don’t know what our future looks like anymore. Sometimes I think about what will happen to this craft and I cry. This wasn’t just our profession; it was our identity, our heritage and everything we were known for.” Still, Hussain clings to the hope that silver prices will decline and orders will return. Economists and market analysts are less optimistic. Ayyub said silver prices are expected to remain above $2,085 per (200,000 rupees) kg for the foreseeable future because once precious metal prices rise sharply, they rarely fall significantly enough to return to their previous levels. Historically, the same has been the case with gold. “Even if prices decline, they are unlikely to return to their earlier levels,” Ayyub said. Not far from Hussain’s workshop, 40-year-old former silver nagras maker Kuldeep Gautam now spends his days behind the counter of a jewellery shop. Known for his intricate workmanship, Gautam once earned between $415 and $518 (40,000 and 50,000 rupees) a month making the ornate footwear. But he has not received a single order since January, he says. As orders disappeared and his savings dwindled, Gautam was forced to abandon the craft and take up a job as a salesman. “I left the craft because I had no other choice,” he said. “Whenever I pass my old workshop, I don’t even look at it. It hurts too much.” Beyond the loss of income, Kuldeep says he mourns the loss of the identity his craft had given him. “People knew me for my work and appreciated my craftsmanship. It gave me dignity. Today, I earn only $155 (15,000 rupees) a month, and I struggle to pay my children’s school fees. I never imagined my life would come to this.” “I still yearn to make nagras, but there are no buyers anymore. The war has destroyed our lives.” Back in his shop, Azhar Hussain also faces the prospect of abandoning a craft that has carried his family for more than a century. snapshot.title: Codebreaker, 103, kept his WW2 heroics a secret for decades
snapshot.evidenceText: Fred Vanke was sworn to secrecy but his work as a codebreaker has finally been recognised "My wife died and didn't know. I never told anybody. In fact, she always complained - all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell and you never tell anything." From fleeing the Nazi invasion of his native Poland, to training as an operative to work behind enemy lines, to helping to crack the codes which turned the tide of the conflict, Fred Vanke had an eventful World War Two. Sworn to secrecy however, his family and friends almost never learned of the true role the 103-year-old played in the Allied war effort. But research into the life story of Vanke, now living in Breaston, Derbyshire, has written a new chapter on the history of Bletchley Park's famed codebreakers. About 100 Poles based in the UK carried out work on behalf of Bletchley Park between 1940 and 1945. After Fred shared his story, research has added the names of 27 Polish codebreakers and signals intelligence (sigint) to the Bletchley Park Roll of Honour, and more could follow. The additions represent one of the most significant expansions of the documented Polish contribution to Britain's wartime codebreaking effort in recent years, helping historians better understand the scale of the intelligence partnership between Britain and the Polish government-in-exile. Fred fled Poland after a happy childhood in Krakow Believed to be the last surviving member of these Polish codebreakers, Ferdynand Stanislaw Vanke grew up in Krakow, but fled at the age of 16 when war arrived on his doorstep in 1939. He said: "I did wake up in the morning hearing the planes. I ran to the window and I could see Germans coming over but I thought it was Polish Air Force training. "People were screaming and falling to the ground and we could hear machine gun fire. My father burst in and said 'in to the cellar, the Germans are coming'. That's how my war started." Fred, his sister and a friend travelled east in a Polish Army Hospital van, to his grandparents' home, avoiding Nazi gunfire on the roads. "I could see people coming from all over the place, masses of people," he said. "When Germans would come, my sister said to me 'under the van, under the van'. That's the first time I've seen people being injured to that extent." Fred and his father served together in the Middle East After his initial destination Syria was lost with the invasion of France, he instead made his way to British-controlled Palestine where he joined the newly-formed Polish brigade, the Carpathian Rifle Brigade alongside his father. "I'm going to be a soldier at last," Fred remembers thinking. He proved his worth and after officer training in Tel Aviv he was sent to Glasgow to join the Cichociemni, a Polish special forces unit trained for occupied Poland. "Cichociemni in Polish means dark and quiet," he said. "I've gone right through the courses, how to use the poison, how to kill people quietly, and all that sort of thing. "One day my commanding officer, Colonel Mayer, called me and explained 'you're young, I've got a son like you, you volunteer to be dropped in Poland you will last four or five months on average and that's the end of you. I've got something better'. Fred served in the Middle East before his service took an unexpected turn Instead, a captain visited from Bletchley Park, the then-secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School, the forerunner of GCHQ, and the base for Allied codebreaking. "He gave us all a lecture and a little puzzle," said Fred. After cracking the first, he was given a second which he also deciphered. "He said, 'you've got a gift which very few people have'," Fred recalled. So despite being in his early 20s, several years younger than anyone else on the unit, Fred was recruited to work at The Arches in Boxmoor, a Polish sigint station near Hemel Hempstead which supported Bletchley Park. The Arches was from the street a large but unassuming house but inside the building featured more than a dozen rooms turned into offices for codebreakers, and its garden was filled with huts housing radio operators. One of dozens of Polish codebreakers based there, Fred would work in a team listening to German signals and attempting to decode them. Poles like Fred worked in secret under the guidance of Bletchley Park Fred said: "You start with the simple things. You've got to learn the language, how it is built, and what is the quirk in that language, and you base your guessing on that. "When I arrived there first, I never knew anybody there, it was a little strange, but very very soon it was like a holiday." However outside of The Arches, life was tougher for Fred. He said: "The people in Hemel Hempstead, because we had uniforms with Poland, they spat on you and called 'why don't you eff off to fight Germans instead'. "You couldn't say what you're doing, so that was a little bit upsetting." But what Fred and his Polish compatriots were doing, both before the war and during it, was pivotal in the Allied war effort. Bletchley Park was the secret headquarters of the Government Code and Cypher School Among those identified during the research were Marian Rejewski and Henryk Zygalski, two of the three Polish mathematicians who alongside Jerzy Różycki first broke the German military Enigma cipher before the war, and who continued codebreaking work in Britain after escaping occupied Europe. At the Pyry Conference near Warsaw in 1939, Polish cryptologists invited French and British counterparts, including Alastair Denniston and Dilly Knox, to share their pioneering success in breaking the German Enigma machine cipher. Dr David Kenyon, the research historian at Bletchley Park Trust who investigated Fred's story, said: "This meeting was important because it laid the groundwork for partnership between the British and the Polish and significantly helped the subsequent British attack on Enigma." Fred said: "I was very pleased when I received a letter from the British government for what I've done. But I was very proud of Zygalski, Rejewski and Różycki - that's our three real codebreakers." Fred and Patricia met in Nottingham after the war After the war, Fred moved to Nottingham where he started a photography firm with a fellow Polish ex-paratrooper. "I met my wife in Jessops in one of the shops," he said. "She was a model there, once I saw her, I said 'this is my wife'." The couple raised three children, and were together until her death in 1996 - but Fred never told her about his wartime role. "My wife died and she still didn't know what I was doing. I never told anybody," he said. "In fact, she always complained - 'all your friends, when they come visit, they all have stories to tell, you never tell anything'. "You were sworn not to tell, so I kept that." Having reached the age of 103, Fred puts his long life down to luck, whiskey and stopping smoking in 1963, and believes he must now be the last surviving Polish codebreaker. "I'm bound to be, I am 103-and-a-half, and I was the youngest by two years," he said. Fred and 26 other Poles who served under Bletchley Park have been added to its Roll of Honour Kenyon said: "Due to the secrecy of the work at Bletchley Park, so much of this work remained classified for decades - the full scale of Polish involvement in Britain's WW2 codebreaking effort is still being pieced together. "Adding these Polish names to our Roll of Honour pays tribute to the contribution made by Polish citizens in the wider Allied effort in WW2, not only on the fighting fronts, but also at Bletchley Park, and in other secret intelligence work, a contribution which may have been overlooked in the past." Rafał Wiśniewski, Chargé d'Affaires a.i. at the Embassy of the Republic of Poland in London, said: "The work of Polish cryptologists, well before and during WW2, was instrumental in cracking the Enigma cypher and, ultimately, in the Allied victory, which helped save countless lives. "The evidence proving direct links to Bletchley Park and other secret intelligence work is truly important and shows the depth of our co-operation, which needs to be recognised." Caroline Whelan said her father's story showed the importance of intelligence and the role it can play in bringing about peace Fred's daughter Caroline Whelan, 60, said: "We've had a very happy, normal life, considering dad had a really traumatic start to his. "It is unbelievably fantastic that he is able to witness the acknowledgement that so many people haven't been able to," she said. "He's one of the people that you never get bored of talking to, and he's always got a story to tell now." representative.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
representative.author: Sarah Rainsford

snapshot.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
snapshot.evidenceText: Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children. Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks. But German police were already closing in on him. After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany. Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine". Both he and his country have denied any involvement. Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov. It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea. There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas. Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers. They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda. Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat. As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow. Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure. But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise. The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services. In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich. That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy. He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks. But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected. Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him. By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert. Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs. None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions. But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them. "Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that." Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe. That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it. Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution. "Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out. The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution. Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence. "At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained. Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned". Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far. Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August. He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation. Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him. Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning. He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver. Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him. In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war". As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more." The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg. After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop. It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv. It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone. When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that". This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further. "I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully. He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did." Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial. Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated. He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023. His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing. And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either. His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up. I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot. Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the tech firm admits customers may experience disruption to digital services due to the attacks. A Kyiv resident told the BBC she has moved away from "everything that can be a Russian target" as Ukraine braces for another cold winter under intense attacks. representative.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
representative.author: Sarah Rainsford

snapshot.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
snapshot.evidenceText: Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children. Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks. But German police were already closing in on him. After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany. Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine". Both he and his country have denied any involvement. Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov. It was 02:03 on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea. There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas. Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers. They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda. Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat. As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow. Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure. But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise. The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services. In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich. That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy. He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks. But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected. Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him. By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert. Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs. None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions. But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them. "Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that." Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe. That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it. Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution. "Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out. The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution. Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence. "At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained. Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned". Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far. Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August. He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation. Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him. Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning. He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver. Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him. In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war". As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more." The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg. After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop. It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv. It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone. When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that". This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further. "I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully. He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did." Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial. Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated. He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023. His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing. And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either. His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up. I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot. representative.title: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students - BBC News
representative.author: Endang Nurdin, Rebecca Henschke, BBC Indonesia

snapshot.title: Headmaster detained after BBC investigation into alleged sexual abuse of students
snapshot.evidenceText: Ex-headmaster Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, has been accused of sexual abuse A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report. Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok. Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him , and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities. The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police. Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault Two ex-students expose sexual abuse by teachers at Islamic boarding schools in Indonesia Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube , external . Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar. They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school. By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta. Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school. Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school. Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations. In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation. "Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said. Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC. In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent. Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions. Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name". The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases. Watch: BBC tracks down abusive teacher secretly released early The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands. One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter. "I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school." Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married , were overwhelmed by the response from former students. "It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'." Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse. "They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said. Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously. "It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC. Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process. The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time. NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals. In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward. representative.title: This 345-Million-Year-Old Fossil Fooled Scientists for Decades
representative.author: American Museum of Natural History

snapshot.title: This 345-Million-Year-Old Fossil Fooled Scientists for Decades
snapshot.evidenceText: A famous Scottish fossil is forcing scientists to rethink what claw-like feet really reveal about the move onto land. Pressed flat inside two slabs of Scottish rock, a 345-million-year-old skeleton seemed to carry some unmistakable signs of life on land. Its four limbs ended in five-digit feet, and the tips of its fingers and toes looked strikingly like claws. For decades, those features helped make Westlothiana lizziae , better known as “Lizzie,” a landmark in the story of how vertebrates moved away from water and gave rise to reptiles, birds, and mammals. Yet the fossil had been crushed so badly that much of its anatomy remained hidden inside the stone. Peering through that rock with X-rays has now exposed a very different animal. Researchers from the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, reconstructed structures that could not be seen from the fossil’s surface. Their results, published in Nature , revealed a primitive skull, ossified internal gills, and a fish-like mouth packed with thousands of tiny teeth. “Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades,” said Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum’s Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. “But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected.” Discovered in Scotland in 1984 and formally described in 1990, Westlothiana had initially been interpreted largely from the anatomy exposed on the surfaces of its two slabs. Its nearly complete skeleton stood apart from many animals living around the same time because its limbs looked more suited to supporting a body than the more fin-like appendages seen in some early tetrapod relatives. Those visible feet helped secure Lizzie’s reputation as an early amniote, the branch of vertebrates that eventually produced reptiles, birds, and mammals. Researchers repeatedly used the fossil as an important reference point when estimating when animals with fully land-adapted lifestyles began appearing. Inside Lizzie’s skull, however, the synchrotron scans uncovered features that do not fit that interpretation. The internal gills and tooth-filled, fish-like mouth instead place the animal on a much older branch of the tetrapod family tree and indicate that it was aquatic or amphibious rather than a fully terrestrial reptile ancestor. “The surprisingly primitive features of the skull show us that Lizzie was not only not a reptile but belonged to a much more ancient lineage. It turns out looks can be deceiving, and Lizzie lived a completely different lifestyle than we previously thought,” said Ben Igielman, co-lead author of the study, who started this research during his graduate work at the University of Oxford. Keeping those reptile-like feet creates another surprise. Five toes, claw-like tips, and limb structures once treated as hallmarks of land-adapted amniotes were apparently already present in more ancient members of the stem lineage leading toward tetrapods. In other words, some pieces of the body plan associated with later land animals evolved before the animals carrying them had fully left the water behind. “This is a big surprise,” said study co-author Roger Benson, the Museum’s Macaulay Curator of Paleontology. “It shows that, although we think of amphibians as being more ‘primitive’ than reptiles today, some of the traits of reptiles were already there in the ancestor of both amphibians and reptiles.” Claw-shaped impressions preserved in still older fossil trackways may now need the same kind of caution. Some tracks dating to the Devonian Period, more than 359 million years ago, have been interpreted as evidence that amniotes had already evolved because they record four-limbed animals walking on claw-like digits. If creatures as primitive as Westlothiana could also possess claw-like structures, those tracks no longer provide a simple fingerprint of an amniote. Some may instead have been left by amphibious tetrapod relatives that carried land-like anatomical features while still dividing their lives between water and shore. “The broader lesson is that terrestrial-looking traits, such as a reptile-like foot, a weight-bearing forelimb, and claw-like phalanges were not unique features of tetrapods, but rather accumulated piecemeal in their close relatives, in animals that were still living in and out of the water,” Jenkins said. Reference: “Evolution of terrestrial anatomy revealed by a derived stem tetrapod” by Ben Igielman, Xavier Jenkins, Jason Head, Vincent Fernandez, Lucy Roberts, Timothy Smithson and Roger Benson, 30 September 2026, Nature . representative.title: A Flat-Tailed, Platypus-Like Mammal Relative Hunted Salamanders in China's Jurassic Lakes About 168 Million Years Ago
representative.author: Avery Porter

snapshot.title: A Flat-Tailed, Platypus-Like Mammal Relative Hunted Salamanders in China's Jurassic Lakes About 168 Million Years Ago
snapshot.evidenceText: About 168 million years ago, while dinosaurs roamed the land, a Chihuahua-sized swimmer with a broad, flattened tail and powerful canine teeth hunted salamanders in the lakes and rivers of what is now Inner Mongolia, China. Scientists described the animal, named Megacauda sungei, a name meaning big tail, in a study published Oct. 7 in Nature.The creature was not a true mammal — it was a close relative from an extinct group called docodonts. It weighed about 1 to 2 kilograms (2.2 to 4.4 pounds), making it the largest known mammal relative from the Jurassic, and it may be the earliest known semiaquatic member of the broader mammal family tree.Its body mixed features seen today in very different animals. "It's like a chimera," senior author Zhe-Xi Luo, a paleontologist at the University of Chicago, told Live Science.A Swimmer Built for HuntingThe rear half of Megacauda resembled a platypus, with short hind legs, relatively long feet and a broad, flat tail suited to powerful swimming. Its feet may also have helped it dig burrows in riverbanks, according to the researchers.The front end told a different story — one of a predator. Unlike the toothless bill of a modern platypus, Megacauda had robust, highly specialized canines and shearing cheek teeth suited to cutting meat, features Luo compared to an otter's.The fossil came from the Haifanggou Formation, a Middle Jurassic deposit that Luo described to ABC News as teeming with salamanders. Tiny vertebrate bone fragments in the animal's stomach region and in surrounding rock suggest it ate salamanders and likely small fish and invertebrates as well.Throat Bones That Point to NursingThe most significant finding for evolutionary biologists lies in the throat. The exceptionally preserved fossil retains hyoid bones, the small bones that support the tongue and throat, arranged in a U-shaped saddle like those in modern mammals.That arrangement suggests Megacauda had the anatomy needed to swallow food in a mammal-like way and to suckle milk as an infant. If so, the soft-tissue machinery for nursing evolved before the split between the docodont line and true mammals, pushing that history back into the Middle Jurassic.Luo called the throat structure "an incredibly important evolutionary innovation" in comments to Live Science, a step that set mammals apart from other animals. Nursing allowed mammal mothers to feed their young directly, a key part of the group's later success.An Evidence Check on the FossilThe study describes a single, nearly complete fossil analyzed with CT scanning. Its diet is inferred from tooth shape and small bone fragments rather than an intact meal, and the ability to suckle is inferred from throat anatomy rather than direct evidence of nursing. Burrowing remains a possibility, not a demonstrated behavior.Sources differ slightly on when the fossil was found, with Live Science reporting 2016 and ABC Australia reporting 2015. The age of the rock, about 168 to 163 million years old, is consistent across the study coverage.Independent scientists praised the find. Suzanne Hand, an emeritus professor and vertebrate paleontologist at the University of New South Wales who was not involved in the work, told ABC Australia that "semiaquatic animals have also been shown to survive catastrophic events," a reason the lifestyle may have helped early mammal relatives endure.The research team spanned Shenyang Normal University and the Shandong University of Science and Technology in China, the University of Chicago and Ohio University in the U.S., and the University of Bonn in Germany. The detailed preservation, including soft tissue in the throat, is what allowed the team to examine anatomy that rarely survives in fossils this old. Funding came from the National Natural Science Foundation of China, the German Research Foundation and the U.S. National Science Foundation, among others.An Ancient Lifestyle That Still Shapes Rivers TodayMegacauda joins a growing list of docodonts that adapted to water long before modern mammals did. The earliest known semiaquatic true mammal, Dongoconodon platycauda, comes from a Chinese deposit about 120 million years old, while Kryoryctes cadburyi, an Australian semiaquatic monotreme, lived about 100 million years ago, according to ABC Australia. By contrast, platypuses split from echidnas only about 55 million years ago, and the oldest platypus fossil is about 3.8 million years old, which makes Megacauda's resemblance a case of similar lifestyles producing similar bodies rather than a family link. It is related to Castorocauda, a beaver-like animal from the same region about 164 million years ago that previously held the title of earliest known semiaquatic mammal relative and that Luo also helped describe.The authors say docodonts repeatedly evolved specialized lifestyles, from swimming to digging, during the age of dinosaurs. That challenges an older view of early mammal relatives as small, generalized insect-eaters living in the dinosaurs' shadow.The lifestyle Megacauda pioneered remains important. Luo told ABC that about 140 living mammal species depend on riverside habitats. In North America, beavers, river otters and muskrats fill similar roles, shaping wetlands, controlling prey populations and influencing water flow.That modern connection gives the fossil a conservation angle. Semiaquatic mammals depend on healthy streams, wetlands and riverbanks, habitats that are often the first to be altered by dams, development and drought.Further study of the fossil, and comparisons with other docodonts, may clarify how many times mammal relatives took to the water and how early nursing evolved. The bottom line is that a single, unusually complete fossil has added an aquatic predator to the Jurassic mammal story and moved key features of mammal biology millions of years earlier.What Readers Want to KnowWhat is Megacauda sungei?It is an extinct mammal relative from the docodont group that lived about 168 to 163 million years ago in what is now Inner Mongolia, China.Was it a platypus ancestor?No. It resembled a platypus in body shape but belonged to a separate extinct lineage. Platypuses split from other mammals much later.What did it eat?Its teeth and nearby bone fragments suggest it hunted salamanders and likely small fish and invertebrates in lakes and rivers.How big was it?It weighed about 1 to 2 kilograms (2.2 to 4.4 pounds), roughly the size of a Chihuahua, making it the largest known Jurassic mammal relative.Why do its throat bones matter?The U-shaped arrangement of its hyoid bones suggests it could swallow like a mammal and suckle as an infant, pushing that ability back into the Middle Jurassic.Where was the study published?The study was published on Oct. 7, 2026, in the journal Nature.

snapshot.title: This 345-Million-Year-Old Fossil Fooled Scientists for Decades
snapshot.evidenceText: A famous Scottish fossil is forcing scientists to rethink what claw-like feet really reveal about the move onto land. Pressed flat inside two slabs of Scottish rock, a 345-million-year-old skeleton seemed to carry some unmistakable signs of life on land. Its four limbs ended in five-digit feet, and the tips of its fingers and toes looked strikingly like claws. For decades, those features helped make Westlothiana lizziae , better known as “Lizzie,” a landmark in the story of how vertebrates moved away from water and gave rise to reptiles, birds, and mammals. Yet the fossil had been crushed so badly that much of its anatomy remained hidden inside the stone. Peering through that rock with X-rays has now exposed a very different animal. Researchers from the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, working with the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility in Grenoble, France, reconstructed structures that could not be seen from the fossil’s surface. Their results, published in Nature , revealed a primitive skull, ossified internal gills, and a fish-like mouth packed with thousands of tiny teeth. “Lizzie has been an icon for the early evolution of amniotes for decades,” said Xavier Jenkins, a postdoctoral fellow in the Museum’s Division of Paleontology and co-lead author of the study. “But when we were finally able to see inside the fossil, we found an animal that looked very different from what we expected.” Discovered in Scotland in 1984 and formally described in 1990, Westlothiana had initially been interpreted largely from the anatomy exposed on the surfaces of its two slabs. Its nearly complete skeleton stood apart from many animals living around the same time because its limbs looked more suited to supporting a body than the more fin-like appendages seen in some early tetrapod relatives. Those visible feet helped secure Lizzie’s reputation as an early amniote, the branch of vertebrates that eventually produced reptiles, birds, and mammals. Researchers repeatedly used the fossil as an important reference point when estimating when animals with fully land-adapted lifestyles began appearing. Inside Lizzie’s skull, however, the synchrotron scans uncovered features that do not fit that interpretation. The internal gills and tooth-filled, fish-like mouth instead place the animal on a much older branch of the tetrapod family tree and indicate that it was aquatic or amphibious rather than a fully terrestrial reptile ancestor. “The surprisingly primitive features of the skull show us that Lizzie was not only not a reptile but belonged to a much more ancient lineage. It turns out looks can be deceiving, and Lizzie lived a completely different lifestyle than we previously thought,” said Ben Igielman, co-lead author of the study, who started this research during his graduate work at the University of Oxford. Keeping those reptile-like feet creates another surprise. Five toes, claw-like tips, and limb structures once treated as hallmarks of land-adapted amniotes were apparently already present in more ancient members of the stem lineage leading toward tetrapods. In other words, some pieces of the body plan associated with later land animals evolved before the animals carrying them had fully left the water behind. “This is a big surprise,” said study co-author Roger Benson, the Museum’s Macaulay Curator of Paleontology. “It shows that, although we think of amphibians as being more ‘primitive’ than reptiles today, some of the traits of reptiles were already there in the ancestor of both amphibians and reptiles.” Claw-shaped impressions preserved in still older fossil trackways may now need the same kind of caution. Some tracks dating to the Devonian Period, more than 359 million years ago, have been interpreted as evidence that amniotes had already evolved because they record four-limbed animals walking on claw-like digits. If creatures as primitive as Westlothiana could also possess claw-like structures, those tracks no longer provide a simple fingerprint of an amniote. Some may instead have been left by amphibious tetrapod relatives that carried land-like anatomical features while still dividing their lives between water and shore. “The broader lesson is that terrestrial-looking traits, such as a reptile-like foot, a weight-bearing forelimb, and claw-like phalanges were not unique features of tetrapods, but rather accumulated piecemeal in their close relatives, in animals that were still living in and out of the water,” Jenkins said. Reference: “Evolution of terrestrial anatomy revealed by a derived stem tetrapod” by Ben Igielman, Xavier Jenkins, Jason Head, Vincent Fernandez, Lucy Roberts, Timothy Smithson and Roger Benson, 30 September 2026, Nature . representative.title: Bangladesh flood death toll rises to 44 as more than one million people affected - [İLKHA] Ilke News Agency
representative.author: WORLD

snapshot.title: Bangladesh flood death toll rises to 44 as more than one million people affected
snapshot.evidenceText: Relentless monsoon rains, flash floods and landslides have left at least 44 people dead and affected more than one million people across seven districts in Bangladesh, authorities said on Sunday, as emergency responders continued relief operations amid warnings of further flooding. According to the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, more than 1.022 million people have been affected by the flooding, with 267,918 families remaining stranded by rising waters. At least 39 people have been injured since the severe weather began. The worst-hit districts include Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, Chattogram, Moulvibazar and Habiganj, where floodwaters have inundated 58 sub-districts (upazilas), damaging homes, roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure. Although rainfall eased over the past 24 hours in several parts of the country, flood risks remain elevated. The Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) warned that fresh short-term flooding could occur in Feni, Sylhet and northern districts, particularly along the Teesta River basin, due to continued upstream inflows and additional rainfall. The agency said water levels at seven monitoring stations on the Sangu, Matamuhuri, Kushiyara, Manu and Someswari rivers remained above danger levels, keeping low-lying communities at risk. Authorities have opened 1,131 emergency shelters, where 44,457 displaced people are currently staying after being evacuated from flood-affected areas. The Disaster Management Ministry said it had allocated 145 million taka ($1.2 million) and 2,650 metric tonnes of rice to the seven worst-hit districts to support relief efforts. Since July 7, district administrations across the country have also received 345 million taka and 6,900 metric tonnes of rice for emergency response operations. However, aid workers and local officials said many flood-affected families have yet to receive sufficient assistance as access to some remote communities remains difficult. Shortages of food, clean drinking water and essential medicines have been reported in several inundated areas, raising concerns over the risk of waterborne diseases. Health officials said pregnant women, young children and elderly residents remain among the most vulnerable groups as floodwaters continue to submerge homes and farmland. Bangladesh, one of the world's most climate-vulnerable countries, experiences severe monsoon flooding almost every year. Scientists say climate change is increasing the intensity of extreme rainfall events, contributing to more frequent floods and landslides across South Asia. Authorities said relief operations were continuing while closely monitoring river levels and weather forecasts, warning that additional rainfall could worsen conditions in low-lying areas over the coming days. Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Iran’s vision for a possible resolution to the war to US President Donald Trump during a telephone conversation on Friday, coordinating the message with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, the Kremlin said Saturday. Eight people, including two children, were killed in a mass shooting at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday, while the suspected gunman also died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, bringing the total death toll to nine, authorities said. A Russian strike on the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia killed at least 11 people, including three children, and wounded at least 16 others on Saturday, Oct. 10, local authorities said, as Russia launched a large-scale overnight drone attack across Ukraine. Heavy rains have triggered flash floods and mudslides in Chile's capital, Santiago, and surrounding areas, injuring at least six people, forcing the evacuation of hundreds of households and damaging thousands of homes, according to authorities. representative.title: BRICS: Cabinet’s decision is that we should begin as a partner country - Ablakwa | 3News
representative.author: Laud Nartey

snapshot.title: BRICS: Cabinet’s decision is that we should begin as a partner country - Ablakwa
snapshot.evidenceText: We want to start as a partner country, and then we will gradually progress into full membership as the situation evolves The Minister of Foreign Affairs Samuel Okudzeto Abklakwa has explained that Ghana will join BRICS as a partner country. According to him, Cabinet's decision forms part of the government’s efforts to expand Ghana’s economic options and diversify its international partnerships. He said the move would also strengthen Ghana’s engagement with countries in the Global South and create opportunities for deeper South-South cooperation. "We want to start as a partner country, and then we will gradually progress into full membership as the situation evolves," he said on the Key Points on TV3 Saturday October 10. “The major highlight, which I am disclosing to the Ghanaian people for the first time, is that the Cabinet of President John Dramani Mahama has decided that Ghana will be joining BRICS,” he said. Ablakwa explained that Ghana believes membership of the bloc, which brings together major emerging economies, could provide the country with alternative economic and diplomatic partnerships. “We believe that joining India in BRICS will give us economic options, will diversify our base and our partnerships, and will also allow us to have more cooperation within the Global South framework, as far as South-South engagements are concerned,” he added. The Foreign Affairs Minister’s disclosure signals Ghana’s intention to deepen its engagement with emerging economies as the government seeks to broaden the country’s international economic partnerships. He also announced plans for Ghana and India to deepen cooperation in railway development, pharmaceuticals, ICT, defence, agriculture, science and technology. He said the two countries had signed two Memoranda of Understanding covering agriculture and science and technology as part of efforts to strengthen their comprehensive partnership. BRICS is an intergovernmental organization and geopolitical coalition comprising 11 core member nations—Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, and the United Arab Emirates—alongside 10 partner countries, representing roughly 49.5% of the global population and 40% of world GDP. The group operates as an informal economic powerhouse designed to amplify the voice of the Global South and counterbalance Western-dominated institutions. representative.title: Kauai’s Hawaiian salt makers seek help restoring harvest area | Hawaii News Now
representative.author: Dillon Ancheta

snapshot.title: Kauai’s Hawaiian salt makers seek help restoring harvest area
snapshot.evidenceText: HANAPEPE (HawaiiNewsNow) - The 22 Kauai families keeping traditional Hawaiian salt making alive in Hanapepe are seeking the community’s help to restore their harvest site. Storm surge from Hurricane Lowell drastically changed the area. “The sand dunes were depleted. It was gone. It was a new landscape. I didn’t recognize it,” said Malia Nobrega-Olivera. Nobrega-Olivera and her ‘ohana have been Hawaiian salt makers for decades. She said the storm damage was the worst she’s seen. “It is different from all of my 55 years growing up in Hanapepe. It was a new space,” she said. Lowell pushed incredible amounts of sand into the beach park and salt beds, changing the composition of the land, making the clay more porous. “We are using this clay to seal the aina so that it can evaporate over time. But with the mixture of the sand, the practice doesn’t exist,” she said. Nobrega-Olivera is also the president of Hui Hana Pa’akai O Hanapepe, the group established for the salt makers. Together, they’re hosting a community work day on Saturday to restore the area. “Bring your tools. If you don’t have, just show up and your hands will be a good enough tools to be with us,” she said. They’ve also been getting assistance from the county and other partners to move sand as they prepare for the work day. There have been floods in recent years, and the group was already working on a dune restoration project. “Our practice is dictated by the weather, so you know, we wait until everything dries up and then we’re ready to go back in,” Nobrega-Olivera said. “And once the place is flooded, our salt-making time gets shorter and shorter.” She added the best harvest she’s had yielded 55 large buckets worth of salt. But if conditions aren’t right, that number is drastically less. Steeped in tradition, Hawaiian Salt is crucial to the culture. “Salt is not only used for our food, salt is used for medicinal purposes, for healing in all different ways,” she said. The workday runs from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., and more will be scheduled in the future. To stay connected with the group, contact them online at ProtectPaakai.org .

representative.title: Syria Begins Destroying Chemical Weapons Remnants

snapshot.title: Syria Begins Destroying Chemical Weapons Remnants
snapshot.evidenceText: Syria's Permanent Representative to the OPCW, Mohammad Katoub, announced that operations to destroy remnants of the Assad-era chemical program have begun, while warning that Israeli attacks hinder the process and that a timeframe for completion has not yet been set. Syria's Permanent Representative to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), Mohammad Katoub, stated that his country continues full cooperation with the organisation's Technical Secretariat to completely eliminate remnants of the chemical weapons program from the Assad era. He confirmed that destruction operations have already begun, describing this as tangible progress in the capabilities of Syria's national teams working on this sensitive file. The announcement falls within an internationally monitored process overseen by the OPCW, the body responsible for verifying the elimination of banned weapons programs. Ongoing work includes verification, inspection, and destruction of remaining materials and facilities linked to the former program. Katoub pointed out that Israeli attacks constitute a real obstacle to the removal of the chemical program's remnants, imposing security challenges and operational complications on field teams. In practical terms, these obstacles tie the pace of work to security conditions at the affected sites, making movement, equipment handling, and field coordination more difficult. He explained that Syria is working with OPCW teams to develop a realistic timeframe for completing verification, inspection, and destruction operations, but this framework has not yet been announced, as work continues on shaping it in light of field and security conditions. The Syrian envoy stressed that pursuing and holding accountable those involved in developing and using chemical weapons is among Syria's top priorities at this stage. This judicial track runs parallel to the technical work of destroying the remnants, as part of an effort to close the file of the former chemical program from both ends: materially through destruction, and legally through accountability. The step marks a shift of the chemical file from declarations to actual destruction on the ground — a significant development for Syria's international standing and its relations with international organisations, which could gradually reflect in reduced pressures and isolation on the country. However, the absence of an announced timeframe means Syrians will not see a defined end to this file any time soon. The continued Israeli attacks as a disrupting factor also serve as a reminder that security conditions remain the key variable determining the pace of sensitive files like this one, directly affecting civilians in the affected areas.
