representative.title: Nearly 600 Floyd County, Ind. voters receive incorrect ballots
representative.author: Aprile Rickert

snapshot.title: Nearly 600 Floyd County, Ind. voters receive incorrect ballots
snapshot.evidenceText: Floyd County election officials say nearly 600 voters received incomplete ballots, and they’re reaching out to people affected to help them cast their full vote. The Floyd County Election Board met for an emergency meeting Friday afternoon to address a programming error that omitted the Floyd County Commissioners District 1 race from four precincts: Franklin, Greenville, Georgetown and Lafayette. The race is between Republican incumbent Al Knable and Democratic challenger Ellen Morrison Kelley. The board said Friday afternoon they had identified 572 impacted voters. They include people who voted early in-person between Tuesday, Oct. 6 through Thursday, Oct. 8. Absentee ballots were also impacted. “The Election Board’s immediate priority is to provide each identified voter a lawful opportunity to vote in the omitted race,” according to a news release provided by the board. “The Election Board recognizes the importance of providing every voter a complete and accurate ballot and apologizes to the affected voters for this error.” The board, which includes Floyd County Clerk Danita Burks, did not speak to news media following the meeting. Officials say they have corrected the error and that early voting resumed Friday with the corrected ballot styles on voting machines. Voters who got the incomplete ballots will receive a written explanation and ABS-5 form, officials said. That is a “statement concerning defective, lost, destroyed, or spoiled absentee ballot.” After that is processed, they'll receive instructions and a chance to vote a corrected ballot. Susan Lockhart and her husband Jerry voted Tuesday, the first day of early voting, at the Floyd County 4-H Fairgrounds. She told LPM News this week they started questioning their ballots after they left. “It wasn't until we left that I said, ‘Hey, did you vote for Ellen?’ And he said, ‘There was no place to vote for Ellen,’” Lockhart said Thursday. She questioned how the faulty ballots were issued in the first place, and said it shouldn't be up to the voters to catch it. “There's no reason for the ballot to go out incomplete if that many people have their eyes on it,” she said. “And the Floyd County clerk, the buck stops with her.” Kelley, the Democratic candidate, said after the meeting she learned about the error when she started getting text messages from people saying her name hadn’t been on their ballots. And she’s not confident the process to address the problem will work. “I know that for the average person, getting out to vote once is can be a big deal when you're trying to get to work and go to soccer practice and make sure the laundry's done,” she said. ‘“And to receive a letter in the mail that says something very weird like this, I don't think people are gonna have the time, maybe.” Knable, the Republican incumbent, said after the meeting he had concerns about people who might be out of town or have trouble getting around. “That's a great concern because I want to make sure that those people do have a chance to be heard,” he said. He also said he was concerned about the whole situation. He said he doesn’t think this incident will affect the outcome of the race. “But even if it does, that's a meager consideration when you consider the fact that we might potentially disenfranchise some of these 572 folks,” he said. Election officials did not provide a reason for the error. They said that ballot information and styles are usually reviewed and proofed before going out to voters, and they’re reviewing the process to see what happened. Voters with questions or concerns can contact the Floyd County Election Division at (812) 948-5419. Coverage of Southern Indiana is funded, in part, by Samtec Inc., the Hazel & Walter T. representative.title: Athens-Clarke County Duplicate Absentee Ballot Error Explained
representative.author: Rohit Mehta

snapshot.title: Athens-Clarke County Duplicate Absentee Ballot Error Explained
snapshot.evidenceText: More than 1,100 registered voters in Athens-Clarke County opened their mailboxes this week to find something they weren't expecting: a second absentee ballot for the November 3 midterm election. County elections officials say the mix-up affected 1,154 voters and stemmed from a data error sent to the printer responsible for producing the ballots. According to CBS News , the Athens-Clarke County Unified Government Elections Department confirmed the duplicate mailing after voters began reporting the problem. Athens-Clarke County Elections Director Pam Long said the mailing error traced back to an address file sent to a state-authorized printer that included entries duplicated from an earlier mailing list. The first batch of absentee ballots went out October 5, as required under Georgia law, and the county learned of the duplicate mailing just two days later, on October 7, when voters alerted the department. The county sent a voter address list to a state-authorized printer, and in this case, officials say an older list got mixed in with the current one, resulting in duplicate entries for 1,154 voters. The county has not detailed how many of the roughly 1,100-plus affected voters have already received their notices or returned extra ballots, and whether the supplemental manual review will slow down processing remains an open question. Long said her department identified the issue and is now tracking every affected ballot individually. The Elections Department says it is issuing expedited notices to all 1,154 impacted voters and has put supplemental manual reviews in place for returned absentee ballots, so that only one ballot per voter gets accepted, per WXIA 11Alive . County authorities have specific instructions for anyone holding a duplicate ballot: shred the extra copy, or bring it in person to the elections office at 155 E. Washington Street. Voters are explicitly warned against mailing the extra ballot back separately, tossing it intact in the trash or recycling, handing it off to someone else, or stuffing both ballots into a single envelope — any of those moves could create confusion during processing, CBS News reports. Officials stress that Georgia's statewide system is designed to prevent anyone from actually casting two ballots, regardless of how many copies land in a mailbox. GARViS, the Georgia Registered Voters Information System, replaced the state's legacy ElectioNet database when it launched in March 2023 across all 159 counties, according to Grady Newsource . The system manages more than 12 million voter records statewide and provides voter and election information. While the database is designed to catch any attempt at casting more than one ballot, state law treats the act of trying as a serious crime. Fraudulent double voting is a felony, carrying a prison sentence of one to 10 years and fines of up to $100,000. Georgia lawmakers classify repeat voting as a felony offense rather than a minor administrative slip-up, underscoring why officials are urging affected voters to dispose of or return extras rather than hang onto them. The timing adds another wrinkle for Athens-Clarke County voters navigating the mix-up. Under Senate Bill 202, absentee ballot applications for the November 3 election can only be submitted between 78 and 11 days before Election Day, which puts the final application deadline at Friday, October 23, per the same CBS News report. That narrowed window, a significant tightening from pre-2021 rules, leaves less room for voters to sort out paperwork problems before the deadline closes. For now, county officials maintain that the duplicate mailing is a printing and address-list error rather than a security breach, and that the safeguards built into the state's voter database will keep the midterm election count accurate. representative.title: Nearly 600 Floyd County, Ind. voters receive incorrect ballots
representative.author: Aprile Rickert

snapshot.title: Nearly 600 Floyd County, Ind. voters receive incorrect ballots
snapshot.evidenceText: Floyd County election officials say nearly 600 voters received incomplete ballots, and they’re reaching out to people affected to help them cast their full vote. The Floyd County Election Board met for an emergency meeting Friday afternoon to address a programming error that omitted the Floyd County Commissioners District 1 race from four precincts: Franklin, Greenville, Georgetown and Lafayette. The race is between Republican incumbent Al Knable and Democratic challenger Ellen Morrison Kelley. The board said Friday afternoon they had identified 572 impacted voters. They include people who voted early in-person between Tuesday, Oct. 6 through Thursday, Oct. 8. Absentee ballots were also impacted. “The Election Board’s immediate priority is to provide each identified voter a lawful opportunity to vote in the omitted race,” according to a news release provided by the board. “The Election Board recognizes the importance of providing every voter a complete and accurate ballot and apologizes to the affected voters for this error.” The board, which includes Floyd County Clerk Danita Burks, did not speak to news media following the meeting. Officials say they have corrected the error and that early voting resumed Friday with the corrected ballot styles on voting machines. Voters who got the incomplete ballots will receive a written explanation and ABS-5 form, officials said. That is a “statement concerning defective, lost, destroyed, or spoiled absentee ballot.” After that is processed, they'll receive instructions and a chance to vote a corrected ballot. Susan Lockhart and her husband Jerry voted Tuesday, the first day of early voting, at the Floyd County 4-H Fairgrounds. She told LPM News this week they started questioning their ballots after they left. “It wasn't until we left that I said, ‘Hey, did you vote for Ellen?’ And he said, ‘There was no place to vote for Ellen,’” Lockhart said Thursday. She questioned how the faulty ballots were issued in the first place, and said it shouldn't be up to the voters to catch it. “There's no reason for the ballot to go out incomplete if that many people have their eyes on it,” she said. “And the Floyd County clerk, the buck stops with her.” Kelley, the Democratic candidate, said after the meeting she learned about the error when she started getting text messages from people saying her name hadn’t been on their ballots. And she’s not confident the process to address the problem will work. “I know that for the average person, getting out to vote once is can be a big deal when you're trying to get to work and go to soccer practice and make sure the laundry's done,” she said. ‘“And to receive a letter in the mail that says something very weird like this, I don't think people are gonna have the time, maybe.” Knable, the Republican incumbent, said after the meeting he had concerns about people who might be out of town or have trouble getting around. “That's a great concern because I want to make sure that those people do have a chance to be heard,” he said. He also said he was concerned about the whole situation. He said he doesn’t think this incident will affect the outcome of the race. “But even if it does, that's a meager consideration when you consider the fact that we might potentially disenfranchise some of these 572 folks,” he said. Election officials did not provide a reason for the error. They said that ballot information and styles are usually reviewed and proofed before going out to voters, and they’re reviewing the process to see what happened. Voters with questions or concerns can contact the Floyd County Election Division at (812) 948-5419. Coverage of Southern Indiana is funded, in part, by Samtec Inc., the Hazel & Walter T. Bales Foundation, and the Caesars Foundation of Floyd County.

representative.author: Charlotte Grieve, Kyle Taylor, Daryna Zadvirna

snapshot.title: Retracing the steps of Mark Dennis, 'brilliant' barrister with a dark side
snapshot.evidenceText: Mark Dennis built a reputation defending accused criminals before he himself became the accused. ( ABC News: Sharon Gordon ) Warning: This article contains references to child sexual abuse and suicide. There is a small terrace house in Sydney's inner west that always gave builder Chad Loxsom an uneasy feeling. "I've been in thousands and thousands of people's houses," he said, but this one "was a little bit strange". The Leichhardt property belonged to Mark Dennis SC, a criminal defence barrister, who Loxsom said had a "weird demeanour" and was "just odd". But what he saw inside is what gnawed at him for years. "All over the walls of his house, he had dozens upon dozens upon dozens of pictures of him with little kids," he said. In some photos, Loxsom said Dennis was hugging shirtless children. Loxsom shared his suspicions with an electrician. "His gut was this guy was doing something bad with kids as well," he said. The electrician first noticed the "come back with a warrant" doormat, and then the large mirror fixed to the ceiling above Dennis's bed. But, like Loxsom, what really alarmed him was the sheer volume of photographs in almost every room, even the kitchen. "It was just disturbing. Like, these kids weren't happy," he said. Dennis was found dead in his home in Sydney's inner west in February. ( ABC News: Sissy Reyes ) Eventually, Loxsom decided to make a report with the child protection hotline. "I didn't do it straight away, which now I regret," he said. In January, Dennis came onto the police's radar again when he was searched at Sydney Airport as he returned from a trip to Cambodia. What was found on his devices led to his arrest, a raid of his house, and child abuse material charges from evidence prosecutors described as "disturbing". Dennis was released on bail, and soon after, was found dead in his home . Last week, Background Briefing and ABC Investigations revealed his death did not bring the police investigation to an end . Codenamed Operation Queenstown, Cambodian and Australian national police have been quietly probing Dennis's network and links to famous children's charity Sunrise Cambodia all year. The ABC travelled to Cambodia in June to retrace Dennis's steps to reveal the inside story of how an accused predator accumulated power within a high-profile charity and gained access to vulnerable children. In an investigation that combines a tranche of internal documents with dozens of interviews, the ABC can reveal allegations that Dennis sexually harassed a former Sunrise staff member and made teenage girls feel uncomfortable by excessive touching. Listen to Dark Menace , a new three-part investigative podcast from Background Briefing and ABC Investigations, via the ABC Listen app or wherever you get your podcasts. The claims raise important questions for all children's charities that must balance the need to fundraise with child safety, as multiple former Sunrise staff say they saw Dennis's bad behaviour but felt they could not report it. "They saw this," one former staff member told the ABC through a translator. "But they could not do anything because he's a big sponsor." A spokesperson for Sunrise said they were never aware of any complaints about Dennis and police had told them no current or former Sunrise child had been identified as one of his victims. The charity defended its child protection policies, saying the children always came first. Dennis grew up in a large family on Sydney's northern beaches, and by 2001, was a criminal defence barrister with a room at the prestigious Forbes Chambers. "You don't get to go to Forbes unless you are absolutely brilliant," says one solicitor who briefed Dennis. "He was one of those people who was married to the profession." His nickname was "Dark Menace" — a play on words that several acquaintances said reflected his personality and black sense of humour, exemplified by his "WASNTME" personalised number plate. Across his career, Dennis was known to have mentored junior lawyers and published papers under provocative titles and on topics like defending accused paedophiles and cross-examining child witnesses. Some of the legal papers authored by Dennis. ( ABC News / supplied ) "You need to watch the child witness carefully and assess matters such as intelligence, level of vocabulary and articulation, degree of self-confidence, general demeanour," he wrote in 2017. One lawyer who knew Dennis for more than a decade said he was "not shocked" by the charges because he had a reputation for sexual harassment and aggression towards women. "It's one of those situations where, and I know I'm not the only person who's thought about this, I think a lot of us in retrospect are like, 'This was actually f***ing obvious,'" he said. Three lawyers told the ABC about an incident where Dennis was intoxicated at the 2012 Aboriginal Legal Service (ALS) Christmas party in Sydney, when he lunged at a woman with an open fist. He was then banned from ALS Christmas parties. Barrister Charles Waterstreet, who worked at Forbes alongside Dennis for more than a decade until facing his own sexual misconduct allegations, described his former colleague as "very ambitious" but "an oddball". "He loved a drink, especially on Friday nights," he said. "He sort of became another personality." Forbes Chambers is on the 11th floor of a building overlooking Sydney's Hyde Park. ( ABC News: Sissy Reyes ) In 2011, Dennis began hosting legal conferences to raise funds for his charity, Reasonable Cause, that pledged to help "disadvantaged young Cambodians to further their education". Tickets cost $450, and the guest list included magistrates, silks and politicians, according to the 2024 invitation. In interviews with more than 20 sitting Forbes barristers, some were quick to defend their late colleague — insinuating the evidence was thin, based on industry rumours, and one said they did not think his charity work should be "smeared". "It did such good work. I don't think it was connected … to some sexual interest," they said. However, despite some celebrating his work and attending his legal conferences, many could not name the charity the money went to. The largest recipient of Dennis's fundraising was Sunrise Cambodia — a high-profile children's charity founded by Adelaide-born Geraldine Cox. Cox has spent decades crisscrossing the globe, and according to her 2011 report, delivering speeches to company executives in the United Arab Emirates, government officials in Australia, private schools, and lawyers like Dennis. "I flew to Sydney to address a group of lawyers at an event arranged by sponsor Mark Dennis, where over $14,000 was raised. Who said lawyers do not have hearts!" Cox wrote. Her work has been celebrated internationally. She has won awards, been praised by Australian media and rubbed shoulders with Hollywood celebrities and Australian prime ministers. Geraldine Cox's work has brought her into contact with the likes of Angelina Jolie, Brad Pitt and Anthony Albanese. ( ABC News / supplied ) Starting in 2008, Dennis personally sponsored a handful of children at Sunrise whom he visited in the orphanages each year. Over time, he backed the whole organisation — raising at least $340,000 in seven years through the legal conferences. In 2010, he also began funding and attending Sunrise's annual beach holidays to Sihanoukville, a once-sleepy Cambodian coastal town now filled with scam compounds and casinos. Itineraries for these trips obtained by the ABC show the children played football, shared meals, performed concerts and socialised with sponsors, including Dennis. Photographs from these trips show Dennis on the beach, and hugging and playing with young children at the hotel. There is no suggestion the photographs are sexual. Dennis playing with children during one of the Sunrise trips to Sihanoukville. ( ABC News / supplied ) A spokesperson for Sunrise said sponsors were not permitted to initiate contact with children. "However, if a child comes running at a sponsor for a hug, the sponsor is not expected to push them away as this can be very emotionally damaging to a kid who may actually feel safe for the first time in his/her life," they said. A former Sunrise employee told the ABC it was during one of these beach trips that Dennis was swimming when he went under the water and touched her leg in a sexual manner. "I felt really afraid," she said. "I kicked Mark off. I was very terrified. He apologised later." A Sunrise spokesperson said the charity did not know about this allegation and was "very sorry to hear this". "Had they reported this, we could and would have dealt with it at the time," the spokesperson said. The woman did not complain formally, but said staff were concerned about Dennis's behaviour and agreed they needed to be "careful" around him to "protect the kids". Geraldine Cox (second from left) and Dennis (seated with arms crossed) on a beach at Sihanoukville. ( Supplied ) The same former employee said she was also concerned about Dennis's behaviour towards an autistic teenage girl living in Sunrise, whom he regularly tried to come close to, and touched her breasts. She said she saw Dennis entering the girls' and boys' bedrooms at Sunrise, but staff felt there was nothing they could do "because he's a big sponsor" and therefore did not report this. Eng Sopheak, who lived at Sunrise from the age of five and then worked as Cox's personal driver, also said he witnessed Dennis regularly entering the girls' dormitories. "I was personally worried," he said, because men were typically not allowed to enter the dormitories. Eng Sopheak became Cox's personal driver after living at Sunrise as a child. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) Sopheak said there needed to be greater separation between sponsors and children. "My recommendation to sponsors is just that they donate the money, but they don't need to have a relationship with the child," he said. A spokesperson for Sunrise said dormitories were private areas and as of last year, sponsors were no longer invited to Sihanoukville. They said they had plans to phase out individual child sponsorship but did not specify when. However, Sunrise's website still allows sponsors to preference the age and gender of children whom they can visit for $50 per month. By 2018, Dennis was appointed chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered Australian charity managing donations for Sunrise at the time. In this role, Dennis was involved in almost every aspect of Sunrise's operations — managing redundancies, approving wages, signing off on hiring policies and even becoming a 49 per cent shareholder of Sunrise's Sihanoukville property, which was valued at more than $US3 million in 2017. "He was the big boss," said Yi Soksan, who held senior positions at Sunrise between 2011 and 2018. Soksan said staff were told by Cox to "just trust" Dennis because he was a donor and lawyer, and recalls her saying: "He's my friend, he's one of the big donors and sponsors. He loves Sunrise." Yi Soksan says he knew Dennis as "the big boss". ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) "She advised us, 'He's also the lawyer, so he understands, you know, the rules, the laws. So, just trust him.'" Cox said she had no recollection of discussing Dennis with staff. While she considered him a friend, she said she had no knowledge of his personal life and never witnessed any bad behaviour. While chairman, Dennis wielded power over Cox. In an email sent in November 2019, Cox asked for his approval for Sunrise to cover personal expenses. "Since I offered to reduce my salary … around the time you took over, Mark, I am finding it increasingly difficult to have any sort of normal life," she wrote. While their relationship was financial and social, it was also fractious. Emails show Dennis privately described Cox as an "unreliable historian" and "something of a compulsive spender" — descriptions Cox said she could not comment on. Dennis was granted access to Sunrise's bank accounts in 2018, allowing him to use Sunrise's money to make purchases for children. A note from Dennis acknowledging receipt of $US4,000 for the purchase of two motorbikes and a computer. ( Supplied ) Sunrise said this was normal practice, and its current policy permitted donors to purchase gifts for individual children on special occasions like birthdays, capped at $20 per year. Maggie Eno, who runs Cambodian child welfare charity M'Lop Tapang, was critical of everything from sponsors attending beach holidays to giving gifts to children. "Individual purchasing … it's grooming," Eno says. "It's horrifying." Maggie Eno runs Cambodian child welfare charity M'Lop Tapang. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) Eno, who did not want to comment on Sunrise specifically, said sponsors should never have access to children because criminals were "sophisticated" and "always" had the goal of getting "direct access to the children". "Paedophiles or child sex offenders don't just groom the child, they groom the family of the child, and they groom the organisation taking care of the child," she said. "The majority of people are good, kind people, but there is always a risk." A spokesperson for Sunrise said work was underway to distance relationships between sponsors and children. Former Sunrise resident Sok San, now aged 28, was among the children Dennis bought gifts for and socialised with on the beach trips. He first learned that Dennis was charged and had died when contacted by the ABC, and said he cried. "He promised to buy me an iPad," San said in June, adding Dennis wanted him to download Facebook on the device. Former Sunrise resident Sok San says he kept in touch with Dennis after leaving the orphanage. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) San said his mother died when he was young, there was violence in his childhood, and he started living in Sunrise at around 10 years old. "He's a good person, and he also came to watch a traditional dance," San said. He called Dennis "godfather" and said they kept in touch outside Sunrise when he became an adult. They met for ice cream in Siem Reap, and Dennis made promises, like paying for his university studies in America, he said. Dennis also continued relationships with other children outside Sunrise after his chairmanship ended in 2020. Two boys told the ABC that Dennis took groups of former Sunrise children to dinners at a restaurant in the high-end part of Phnom Penh where alcohol was served. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) Facebook messages obtained by the ABC show Dennis maintained direct contact online with children he met through Sunrise. "I am incredibly proud of you," Dennis wrote to one boy in September 2024. "Thank you for your support all the years," the boy responded. Behind Sunrise's gates, emails show staff had been concerned about these relationships for years. One email shows an employee contacted Sunrise's former operations manager, Rob Madsen, in 2020 for help when he learned Dennis was sending money to a 17-year-old outside Sunrise. "He has been still supported by Mak [sic] Dennis," the email said. "Many kids living outside [Sunrise] have been supported/sponsored by him secretly." "Kids requested me to keep it secret as he doesn't want [Sunrise's] managers to know about his support. He buys motorbikes for all kids, school fees, etc." Sunrise said it had no record of this. They said all children were trained on the dangers of maintaining contact with sponsors after leaving the orphanage, but Sunrise did not have the power or resources to monitor what graduates did. Dennis flew to Cambodia for one final trip in January this year, where he visited Cox's personal residence, a wooden villa on the grounds of Sunrise. He was in Cambodia on a golfing trip, Cox said, and saw her as a "concerned friend" after hearing she was bedridden following a fall. Little did she know, this would be Dennis's last visit to Sunrise. When he returned to Sydney, he was intercepted by Australian Border Force officers at the airport who searched his devices and allegedly discovered child abuse material. Documents released to the ABC under Freedom of Information laws reveal Dennis was communicating this material between 2023 and 2025 to two people, including an account with an Australian number and username "Kanje". Dennis denied possessing child abuse material in a police interview, but never entered a formal plea. In a bail hearing the following day, prosecutors said they had discovered an image of a boy aged between six and 10 on his phone, and chat logs where he expressed a desire to rape a 16-year-old. Commonwealth prosecutor Jon Kisch described the material on Dennis's phone as "disturbing" and "very serious offending", which, if proven, would attract a long jail sentence. The judge allowed Dennis to be released under strict conditions. Less than three weeks later, he was found dead, leaving behind many unanswered questions. "I want to know what happened," said one young woman Dennis met through Sunrise. “I want to know [if] this is true or not. I want to know why. I want to know what happened to him.” Listen to Dark Menace , a new three-part investigative podcast from Background Briefing and ABC Investigations, via the ABC Listen app or wherever you get your podcasts. "However, if a child comes running at a sponsor for a hug, the sponsor is not expected to push them away as this can be very emotionally damaging to a kid who may actually feel safe for the first time in his/her life," they said. A former Sunrise employee told the ABC it was during one of these beach trips that Dennis was swimming when he went under the water and touched her leg in a sexual manner. "I felt really afraid," she said. "I kicked Mark off. I was very terrified. He apologised later." A Sunrise spokesperson said the charity did not know about this allegation and was "very sorry to hear this". "Had they reported this, we could and would have dealt with it at the time," the spokesperson said. The woman did not complain formally, but said staff were concerned about Dennis's behaviour and agreed they needed to be "careful" around him to "protect the kids". Geraldine Cox (second from left) and Dennis (seated with arms crossed) on a beach at Sihanoukville. ( Supplied ) The same former employee said she was also concerned about Dennis's behaviour towards an autistic teenage girl living in Sunrise, whom he regularly tried to come close to, and touched her breasts. She said she saw Dennis entering the girls' and boys' bedrooms at Sunrise, but staff felt there was nothing they could do "because he's a big sponsor" and therefore did not report this. Eng Sopheak, who lived at Sunrise from the age of five and then worked as Cox's personal driver, also said he witnessed Dennis regularly entering the girls' dormitories. "I was personally worried," he said, because men were typically not allowed to enter the dormitories. Eng Sopheak became Cox's personal driver after living at Sunrise as a child. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) Sopheak said there needed to be greater separation between sponsors and children. "My recommendation to sponsors is just that they donate the money, but they don't need to have a relationship with the child," he said. A spokesperson for Sunrise said dormitories were private areas and as of last year, sponsors were no longer invited to Sihanoukville. They said they had plans to phase out individual child sponsorship but did not specify when. However, Sunrise's website still allows sponsors to preference the age and gender of children whom they can visit for $50 per month. By 2018, Dennis was appointed chairman of the Australian Cambodian Foundation, the registered Australian charity managing donations for Sunrise at the time. In this role, Dennis was involved in almost every aspect of Sunrise's operations — managing redundancies, approving wages, signing off on hiring policies and even becoming a 49 per cent shareholder of Sunrise's Sihanoukville property, which was valued at more than $US3 million in 2017. "He was the big boss," said Yi Soksan, who held senior positions at Sunrise between 2011 and 2018. Soksan said staff were told by Cox to "just trust" Dennis because he was a donor and lawyer, and recalls her saying: "He's my friend, he's one of the big donors and sponsors. He loves Sunrise." Yi Soksan says he knew Dennis as "the big boss". ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) "She advised us, 'He's also the lawyer, so he understands, you know, the rules, the laws. So, just trust him.'" Cox said she had no recollection of discussing Dennis with staff. While she considered him a friend, she said she had no knowledge of his personal life and never witnessed any bad behaviour. While chairman, Dennis wielded power over Cox. In an email sent in November 2019, Cox asked for his approval for Sunrise to cover personal expenses. "Since I offered to reduce my salary … around the time you took over, Mark, I am finding it increasingly difficult to have any sort of normal life," she wrote. While their relationship was financial and social, it was also fractious. Emails show Dennis privately described Cox as an "unreliable historian" and "something of a compulsive spender" — descriptions Cox said she could not comment on. Dennis was granted access to Sunrise's bank accounts in 2018, allowing him to use Sunrise's money to make purchases for children. A note from Dennis acknowledging receipt of $US4,000 for the purchase of two motorbikes and a computer. ( Supplied ) Sunrise said this was normal practice, and its current policy permitted donors to purchase gifts for individual children on special occasions like birthdays, capped at $20 per year. Maggie Eno, who runs Cambodian child welfare charity M'Lop Tapang, was critical of everything from sponsors attending beach holidays to giving gifts to children. "Individual purchasing … it's grooming," Eno says. "It's horrifying." Maggie Eno runs Cambodian child welfare charity M'Lop Tapang. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) Eno, who did not want to comment on Sunrise specifically, said sponsors should never have access to children because criminals were "sophisticated" and "always" had the goal of getting "direct access to the children". "Paedophiles or child sex offenders don't just groom the child, they groom the family of the child, and they groom the organisation taking care of the child," she said. "The majority of people are good, kind people, but there is always a risk." A spokesperson for Sunrise said work was underway to distance relationships between sponsors and children. Former Sunrise resident Sok San, now aged 28, was among the children Dennis bought gifts for and socialised with on the beach trips. He first learned that Dennis was charged and had died when contacted by the ABC, and said he cried. "He promised to buy me an iPad," San said in June, adding Dennis wanted him to download Facebook on the device. Former Sunrise resident Sok San says he kept in touch with Dennis after leaving the orphanage. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) San said his mother died when he was young, there was violence in his childhood, and he started living in Sunrise at around 10 years old. "He's a good person, and he also came to watch a traditional dance," San said. He called Dennis "godfather" and said they kept in touch outside Sunrise when he became an adult. They met for ice cream in Siem Reap, and Dennis made promises, like paying for his university studies in America, he said. Dennis also continued relationships with other children outside Sunrise after his chairmanship ended in 2020. Two boys told the ABC that Dennis took groups of former Sunrise children to dinners at a restaurant in the high-end part of Phnom Penh where alcohol was served. ( ABC News: Haidarr Jones ) Facebook messages obtained by the ABC show Dennis maintained direct contact online with children he met through Sunrise. "I am incredibly proud of you," Dennis wrote to one boy in September 2024. "Thank you for your support all the years," the boy responded. Behind Sunrise's gates, emails show staff had been concerned about these relationships for years. One email shows an employee contacted Sunrise's former operations manager, Rob Madsen, in 2020 for help when he learned Dennis was sending money to a 17-year-old outside Sunrise. "He has been still supported by Mak [sic] Dennis," the email said. "Many kids living outside [Sunrise] have been supported/sponsored by him secretly." "Kids requested me to keep it secret as he doesn't want [Sunrise's] managers to know about his support. He buys motorbikes for all kids, school fees, etc." Sunrise said it had no record of this. They said all children were trained on the dangers of maintaining contact with sponsors after leaving the orphanage, but Sunrise did not have the power or resources to monitor what graduates did. Dennis flew to Cambodia for one final trip in January this year, where he visited Cox's personal residence, a wooden villa on the grounds of Sunrise. He was in Cambodia on a golfing trip, Cox said, and saw her as a "concerned friend" after hearing she was bedridden following a fall. Little did she know, this would be Dennis's last visit to Sunrise. When he returned to Sydney, he was intercepted by Australian Border Force officers at the airport who searched his devices and allegedly discovered child abuse material. Documents released to the ABC under Freedom of Information laws reveal Dennis was communicating this material between 2023 and 2025 to two people, including an account with an Australian number and username "Kanje". Dennis denied possessing child abuse material in a police interview, but never entered a formal plea. In a bail hearing the following day, prosecutors said they had discovered an image of a boy aged between six and 10 on his phone, and chat logs where he expressed a desire to rape a 16-year-old. Commonwealth prosecutor Jon Kisch described the material on Dennis's phone as "disturbing" and "very serious offending", which, if proven, would attract a long jail sentence. The judge allowed Dennis to be released under strict conditions. Less than three weeks later, he was found dead, leaving behind many unanswered questions. "I want to know what happened," said one young woman Dennis met through Sunrise. “I want to know [if] this is true or not. I want to know why. I want to know what happened to him.” Listen to Dark Menace , a new three-part investigative podcast from Background Briefing and ABC Investigations, via the ABC Listen app or wherever you get your podcasts. Students of Sri Ramana Vidyalaya Matriculation School in Tambaram tend to the plants at the terrace garden Every second Sunday, Sri Ramana Vidyalaya Matriculation School in Tambaram turns into a mini-market with the management opening its gates for farmers to come and sell their organic produce. For the last three months, Thalir Karima Velaan Santhai has enabled at least 30 farmers from different villages to sell their bounty, parents of the school and neighbours being their biggest patrons. The school management looks at this initiative as an extension of its eco-club activities where it operates a terrace garden maintained by the students. The garden has evolved with every passing year and currently has a good variety of vegetable growing plants. Students of classes VII to IX have one period a week allotted in their timetable to engage in terrace garden work, where they till the soil, plant saplings in used containers that serve as pots, water them and do all other things to ensure they grow. Workshops and other engaging activities are conducted at the farmers market “This time, our produce has not been great, but whatever we get is shared among students who take it home. Recently, when we got a decent amount of lady’s finger and cluster beans, we left it to the students to decide who wants to take it,” says V. Selvamani, correspondent of the school. When students have a free period, they are encouraged to spend time in the terrace garden. Traditional rice varieties, cold-pressed oils, pulses, organic gardening inputs and local pottery are among the stalls at the market. Selvamani says they charge a nominal amount for arranging tables and chairs, and the larger goal is to eliminate middle men. To encourage visitors to understand what goes into their plate, the organisers conduct various knowledge sharing sessions. For example, in the last few months, they had a session on tips for terrace gardening and free seed sharing, and another on making seed Ganesha using clay. This time, there’s a special workshop, “21 Plate Balanced Meal for 7 Days,” from 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. by culinary artisan Akila Kunalan. Like other farmers market happening in the city, visitors are encouraged to bring cloth bags. For registration, call 97909 72612 or 99403 37100. representative.title: New island to be removed after bus 'shambles' in Queniborough
representative.author: Dan Martin

snapshot.title: New island to be removed after bus 'shambles' in Queniborough
snapshot.evidenceText: A newly-installed pedestrian island is to be removed after it left a road in a village in Leicestershire too narrow for buses to get through. Arriva Midlands has withdrawn its services from the centre of Queniborough because it said its drivers were unable to get along Rearsby Road without mounting the pavement. The island was installed as part of work to upgrade a nearby junction, which was completed on Saturday 3 October, but has not left enough space in the road for larger vehicles to get round it. Leicestershire County Council said the junction work had been carried out by contractors for developer David Wilson Homes but the design had "not proved correct". David Wilson Homes said it would "implement any changes identified as quickly as possible so that the bus service can operate as normal". James Poland, county councillor for the village, said the island needed to be taken out quickly so Arriva could resume its 5 and 5A services. "The whole situation is a total shambles and it's hard to understand how it has happened," he said. The county council said the island would be taken out temporarily while a new design for the junction, able to take buses, was drawn up. A council spokesperson said: "We recognise the frustration this issue has caused residents who rely on local bus services. "The central crossing island is part of a wider scheme of work to enhance junction capacity following a recent David Wilson Homes development. "We have met with the developers of the scheme and highlighted the issues raised and they will be rectifying the situation as soon as possible. "Whilst a permanent rework of the scheme is finalised, the pedestrian crossing point is set to be removed so buses can use the road." Poland said he had warned highways officials the new island would leave Rearsby Road unusable for large buses but had not been listened to. "It's really frustrating because people have had to put up with three months of disruption while the work was done in the first place. "Now there will be more messing about while they take the thing out. "I've been told it could happen as early as next week. "People rely on buses getting into the village. "I have heard from the family of an 11-year-old girl who now has to walk 500 metres up to Melton Road to get her school bus. "I want to know what's gone wrong and I want to know that this kind of mess won't happen anywhere in the future." A spokesperson for Arriva said: "Safety is our first priority. After the junction in Queniborough reopened, we carried out a risk assessment and found our buses can't get through the new layout without mounting the pavement. "That isn't something we can ask our drivers to do and it puts pedestrians and other road users at risk. "We're sorry that, as a result, services 5 and 5A are not currently serving Queniborough village. Customers can use the nearest stop on Melton Road, which is 500 metres away. "We're in dialogue with Leicestershire County Council Highways and we're keen to work with them to find a solution that lets buses serve the village safely and reliably." The county council said it would run a free taxi service from the Rearsby Road, near the crossroads, to take people to the nearest bus stop 500 metres (1,640ft) away in Melton Road. representative.title: Toronto approves 2026 budget with historic capital plan | The Canada Voice
representative.author: Toronto Voice Staff

snapshot.title: City Council approves Toronto's 2026 budget with $63.1-billion capital plan, frozen TTC fares
snapshot.evidenceText: The Canada Voice network · 13 local news sites across Ontario Toronto City Council has signed off on an $18.9-billion operating budget and the largest 10-year capital plan in the city's history, including frozen TTC fares and a property tax increase below inflation. Toronto City Council has approved the city's 2026 budget, signing off on an $18.9-billion operating plan and a 10-year capital budget that the city says is the largest in its history. The budget — Mayor Olivia Chow's third since her election in 2023 — was passed at a special meeting of council on Tuesday, according to a statement from Councillor Paula Fletcher , who represents Toronto-Danforth and published a budget breakdown on her website. The centrepiece of the plan is a $63.1-billion capital budget and plan covering 2026 to 2035, which Fletcher described as the biggest 10-year capital commitment the city has ever made. Fletcher said the budget's affordability measures — including frozen TTC fares and free meals for students — would save a working family with two children about $1,200 a year on groceries and transportation costs alone. The property tax increase for 2026 is set at 2.2 per cent, which Fletcher noted is below the rate of inflation. The budget also proposes what she called a fairer approach to funding city services, asking "empty home speculators and luxury property buyers" — the top 2 per cent of all buyers — to contribute more. The budget also includes $788 million in new savings and efficiencies, according to Fletcher, who said the city's financial position has improved over the past two years under Chow's leadership. Among the service investments, the budget funds seven-day-a-week library access and increases funding for tenant supports, home upgrade grants, flood protection, and programs that help seniors stay in their homes. On public safety, Fletcher said shootings, youth violence and 911 wait times have all significantly decreased. The budget builds on that trend, she said, by investing in more firefighters, paramedics, police officers and mental health workers, while boosting crime prevention programs. More than 25,000 residents took part in budget consultations held in October 2025, including telephone town halls and local events such as Fletcher's own budget town hall, ensuring the final plan reflected residents' priorities, her statement said. "I was pleased to support Mayor Chow's budget and her progressive vision of a more affordable, caring and safe Toronto," Fletcher wrote in her post. The budget vote came during a busy final stretch of the 2022-2026 council term. According to Fletcher's update, councillors also dealt with a maximum heat bylaw to protect tenants during extreme heat, a new funding deal to build more housing, and the provincial upload of the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway. Other items on the agenda included Fletcher's motion about odours from the Ashbridges Bay sewage treatment plant, a redevelopment plan for Ookwemin Minising, and increased support from the mayor's office for vulnerable youth and low-income tenants. representative.author: WORLD

snapshot.title: Syrian army takes control of al-Shaddadi base after coordination with U.S.
snapshot.evidenceText: The Syrian Army has assumed control of the al-Shaddadi military base in northeastern Syria’s Hasakah province, following coordination with U.S. officials, according to the Syrian Defense Ministry’s media department. In a statement carried by Syrian Arab News Agency, the ministry said the base was formally handed over after arrangements were completed with U.S. authorities. Syrian army units have since moved to secure the facility and its surrounding perimeter. The transfer comes just days after Damascus announced it had taken control of the al-Tanf military base in southeastern Syria. On February 12, the Defense Ministry said the handover of al-Tanf followed direct coordination between Syrian and American officials, marking a significant shift in the military presence in the area. United States Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed its withdrawal from al-Tanf after nearly a decade of operations there. In a statement, CENTCOM said U.S. forces remain prepared to respond to any potential threats from ISIS and will continue supporting partner-led efforts aimed at preventing the group’s resurgence in the region. The twin handovers of al-Shaddadi and al-Tanf signal a broader reconfiguration of military deployments in Syria’s northeast and southeast, areas that have long been focal points in the fight against ISIS and in wider regional dynamics. Syrian officials described the developments as part of ongoing efforts to reassert state authority over strategic sites, while U.S. officials emphasized that counterterrorism operations against ISIS remain a priority despite the withdrawal from specific bases. Eight people, including two children, were killed in a mass shooting at a home in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday, while the suspected gunman also died from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, bringing the total death toll to nine, authorities said. A Russian strike on the southeastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia killed at least 11 people, including three children, and wounded at least 16 others on Saturday, Oct. 10, local authorities said, as Russia launched a large-scale overnight drone attack across Ukraine. Heavy rains have triggered flash floods and mudslides in Chile's capital, Santiago, and surrounding areas, injuring at least six people, forcing the evacuation of hundreds of households and damaging thousands of homes, according to authorities. snapshot.title: Syrian army takes control of al-Shaddadi base after coordination with U.S.
snapshot.evidenceText: The Syrian Army has assumed control of the al-Shaddadi military base in northeastern Syria’s Hasakah province, following coordination with U.S. officials, according to the Syrian Defense Ministry’s media department. In a statement carried by Syrian Arab News Agency, the ministry said the base was formally handed over after arrangements were completed with U.S. authorities. Syrian army units have since moved to secure the facility and its surrounding perimeter. The transfer comes just days after Damascus announced it had taken control of the al-Tanf military base in southeastern Syria. On February 12, the Defense Ministry said the handover of al-Tanf followed direct coordination between Syrian and American officials, marking a significant shift in the military presence in the area. United States Central Command (CENTCOM) confirmed its withdrawal from al-Tanf after nearly a decade of operations there. In a statement, CENTCOM said U.S. forces remain prepared to respond to any potential threats from ISIS and will continue supporting partner-led efforts aimed at preventing the group’s resurgence in the region. The twin handovers of al-Shaddadi and al-Tanf signal a broader reconfiguration of military deployments in Syria’s northeast and southeast, areas that have long been focal points in the fight against ISIS and in wider regional dynamics. Syrian officials described the developments as part of ongoing efforts to reassert state authority over strategic sites, while U.S. officials emphasized that counterterrorism operations against ISIS remain a priority despite the withdrawal from specific bases. representative.title: Gaza: Ceasefire Anniversary Marks Year of Failed Promises | Human Rights Watch

snapshot.title: Gaza: Ceasefire Anniversary Marks Year of Failed Promises
snapshot.evidenceText: No Reconstruction; Acute Humanitarian Needs; Killing Continues Share this via Bluesky Share this via Facebook Share this via X Share this via WhatsApp Share this via Email More sharing options Share this via LinkedIn Share this via Reddit Share this via Telegram Share this via Printer (Beirut) – Israeli forces continue to kill and wound civilians and deny sufficient food, aid, and water to Palestinians in Gaza one year after a ceasefire agreement took effect on October 10, 2025, Human Rights Watch said today. Israel’s acts of genocide and crimes against humanity , including forced displacement and extermination, have persisted throughout the ceasefire. Other countries should take immediate measures to protect civilians and ensure that rights-based reconstruction begins. The Board of Peace, authorized under United Nations Security Council Resolution 2803, is tasked with assessing parties’ compliance with the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict. Promises of humanitarian relief and the restoration of essential civilian infrastructure are central to the plan. Yet, a year on, aid volumes remain far below required levels , critical humanitarian access routes have been repeatedly obstructed, and reconstruction has not yet begun. Continuing Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,400 Palestinians and wounded 4,881 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry, bringing the death toll since October 2023 to over 74,000, including over 21,000 children. “The outside world may be under a dangerous illusion that life in Gaza is returning to normal, but reality tells a very different story, ” said Sarah Sanbar , acting Israel and Palestine researcher at Human Rights Watch. “There is nothing normal about living in a tent under bombardment, without enough food or drinking water for your family.” With winter approaching, families living in an Israel-engineered shelter crisis face preventable deaths and suffering affecting key human rights such as the rights to housing, health, and education. Ninety-four percent of Gaza’s population lacks adequate shelter, the Palestine Shelter Cluster reported based on a survey of nearly 2,000 households across Gaza. Nearly two-thirds of housing units have been destroyed , and many of those still standing are damaged and unsafe. The survey showed that over half of the nearly 2,000 households are living in tents. In September 2026, a damaged building housing about 100 people collapsed , killing 21, including 12 children. Gaza’s education and health sectors remain shattered. The new academic year began last month with 93 percent of schools destroyed or damaged. The World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 56 attacks on health care in Gaza between January and August 2026, with just 35 of Gaza’s 57 hospitals and field hospitals partially functional and not one fully operational. Meanwhile, humanitarian organizations report an increase in disease due to the living conditions in overcrowded camps and shelters, including poor waste management, sewage overflow, and rodent infestation. The risks of famine and acute food insecurity loom over Gaza, as the entry of humanitarian aid remains limited and inconsistent , and people in Gaza are unable to produce their own food due to Israeli forces’ widespread destruction of agricultural land and restrictions on fishing. In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC), the world’s foremost experts on food security, reported that 67 percent of the population—over 1.4 million people—are “expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026.” According to the European Union and UN, the recovery and reconstruction needs in Gaza are estimated at US$71.4 billion over the next decade. On September 23, the Board of Peace presented a “6-Month Gaza Recovery Program” ready to begin “the moment funding and access allow,” but one year on, no recovery efforts have begun. Israel continues to move the “ Yellow Line ,” the stated limit of the physical presence of Israeli ground forces under the ceasefire, westward beyond its agreed boundaries as Israeli officials call the line Israel’s “new border.” The area within the Yellow Line now amounts to about 64 percent of the Gaza Strip, and Israeli forces are displacing Palestinians as the line moves while preventing residents from returning to their homes beyond the line, corralling Gaza’s 2.1 million people into an ever-shrinking strip of land. In June, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs ( OCHA ) documented that 196 Palestinians had been killed near the Yellow Line and its westward movement is swallowing up water points and health facilities , further restricting Palestinians’ access to key services. Alongside these actions, Israeli officials continue to openly declare a goal of ethnically cleansing Gaza. For example, in September, Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir proposed the “ 710 Disengagement Plan ,” aiming to depopulate Gaza in seven years, and establishing a ministry of “voluntary emigration” for that purpose. According to Palestinian civil defense authorities, over 630 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble since November 2025, and they estimate that over 8,000 remain buried under the rubble. The UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory warned in September 2026 that the large-scale removal of rubble in areas of Gaza under Israeli military control should not become a way to erase traces of atrocity crimes. Finding the remains of those lost under the rubble is essential so that families can know what happened to their loved ones, offer them dignified burial, and start a long process of recovery and remedy, Human Rights Watch said. As world leaders discuss the future of Gaza, it is essential for them to urgently address the rights of Palestinians to rebuild their lives in Gaza, categorically reject all Israeli propositions of forced displacement and ethnic cleansing, and support all measures of accountability to put an end to the catastrophic situation for rights in Gaza. “Palestinians deserve a better future where their rights are respected and they can live in dignity, but none of this is possible unless the atrocities stop and justice and redress become a reality,” Sanbar said. representative.title: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion-year-old millisecond signal from space
representative.author: Themiya Nanayakkara, Manisha Caleb

snapshot.title: Astronomers pinpoint the origin of a 10 billion-year-old millisecond signal from space
snapshot.evidenceText: More than 10 billion years ago, something in a distant galaxy gave off an incredibly bright burst of radio waves which lasted just a few milliseconds. In new research published today in Science , our team tracked it back to its origin in a small galaxy filled with many young stars, when the universe was only one-fifth of its current age. Fast radio bursts like this one are a mystery scientists have been trying to unravel for almost 20 years since they were first discovered. Our discovery is the most distant such burst whose host galaxy has yet been identified. We detected the burst, dubbed FRB 20240304B, with the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, using a system called MeerTRAP which is designed to catch fast-changing transient radio signals from space in real time. The different frequencies of the radio burst arrived at slightly different times. We call this effect “dispersion”, and it happens because the signal has travelled through a lot of electrically charged material in space on its journey to Earth. By measuring the amount of dispersion, we can tell how much of this material the signal has passed through – which in turn lets us calculate how far the signal has travelled and how far away from us it was created. The FRB 20240304B burst showed a large amount of dispersion, which suggested it was probably coming from a great distance. We were also able to pinpoint its position on the sky. But when we looked at that position with large ground-based telescopes like the Keck Telescopes , we couldn’t see a host galaxy. The galaxy was simply too faint. So we turned to the James Webb Space Telescope ( JWST ). The space telescope’s infrared camera revealed a tiny galaxy very close to the position of the fast radio burst. We then broke down light from the galaxy into the spectrum of different frequencies that made it up. We know what part of this spectrum “should” look like, and seeing how those frequencies have changed lets us calculate how fast the galaxy is moving away from us due to the expansion of the universe – which in turn lets us figure out how old it is. These calculations confirmed that we were looking at a galaxy 10.6 billion years ago. It contains only about 10 million times the mass of our Sun, which is a tiny fraction of the mass of our own Milky Way galaxy. The host galaxy appears to be a young galaxy still forming many stars, with a very low amount of metal content, and very different from many of the larger galaxies in which most other fast radio bursts have been found. This is consistent with one theory about the source of at least some fast radio bursts – that they are produced by young, highly magnetised neutron stars called magnetars . At the same time, fast radio bursts come in different shapes and sizes, we don’t think all of them necessarily have the same kind of origin. However, observations like ours give us another piece of the puzzle. By studying the host galaxies and the environments of fast radio bursts across cosmic time, we can start to understand which types of galaxies and stellar environments produce them. The most exciting thing about this discovery, however, may not be the distance itself. As the radio signal made its way to Earth, it picked up the imprint of everything it passed through, bearing a record of the magnetic fields, changes in the space environment, and turbulence that it encountered. This makes it a gold mine of information about the cosmos that is otherwise difficult to access. This includes how electrons are distributed through the cosmic web, as well as information on magnetic fields that pervade the universe. As the signal encounters magnetic fields along the way they subtly twist the orientation of its radio waves. By measuring this twist, we learn about the magnetic field complexities across many billions of light years. FRB 20240304B does more than tell us about one distant galaxy. It gives us a new data point for studying how electrically charged matter has been distributed through the universe over cosmic time, and also how magnetised the cosmos is. Our discovery has shown for the first time that fast radio bursts were being produced all the way back to around 3 billion years after the Big Bang, during the period when the universe was most actively forming stars and galaxies. This lets us probe electrically charged matter across about 80% of cosmic history. Finding fast radio bursts at such large distances is difficult because of the combination of detecting increasingly faint bursts and identifying galaxies that are themselves extremely faint. With larger samples of distant fast radio bursts, we can use these brief flashes as cosmic signposts, revealing how matter is spread through the universe, how galaxies grow, and how the space between them changes over time. representative.title: New large docodont fossil sheds light on Jurassic mammaliaform diversity-Xinhua

snapshot.title: New large docodont fossil sheds light on Jurassic mammaliaform diversity
snapshot.evidenceText: SHENYANG, Oct. 11 (Xinhua) -- An international team led by Chinese scientists has discovered a new docodont mammaliaform species, the largest known of its kind, in Jurassic strata dating back about 160 million years, enriching scientific understanding of Jurassic mammaliaform diversity. The new species has been named Megacauda sungei. Its fossil specimen, discovered in Ningcheng, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, measures roughly 52 centimeters in length and is estimated to have weighed around 2 kilograms, making it the largest known docodont mammaliaform. Its skull is clearly preserved, its trunk is robust, and its most striking feature is an unusually long, coiled tail. The specimen also retains well-preserved pelvic bones, hind limbs and tail vertebrae, suggesting it was adapted for swimming. Based on its distinctive teeth, researchers believe it could have hunted small animals living in the same environment, with a lifestyle possibly similar to that of the modern platypus. The study also sheds light on the animal's throat structure. The bones in its throat are similar to those of modern mammals, suggesting that behaviors such as swallowing, lapping and suckling may have already existed in the early ancestors of mammals, long before modern mammal groups appeared. "Mammaliaforms from the Mesozoic are often imagined as tiny creatures under dinosaur feet, but Megacauda sungei clearly raises the size limit of this group," said Li Yikun, an associate professor at Shenyang Normal University in northeast China. The study was published online in the journal Nature on Oct. 7. ■

representative.title: China Unveils First Nationwide Labor Rules to Protect Gig Economy Workers - Caixin Global
representative.author: Tang Hanyu

snapshot.title: China Unveils First Nationwide Labor Rules to Protect Gig Economy Workers
snapshot.evidenceText: China’s labor ministry on Thursday released draft rules that would set nationwide protections for workers in the fast-growing gig economy, including minimum-pay safeguards, limits on algorithmic decision-making and stronger obligations for internet platforms. The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security is seeking public comment through Nov. 8 on the 54-article draft, which would be China’s first ministerial regulation specifically governing the rights of workers in new forms of employment, such as food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers and truck drivers. China Proposes Sweeping E-Commerce Overhaul to Protect Gig Workers, Counter Foreign Curbs Pioneering Injury Lawsuit Could Finally Hold China’s Gig Platforms Liable 1. China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security has released a 54-article draft rule, open for public comment until Nov. 8, that would establish the country’s first ministerial regulation specifically protecting workers in the gig economy, including food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers, and truck drivers. The proposal reflects Beijing’s effort to extend labor protections to a workforce that has grown rapidly alongside internet platforms but often falls outside conventional labor-law definitions due to flexible and complex employment arrangements. [para. 1 ] [para. 2 ] [para. 3 ] 2. The draft determines employment relationships based on whether a platform exercises “controlling labor management” over workers. Workers subject to such control and meeting employment-relationship conditions must receive labor contracts; the same applies when a platform’s partner company recruits and manages workers in an employment relationship. If the relationship does not meet the formal threshold, platforms must sign a written work agreement—or a three-party agreement when both platform and partner jointly manage the worker. The rules do not apply to independent business operators or freelancers using platforms. Platforms must vet partners, bear employer responsibility for unqualified partners, and are prohibited from encouraging workers to register as sole proprietors or using multilayer subcontracting to evade obligations. In disputes, workers may name both platform and labor-service partner as joint parties. [para. 7 ] [para. 8 ] [para. 9 ] [para. 10 ] [para. 11 ] [para. 12 ] 3. The proposal sets detailed pay protections: minimum-wage calculations must subtract workers’ costs for providing their own equipment or tools, ensuring net earnings do not fall below local minimum wage. Workers can withdraw compensation on the agreed cycle without fees. The draft encourages positive incentives and prohibits abuse of fines and punitive measures, addressing complaints about arbitrary deductions. It also requires transparent rules and breaks to protect rest rights, as well as labor protections in severe weather, given the outdoor nature of much gig work. [para. 13 ] [para. 14 ] [para. 15 ] 4. The draft restricts platforms’ handling of worker data. Personal information may be processed only lawfully, properly, necessarily, in good faith, and only to the extent required for work management. Platforms must establish accurate work records that workers can conveniently view and download through apps or other channels, and companies must retain records for at least two years after a worker leaves. [para. 16 ] [para. 17 ] 5. A prominent section targets algorithmic management. Platforms must explain the basic principles and operating mechanisms of their algorithms to workers and are barred from algorithmic discrimination. Decisions with major consequences—such as suspending order assignments or banning accounts—cannot be made automatically by an algorithm and require human review. Wang Tianyu, deputy director of the social-law research division at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Law, said this provision addresses public concern that delivery riders and other platform workers have become trapped by algorithmically imposed targets. [para. 18 ] [para. 19 ] [para. 20 ] 6. The ministry noted existing labor laws do not always apply directly to platform work, but experience since a 2021 policy guideline on protecting gig workers allowed mature policies to be turned into binding institutional rules and address gaps. Wang said platform work has become an important part of China’s employment landscape, with complaints including withheld compensation, excessively long hours, inadequate safety protections, opaque algorithmic rules, and lack of occupational-injury coverage. Shen Jianfeng, a law professor at the Central University of Finance and Economics, said parts of the draft adapt traditional labor standards to platform conditions, while provisions on data protection and algorithm rules represent institutional innovations. Public comments can be submitted via the ministry’s website, mail, or email. snapshot.title: China Unveils First Nationwide Labor Rules to Protect Gig Economy Workers
snapshot.evidenceText: China’s labor ministry on Thursday released draft rules that would set nationwide protections for workers in the fast-growing gig economy, including minimum-pay safeguards, limits on algorithmic decision-making and stronger obligations for internet platforms. The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security is seeking public comment through Nov. 8 on the 54-article draft, which would be China’s first ministerial regulation specifically governing the rights of workers in new forms of employment, such as food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers and truck drivers. China Proposes Sweeping E-Commerce Overhaul to Protect Gig Workers, Counter Foreign Curbs Pioneering Injury Lawsuit Could Finally Hold China’s Gig Platforms Liable 1. China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security has released a 54-article draft rule, open for public comment until Nov. 8, that would establish the country’s first ministerial regulation specifically protecting workers in the gig economy, including food-delivery riders, couriers, ride-hailing drivers, and truck drivers. The proposal reflects Beijing’s effort to extend labor protections to a workforce that has grown rapidly alongside internet platforms but often falls outside conventional labor-law definitions due to flexible and complex employment arrangements. [para. 1 ] [para. 2 ] [para. 3 ] 2. The draft determines employment relationships based on whether a platform exercises “controlling labor management” over workers. Workers subject to such control and meeting employment-relationship conditions must receive labor contracts; the same applies when a platform’s partner company recruits and manages workers in an employment relationship. If the relationship does not meet the formal threshold, platforms must sign a written work agreement—or a three-party agreement when both platform and partner jointly manage the worker. The rules do not apply to independent business operators or freelancers using platforms. Platforms must vet partners, bear employer responsibility for unqualified partners, and are prohibited from encouraging workers to register as sole proprietors or using multilayer subcontracting to evade obligations. In disputes, workers may name both platform and labor-service partner as joint parties. [para. 7 ] [para. 8 ] [para. 9 ] [para. 10 ] [para. 11 ] [para. 12 ] 3. The proposal sets detailed pay protections: minimum-wage calculations must subtract workers’ costs for providing their own equipment or tools, ensuring net earnings do not fall below local minimum wage. Workers can withdraw compensation on the agreed cycle without fees. The draft encourages positive incentives and prohibits abuse of fines and punitive measures, addressing complaints about arbitrary deductions. It also requires transparent rules and breaks to protect rest rights, as well as labor protections in severe weather, given the outdoor nature of much gig work. [para. 13 ] [para. 14 ] [para. 15 ] 4. The draft restricts platforms’ handling of worker data. Personal information may be processed only lawfully, properly, necessarily, in good faith, and only to the extent required for work management. Platforms must establish accurate work records that workers can conveniently view and download through apps or other channels, and companies must retain records for at least two years after a worker leaves. [para. 16 ] [para. 17 ] 5. A prominent section targets algorithmic management. Platforms must explain the basic principles and operating mechanisms of their algorithms to workers and are barred from algorithmic discrimination. Decisions with major consequences—such as suspending order assignments or banning accounts—cannot be made automatically by an algorithm and require human review. Wang Tianyu, deputy director of the social-law research division at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences’ Institute of Law, said this provision addresses public concern that delivery riders and other platform workers have become trapped by algorithmically imposed targets. [para. 18 ] [para. 19 ] [para. 20 ] 6. The ministry noted existing labor laws do not always apply directly to platform work, but experience since a 2021 policy guideline on protecting gig workers allowed mature policies to be turned into binding institutional rules and address gaps. Wang said platform work has become an important part of China’s employment landscape, with complaints including withheld compensation, excessively long hours, inadequate safety protections, opaque algorithmic rules, and lack of occupational-injury coverage. Shen Jianfeng, a law professor at the Central University of Finance and Economics, said parts of the draft adapt traditional labor standards to platform conditions, while provisions on data protection and algorithm rules represent institutional innovations.
