"This is an extraordinary glimpse into the distant universe." When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . Astronomers have discovered the most distant Fast Radio Burst (FRB) ever detected. Not only could this help untangle the mystery of what causes these powerful but brief explosions of radio waves, but because FRBs are incredible celestial messengers, it could also reveal details of 11 billion years of cosmic evolution. This FRB , designated FRB 20240304B, was first observed by astronomers using the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa. Then, using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), astronomers tracked it back to its home galaxy, located around 11 billion light-years away. This revealed that FRB 20240304B has been travelling to Earth since the universe was just 3 billion years old or so. That doesn't just make this FRB 20240304B the most distant and earliest FRB ever detected; it more than doubles the distance of the previous record holder! "This is an extraordinary glimpse into the distant universe," team co-leader Manisha Caleb from the Sydney Institute for Astronomy said in a statement sent to Space.com. "We have caught a fast radio burst from a time when the universe was only about three billion years old, and we have used that brief flash of radio light to learn about the matter it has travelled through over billions of years." The team's research was published on Thursday (Oct. 8) in the journal Science. Fast Radio Bursts are mysterious blasts of radio waves that usually flare just once, and in the mere milliseconds they last, emit many times more energy than the sun can radiate in a year. As these powerful millisecond-long blasts of radio waves travel billions of light-years to reach Earth, they pass through gas and dust in galaxies and through the "cosmic fog" lying between these galaxies, the so-called intergalactic medium . By measuring how much the signal slows down, scientists can effectively weigh this fog of gas to map the distribution of matter in galaxies. That makes them crucial tools for understanding how galaxies use gas and dust to form stars and grow. Thus, FRBs are a metaphorical cosmic 'fossil record' blasting through space at light speed with the energy of a multitude of stars. With that in mind, it is little wonder that as a record-breaking example of a fast radio burst, FRB 20240304B has already shocked astronomers. It did this by delivering a surprise about its home galaxy. "The galaxy hosting this burst is surprisingly small, metal-poor and undergoing a very active episode of star formation," team member Laura Driessen, of the University of Sydney, said. "That gives us an important clue about the environments in which FRBs are born and shows that these brief radio flashes can tell us not only about the distant universe, but also about how galaxies and their stellar populations evolve." One of the leading suspects in the creation of FRBs are magnetars , a type of neutron star created when a massive star collapses and dies in a supernova explosion. Unlike "standard" neutron stars, magnetars have fearsomely strong magnetic fields — the strongest magnetic fields in the known universe, in fact. There are different theories about how magnetars are born: one involving existing older neutron stars colliding and merging, the other involving environments with burgeoning star formation. The galaxy from which FRB 20240304B originates seems to support that latter formation route, as it is young in the midst of "starburst," a period of extreme star formation. Scientists will work on the mystery of the FRB/magnetar connection. In the meantime, this newly detected and tracked blast of radio waves definitely has expanded the boundaries of the cosmos that can be probed with FRBs. "In principle, sufficiently powerful bursts could be detectable from the very early universe," team member Kavya Shaji said. That means that FRBs are emerging as a promising way to study the first stars and galaxies in the universe. This is even more exciting considering that this research validates teaming the JWST with radio telescopes to detect and track FRBs back to their points of origin. "Our results further show the amazing capability of the JWST, where we can push boundaries beyond what was previously possible," team member Themiya Nanayakkara of the University of Sydney said. representative.title: US forces disable ship ‘attempting to run’ Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman | US-Israel war on Iran News | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Al Jazeera Staff

snapshot.title: US forces disable ship ‘attempting to run’ Iran blockade in Gulf of Oman
snapshot.evidenceText: US military jet strikes stern of commercial cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman ‘without harming the crew’, CENTCOM says. United States forces have disabled a commercial cargo vessel in the Gulf of Oman after its crew “ignored repeated warnings and attempted to run the ongoing naval blockade against Iran”, according to Central Command (CENTCOM). A US military fighter jet struck the stern of the Panama-flagged M/V Ocean Molica, also known as the Arika Sun, with a precision munition on Saturday, “fully disabling the ship’s propulsion without harming the crew”, CENTCOM said in a statement. The vessel was attempting to transit regional waters after “having previously departed an Iranian port”. CENTCOM said its forces resumed their blockade against all ships “entering or departing Iranian ports on July 14”, disabling four commercial vessels and turning around 135 ships during “three months of strict enforcement”. US forces also destroyed 10 tankers linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) “multibillion-dollar shadow network” over the same period, CENTCOM said. US Senator Chris Murphy questioned the military strike, writing on X: “What is this all for? Why are taxpayers paying billions to hit commercial ships?” “Apparently the goal is to gain leverage in order to convince the Iranians to let us pay them billions to return everything to the way it all was before the war,” the Democratic politician added. “What a disaster.” The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency acknowledged the incident on Sunday, saying that it had received “a report of an incident involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman” and that authorities were investigating. Meanwhile, the IRGC said it struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz for attempting to take an “illegal route”, as Tehran seeks to enforce its own blockade on the vital waterway. In a statement carried by official Iranian media, the IRGC claimed Iranian forces “have taken control of the administration of the strait”. “In carrying out this mission, a few hours ago, a giant LPG carrier named NV Sunshine, owned by NatWit, which was attempting to transit via the illegal route south of the Strait of Hormuz, was struck,” the statement said. The UKMTO said on Sunday that an outbound tanker in the strait was struck on the port side by an unknown projectile, causing a fire on board. The UK agency said crew members were reported safe, while the damage and environmental impact remained unknown at the time of the report. Tehran has attempted to enforce control over the Strait of Hormuz during the US-Israel war on Iran, insisting that ships obtain permission to cross via its preferred routes. However, vessels have increasingly risked taking an alternative route hugging the strait’s southern coast. The UK maritime agency said on Thursday that a vessel sailing 94km (58 miles) north of Madinat ash Shamal, off the north coast of Qatar, was struck by multiple projectiles, resulting in several casualties. The agency did not specify the origin of the ship or the number of people killed or injured, adding that authorities were investigating the incident amid a recent rise in attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz. Ships in the Gulf attempting to cross the strait, which is the sole maritime route in or out of the oil-rich region, have faced repeated attacks since the US and Israel began the war in late February. The Strait of Hormuz remains vital to the global economy, with about a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passing through the passage before the war began.

representative.title: China shock: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports | Fortune
representative.author: Sam McNeil, Kanis Leung, Elaine Kurtenbach, The Associated Press

snapshot.title: EU says trade deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese EV and plug-in hybrid imports and lower tariffs for some European exports to China | Fortune
snapshot.evidenceText: The top trade envoys for China and the European Union agreed Friday on a broad initial deal following two days of talks aimed at calming escalating tensions over trade imbalances, the EU trade commissioner said. Neither side provided clear details on the preliminary deal, but European Commissioner for Trade Maros Sefcovic said it includes lower tariffs for some European goods to China as well as measures to stabilize rare earth supply chains. The EU trade envoy said the deal could cut up to 50% of Chinese electric and plug-in hybrid vehicle imports to the EU and could lower tariffs on products benefiting “almost every” EU nation. The deal would require approval from leaders across the 27-nation EU. He said that “by this step we are actually preventing several millions of car exports from China to the European Union.” The two sides were seeking to resolve key factors behind China’s growing trade surplus, which hit 360 billion euros ($403 billion) last year. China’s Commerce Ministry posted online that Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao expressed concerns about the EU’s recent restrictive measures. He said that China is not the root of the EU’s problems but a partner in solving them. The head of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association, Sigrid de Vries, said that the deal appears to avert further instability in the EU and “can help facilitate the transition to a new era of Chinese presence in the European market in an orderly way and this is in the long-term interests of all parties.” Sefcovic said he will brief EU leaders meeting in Brussels next week and seek their approval. “They would have to see that this is convincing enough to take the other steps,” he said. “We are in a situation that they (China) could put under the threat whole sectors in the European industry, literally thousands of jobs and the public opinion and the leaders clearly expect very fast action from our side.” Sefcovic also said both sides reached understandings to further facilitate China’s export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets, as well as to improve access to the Chinese market for various EU products through lower most-favored-nation tariffs, including car parts, olive oil and footwear, totaling almost 4 billion euros (about $4.5 billion) in current export value. The two sides will meet next by video in January and then in person in March. China has been pushing for the EU to stop blocking Chinese imports of advanced computer chipmaking machines, restrictions imposed on national security grounds at Washington’s behest. Earlier, Sefcovic had said the talks this week were the culmination of three months of intensive work. He had set an October deadline for meaningful results on trade rebalancing. Earlier in the week, the Chinese Commerce Ministry issued a statement urging the EU to avoid protectionist measures, warning that such moves could backfire. Trade tensions have grown in recent months, with both sides imposing or considering curbs on each other’s imports. The EU has moved to limit imports of Chinese-made electric vehicles and EV batteries and enacted measures to protect the European steel industry. It also is limiting duty-free imports of e-commerce small parcels, essentially targeting Chinese fast fashion firms. Last week, China launched an anti-dumping investigation into imports from the EU of p-nitrotoluene, a chemical compound used in dyes and pharmaceuticals. Chinese officials and businesses have raised concerns over reports some EU members are pushing for new measures to protect local industries. Worries over surging Chinese exports to Europe and other parts of the world in what some are calling a China shock 2.0 have deepened as the U.S., especially since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to the White House, has raised tariffs and enacted other measures to try to reduce its own huge trade deficit with Beijing. Despite the backlash from some of its trading partners, China’s global trade surplus hit $1.2 trillion in 2025 and is forecast to surpass $1 trillion again this year. The EU’s trade deficit with China widened to 103.3 billion euros (about $116 billion) in the second quarter, as imports rose to 153.6 billion euros ($172 billion), while European exports to China climbed to 50.3 billion euros ($56 billion), according to EU statistics. And on Wednesday, Germany blocked the sale of a major logistics firm in the port of Hamburg to the state-owned Chinese shipping behemoth Cosco over security concerns. “As Europe’s largest economy, Germany welcomes foreign investment. At the same time, some investments can endanger the country’s security,” the German economic ministry said in a statement. “The acquisition would have deepened dependencies and jeopardized the resilience of supply chains in Germany and the EU.”
snapshot.imageAlt: Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, meets with European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 9, 2026.

representative.title: Singapore Parliament passes 2026 Finance Bill with Pillar Two amendments – oecdpillars.com
representative.author: Lee Hadnum

snapshot.title: Singapore Parliament passes 2026 Finance Bill with Pillar Two amendments – oecdpillars.com
snapshot.evidenceText: Singapore’s Parliament passed the Finance (Income Taxes) Bill 2026 (Bill No. 22/2026) on 6 October 2026. The Bill contains a substantial package of amendments to the Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Act 2024 (MMTA), including statutory powers for Singapore’s implementation of the OECD Side-by-Side Safe Harbour, revised GloBE Information Return (GIR) filing and exchange rules, return-exemption powers and detailed domestic top-up tax accounting provisions. Parliamentary passage is not the same as commencement. The Bill still requires presidential assent and publication as an Act. Several provisions will then depend on ministerial commencement notifications or regulations. This article therefore describes the passed Bill, not law already in force. The official second-reading speech confirms the policy purpose of the amendments, while the Bill supplies the operative text. Singapore consulted in June 2026 on a narrower set of Side-by-Side changes. As discussed in our earlier analysis , those proposals focused on allowing the safe harbour to apply to stateless entities and on a dynamic reference to OECD qualification decisions. The introduced Bill, first read on 8 September, is materially broader. Clauses 36–50 now amend the MMTA across definitions, filing, exchange, penalties, exemptions, appeals, secrecy, regulation-making and DTT accounting. The renumbering is also important. The Side-by-Side provisions appear in clauses 38 and 49(b) of Bill 22/2026, rather than the clause numbers used in the consultation draft. The remaining clauses are not merely drafting support for that safe harbour; they establish separate compliance and administrative rules that groups will need to map into Singapore processes. Clause 38 amends MMTA section 20 so that a GloBE safe harbour may apply in relation to a stateless entity. That change is needed for Singapore to give effect to the Side-by-Side Safe Harbour, which uses a simplified jurisdictional effective tax rate test and can require stateless entities to be taken into account. Clause 49(b) allows regulations to identify the relevant OECD qualification material by reference to the version published on the OECD website at a specified time. The Bill treats both provisions as effective from 1 January 2026. The second-reading speech states that US-parented groups qualifying for the Side-by-Side Safe Harbour would be exempt from Singapore’s multinational enterprise top-up tax (MTT), while Singapore’s domestic top-up tax (DTT) would continue to apply. That distinction follows the architecture of the safe harbour: it protects qualifying groups from specified IIR and UTPR exposure, but does not disapply a jurisdiction’s QDMTT. Clause 36 expands the statutory definition of a GIR so that it can include an equivalent return required under the domestic law of a foreign jurisdiction for a qualified UTPR, QDMTT, MTT or DTT. Clauses 40 and 41 then separate two legal questions: whether the return is required under the foreign jurisdiction’s domestic law, and whether Singapore has a qualifying exchange relationship with that jurisdiction. The distinction is significant because central filing relies on both an obligation to file and an effective mechanism for Singapore to receive the information. The Bill also creates a local fallback where exchange does not deliver the return. These amendments move Singapore beyond the consultation-stage safe-harbour proposal and towards an integrated statutory framework for administration of the first MMTA reporting cycles. Clause 42 inserts a new MMTA section 40(4A). Where a GIR has been filed centrally outside Singapore but is not received by the Comptroller within the required period under a qualifying competent authority agreement, the Comptroller may require the designated local GIR filing entity to file it in Singapore. The deadline specified in the notice must be at least one month after the notice is given. If you haven’t got a subscription you can join up below. representative.title: Falling catches threaten Ho Chi Minh City’s oldest fishing village | DTiNews

snapshot.title: Falling catches threaten Ho Chi Minh City’s oldest fishing village | DTiNews
snapshot.evidenceText: Dawn comes early in Phuoc Hai, in Ho Chi Minh City’s Vung Tau area. At around 6 am, small round basket boats return to shore after a night at sea, carrying catches of fish, squid, shrimp and crabs. The sight of the little circular boats against the blue water has become a defining feature of the fishing village beneath Minh Dam Mountain. As the boats reach shore, fishermen hurry to untangle their nets and sort their seafood to keep it fresh before taking it to market. Nguyen Ngoc Chau, 55, was visibly disappointed after returning from a night at sea with only a few crabs. “Seafood catches have fallen significantly in recent years,” he said. “We used to earn an average of VND 500,000 (about USD 19) a night. Now we make only around VND 200,000 (about USD 7.70).” Nguyen, 46, who has been part of the village since childhood, said about 80 per cent of residents depended on fishing for their livelihoods. “Things are different now. There are fewer fish. Those who can afford it have replaced their basket boats with larger vessels equipped with GPS, fish-finding equipment and radios so they can fish farther offshore. Those of us who fish close to shore earn very little,” he said. More than a century after its establishment, Phuoc Hai continues to follow the rhythms of life at sea. After selling their catch, fishermen return home to mend nets and rest before preparing their gear for the next trip in the late afternoon or evening. Le Huu Duc, 58, said basket boats used relatively little fuel but yielded smaller catches. On calm days, he might bring home several dozen kilos of fish; in rough seas, the catch could fall to just 5-7kg. He said he had to make two trips a day to earn enough to support his three-member household. representative.title: The Man Behind a West Bank Telegram Channel Trying to Keep Palestinian Drivers Safe | WIRED
representative.author: Lama Rabah

snapshot.title: The Man Behind a West Bank Telegram Channel Trying to Keep Palestinian Drivers Safe
snapshot.evidenceText: At 30, Hattab’s life now revolves around these checkpoints—perhaps more than any other Palestinian in the occupied West Bank. But he has also transformed his community’s approach to them: Nearly 350,000 people follow his traffic Telegram group, which has closed a gap left open by major navigation apps that fail Palestinian users. Local radio stations build their hourly road segments off his dispatches. A routing system used by West Bank companies and a new local app pull his data into their own. It began in 2019. Hattab was working during the day as a digital designer at a newspaper in Ramallah. When one shift ended, he started another, this time as the paper’s delivery driver. That meant that most nights, Hattab had to drive all around the West Bank. After loading the fresh editions into his car, he would drive north, looping through the cities of Nablus and Jenin, eventually reaching his home in Tulkarm by dawn. He found himself dodging Israeli military raids, settlements he had to route around and, most of all, unpredictable checkpoints, which could cause hours-long delays and where armed Israeli soldiers could search him or his car. For decades, Israel has restricted or barred Palestinian vehicles from many of the main arteries through the West Bank, while Israeli vehicles pass freely. Popular navigation apps like Google Maps don't account for any of it. They do not mark the 942 checkpoints, gates, and other barriers that now fragment the territory, and they default to what their algorithms deem the fastest routes, many of which run through settlements and areas under Israeli control. A Palestinian driver who follows their directions risks being arrested, fined, or shot. Navigating these uncertain roads, night after night, wore on Hattab. He knew he wasn't the only one. “People were scared to leave their governorates,” he says. At the core of that fear was an information void. So he began devising a way to fill it, for himself and every other Palestinian in the West Bank. Seven years ago, Hattab launched a Telegram group called “Road Conditions.” The idea was that people would share information with each other about movements at checkpoints—warn each other about delays or closures, about settler or military presence and violence. Hattab posted the link in local news groups, and waited. They came in a trickle, at first, and then, as checkpoints began to multiply in 2022 and delays got worse, they came in a flood. As more people joined Road Conditions, the pressure on Hattab mounted. When checkpoints locked down major cities, the number of users could spike, sometimes by thousands at a time. Dozens of commuters would ask about the same checkpoint, and answers would pour in at once. “Clear,” “open,” “closed.” All three could be true within the same hour. "Ten minutes is a long time," Hattab says. "Things change instantly." The questions landed on him, thousands of messages a day. “In the beginning,” he says, “I barely slept.” When Hattab started Road Conditions, his odometer read 70,000 kilometers. Within four years it read 274,000, inside a territory barely 130 kilometers from tip to tip. It is the equivalent of driving around the Earth more than five times, without ever leaving the West Bank. What began as a crowdsourced tool for people to help each other navigate the occupied West Bank was becoming an essential utility. To keep Road Conditions reliable, soon after launching the group in 2019, Hattab closed the public chat and asked the most active contributors to become moderators. More than a dozen volunteers now run the feed. Drivers from every corner of the West Bank send them reports, usually with a photo or video. Moderators check these updates by asking others on the ground, cross-checking other local pages, or driving the roads themselves. As Road Conditions grew, users asked about roads in cities Hattab had never been to. Nothing goes out until he or the moderators have checked it. Before posting a checkpoint is closed, they need to know where it is, whom to ask to verify the update, and what route a driver can take instead. So for six months, Hattab spent his days off driving with no destination. "I'd get in the car, get lost, wherever I ended up, I ended up," he says. He stopped to ask locals for the name of every checkpoint and bypass road until he held the whole map of alternative routes in his head. After October 7, 2023, a situation that was already dangerous became a crisis. An investigation we published in September, in partnership with the Palestine Reporting Lab, Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism, and Lighthouse Reports, found that checkpoint delays have increased by more than 50 percent since then. Our analysis found that the average commuter in the West Bank now loses about 77 hours every year taking roundabout routes to avoid checkpoints. Towns that were once quick, 10-minute drives apart have been severed by gates and other obstacles that turn those trips into hour-long voyages. To arrive at our analysis, we went searching for data about checkpoint delays, about when they are open and closed. No official data exists. So our reporting team looked to the Telegram group that Hattab built, scraping the updates that originated from Road Conditions to produce a comprehensive database of the way checkpoints work. Not long after October 2023, Hattab was driving home at 2 in the morning when a soldier at a checkpoint near the city of Qalqilya stopped him and took his phone. The soldier scrolled through some 20,000 photos Hattab had received on the group of traffic around checkpoints. “You photographed a military site!” the soldier said, then stepped aside to speak with an officer on his radio. The soldier came back and ordered Hattab to delete everything. “I started deleting, in all naivety,” Hattab says. He had erased thousands of photos before the soldier walked back over and told him to go. “I make sure not to show the military jeeps, not to show one soldier,” Hattab says. Hattab quit the newspaper and took a job as a sales representative for a construction equipment company because it would put him on a different road every day. “My point is not sales,” he said. “It's Road Conditions.” Israeli settlers, living in the nearly 150 official settlements and an additional 185 new “outposts” established in the West Bank since 2023—all of which are illegal under international law—have in recent years become a daily threat. In March 2025, at the Yitzhar junction on Route 60, near Nablus, Hattab watched a settler cut off a coffee bean delivery truck directly ahead of him, get out, and beat the driver in the middle of the road. “He was screaming and cursing, armed, beating the driver, grabbing him, punching him, grabbing him again,” he says. Hattab posted the update to the group. That year, the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission documented nearly 5,443 settler attacks. In the first eight months of 2026, it recorded about 4,766. At 4 o’clock one January morning in 2025, news was circulating about Israeli troops on the road out of the city of Tulkarm. By 7, no one knew if they were still there, and no one wanted to be the one to find out. Hattab was heading from his home in Tulkarm to Ramallah that morning. He started the car. He turned onto the road that people had been asking about and drove slowly, watching the road ahead. The path was clear. He posted it to the group. “By the grace of God, it was easy this time,” he says. Hattab knows the roads better, he would wager, than almost anyone now. When a major junction closes, he can predict the closures that follow across a whole corridor, “like dominoes,” he says. “Think of ants. You set their path with a toothpick on the ground.” With no institutional support and two young children, Hattab sometimes doubts if he can keep going: “You’re supposed to give your family the best life, not give up stable income for a Telegram group.” To him, it's already more than that. Other innovators have stepped into the fray, launching new apps and groups to help drivers manage traffic. In 2025, for instance, computer engineers Musab Nuirat and Ahmed Gharib launched A Ween Rayeh (Where Are You Heading?). It’s a Palestinian application that aggregates data to produce a real-time heat map of traffic. It was, by Nuirat’s count, the seventh local attempt to build a functional navigation system in the West Bank. And like nearly all the other efforts, A Ween Rayeh relied on Hattab’s data to update its map. Hattab knows how important what he’s built has become. So he continues. Hattab knows the operation should be 10 times the size. And he knows he should be able to compensate the moderators. But as a volunteer himself, he has no way to pay them. “I can't give them more than a thank you,” he says. Hattab considers it his duty. “You know how a taxi driver has souls with him in the car, and he has to drive carefully? Same principle.” Mistakes happen, no one can verify every update in real time. “In the end,” he says, “aren't we living in this country at our own risk?”

representative.title: Still wielding a chainsaw at 85: the Australians restoring nature in retirement | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
representative.author: Rosamund Brennan

snapshot.title: Still wielding a chainsaw at 85: the Australians restoring nature in retirement
snapshot.evidenceText: For a growing band of older Australians, retirement has become an unlikely second act, spent rewilding mountains, counting sea slugs and coaxing damaged country back to life When Susan Downes stepped into the hallway of an old farmhouse for sale in York, Western Australia , she felt an oddly certain sense of knowing. “Oh, this is my house,” the retired GP remembers thinking. There was just one problem: it came with 200 hectares. Widowed and with her children grown, Downes, then in her 60s, was finally able to act on a long-held wish to move to the countryside. She had imagined something modest: an old house with “a little bit of garden and stuff”. Two hundred hectares was rather more than she had in mind, no matter how charming she found the high ceilings. “I thought, the house is lovely, but I can’t possibly do that.” But the property had gotten under her skin. Returning for another look two weeks later, she discovered Mount Mackie, a 295-metre hill at the back of the farm where ancient York gums and wandoos had survived about 150 years of grazing. Almost all of the understorey had disappeared. “These magnificent old trees” were all that remained. “I felt a great connection to the land,” she says. Downes, now 76, bought the property and slowly began restoring it. She started with a small local grant to control foxes and feral cats. Then she applied for another, and was awarded 24,000 trees over three years. “I thought, OK, I can start doing this,” says Downes, who began her career as a botanist. “This is what I really want to do.” Today, about 45,000 native seedlings have been planted, while a further 45 plant species have reappeared naturally from the seed bank. The restoration now spans 120 hectares of Downes’ working farm, which she is placing under a conservation covenant so it can never again be cleared. The work is supported by Friends of Mt Mackie, a volunteer group with a core crew of about eight alongside more than 80 volunteers who join organised planting and seed-collecting days. Downes’ days are spent rebaiting live traps, weeding and planting, and dealing with what she jokingly calls “all this bloody admin”. But the payoff is considerable. “Some of the trees are now taller than I am,” she says proudly. “You can see them from two or three kilometres away.” Downes is part of a large cohort of Australians spending their spare time repairing the natural world. The latest Australian Bureau of Statistics data suggests roughly 290,000 Australians volunteer through environmental protection or animal welfare organisations. Older Australians are particularly prominent: in Landcare Australia’s 2026 national survey, 80% of respondents were aged 55 or over. Peter Garrett, Landcare Australia’s chair, calls older Australians “the backbone” of the movement. Retirement brings more time, he says, but also a chance to reassess priorities and think about what will be left for children and grandchildren. “The sort of stirring song of the Australian bush calls to them,” he says. In a world of crises that can feel beyond individual control, conservation offers something tangible. People may not be able to change everything, Garrett says, but they can look after “our back yard, our bit of bush down in the gully, our creeks and streams”. This can bring “a lot of purpose” in later life. For 70-year-old Lyn Sharp of the Gold Coast , conservation volunteering began with sea slugs. Five years ago she joined a project to count and monitor them at Burleigh Heads. Immediately she felt she had found her place. “That was it,” she says. “I was hooked.” Sharp spent most of her career in the cheese industry and, for 23 years, lived on a steep bush block on Tamborine Mountain that absorbed much of her spare time. After retiring and downsizing to a townhouse in Nerang, she redirected that energy into national parks, council reserves, waterways and beaches. Sea slugs were just the beginning. Sharp soon added water bug, turtle and platypus surveys, seagrass monitoring and bush regeneration. Cane toad season brought nocturnal hunts and calls from people needing somewhere to drop them off. She now volunteers up to 15 hours a week. Some of the work is becoming harder. Bursitis in her hip makes the repeated squatting involved in surveys painful, while a troublesome shoulder has flared up too. Sharp remains determined. “What am I going to do? Sit around like a veggie?” she says. “No one’s gonna stop me.” On the Edward River in New South Wales , 30km outside Deniliquin in the Riverina, 85-year-old Ken Hooper and his wife, Jill, 82, have spent decades restoring damaged country. “It’s a bit addictive,” Ken says. In 1992 the Hoopers bought Wirra-Lo, a 180-hectare property in northern Victoria, as part of their dairy farming operation. When they retired, they kept it, placed it under a conservation covenant and began the painstaking work of restoring its bush and wetlands. Even that was not enough. Looking for somewhere to spend their retirement, they found Moona-Bingel in NSW, where a conservation agreement now covers 970 hectares of country they have spent more than 20 years restoring. For a time, they ran both projects, with Ken frequently driving 100km back to Wirra-Lo – and sometimes camping there. In 2023 the pair sold it to the Wetland Revival Trust. Ken is still nowhere near done. “No retirement involved,” he says. At Moona-Bingel, the work is relentless: weeds, feral animals, revegetation and flood management. Despite osteoarthritis and two replacement knees, he still uses a chainsaw. Red deer are a particular irritation, capable of smashing a carefully nurtured 2-metre tree below knee height. “The rotten bugger,” he says. But there are rewards almost daily: new birds, breeding carpet pythons and native vegetation spreading by itself. “You’ve got to have something, because that’s what keeps you going,” Ken says. Jill jokes that “there needs to be three of us … There’s just not enough time in the day.” Ken reckons even three might not be enough. “We need another two lifetimes to do what we’d like to do.” Back at Mount Mackie, Downes contemplates what will remain when she is gone. The deaths and dementia diagnoses of friends have changed the way she thinks about the time she has left. “I suddenly realised I might not even have a day,” she says. What remains unresolved is who will ultimately take responsibility for it, her grandchildren or some kind of society or organisation: “I need to have it set in stone.” She hopes her children and grandchildren, seeing what she has done, will be inspired to care for the natural world in their own way. She also wants Mount Mackie to remain a place the wider community can use and share. Several times a year, Ballardong women from York come to the hill for cultural healing sessions. Downes is working with Ballardong elders to find an Aboriginal name for Mount Mackie, with planning also under way for a 2030 reconciliation event marking 200 years since European arrival in the region. “It’s no use to me being there by myself,” Downes says. What brings her the most joy is “seeing people love the place … having people share it with me”.

representative.author: Derrick A Paulo

snapshot.title: Inside Thailand’s cyanide murders and the search for its ‘most prolific serial killer’ in history
snapshot.evidenceText: When healthy people suddenly began dying, grieving families struggled to get answers. The series, Death Loans, retraces how a dogged investigator looking into a friend’s death helped police connect 15 cases to one woman eventually. BANGKOK: When her friend gave her some herbal medicine for her cough, Kantima “Pla” Paesaard did not think too much about it. She wasn’t to know it would turn out to be an alleged murder attempt. Less than 10 minutes after they went their separate ways, Pla started feeling short of breath. So she turned on the air-conditioner in her car and got a strong draught blowing at her face. “But no matter how I tried to breathe, I still couldn’t,” she recalled. After she called an ambulance, her hands started to stiffen. When the ambulance arrived a few minutes later, only her little finger could move a bit, she said. And once she was in the ambulance, “everything just went black”. This service is not intended for persons residing in the E.U. By clicking subscribe, I agree to receive news updates and promotional material from Mediacorp and Mediacorp’s partners. Loading Hours went by before she started to awake. “After I regained consciousness, my husband told me, ‘Do you know that earlier, your heart had actually stopped beating?’” she recounted. “The doctor told me they did a brain scan. They checked my blood and examined my whole body, and there was nothing abnormal. So I thought it was an allergic reaction to the herbal medicine.” Her friend, Sararat “Aem” Rangsiwuthaporn, checked on her in hospital, seemingly worried for her health. Pla did not suspect anything. They had known each other for about 10 years. Their husbands — or ex-husband, in Aem’s case — were from the same police academy class. “I felt like Aem was part of the family. We’d always visit each other,” she said. Two months later, in November 2022, when the two friends went to a gathering together, Pla’s mum asked Aem (also spelt as Am) why she looked thinner. Weight-loss pills, she replied. “So my mum said, ‘If that’s the case, bring some for Pla to try so she can lose weight too,’” Pla recounted. After the gathering ended, Aem brought over the pills to their house in Thailand’s Kanchanaburi province. But Pla chose not to take them. She still did not have any suspicions of her friend, not until she heard the news about a woman who had been poisoned with cyanide months later, with Aem present at the scene. Pla, then 36, started googling the symptoms of cyanide poisoning and found that they included difficulty breathing and stiff hands. “At that moment, I was very shocked,” she said. She was the only survivor out of 15 victims identified by the police in what has become a historic set of cases, involving a pattern of deaths in different provinces starting as far back as 2015. Aem, now 39, is the “most prolific serial killer in Thai history”, according to Surachate Hakparn, the deputy police chief from 2022 to 2024. “She’s killed more people than Jack the Ripper, the Zodiac and BTK (did individually),” he charged. Only one of those three — BTK (Bind, Torture, Kill), the moniker for American killer Dennis Rader — was caught. And it took one of the largest investigations ever conducted in Thailand for the Royal Thai Police to catch their killer better known as Aem Cyanide. The series, Death Loans , tells how the country’s cyanide murders finally ended. WATCH PART 1: ‘She didn’t go alone’ — This CCTV footage helped expose Thai serial killer (46:57) Most of the victims were in their 30s and healthy. All died under mysterious circumstances. In Mukdahan province, Sawitree “Nim” Budsrirak, 40, had just given birth to a baby girl, “exactly as we’d hoped”, said her husband, Nitipon “Ta” Nuchit. A month later, in November 2020, he was back at work in Bangkok, 650km away. Nim was taking care of the children — their newborn and their five-year-old son — and cleaning the house. One day when he was on his break, he tried video-calling Nim. She did not answer. Then he sent her a message. It was left unread. So he video-called his son, Neo. “I asked him, ‘Who are you with? Where’s Mummy? I want to talk to Mummy.’ Neo turned the camera towards the mattress. I saw Nim lying face down, with her face resting on the edge of the mattress,” he recounted. Thinking that Nim was tired and had taken a nap, he decided to end the call. “After no more than 30 minutes, I tried video-calling again,” he continued. “Neo answered as before and turned the camera towards Nim, who was still lying in the same position. That’s when I realised something was wrong.” He immediately called a neighbour to check on Nim. Her lips had turned dark bluish, a trickle of blood was oozing from her mouth, and her body was covered in sweat. “Nim was found dead on the bed while our daughter was sleeping only a few feet away,” Ta said. “Nim was playing just fine with the children. It’s impossible that she’d then die. How could something like this happen?” At that time, he wasn’t to know the answer lay in Thailand’s money-sharing circles. These are rotating savings groups whose members save together. The money they contribute regularly is pooled, which members can borrow when needed. These loans are not free. Members pay a monthly interest — setting the rate themselves beforehand — on loans taken out from the group’s fund. They must also continue their regular contributions as they repay the loans. “It’s estimated that millions of Thais participate in share groups, with billions of baht estimated to be in circulation,” said Piriya Pholphirul, an economics professor at the National Institute of Development Administration. Nim was one of them, joining in as a way of earning additional income, said Ta. Sharing circles have existed for generations, built on friendship and trust. But the problem was that she joined an online sharing group with Aem. For another victim, Surat “Bee” Toraphap, 35, his friendship with Aem went back to childhood. They had been schoolmates. In January 2021, his brother “Koon” was at a temple when a neighbour in Kanchanaburi’s Tha Maka district called to say that Bee was in the bathroom and turning blue. Koon hurried over. “There were police all over the house. I saw my younger sibling sitting on the toilet in the bathroom, leaning to the right. I realised my sibling was no longer with me,” he said. “My younger brother was healthy, didn’t drink and didn’t smoke. His death was abnormal. I started getting suspicious and unlocked my brother’s phone and wondered why this friend named ‘Aem’ wasn’t responding to him.” It turned out that Bee had lent her money: 50,000 baht (US$1,500) at first and then another 10,000 baht. But for all of Koon’s suspicions, his brother’s death was classified as natural, as was the case for Nim and other victims. Aem’s victims could be categorised in a few groups, such as those in savings groups where she was the organiser, those whom she borrowed money from and those who loaned her money to lend out to others. One of the people she invited to lend money through her was her friend Siriporn “Koy” Khanwong, 32. On Apr 14, 2023, Koy told her mother she was going to run an errand. “She told me to wait,” recalled Thongpin Kiatchanasiri. “She said she’d come back in the evening and take me shopping. But she never came back.” Koy had two phones. “If one phone was off, the other one would still be on,” said her elder sister, Nipawan “Som” Khanwong. “But that day, both phones were off at the same time. I was so anxious, wondering why.” As Koy’s family tried to figure out where she was, a friend of hers, independent investigator Rapee Chamnanrua, received a photo of a person the police in Ratchaburi province were trying to identify. It was Koy. She had fainted and died by the Mae Klong River, 80km west of Bangkok. The police cited the official cause of death as a heart attack. But her mother “didn’t believe that her heart would fail”. “My daughter was only 32, healthy and strong,” said Thongpin, now 65. “I was shocked. I felt I was losing my sanity. … I kept asking where her bag went, where her phone went, because they were all gone.” Som also “felt something was wrong”, but the police “wouldn’t listen”, she recounted. The family’s request for a further probe into Koy’s death was turned down. Her body was returned to them the next day for Buddhist rites and cremation. The first person who listened to the family and thought her death was unnatural was Rapee. “How could someone so young just die so suddenly?” he questioned. “Because I knew her, this case was special (to me).” But at first, his investigation went down the wrong path. The family suspected a former boyfriend who had allegedly threatened her. This was a police officer named Navin — whose alibi ruled him out, according to the police. Doubting that the police would implicate one of their own, Rapee “asked people to go check on Navin”. He reasoned: “Navin had an intimate relationship with Koy.” Above all else, however, he wanted “someone in authority” to hear the family out before her cremation. So they met the police general Surachate, who is known in Thailand by his nickname, “Big Joke”. “I put all the evidence in front of him and asked him if he felt the local police had done their job,” recounted Rapee, who cited Koy’s missing belongings, among other things. “A heart attack doesn’t make belongings disappear.” Surachate gave credit to Rapee for getting him involved in the case. His own suspicions were aroused when Rapee showed him the autopsy report, which recorded that Koy was healthy. “This was unusual,” he said, adding that Navin’s alleged threats were also “concerning”. Things started moving “much faster” after Surachate got involved in the case, said Som. For example, the police called her in to watch the footage from the closed-circuit television cameras pointed towards the walkway along the river. Rapee said they were “very lucky” because the cameras had been recently repaired after being “broken for a long time”. Meanwhile, a second, more detailed autopsy was performed on Koy. When the toxicology results came out, forensic pathologist Smith Srisont, who ran the test, “was very shocked”. It was a cyanide poisoning case. His colleague at Ramathibodi Hospital, internal medicine doctor Sahaphume Srisuma, had “never seen this before” in his practice in Thailand. “Cyanide is one of the most lethal chemical compounds known to mankind. It’s virtually untraceable,” said Sahaphume. “The most dangerous thing is cyanide is lethal either by ingestion or inhalation. All it takes is a tiny dose, maybe smaller than a grain of rice.” That was not the only evidence that “changed the case immediately” as Surachate described. CCTV footage showed that when Koy went to release fish at the Mae Klong pier, she did not go alone. She was with Aem. It turned out Koy had transferred 300,000 baht to Aem for her to invest “because she was a friend and we trusted her”, said Som, who shared that she herself first met Aem at age 16. “Aem was very chatty, and she got along with people easily,” Som added. “But her personality changed when it came to money. She started getting involved with money matters, talking about it, pushing it, things like that.” Aem’s financial motives led the police to follow the money trail, which eventually led to gambling websites and gambling dens. “I’ll give one example. She was travelling from Kanchanaburi to Nakhon Pathom. She found a gambling den along the way. She goes straight in, plays and loses 10 million baht,” cited Surachate. “Whose money was that? Money she’d just borrowed from people.” Online savings groups and instant bank transfers — plus misplaced trust — allowed money to move with ease and feed her gambling addiction. “When asked to repay, if there’s no money to clear debts, what do you do?” remarked Surachate. Citing what he learnt from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, he added: “Serial killers, if they’re men, will commit crimes outside the city, and the motive is sexual in nature. But if it’s a woman, the motive must be money.” Prior to Aem, there was the case of serial killer Somkid Phumphuang, who raped and killed his victims — six of them — between 2005 and 2019. There are “many contributing factors”, however, in cases like Aem, according to Somdet Chaopraya Institute of Psychiatry deputy director Winyoo Chanakul, who has over 20 years’ experience in caring for psychiatric patients who have committed violent acts or even homicide. “Someone who has financial problems to the point of being able to kill others, and to do so repeatedly, can’t be explained by financial reasons alone. Otherwise, everyone in debt would be killing people,” he said. “The person must have certain personality traits that allow them to commit serious wrongdoing for their own benefit without feeling guilt. This includes a lack of empathy and a disregard for social rules.” Thinking back on Aem’s personality, Som remembered her once saying that if anyone were to fight with her or say something bad, “she wouldn’t let it go” and would “go as far as killing”. When the police arrested Aem, however, senior staff writer Pravit Rojanaphruk at news outlet Khaosod English remembers that “everyone was confused” by this woman from a middle-class background. “She looks just like anyone from an average neighbourhood,” he said. It became a major news story that many people have followed. “No one person has caused this much of an uproar before,” he added, citing the 14 murder charges. She has contested all the charges so far. One of her lawyers, Thannicha “Pat” Aeksuwannawat, said it was “impossible that Aem committed all 14 murders”. “The police want to dump the murder cases onto Aem so they don’t have to find the real perpetrator. It was clear that she was being targeted,” said Pat. “It’s media-driven momentum more than facts. “They said death was due to cyanide. … That cyanide mightn’t have come from Aem. This is the weakness of the case.” Buying cyanide in Thailand is not suspicious on its own. It is used in factories in metal-related industries, such as for metal plating and electroplating. It is used in gold shops and in research. And what the police found was that Aem “never used her own name to order cyanide”, said Surachate. “She had others order it, and then it reached her.” One of the cyanide bottles that the police seized had been sold by a company that called Grab to do the delivery. And the rider took a photo when delivering the cyanide to Aem in her Toyota Fortuner, recounted Rapee. “In that photo, a small pink Hello Kitty bag was visible beside the gear stick. Once the police … impounded the bag, we found this bottle,” he said, adding that the bottle had a registration number showing who the importer was. “Aem used her phone number to contact the company. All the evidence pointed directly to Aem. Game over.” Although Rapee said it was Aem’s “own mistakes that brought her down”, his involvement led to a breakthrough in the case in more ways than one. After he and Koy’s family appealed publicly for information once Aem was fingered as a suspect, his phone began ringing nonstop. Families across Thailand told of similar stories: sudden deaths, missing money and a connection to savings groups. One of those who came forward was Pla. She said Aem had asked for a loan to repay a fund, so she gave her 250,000 baht. “She was my friend. Why would I refuse?” said Pla. But she was lending the money only for a month. Then she asked Aem to return the entire amount as agreed because she had to pay for her car. “Reliving my ordeal wasn’t easy,” said Pla, who did it so that Aem “won’t be able to hurt anyone else again”. Pravit described her role as the “nail in the coffin” for Aem, who was sentenced to death in November 2024 for the murder of Koy. WATCH PART 2: ‘She tried to kill me twice’ — The witness who survived a serial killer (46:59) It is a penalty she deserves, said Thongpin, who was “very close” to Koy. “We’d travel together, perform Buddhist rituals together.” Koy and her sister were also close. Som called her the “pillar of the family” who took care of everyone. “Koy only had one child, so she doted on her. She loved her so much. Whatever the child wanted, she got,” said Som, referring to Koy’s daughter, now 13. “Everything she built, she built it for her daughter.” The murders of Nim and Bee, meanwhile, have not gone to trial yet. Koon said he thinks about his younger brother every day. “And whenever I do, my heart feels as if it’s going to break,” he lamented. As for Ta, if he had the chance, he would want to speak to Nim — whom he lovingly described as “good-hearted” and “always willing to help others” — one more time. “I’d want to thank her for coming into my life as my wife and as the mother of our children, for making my life better and helping me grow and become more mature,” he said. As of Sep 22, the criminal court has delivered three death sentences and two life imprisonments for Aem’s string of cyanide murders, plus acquittals in three cases where the court cited a lack of evidence in her favour. Since the end of 2009, Thailand has carried out only one execution, in 2018, even as several death sentences have been imposed. Aem’s next trial date is Nov 25, for the attempted murder of Pla. Weight-loss pills, she replied. “So my mum said, ‘If that’s the case, bring some for Pla to try so she can lose weight too,’” Pla recounted. After the gathering ended, Aem brought over the pills to their house in Thailand’s Kanchanaburi province. But Pla chose not to take them. She still did not have any suspicions of her friend, not until she heard the news about a woman who had been poisoned with cyanide months later, with Aem present at the scene. Pla, then 36, started googling the symptoms of cyanide poisoning and found that they included difficulty breathing and stiff hands. “At that moment, I was very shocked,” she said. She was the only survivor out of 15 victims identified by the police in what has become a historic set of cases, involving a pattern of deaths in different provinces starting as far back as 2015. Aem, now 39, is the “most prolific serial killer in Thai history”, according to Surachate Hakparn, the deputy police chief from 2022 to 2024. “She’s killed more people than Jack the Ripper, the Zodiac and BTK (did individually),” he charged. Only one of those three — BTK (Bind, Torture, Kill), the moniker for American killer Dennis Rader — was caught. And it took one of the largest investigations ever conducted in Thailand for the Royal Thai Police to catch their killer better known as Aem Cyanide. The series, Death Loans , tells how the country’s cyanide murders finally ended. WATCH PART 1: ‘She didn’t go alone’ — This CCTV footage helped expose Thai serial killer (46:57) Most of the victims were in their 30s and healthy. All died under mysterious circumstances. In Mukdahan province, Sawitree “Nim” Budsrirak, 40, had just given birth to a baby girl, “exactly as we’d hoped”, said her husband, Nitipon “Ta” Nuchit. A month later, in November 2020, he was back at work in Bangkok, 650km away. Nim was taking care of the children — their newborn and their five-year-old son — and cleaning the house. One day when he was on his break, he tried video-calling Nim. She did not answer. Then he sent her a message. It was left unread. So he video-called his son, Neo. “I asked him, ‘Who are you with? Where’s Mummy? I want to talk to Mummy.’ Neo turned the camera towards the mattress. I saw Nim lying face down, with her face resting on the edge of the mattress,” he recounted. Thinking that Nim was tired and had taken a nap, he decided to end the call. “After no more than 30 minutes, I tried video-calling again,” he continued. “Neo answered as before and turned the camera towards Nim, who was still lying in the same position. That’s when I realised something was wrong.” He immediately called a neighbour to check on Nim. Her lips had turned dark bluish, a trickle of blood was oozing from her mouth, and her body was covered in sweat. “Nim was found dead on the bed while our daughter was sleeping only a few feet away,” Ta said. “Nim was playing just fine with the children. It’s impossible that she’d then die. How could something like this happen?” At that time, he wasn’t to know the answer lay in Thailand’s money-sharing circles. These are rotating savings groups whose members save together. The money they contribute regularly is pooled, which members can borrow when needed. These loans are not free. Members pay a monthly interest — setting the rate themselves beforehand — on loans taken out from the group’s fund. They must also continue their regular contributions as they repay the loans. “It’s estimated that millions of Thais participate in share groups, with billions of baht estimated to be in circulation,” said Piriya Pholphirul, an economics professor at the National Institute of Development Administration. Nim was one of them, joining in as a way of earning additional income, said Ta. Sharing circles have existed for generations, built on friendship and trust. But the problem was that she joined an online sharing group with Aem. For another victim, Surat “Bee” Toraphap, 35, his friendship with Aem went back to childhood. They had been schoolmates. In January 2021, his brother “Koon” was at a temple when a neighbour in Kanchanaburi’s Tha Maka district called to say that Bee was in the bathroom and turning blue. Koon hurried over. “There were police all over the house. I saw my younger sibling sitting on the toilet in the bathroom, leaning to the right. I realised my sibling was no longer with me,” he said. “My younger brother was healthy, didn’t drink and didn’t smoke. His death was abnormal. I started getting suspicious and unlocked my brother’s phone and wondered why this friend named ‘Aem’ wasn’t responding to him.” It turned out that Bee had lent her money: 50,000 baht (US$1,500) at first and then another 10,000 baht. But for all of Koon’s suspicions, his brother’s death was classified as natural, as was the case for Nim and other victims. Aem’s victims could be categorised in a few groups, such as those in savings groups where she was the organiser, those whom she borrowed money from and those who loaned her money to lend out to others. One of the people she invited to lend money through her was her friend Siriporn “Koy” Khanwong, 32. On Apr 14, 2023, Koy told her mother she was going to run an errand. “She told me to wait,” recalled Thongpin Kiatchanasiri. “She said she’d come back in the evening and take me shopping. But she never came back.” Koy had two phones. “If one phone was off, the other one would still be on,” said her elder sister, Nipawan “Som” Khanwong. “But that day, both phones were off at the same time. I was so anxious, wondering why.” As Koy’s family tried to figure out where she was, a friend of hers, independent investigator Rapee Chamnanrua, received a photo of a person the police in Ratchaburi province were trying to identify. It was Koy. She had fainted and died by the Mae Klong River, 80km west of Bangkok. The police cited the official cause of death as a heart attack. But her mother “didn’t believe that her heart would fail”. “My daughter was only 32, healthy and strong,” said Thongpin, now 65. “I was shocked. I felt I was losing my sanity. … I kept asking where her bag went, where her phone went, because they were all gone.” Som also “felt something was wrong”, but the police “wouldn’t listen”, she recounted. The family’s request for a further probe into Koy’s death was turned down. Her body was returned to them the next day for Buddhist rites and cremation. The first person who listened to the family and thought her death was unnatural was Rapee. “How could someone so young just die so suddenly?” he questioned. “Because I knew her, this case was special (to me).” But at first, his investigation went down the wrong path. The family suspected a former boyfriend who had allegedly threatened her. This was a police officer named Navin — whose alibi ruled him out, according to the police. Doubting that the police would implicate one of their own, Rapee “asked people to go check on Navin”. He reasoned: “Navin had an intimate relationship with Koy.” Above all else, however, he wanted “someone in authority” to hear the family out before her cremation. So they met the police general Surachate, who is known in Thailand by his nickname, “Big Joke”. “I put all the evidence in front of him and asked him if he felt the local police had done their job,” recounted Rapee, who cited Koy’s missing belongings, among other things. “A heart attack doesn’t make belongings disappear.” Surachate gave credit to Rapee for getting him involved in the case. His own suspicions were aroused when Rapee showed him the autopsy report, which recorded that Koy was healthy. “This was unusual,” he said, adding that Navin’s alleged threats were also “concerning”. Things started moving “much faster” after Surachate got involved in the case, said Som. For example, the police called her in to watch the footage from the closed-circuit television cameras pointed towards the walkway along the river. Rapee said they were “very lucky” because the cameras had been recently repaired after being “broken for a long time”. Meanwhile, a second, more detailed autopsy was performed on Koy. When the toxicology results came out, forensic pathologist Smith Srisont, who ran the test, “was very shocked”. It was a cyanide poisoning case. His colleague at Ramathibodi Hospital, internal medicine doctor Sahaphume Srisuma, had “never seen this before” in his practice in Thailand. “Cyanide is one of the most lethal chemical compounds known to mankind. It’s virtually untraceable,” said Sahaphume. “The most dangerous thing is cyanide is lethal either by ingestion or inhalation. All it takes is a tiny dose, maybe smaller than a grain of rice.” That was not the only evidence that “changed the case immediately” as Surachate described. CCTV footage showed that when Koy went to release fish at the Mae Klong pier, she did not go alone. She was with Aem. It turned out Koy had transferred 300,000 baht to Aem for her to invest “because she was a friend and we trusted her”, said Som, who shared that she herself first met Aem at age 16. “Aem was very chatty, and she got along with people easily,” Som added. “But her personality changed when it came to money. She started getting involved with money matters, talking about it, pushing it, things like that.” Aem’s financial motives led the police to follow the money trail, which eventually led to gambling websites and gambling dens. “I’ll give one example. She was travelling from Kanchanaburi to Nakhon Pathom. She found a gambling den along the way. She goes straight in, plays and loses 10 million baht,” cited Surachate. “Whose money was that? Money she’d just borrowed from people.” Online savings groups and instant bank transfers — plus misplaced trust — allowed money to move with ease and feed her gambling addiction. “When asked to repay, if there’s no money to clear debts, what do you do?” remarked Surachate. Citing what he learnt from the Federal Bureau of Investigation, he added: “Serial killers, if they’re men, will commit crimes outside the city, and the motive is sexual in nature. But if it’s a woman, the motive must be money.” Prior to Aem, there was the case of serial killer Somkid Phumphuang, who raped and killed his victims — six of them — between 2005 and 2019. There are “many contributing factors”, however, in cases like Aem, according to Somdet Chaopraya Institute of Psychiatry deputy director Winyoo Chanakul, who has over 20 years’ experience in caring for psychiatric patients who have committed violent acts or even homicide. “Someone who has financial problems to the point of being able to kill others, and to do so repeatedly, can’t be explained by financial reasons alone. Otherwise, everyone in debt would be killing people,” he said. “The person must have certain personality traits that allow them to commit serious wrongdoing for their own benefit without feeling guilt. This includes a lack of empathy and a disregard for social rules.” Thinking back on Aem’s personality, Som remembered her once saying that if anyone were to fight with her or say something bad, “she wouldn’t let it go” and would “go as far as killing”. When the police arrested Aem, however, senior staff writer Pravit Rojanaphruk at news outlet Khaosod English remembers that “everyone was confused” by this woman from a middle-class background. “She looks just like anyone from an average neighbourhood,” he said. It became a major news story that many people have followed. “No one person has caused this much of an uproar before,” he added, citing the 14 murder charges. She has contested all the charges so far. One of her lawyers, Thannicha “Pat” Aeksuwannawat, said it was “impossible that Aem committed all 14 murders”. “The police want to dump the murder cases onto Aem so they don’t have to find the real perpetrator. It was clear that she was being targeted,” said Pat. “It’s media-driven momentum more than facts. “They said death was due to cyanide. … That cyanide mightn’t have come from Aem. This is the weakness of the case.” Buying cyanide in Thailand is not suspicious on its own. It is used in factories in metal-related industries, such as for metal plating and electroplating. It is used in gold shops and in research. And what the police found was that Aem “never used her own name to order cyanide”, said Surachate. “She had others order it, and then it reached her.” One of the cyanide bottles that the police seized had been sold by a company that called Grab to do the delivery. And the rider took a photo when delivering the cyanide to Aem in her Toyota Fortuner, recounted Rapee. “In that photo, a small pink Hello Kitty bag was visible beside the gear stick. Once the police … impounded the bag, we found this bottle,” he said, adding that the bottle had a registration number showing who the importer was. “Aem used her phone number to contact the company. All the evidence pointed directly to Aem. Game over.” Although Rapee said it was Aem’s “own mistakes that brought her down”, his involvement led to a breakthrough in the case in more ways than one. After he and Koy’s family appealed publicly for information once Aem was fingered as a suspect, his phone began ringing nonstop. Families across Thailand told of similar stories: sudden deaths, missing money and a connection to savings groups. One of those who came forward was Pla. She said Aem had asked for a loan to repay a fund, so she gave her 250,000 baht. “She was my friend. Why would I refuse?” said Pla. But she was lending the money only for a month. Then she asked Aem to return the entire amount as agreed because she had to pay for her car. “Reliving my ordeal wasn’t easy,” said Pla, who did it so that Aem “won’t be able to hurt anyone else again”. Pravit described her role as the “nail in the coffin” for Aem, who was sentenced to death in November 2024 for the murder of Koy. WATCH PART 2: ‘She tried to kill me twice’ — The witness who survived a serial killer (46:59) It is a penalty she deserves, said Thongpin, who was “very close” to Koy. “We’d travel together, perform Buddhist rituals together.” Koy and her sister were also close. Som called her the “pillar of the family” who took care of everyone. “Koy only had one child, so she doted on her. She loved her so much. Whatever the child wanted, she got,” said Som, referring to Koy’s daughter, now 13. “Everything she built, she built it for her daughter.” The murders of Nim and Bee, meanwhile, have not gone to trial yet. Koon said he thinks about his younger brother every day. “And whenever I do, my heart feels as if it’s going to break,” he lamented. As for Ta, if he had the chance, he would want to speak to Nim — whom he lovingly described as “good-hearted” and “always willing to help others” — one more time. “I’d want to thank her for coming into my life as my wife and as the mother of our children, for making my life better and helping me grow and become more mature,” he said. As of Sep 22, the criminal court has delivered three death sentences and two life imprisonments for Aem’s string of cyanide murders, plus acquittals in three cases where the court cited a lack of evidence in her favour. Since the end of 2009, Thailand has carried out only one execution, in 2018, even as several death sentences have been imposed. Aem’s next trial date is Nov 25, for the attempted murder of Pla. Watch Part 1 and Part 2 of the series, Death Loans: Thailand’s Cyanide Murders. CNA's best current affairs documentaries with a deeper look at issues affecting Asia, sent to your inbox weekly.
