snapshot.title: UN Geneva Press Briefing - 09 October 2026
snapshot.evidenceText: Press Conferences | UNHCR , UNICEF , IFRC , OHCHR , UN WOMEN , IOM , OCHA , WHO Recovery and preparedness in Nepal James Elder, for the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), speaking from Kathmandu, said that more than 32,000 children in Nepal had been affected by floods that had begun when a mountain of glacial ice and rock collapsed into a Himalayan river in late August. Parts of towns and villages still looked like war zones. Scientists warned that, as the Himalayas warmed, this kind of disaster was becoming more likely, and the countries that had done least to cause it were being left to pay for it. Mr. Elder stressed that this problem reached far beyond Nepal. The Hindu Kush Himalaya held more ice than anywhere on Earth, outside the polar regions. Two hundred and forty million people lived in these mountains. Another 1.65 billion lived downstream and relied on the rivers this ice fed, which was nearly two billion people – about a quarter of humanity. That system was now being pushed out of balance. Faster melting brought more water and more flood risk now, and serious shortages later as the glaciers disappeared. Both were driven by a heating planet. Nepal produced only around 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet children, who were least responsible for the climate crisis, were among those bearing its heaviest consequences. This disaster had not begun when the waters rose. Before the floods, more than half a million children in Nepal had been already exposed to at least multiple overlapping climate and environmental hazards. On a positive side, the response from Government, communities and the UN was comprehensive, with new bridges built just weeks after a mountain of water and rock ripped through such infrastructure. However, unless the world acted to reduce climate risks, we would keep returning to the same valleys after the next flood and the next landslide, and yet again find children once paying the highest price. That was true in Nepal, across Asia and the Pacific, and around the world, concluded Mr. Elder. Caroline Holt, Director for Disasters, Climate and Crises at the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), had just returned from Nepal and shared what she had seen. She had witnessed stories of both loss and resilience. Ms. Holt provided an example of a teacher who had reacted quickly and warned his 900 students, making sure no child in his school lost a life. This teacher had been trained on disaster preparedness by the Nepal Red Cross. Investment in early warning and preparedness mattered and saved lives, stressed Ms. Holt. Now, the focus was shifting from immediate life-saving assistance to recovery. The Nepal Red Cross was the first organization to provide cash assistance, which allowed people to continue their lives with dignity. In the hardest-hit locations families faced numerous obstacles, and people now needed confidence in the future, which required planning. Sustained, reliable resources were very much needed as the recovery efforts were getting underway, concluded Ms. Holt. Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde, Director of the Regional Bureau for West and Central Africa at the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), who had just returned from the region, said that UNHCR was increasingly concerned about the deepening displacement crisis in the Central Sahel, with nearly four million people uprooted across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, including more than 818,000 refugees and asylum-seekers. This was roughly twice the number recorded in October 2020. The crisis was being compounded by continued attacks affecting civilians, climate-related shocks and severe humanitarian funding shortfalls. Together, these pressures were forcing more families to flee, eroding livelihoods and limiting opportunities for displaced people to rebuild their lives, contributing to further movements within and beyond the region. In Mali, the vast majority of refugees were from neighbouring Burkina Faso. In Koro, in the Bandiagara region, the refugee population was now approaching the size of the local host community, placing mounting pressure on already scarce land and water resources, overstretched health services and limited livelihood opportunities. Climate-related shocks were adding another layer of pressure to communities already struggling with displacement and insecurity. In Koro, agricultural cooperative initiatives bringing together Burkinabè refugees and host-community members had helped expand cultivated land from 21 hectares in 2025 to 45 hectares in 2026, improving food production and household incomes. In Burkina Faso, similar support in Kaya was helping internally displaced people and host communities increase food production, reduce post-harvest losses and generate income. These efforts remained tiny compared with the scale of displacement, but they showed what could be achieved when people forced to flee were given the means to rebuild their lives while longer-term solutions were sought. The crisis was also increasingly extending beyond the Central Sahel. For some, displacement did not end in neighbouring countries. When safety and prospects remained out of reach, refugees might move on, often alongside migrants, taking dangerous routes towards North Africa and Europe. This underscored the wider regional and international consequences of prolonged insecurity and limited opportunities closer to home. UNHCR had been working with governments and partners to establish multi-purpose service hubs that provide critical information, counselling, referral services and essential assistance. As of September 2026, however, UNHCR's response in the Sahel was only 27 per cent funded, forcing difficult choices over which essential services and activities could be sustained, warned Mr, Gnon-Konde. Volatile humanitarian situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo Damien Mama, Humanitarian Coordinator in the Democratic Republic of the Congo , had toured the eastern DRC over the recent weeks, traveling to hard-to-reach areas. Millions of people longed for peace and security, yet both remained out of reach in large parts of the country, particularly in the eastern provinces. More than 6.1 million people were displaced from their homes by conflict and violence. More than 26 million people in the DRC were food insecure and struggling to put food on the table. Children were disproportionately affected, with over four million under five facing malnutrition. Essential services were under enormous pressure, and for some families who managed to return, home no longer looked like home, with their houses destroyed, schools gone, health centres no longer functioning. The Ebola outbreak was adding another layer to an already devastating situation. It was spreading through communities that were already dealing with displacement, hunger, insecurity, and the disruption of basic services. These crises were not separate, stressed Mr. Mama; they fed into one another. When people were forced from their homes, they lost access to healthcare. When health services were disrupted, disease spread more easily. When humanitarian workers could not safely reach communities, both the humanitarian response and the Ebola response were weakened. Despite the constraints, humanitarian workers remained on the frontlines, reaching some of the most vulnerable communities in the country. Protecting both civilians and humanitarian personnel was not optional, the speaker stressed. It was an obligation under international humanitarian law. He concluded by stating that humanitarians needed sustained access, greater protection for civilians and humanitarian workers, and to reinforce the Ebola response and the wider humanitarian response at the same time. The international community had to act with the urgency that this crisis demanded. Sofia Calltorp, Chief of Humanitarian Action at UN Women , stated that the scale of suffering in Gaza could be measured in the lives of women and girls. UN Women estimated that nearly 50,000 women and girls had been killed or severely injured since October 2023: more than 38,000 killed and 11,700 left with injuries so severe that they now lived with lifelong disabilities. This was equivalent to one in every 21 women and girls in Gaza. While most of the casualties had been recorded during the first two years of the war, women and girls continued to be killed and injured even after the ceasefire agreement entered into effect a year ago. 277 women and girls had been killed in Gaza since October 2025. Behind every number was a life: women with hopes and ambitions, mothers caring for their children, daughters, spouses and friends, and women contributing to their families and communities. Today, almost every woman and girl in Gaza remained displaced, with the majority living in tents or among the ruins of their homes. The war had also reshaped family life. The number of women heading households had doubled over the past three years. Women now headed one in four households in Gaza, often while facing deeper poverty, repeated displacement and the responsibility of caring for their families with increasingly limited resources. Women’s organizations were lifelines to women, girls and their families, but funding cuts were threatening their ability to serve those who need them. The consequences were immediate, and nearly two thirds of the organizations surveyed said they had been forced to put women and girls on waiting lists or turn them away altogether. UN Women called for the ceasefire in Gaza to be fully implemented, international law to be upheld, and accountability for violations, alongside the protection of women and girls. Karl Baker, International Organization for Migration (IOM) Regional Crisis Coordinator on Gaza Response, connecting from Amman, said that despite one year since a ceasefire had been announced, nearly the entire population of two million people still required shelter assistance. The reality was that the current shelter response was nowhere near the scale required to protect people. Only 17 per cent of winter-specific shelter needs were covered by the pipeline of humanitarian shelter partners. This was due to the combination of insufficient funding and continued Israeli restrictions on the entry of critical shelter supplies. According to the Palestine Shelter Cluster, coordinated by IOM, half of all existing tents and makeshift shelters were in poor or very poor condition and required replacement. While tents had been entering Gaza this past year, they were temporary solutions made to last only 6-12 months. Current forecasts indicated that a strong El Niño weather pattern could bring a wetter, longer and more intense winter. Most of the 1.8 million people living in displacement sites were in flood-risk areas. This was a frustrating situation, stressed Mr. Baker, because humanitarian organizations had shelter solutions ready. IOM, like all Shelter partners, ensured compliance with Israeli security requirements and specifications, yet supplies continued to be turned away at crossing points. Humanitarian partners were doing everything possible to find alternative materials inside Gaza, but local markets had been exhausted. Mr. Baker concluded by stressing that meeting humanitarian needs and fulfilling the commitments outlined under the ceasefire framework requires the immediate and sustained entry of shelter materials. Simple tents were allowed in, but more durable solutions were needed and at a higher scale, explained Mr. Baker in a response to a question. Arrests and detentions of Syrians by Israeli forces Shabia Mantoo, for the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), said that OHCHR was concerned by the continuing impact of Israeli military operations on civilians in southern Syria. Some 280 incidents involving armed Israeli incursions into Syria had been recorded in September alone, through open-source monitoring —the highest monthly number since the start of the year. These included reported raids on homes, restrictions on movement, harassment and intimidation of civilians, arbitrary detention and destruction of livelihoods. According to information OHCHR had received, 49 Syrians remained in Israeli custody, although OHCHR had not independently verified a comprehensive, current total. Information from released detainees and other sources described prolonged detention periods - in some cases exceeding a year, detainees reportedly not being informed of the reasons for their detention, as well transfers between several and unknown facilities, and allegations of torture and ill-treatment. These included beatings, prolonged forced standing, setting dogs on detainees, and threats to harm them and their families. On 5 October, a 22-year-old man from Jaba town in Quneitra governorate, had been killed by Israeli forces near Al-Hamidiyah town. Information OHCHR received indicated that he had been walking at night in an area unfamiliar to him and had not known an Israeli military position was at the end of the road. No warning shots were known to have been fired. The High Commissioner called for a prompt and impartial investigation. Ms. Mantoo stressed that the Israeli authorities should cease actions that harass or intimidate civilians in Syrian villages, including raids, restrictions on freedom of movement, detention and destruction of crops. No person should be detained absent proper basis in international law. Ricardo Pires, for the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), said that beyond the immediate dangers of violence and displacement in Yemen, there were deeply worrying signs of a worsening health crisis for children, with alarming levels of malnutrition and a sharp rise in disease outbreaks. Access to healthcare continued to shrink. More than one in three children recently screened by UNICEF mobile health teams in Yemen had been found to be suffering from acute malnutrition. Around 1,500 pregnant and breastfeeding women had also been identified as malnourished. Mr. Pires said that disease was now spreading. Cholera cases had tripled in just three weeks, while dengue and malaria cases were also rising. This came as renewed fighting forced families to flee their homes. Since the beginning of September, more than 200,000 people, including an estimated 110,000 children, had been displaced across ten governorates. Since 3 September, UNICEF verified that 28 children had been killed and 25 injured. Three others are reported missing. For Yemen's children, warned Mr. Pires, the ongoing fighting was creating a crisis within a crisis, and every new wave of violence made their chances of survival more precarious. Vijaya Souri, Chief of Mission of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in South Sudan, speaking from Juba, said that for more than a decade, families in South Sudan had been living through protracted displacement. Many had remained displaced since 2013, enduring years of insecurity, repeated flooding and uncertainty about when they would be able to rebuild their lives. Today, nearly 109,000 displaced people in Bentiu were living in a camp surrounded by flood waters. The camp depended on a system of protective dykes to keep the water out. Continuous pumping removed accumulated water, while regular maintenance helped keep the dykes standing. But these defences were under growing pressure and worsened by the risk of flooding with heavy rains were expected anytime between now and December. Humanitarian operations were facing increasingly severe resource constraints. Funding was becoming more limited, even as the needs of displaced communities remained high. By the end of November 2026, funding for IOM's critical water, sanitation and flood protection operations in Bentiu and Malakal would run out. Unless new resources were secured, these services could be interrupted from December. For the nearly 150,000 people in Bentiu and Malakal IDP Camp, this meant water taps could run dry. Around 2,200 latrines could overflow. Drainage pumps could stop operating. Floodwaters could contaminate drinking water sources, increase the spread of disease and trigger further displacement, warned Ms. Souri. IOM urgently needed USD 8.35 million to maintain these services for another 12 months, from December 2026 to December 2027. With continued funding, IOM could keep these systems operating and undertake the maintenance needed to reduce the risk of flooding. Alongside maintaining essential services, IOM was working with UN agencies, non-governmental organizations and local authorities towards more sustainable infrastructure and longer-term solutions to displacement. Essential services should not be allowed to stop while longer-term solutions were still being developed. The coming weeks were critical. Dr. Mark van Ommeren, Head, Mental Health and Substance Use Unit at the World Health Organization (WHO), informed that the theme of this World Mental Health Day on 10 October was the role of lived experience. By putting lived experience at the centre of the conversation in countries, communities around the world would be reflecting on what meaningful engagement really meant; that reflection was fundamental to a much-needed change of culture in mental health care. Deinstitutionalization was a gradual and planned shift from managing people in long-stay psychiatric institutions to supporting them through community-based mental health and social care, so people could live the life they wanted to live. The goal was dignity, freedom, choice and the support to live a full life. In mental health, there now existed vast amounts of advanced science, and there was increasing goodwill for mental health. Yet, at the same time, the paradox was that typically half of countries’ mental health budgets remained tied up in institutions that were largely designed for a past era. Dr. van Ommeren emphasized that listening to people with lived experience was helping see a better path: investing in community-based support, protecting rights, and creating services that people actually want. Today, WHO was focusing on institutions as the elephant in the room in mental health in many countries. By launching a practical guide to the deinstitutionalization/DI of psychiatric hospitals WHO sought to support countries, guiding them to move from managing people in institutions to caring and supporting people in the community to live the lives they wanted to live. This guide supported hospital leaders and policymakers to implement deinstitutionalization/DI locally. It focused on adults staying in psychiatric hospitals for more than six months. It focused on three areas of action: reducing new admissions and shortening stays; improving care practices in the hospitals; and enabling discharge as appropriate supports became available through building community alternatives. Shabia Mantoo, for the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), congratulated Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, the former High Commissioner for Human Rights, who had just been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize . She said that Ms. Pillay had been a staunch defender and advocate of human rights. It was important in this day and age to see that accolade being awarded to those who were speaking out on violations of human rights. Responding to a question on the ongoing protests in France, Shabia Mantoo, for the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), called on everyone to ensure that the protests in France remained peaceful and that there was no disproportionate use of force. On another question, she said that the absolute prohibition of torture also prohibited public executions, anywhere in the world. snapshot.title: UN Geneva Press Briefing - 09 October 2026
snapshot.evidenceText: Press Conferences | UNHCR , UNICEF , IFRC , OHCHR , UN WOMEN , IOM , OCHA , WHO Recovery and preparedness in Nepal James Elder, for the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), speaking from Kathmandu, said that more than 32,000 children in Nepal had been affected by floods that had begun when a mountain of glacial ice and rock collapsed into a Himalayan river in late August. Parts of towns and villages still looked like war zones. Scientists warned that, as the Himalayas warmed, this kind of disaster was becoming more likely, and the countries that had done least to cause it were being left to pay for it. Mr. Elder stressed that this problem reached far beyond Nepal. The Hindu Kush Himalaya held more ice than anywhere on Earth, outside the polar regions. Two hundred and forty million people lived in these mountains. Another 1.65 billion lived downstream and relied on the rivers this ice fed, which was nearly two billion people – about a quarter of humanity. That system was now being pushed out of balance. Faster melting brought more water and more flood risk now, and serious shortages later as the glaciers disappeared. Both were driven by a heating planet. Nepal produced only around 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet children, who were least responsible for the climate crisis, were among those bearing its heaviest consequences. This disaster had not begun when the waters rose. Before the floods, more than half a million children in Nepal had been already exposed to at least multiple overlapping climate and environmental hazards. On a positive side, the response from Government, communities and the UN was comprehensive, with new bridges built just weeks after a mountain of water and rock ripped through such infrastructure. However, unless the world acted to reduce climate risks, we would keep returning to the same valleys after the next flood and the next landslide, and yet again find children once paying the highest price. That was true in Nepal, across Asia and the Pacific, and around the world, concluded Mr. Elder. Caroline Holt, Director for Disasters, Climate and Crises at the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC), had just returned from Nepal and shared what she had seen. She had witnessed stories of both loss and resilience. Ms. Holt provided an example of a teacher who had reacted quickly and warned his 900 students, making sure no child in his school lost a life. This teacher had been trained on disaster preparedness by the Nepal Red Cross. Investment in early warning and preparedness mattered and saved lives, stressed Ms. Holt. Now, the focus was shifting from immediate life-saving assistance to recovery. The Nepal Red Cross was the first organization to provide cash assistance, which allowed people to continue their lives with dignity. In the hardest-hit locations families faced numerous obstacles, and people now needed confidence in the future, which required planning. Sustained, reliable resources were very much needed as the recovery efforts were getting underway, concluded Ms. Holt. Abdouraouf Gnon-Konde, Director of the Regional Bureau for West and Central Africa at the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), who had just returned from the region, said that UNHCR was increasingly concerned about the deepening displacement crisis in the Central Sahel, with nearly four million people uprooted across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, including more than 818,000 refugees and asylum-seekers. This was roughly twice the number recorded in October 2020. The crisis was being compounded by continued attacks affecting civilians, climate-related shocks and severe humanitarian funding shortfalls. Together, these pressures were forcing more families to flee, eroding livelihoods and limiting opportunities for displaced people to rebuild their lives, contributing to further movements within and beyond the region. In Mali, the vast majority of refugees were from neighbouring Burkina Faso. In Koro, in the Bandiagara region, the refugee population was now approaching the size of the local host community, placing mounting pressure on already scarce land and water resources, overstretched health services and limited livelihood opportunities. Climate-related shocks were adding another layer of pressure to communities already struggling with displacement and insecurity. In Koro, agricultural cooperative initiatives bringing together Burkinabè refugees and host-community members had helped expand cultivated land from 21 hectares in 2025 to 45 hectares in 2026, improving food production and household incomes. In Burkina Faso, similar support in Kaya was helping internally displaced people and host communities increase food production, reduce post-harvest losses and generate income. These efforts remained tiny compared with the scale of displacement, but they showed what could be achieved when people forced to flee were given the means to rebuild their lives while longer-term solutions were sought. The crisis was also increasingly extending beyond the Central Sahel. For some, displacement did not end in neighbouring countries. When safety and prospects remained out of reach, refugees might move on, often alongside migrants, taking dangerous routes towards North Africa and Europe. This underscored the wider regional and international consequences of prolonged insecurity and limited opportunities closer to home. UNHCR had been working with governments and partners to establish multi-purpose service hubs that provide critical information, counselling, referral services and essential assistance. As of September 2026, however, UNHCR's response in the Sahel was only 27 per cent funded, forcing difficult choices over which essential services and activities could be sustained, warned Mr, Gnon-Konde. Volatile humanitarian situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo Damien Mama, Humanitarian Coordinator in the Democratic Republic of the Congo , had toured the eastern DRC over the recent weeks, traveling to hard-to-reach areas. Millions of people longed for peace and security, yet both remained out of reach in large parts of the country, particularly in the eastern provinces. More than 6.1 million people were displaced from their homes by conflict and violence. More than 26 million people in the DRC were food insecure and struggling to put food on the table. Children were disproportionately affected, with over four million under five facing malnutrition. Essential services were under enormous pressure, and for some families who managed to return, home no longer looked like home, with their houses destroyed, schools gone, health centres no longer functioning. The Ebola outbreak was adding another layer to an already devastating situation. It was spreading through communities that were already dealing with displacement, hunger, insecurity, and the disruption of basic services. These crises were not separate, stressed Mr. Mama; they fed into one another. When people were forced from their homes, they lost access to healthcare. When health services were disrupted, disease spread more easily. When humanitarian workers could not safely reach communities, both the humanitarian response and the Ebola response were weakened. Despite the constraints, humanitarian workers remained on the frontlines, reaching some of the most vulnerable communities in the country. Protecting both civilians and humanitarian personnel was not optional, the speaker stressed. It was an obligation under international humanitarian law. He concluded by stating that humanitarians needed sustained access, greater protection for civilians and humanitarian workers, and to reinforce the Ebola response and the wider humanitarian response at the same time. The international community had to act with the urgency that this crisis demanded. Sofia Calltorp, Chief of Humanitarian Action at UN Women , stated that the scale of suffering in Gaza could be measured in the lives of women and girls. UN Women estimated that nearly 50,000 women and girls had been killed or severely injured since October 2023: more than 38,000 killed and 11,700 left with injuries so severe that they now lived with lifelong disabilities. This was equivalent to one in every 21 women and girls in Gaza. While most of the casualties had been recorded during the first two years of the war, women and girls continued to be killed and injured even after the ceasefire agreement entered into effect a year ago. 277 women and girls had been killed in Gaza since October 2025. Behind every number was a life: women with hopes and ambitions, mothers caring for their children, daughters, spouses and friends, and women contributing to their families and communities. Today, almost every woman and girl in Gaza remained displaced, with the majority living in tents or among the ruins of their homes. The war had also reshaped family life. The number of women heading households had doubled over the past three years. Women now headed one in four households in Gaza, often while facing deeper poverty, repeated displacement and the responsibility of caring for their families with increasingly limited resources. Women’s organizations were lifelines to women, girls and their families, but funding cuts were threatening their ability to serve those who need them. The consequences were immediate, and nearly two thirds of the organizations surveyed said they had been forced to put women and girls on waiting lists or turn them away altogether. UN Women called for the ceasefire in Gaza to be fully implemented, international law to be upheld, and accountability for violations, alongside the protection of women and girls. Karl Baker, International Organization for Migration (IOM) Regional Crisis Coordinator on Gaza Response, connecting from Amman, said that despite one year since a ceasefire had been announced, nearly the entire population of two million people still required shelter assistance. The reality was that the current shelter response was nowhere near the scale required to protect people. Only 17 per cent of winter-specific shelter needs were covered by the pipeline of humanitarian shelter partners. This was due to the combination of insufficient funding and continued Israeli restrictions on the entry of critical shelter supplies. According to the Palestine Shelter Cluster, coordinated by IOM, half of all existing tents and makeshift shelters were in poor or very poor condition and required replacement. While tents had been entering Gaza this past year, they were temporary solutions made to last only 6-12 months. Current forecasts indicated that a strong El Niño weather pattern could bring a wetter, longer and more intense winter. Most of the 1.8 million people living in displacement sites were in flood-risk areas. This was a frustrating situation, stressed Mr. Baker, because humanitarian organizations had shelter solutions ready. IOM, like all Shelter partners, ensured compliance with Israeli security requirements and specifications, yet supplies continued to be turned away at crossing points. Humanitarian partners were doing everything possible to find alternative materials inside Gaza, but local markets had been exhausted. Mr. Baker concluded by stressing that meeting humanitarian needs and fulfilling the commitments outlined under the ceasefire framework requires the immediate and sustained entry of shelter materials. Simple tents were allowed in, but more durable solutions were needed and at a higher scale, explained Mr. Baker in a response to a question. Arrests and detentions of Syrians by Israeli forces Shabia Mantoo, for the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), said that OHCHR was concerned by the continuing impact of Israeli military operations on civilians in southern Syria. Some 280 incidents involving armed Israeli incursions into Syria had been recorded in September alone, through open-source monitoring —the highest monthly number since the start of the year. These included reported raids on homes, restrictions on movement, harassment and intimidation of civilians, arbitrary detention and destruction of livelihoods. According to information OHCHR had received, 49 Syrians remained in Israeli custody, although OHCHR had not independently verified a comprehensive, current total. Information from released detainees and other sources described prolonged detention periods - in some cases exceeding a year, detainees reportedly not being informed of the reasons for their detention, as well transfers between several and unknown facilities, and allegations of torture and ill-treatment. These included beatings, prolonged forced standing, setting dogs on detainees, and threats to harm them and their families. On 5 October, a 22-year-old man from Jaba town in Quneitra governorate, had been killed by Israeli forces near Al-Hamidiyah town. Information OHCHR received indicated that he had been walking at night in an area unfamiliar to him and had not known an Israeli military position was at the end of the road. No warning shots were known to have been fired. The High Commissioner called for a prompt and impartial investigation. Ms. Mantoo stressed that the Israeli authorities should cease actions that harass or intimidate civilians in Syrian villages, including raids, restrictions on freedom of movement, detention and destruction of crops. No person should be detained absent proper basis in international law. Ricardo Pires, for the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), said that beyond the immediate dangers of violence and displacement in Yemen, there were deeply worrying signs of a worsening health crisis for children, with alarming levels of malnutrition and a sharp rise in disease outbreaks. Access to healthcare continued to shrink. More than one in three children recently screened by UNICEF mobile health teams in Yemen had been found to be suffering from acute malnutrition. Around 1,500 pregnant and breastfeeding women had also been identified as malnourished. Mr. Pires said that disease was now spreading. Cholera cases had tripled in just three weeks, while dengue and malaria cases were also rising. This came as renewed fighting forced families to flee their homes. Since the beginning of September, more than 200,000 people, including an estimated 110,000 children, had been displaced across ten governorates. Since 3 September, UNICEF verified that 28 children had been killed and 25 injured. Three others are reported missing. For Yemen's children, warned Mr. Pires, the ongoing fighting was creating a crisis within a crisis, and every new wave of violence made their chances of survival more precarious. Vijaya Souri, Chief of Mission of the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in South Sudan, speaking from Juba, said that for more than a decade, families in South Sudan had been living through protracted displacement. Many had remained displaced since 2013, enduring years of insecurity, repeated flooding and uncertainty about when they would be able to rebuild their lives. Today, nearly 109,000 displaced people in Bentiu were living in a camp surrounded by flood waters. The camp depended on a system of protective dykes to keep the water out. Continuous pumping removed accumulated water, while regular maintenance helped keep the dykes standing. But these defences were under growing pressure and worsened by the risk of flooding with heavy rains were expected anytime between now and December. Humanitarian operations were facing increasingly severe resource constraints. Funding was becoming more limited, even as the needs of displaced communities remained high. By the end of November 2026, funding for IOM's critical water, sanitation and flood protection operations in Bentiu and Malakal would run out. Unless new resources were secured, these services could be interrupted from December. For the nearly 150,000 people in Bentiu and Malakal IDP Camp, this meant water taps could run dry. Around 2,200 latrines could overflow. Drainage pumps could stop operating. Floodwaters could contaminate drinking water sources, increase the spread of disease and trigger further displacement, warned Ms. Souri. IOM urgently needed USD 8.35 million to maintain these services for another 12 months, from December 2026 to December 2027. With continued funding, IOM could keep these systems operating and undertake the maintenance needed to reduce the risk of flooding. Alongside maintaining essential services, IOM was working with UN agencies, non-governmental organizations and local authorities towards more sustainable infrastructure and longer-term solutions to displacement. Essential services should not be allowed to stop while longer-term solutions were still being developed. The coming weeks were critical. Dr. Mark van Ommeren, Head, Mental Health and Substance Use Unit at the World Health Organization (WHO), informed that the theme of this World Mental Health Day on 10 October was the role of lived experience. By putting lived experience at the centre of the conversation in countries, communities around the world would be reflecting on what meaningful engagement really meant; that reflection was fundamental to a much-needed change of culture in mental health care. Deinstitutionalization was a gradual and planned shift from managing people in long-stay psychiatric institutions to supporting them through community-based mental health and social care, so people could live the life they wanted to live. The goal was dignity, freedom, choice and the support to live a full life. In mental health, there now existed vast amounts of advanced science, and there was increasing goodwill for mental health. Yet, at the same time, the paradox was that typically half of countries’ mental health budgets remained tied up in institutions that were largely designed for a past era. Dr. van Ommeren emphasized that listening to people with lived experience was helping see a better path: investing in community-based support, protecting rights, and creating services that people actually want. Today, WHO was focusing on institutions as the elephant in the room in mental health in many countries. By launching a practical guide to the deinstitutionalization/DI of psychiatric hospitals WHO sought to support countries, guiding them to move from managing people in institutions to caring and supporting people in the community to live the lives they wanted to live. This guide supported hospital leaders and policymakers to implement deinstitutionalization/DI locally. It focused on adults staying in psychiatric hospitals for more than six months. It focused on three areas of action: reducing new admissions and shortening stays; improving care practices in the hospitals; and enabling discharge as appropriate supports became available through building community alternatives. Shabia Mantoo, for the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), congratulated Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, the former High Commissioner for Human Rights, who had just been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize . She said that Ms. Pillay had been a staunch defender and advocate of human rights. It was important in this day and age to see that accolade being awarded to those who were speaking out on violations of human rights. Responding to a question on the ongoing protests in France, Shabia Mantoo, for the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), called on everyone to ensure that the protests in France remained peaceful and that there was no disproportionate use of force. On another question, she said that the absolute prohibition of torture also prohibited public executions, anywhere in the world. representative.title: Campbell River Identifies Ballot Instruction Error in School District 72 Trustee Election
representative.author: Sophie Mitchell

snapshot.title: Campbell River Identifies Ballot Instruction Error in School District 72 Trustee Election
snapshot.evidenceText: CAMPBELL RIVER, B.C., October 9, 2026 – Election officials in Campbell River have identified an error in ballot instructions used during advance voting for the School District 72 school trustee election, raising concerns that some ballots cast on October 7 may be declared invalid. The issue was discovered after voting had already begun at an advance polling opportunity administered by the City of Campbell River. Officials subsequently began providing verbal instructions to voters to ensure ballots were completed correctly. According to the City, some ballots submitted before the error was identified could be considered invalid for the school trustee portion of the election. Any ballots determined to be invalid would not be included in the final trustee election results. The City has contacted provincial authorities seeking a ministerial order to address the situation and protect the integrity of the electoral process. The ballot instruction error occurred during advance voting on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, for the School District 72 trustee election. Election officials discovered that the instructions provided on ballots were incorrect after voters had begun casting their votes. Once the problem was identified, officials took immediate steps to verbally explain the correct voting procedure to those participating. However, ballots completed before the correction may not meet the requirements for valid votes in the trustee election. The City has not disclosed how many ballots may be affected or confirmed whether any votes will ultimately be excluded from the official results. Campbell River residents who have received mail-in ballots but have not yet submitted them are being reminded to select no more than five candidates for School District 72 trustee positions. The clarification is intended to help voters complete their ballots correctly and avoid potential issues during the counting process. Election officials have emphasized that the identified problem relates specifically to the school trustee election and does not affect every component of the local government voting process. The City confirmed that the ballot instruction issue is limited to the October 7 advance voting opportunity for School District 72 trustees conducted in Campbell River, along with the related mail-voting instructions. Advance and mail voting for the 2026 City of Campbell River mayoral and council elections are not impacted by the error. Similarly, voting on the Strathcona Regional District assent question remains unaffected. Advance voting for School District 72 trustees conducted at other locations is also not affected by the identified problem. This distinction is important for residents participating in multiple electoral contests, as the potential ballot validity concerns apply only to the specified school trustee voting process. Following the discovery, officials contacted British Columbia’s Ministry of Housing and Municipal Affairs and Ministry of Education and Child Care. The City has requested a ministerial order to address the ballot instruction error and its possible implications for the trustee election. A ministerial order could provide formal direction on how the situation should be handled under the applicable election framework. However, the City has not announced what specific measures may be authorized or whether previously submitted ballots will be affected. Officials responsible for administering the School District 72 election have committed to continuing all necessary measures to ensure voting proceeds in accordance with governing legislation and applicable election bylaws. Maintaining public confidence in the election process remains a central priority as authorities determine how to address the issue. The City said it will provide further information once the provincial ministries respond to the request for a ministerial order. The ballot instruction error introduces uncertainty for some residents who participated in the October 7 advance vote, particularly those who completed their ballots before election officials began issuing corrected verbal instructions. For voters who have yet to return their mail ballots, the immediate guidance remains unchanged: select no more than five School District 72 trustee candidates. The City has acknowledged that residents may have questions about the situation and has requested patience while officials work toward a resolution. Further announcements are expected to clarify how potentially affected ballots will be handled and whether additional administrative measures will be required before the trustee election results are finalized. representative.title: Justina López honored at 95 for her life in the Valles Calchaquíes - Salta Hoy

snapshot.title: Justina López honored at 95 for her life in the Valles Calchaquíes - Salta Hoy
snapshot.evidenceText: Justina López was honored at age 95 by communities in Argentina's Valles Calchaquíes for her lifelong connection to local traditions and landscapes. Her story reflects decades spent walking mountain paths while serving as caregiver, cheesemaker, midwife, singer—and living link to indigenous heritage. Justina López was recognized on Oct. 8 for her 95th birthday and a lifetime closely connected to the land and culture of the Valles Calchaquíes, as well as to the Diaguita community identity. The Cóndor Huasi indigenous community of San Lucas, together with residents of San Carlos, acknowledged López’s contributions. Her life has been shaped by traversing mountain paths and building family and community ties in remote areas. Born on Oct. 7, 1931, in Abra Pampa-La Ollada in Las Viñas west of San Carlos, she became responsible for her younger siblings at age 13 after the deaths of her parents, Romelia Escalante and Jorge López. López later lived in El Ubillar and Puesto Colorao, where she raised a family. She worked raising animals and producing food such as cow’s and goat’s cheese—a tradition continued by one daughter—while another inherited bread-making skills and another maintained the tradition of singing coplas. In addition to these roles, López also served as a midwife: “Yo les cortaba el cordón, era buena como partera,” she said. López frequently traveled between Puesto Colorao and San Carlos—a distance of about 25 kilometers each way—on foot or horseback. For many years she was accompanied by María Inés Díaz; their friendship extended across families when they became consuegras through their children’s marriage. Her presence is still noted at local celebrations including those in El Barrial, Corralito, Animaná, San Antonio, San Rafael, and Payogastilla. Community members say: “¿Quién no la conoce?” Those who advocated for honoring López see her story as representing living memory for indigenous peoples of the region—their movements across territory over generations—and a unique relationship with their environment built on direct experience rather than maps. In recent years a road suitable for vehicles has made travel easier between these places; previously most journeys were made on foot. Today her family supports her mobility, but stories about past journeys remain part of collective memory. Organizers say that naming Justina López evokes Pachamama itself—both deeply linked to land shaped by mountains (cerros) and spirits (Apus). At age 95 she continues sharing memories with clarity: childhood experiences alongside siblings; work with animals; making cheese; assisting births; singing coplas; participating in carnivals—all rooted along these historic paths. The wire from Salta Hoy, condensed once a morning.

representative.title: How Science, Indigenous Knowledge, and Sea Otters Are Restoring Canada’s Kelp Forests - The Daily Goods
representative.author: Mark Stone

snapshot.title: How Science, Indigenous Knowledge, and Sea Otters Are Restoring Canada’s Kelp Forests - The Daily Goods
snapshot.evidenceText: A stretch of ocean in Clayoquot Sound is being turned into a kelp nursery, as a First Nation, a restoration group and a kelp company try to rebuild an ecosystem under pressure. The partnership between the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation, Redd Fish Restoration Society and West Coast Kelp has planted more than 4,200 square metres of new kelp habitat since launching in early 2026 in the traditional territory of the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation. “We have grown a lot of kelp,” Emily Fulton, marine program manager for the nonprofit Redd Fish Restoration Society, told Mongabay in a phone interview. Organisers describe it as the largest kelp restoration project on the West Coast of North America. The team is growing baby bull kelp and giant kelp on four lines, each 330 metres long, suspended below the water’s surface and away from seafloor predators such as sea urchins. As the kelp matures, some of it will be removed from the lines and transplanted to sites across Clayoquot Sound to restore degraded kelp forests and seed new ones. The project has cost almost a quarter of a million Canadian dollars, with funding from sources including the provincial government, the World Wildlife Fund of Canada and the Clayoquot Biosphere Trust. Fulton said the project is also about preparing before kelp loss becomes worse in Clayoquot Sound. “If and when that happens, we just have to be ready to act rather than, at that point, go, ‘now how do we do it,” she said. Scientists estimate 11,542 square kilometres of kelp forest are lost globally every year. Along British Columbia’s coast, kelp is already under stress. In 2015, a marine heat wave along the central British Columbia coast wiped out kelp forests after warm water triggered an outbreak of an encrusting bryozoan that smothered the kelp and caused it to sink and disintegrate. Masso said one reason the Tla-o-qui-aht joined the project was the return of sea otters to the region. “The otter played a big role in establishing our kelp forest,” Masso said. Historically, the Tla-o-qui-aht did not hunt sea otters because they knew the animals ate sea urchins, which feed on kelp. But European fur traders hunted sea otters to near extinction across northwestern North America between the 1700s and the early 20th century, Hannah Kobluk, a PhD candidate in the Ocean Relations Collaborative at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia, told Mongabay. Now, with protections in place in Canada and the United States, sea otter populations are beginning to recover naturally. Canada’s Department of Oceans and Fisheries estimates close to 1,500 sea otters live in and around Clayoquot Sound. Masso said his ancestors knew kelp forests supported salmon smolts by offering protection and forage until they were ready to enter the open ocean. Tatt Charlie, a tribal guardian of the Tla-o-qui-aht who has been working in the nursery, said he has already seen the kelp develop. “I’ve been out there a couple of times now,” he told Mongabay in a phone interview. “The first time is when they laid the lines, and it was exciting to see it start. representative.title: Why this Canadian farmer is letting his land grow wild - North Bay News
representative.author: Danielle Tocker Photo/Be Giant

snapshot.title: Why this Canadian farmer is letting his land grow wild
snapshot.evidenceText: Lorne Scott calls his farm an island. Given that it’s in the prairie pothole region of southern Saskatchewan – a sweep of shallow wetlands left by glaciers – this is a metaphor, but it works: in all directions from where we stand, on a sunny day in June, are cultivated croplands. They’ve been planted to within an inch of their lives with canola, wheat, lentils. Except for a few shelterbelts, there are no trees from here to the horizon. Then there’s Scott’s land, thick with trees, shrubs and grasses. Parts of his farm grow wild, or “never broke,” as he puts it, with aspen, snowberry, starflower, Solomon’s seal and northern bedstraw, from which the Cree, who were here before settlement, made red dye. The bedstraw seeds, when roasted, work as a coffee substitute. Scott doesn’t drink coffee. Nor does he harvest any of the Indigenous plants on his land, which sits about nine kilometres south of Indian Head and about 75 kilometres southeast of Regina. They’re just here, left to grow any which way. His land is wild on purpose. It’s fair to call Scott a conservationist, one of the most respected in the province, still active in the community at 79. Soft-spoken and gentle, he is still a farmer: he grows wheat and oats, albeit on a small patch – 32 hectares planted this year. His grandfather was a farmer too, on a property two kilometres east, where Scott grew up. Letting more than a quarter of his farm grow wild is a radical act. Scott wouldn’t say so. He does it “for nature,” he says, to protect the life that’s disappearing, from insects to owls to moose. The day before we met, he saw two yearling moose, as well as a whitetail doe with a fawn and a mule deer. There are bluebird nesting boxes all over the property. What makes all of this radical is the context. Modern agriculture is a high-tech, data-driven industry that uses autonomous field equipment that relies on AI, drones and satellite imagery to maximize resources – land – for profit. “Only a wild man could be so reckless as to let a valuable thing like land go free,” says Andrea Olive, a political science professor at the University of Toronto, a friend of Scott’s and the author of Protecting the Prairies: Lorne Scott and the Politics of Conservation . “It must bother his neighbours, who only see cash crops where Lorne sees true growth.” It does, and some have asked, politely, to rent those perfectly good hectares of his, to plow them under, get things going as God and the commodities markets intended. He tells them no, that their equipment is too big, “and they shake their heads and walk away.” There’s a sign at the entrance to his farm that says, “This Property Is Forever Protected.” That means there’s a conservation easement on part of the property to preserve its natural state. Scott still owns the land and can pass it to his children or whoever he wants, but the restrictions on development are permanent. Scott knows about easements: he served as Saskatchewan’s minister of environment and resource management for four years in the late ‘90s, in Roy Romanow’s NDP government, and was responsible for the Conservation Easements Act, aimed at restricting development of wild land on private property. Under the act, the farmer still owns the land but enters into an agreement with a non-profit, like Ducks Unlimited, to keep it wild, as, say, wetland or grassland. There are thousands of hectares under easement in Saskatchewan. Some ranchers find them useful for protecting natural grasslands for grazing. Grazing is good for grasslands. It disturbs the plants (as does wildfire) in ways that help them grow. A conservative estimate is that 80 per cent of the grassland in Saskatchewan has been lost since commercial agriculture began, most recently through the sale of Crown lands after Ottawa dismantled the 74-year-old Prairie Farm Rehabilitation program in 2009. In the first 20 years of the 21st century, the average farm size increased by about 20 per cent, while the number of farms shrank by 23 per cent. Farms are getting bigger, land prices are rising, and while most farms are owned by the families that work them, one to two per cent are owned by investors and 2.4 per cent by large-scale private landowners. From Manitoba to the Cypress Hills, southern Saskatchewan was once grassland where bison grazed and First Nations hunted. It’s now mostly agricultural, and many farms are dotted with oil wells and pumpjacks, sometimes called “nodding donkeys.” To Scott and groups like the Saskatchewan Wildlife Federation, a non-profit he used to head, the mixed grasslands and fescue prairie are home to more than 30 species at risk, including the greater sage-grouse, and are valuable for that fact alone. Ottawa and the private sector (including Mosaic, a potash mining company, and the Weston family, which backs Be Giant ) have donated millions of dollars to prairie habitat preservation. “Everything gets bigger and better, supposedly,” says Scott, a man of few words until he gets wound up. “The biggest impact I see is on the natural environment. The wetlands, the bush are being cleared, and with equipment and technology, everything is workable these days for growing canola or wheat, whatever, and it's really made a big impact on the natural environment, and consequently some bird species have declined by 90 per cent or more, and largely due to agriculture, intensive farming.” According to Environment and Climate Change Canada, burrowing owl numbers declined 90 per cent from 1990 to 2000, then another 64 per cent between 2005 and 2015. They are small, oddball birds with long legs for running that live underground in tunnels dug by badgers. There are now fewer than 800 pairs left in Saskatchewan and Alberta. “Out in the country and the wild west, I call it, anything goes as long as it benefits you,” Scott says. Scott is not a born politician. He’s not an ideologue. He ran for office as a New Democrat, but in the 1980s, he joined the Progressive Conservative Party. As a boy on the farm, he was more interested in birds than politics, particularly the bluebirds that nested near sloughs and aspen bluffs, in grain bins and any natural cavity, including tractor wheel wells. On a farm, bluebirds bring good luck. But as early as the 1920s, they lost habitat to industrial agriculture and urban spread, and Scott took to building simple wood houses and tacking them up on farm fences to give them a place to nest. In 1969, he got a licence to band bluebirds and tree swallows, and in the first year banded nearly 1,000. Since then, he has banded tens of thousands of birds. With other volunteers, he built a “bluebird trail” of nesting boxes, from Brandon, Manitoba, to Raymore, Saskatchewan, north of Regina. He would drive 800 kilometres four times a year to check on the nests. It was, he says, the longest bluebird trail in the world. Then everything changed: the climate, and the business of agriculture. Large grain farms replaced natural aspen bluffs, wetlands and grasslands. Extreme weather in the bluebirds’ Texas breeding grounds changed migration patterns. By 2014, only six came back to nest near Indian Head, and the next year, none. Scott hasn’t seen bluebirds on his property since. To get to the wild acreage on Scott’s farm, we drive there in a Dodge Caravan (licence plate: BLUEB1RD), not by road but over the hummocky farmland itself . He points to an eastern kingbird on the fence. “From central South America,” he says. The place is home to bees and other insect pollinators, owls, hawks, moose and songbirds. Tree swallows have taken to nesting in the old bluebird houses, and we pull up next to one on a fencepost. He opens the top to show me five white eggs in a nest. Past the fence is a new project: a tree and shrub sanctuary with dozens of species, planted on four hectares when the federal sanctuary in Indian Head was shut down in 2012 following cuts by the Stephen Harper government. Scott is growing sea buckthorn, snowberry, high bush cranberry, apples, crabapples, buffalo berry, chokecherry and poplar – 80 different species – to serve as a seed bank. There is an easement on this land, too. Meanwhile, researchers and neighbours are welcome to take cuttings from the trees. His house is cluttered with school pictures of grandchildren and paintings of ducks and birdhouses. Below a picture of a meadowlark is a small, framed photo of Scott in a suit and Canada-flag tie, receiving the Order of Canada in 2008 from Governor General Michaëlle Jean. The Governor General’s website cites his volunteer work, his political life and his reputation “throughout Western Canada as a staunch defender of wildlife and natural habitats.” I ask him why he practises what he preaches on his own farm, whether this kind of “rewilding,” as it’s called, is more than a gesture. After all, a few hectares of aspen and bedstraw won’t save the planet. “That's the way the land was when I grew up on my dad's farm, you know,” he says. “Back then, people lived more in harmony with nature. They didn't feel it necessary to cultivate every acre, and they relied on the sloughs [for water] and the grass for pasture for hay, the aspen bluffs for wood and [the shrubs for] berry picking.” That’s not radical. He’s talking about an idea of land use that accommodates wildlife alongside a less destructive form of agriculture, not either-or. He’s a farmer. But he paraphrases Teddy Roosevelt: wildlife in its habitat can’t speak, so we must and we will. “Somebody has to,” Scott says. Tom Jokinen is a Winnipeg writer and broadcaster. He writes for The Walrus, Literary Review of Canada and is a regular contributor to CBC Radio Ideas. He's won a National Magazine Award, a New York Festivals Gold Award for audio documentary, and his book Curtains , about the funeral industry, was a Canadian bestseller. representative.title: Drones, explosions and soldiers in bulldozers: surrounded by Israelis in Lebanon's 'model town' - AL-MONITOR: The Middle Eastʼs leading independent news source since 2012
representative.author: Maya Gebeily, Emilie Madi, Mohamed Azakir

snapshot.title: Drones, explosions and soldiers in bulldozers: surrounded by Israelis in Lebanon's 'model town'
snapshot.evidenceText: By Maya Gebeily, Emilie Madi and Mohamed Azakir WEST ZAWTAR, Lebanon Oct 8 (Reuters) - Dodging the broken glass carpeting her home in southern Lebanon, Mariam al-Yaghi exited onto her upper balcony and pointed. A few hundred metres away was a sight the 67-year-old had grown accustomed to: military vehicles moving through the adjacent Lebanese village, still occupied by Israeli troops. At night, Israeli soldiers patrol so close to Yaghi's home inWest Zawtar that she can heartheir voices. By day, she is often trailed by a small Israeli surveillance drone as she toils in her garden. Booms echo throughout the morningas Israel's military destroys homes in the surrounding occupied towns with controlled detonations and bulldozers. "We hear them all the time from that house over there with the tile roof. We hear their voices yelling, the tanks when they move this way and that way. We hear all of that. They’re very close to us, but we’re sitting here and we’re not scared. Never," Yaghi told Reuters. Israeli troops withdrew from WestZawtar in July, the first test of a US-backed "pilot zone" plan for Israel to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon, in exchange for the disarmament of the Iranian-backed militant group Hezbollah. But two months on, no further "pilot zones" have been agreed and residents of West Zawtar say their village is no blueprint. In response to questions from Reuters, the Israeli military said work to remove the threat of Hezbollah's weapons had not been completed. Drones were used to identify threats, and restrictions on movement of local villagers were intended to protect troops. A US State Department spokesperson said the pilot zone process was "the only viable path" to security for both Lebanon and Israel. The zone would expand after the Lebanese army carried out clearance operations in the initial zone, and Hezbollah's disarmament "is an integral part of this process." representative.title: Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns | Economics | The Guardian
representative.author: Heather Stewart

snapshot.title: Developing nations face triple shock from energy crisis, El Niño and borrowing costs, UN warns
snapshot.evidenceText: UN’s development arm calls for urgent action as crises could ‘throw tens if not hundreds of millions back into poverty’ UN’s development arm calls for urgent action as crises could ‘throw tens if not hundreds of millions back into poverty’ Developing countries face a triple shock from the energy crisis, El Niño and surging borrowing costs and need urgent support from the international community, the UN’s development arm has warned. Speaking before the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, the UNDP’s administrator, Alexander De Croo, called for “solidarity and global action”. “Developing countries, their hands and legs are being pulled in different directions: it’s truly hard for them,” he said. Before the meetings, the UNDP published a report, No Time to Recover, which lays out the risks of what it calls the “compounding crises” of energy, climate and debt. Oil prices have been driven back above $100 a barrel in recent weeks since hostilities resumed in the Middle East. The report says that since the Iran war broke out earlier this year, up to 130 million of the world’s poorest people have been shielded from the full impact of high prices by emergency government measures. But it warns many of them are now at risk, as governments run out of the resources needed to keep cushioning their populations against soaring costs. “What we see now is that countries are pivoting their policy and letting the price hikes flow through. They’re pivoting the policy because they have no choice, because their fiscal space is completely eaten up,” De Croo said. “We are witnessing a perfect storm that could throw tens if not hundreds of millions of people back into poverty.” Meanwhile, the worst El Niño climate pattern in perhaps 1,000 years is expected to cause widespread crop failures and increase the risk of extreme weather events, while at the same time the global bond sell-off is driving up government borrowing costs. De Croo said: “The cost today for bond financing for developing countries, it’s 9%. That is really, really high.” He added that the situation was expected to deteriorate between now and the spring. “For each of the three things that we mentioned – fuel prices, El Niño and the bond markets – unfortunately for each of those at the moment, we don’t see any light at the end of the tunnel.” His warning chimes with the findings of separate research published on Sunday by the campaign group Debt Justice, underlining the social impact of high debt servicing costs. It shows that low-income countries classified by the IMF as either in, or at risk of, debt distress have cut their education budgets by an average of 8% since 2019, and wider public spending by 2%. Heidi Chow, the executive director of Debt Justice, said: “High levels of debt are having a devastating impact on people’s access to healthcare and education.” Debt Justice is calling for the outright cancellation of some of the most burdensome debts, and overhaul of the IMF-administered common framework for debt restructuring. Chow said: “We urgently need debt cancellation – especially from the highest interest lenders like banks, hedge funds and oil traders.” De Croo said the UNDP did not oppose efforts to secure debt relief for some of the hardest-hit countries – but argued it would take many months to negotiate, and instead called for more urgent action. “We urge the international community – multilateral lenders, donors, and partners – to step up access to affordable finance so countries can sustain support for their most vulnerable households,” De Croo said. He praised the IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva’s recent call for spending restraint in developed countries, in the hope of taming bond yields. But he said: “We also need to have a coordinated policy for developing countries. And that coordinated policy for developing countries cannot just be, ‘you are at the end of the line and we’ll see what happens’.” He declined to say what the specific response should be, but stressed that it should create “time and space” for developing countries to carry out much-needed changes. During the Covid crisis, G20 nations implemented a temporary standstill on debt repayments for developing countries. De Croo also pointed to liquidity measures available to central banks, such as the currency swap lines implemented by the US Federal Reserve during recent financial crises, to prevent markets seizing up. “What would help is a certain level of liquidity,” he said.

snapshot.title: Largest 2D map of the universe helps scientists discover new gravitational lenses
snapshot.evidenceText: edited by Swati Mestri , reviewed by Robert Egan This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: Using data from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, with help from artificial intelligence, an international team of scientists has discovered 70 new gravitational lenses—rare cosmic alignments that act as natural magnifying glasses. The new lenses further expand one of the largest collections of confirmed lenses to date and will allow scientists to study dark matter, galaxy evolution and the structure of the universe. In August 2026, the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys team released the largest 2D map of the universe ever created. The 5.6-trillion-pixel map contains nearly 4 billion celestial objects, including stars, galaxies, black holes and asteroids. This map was created using data from three ground-based sky surveys: The Legacy Surveys map has been 13 years in the making, and regular data releases from the team have enabled scientists to make countless discoveries across a range of subfields in astronomy and astrophysics. In one such research project, an international team led by Xiaosheng Huang (Santa Clara University and DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory) used machine learning to inspect the vast Legacy Surveys data set and identify thousands of new gravitational lens candidates. In an extensive follow-up study published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series , led by Emerald Lin (an undergraduate student at UC Berkeley) and Ivonne Toro Bertolla (a research assistant at NSF NOIRLab and science operations assistant at Las Campanas Observatory), the team spectroscopically confirmed 70 of the candidates, establishing them as true instances of gravitational lensing. A gravitational lens occurs when a massive object such as a galaxy, galaxy cluster or black hole lies directly between Earth and a more distant background object. The foreground object's gravity bends and magnifies the background light, producing arcs, rings and even multiple images of the same object. These natural telescopes allow astronomers to study objects that would otherwise be too distant or faint to detect. They can magnify galaxies from the early universe, reveal the presence and distribution of invisible dark matter , help improve measurements of the universe's expansion rate and enable the detection of exoplanets—planets orbiting other stars. "The DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys' deep and wide-field images have provided an unprecedented foundation for discovering new gravitational lenses," says Aleksandar Cikota, an associate scientist at NSF NOIRLab, co-author of the study and PI of the follow-up observing program. "What we're building now is a carefully confirmed sample that researchers can use for years to come." While the Legacy Surveys provided the foundation for discovering these lenses, that foundation was vast. This created both an opportunity and a challenge: Thousands of gravitational lenses were likely waiting to be found, but visually searching for them was impractical. So the team had to devise a robust and efficient process for scouring the data to identify the lenses buried within them. This is where they turned to artificial intelligence. Using a residual neural network—a form of machine learning designed to recognize subtle patterns in images—the team searched the survey data for the distinctive signatures of gravitational lensing. Earlier work using these techniques had created a catalog containing about 3,500 potential lenses. The machine-learning approach dramatically accelerated the discovery process, allowing astronomers to focus valuable telescope time on follow-up observations of the most promising candidates. "The combination of large surveys and AI-powered searches is transforming how we discover rare objects in the sky," says Cikota. "These tools allow us to systematically search for systems that, previously, only a few years ago, we might have discovered only serendipitously." The initial lens searches also relied on advanced computing resources, including infrastructure provided by the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a DOE Office of Science user facility, underscoring how modern astronomy increasingly depends on powerful computation alongside telescopes. The AI-powered search uncovered 76 gravitational lens candidates, but this was only the first step. To determine whether an object is truly a gravitational lens, astronomers must use telescopes to measure the distances to both the lensing and background objects. To confirm the lens candidates uncovered in the Legacy Surveys, the team used the Multi-Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) instrument on the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope. MUSE was particularly handy for this task since it employs a technique called integral field spectroscopy. Unlike a traditional spectrograph, which records light from only a narrow region of the sky, an integral field spectrograph collects a spectrum at every point across an image. The result is a three-dimensional data set containing both spatial and spectral information. MUSE proved valuable for this study as it allowed the researchers to simultaneously study the lensing and background objects, as well as other nearby objects, in the same observation. The instrument's broad wavelength coverage also enabled the detection of faint spectral features that revealed the distances and physical properties of the objects involved. Using MUSE observations collected between 2022 and 2024, the team confirmed that 70 of the candidates were true gravitational lenses. While the newly confirmed lenses are scientifically interesting on their own, their greatest impact may come from what they enable in the future. The newly discovered gravitational lenses have been added to the DESI Strong Lens Foundry Project, one of the largest collections of confirmed lenses to date. The large, well-characterized lens sample provides an essential foundation for studies of dark matter, galaxy structure and cosmology. Combined with observations from facilities like the Hubble Space Telescope, the James Webb Space Telescope and the recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, as well as with large surveys like NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST), these lenses will help researchers probe the distribution of dark matter, study distant galaxies and test models of cosmic evolution. The work also highlights the enduring scientific value of the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys. What began as a massive imaging campaign to create a 3D map of the universe is now serving as the foundation for a growing catalog of gravitational lenses that will support discoveries for years to come. "Each confirmed lens adds to a resource that will benefit the entire astronomical community," says Cikota. "Together, we are building a powerful foundation for future discoveries." Emerald Lin et al, DESI Strong Lens Foundry. IV. Spectroscopic Confirmation of DESI Lens Candidates with VLT/MUSE, The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series (2026).
