The town also plans to revisit the feasibility of trash incineration — a concept that was shelved following the fire but has proven beneficial in other northern communities, like Nuuk, Nvt. , where the energy generated from burning household garbage is used to heat homes. Eliasson thinks incineration should be given higher priority. “Churchill has been talking about an incinerator [for a long time] and … we’re just not building one. It’s the only solution,” he says. “Polar bears will break into everything else.” The western Hudson Bay subpopulation, which includes Churchill and ranges from Chesterfield Inlet in Nunavut to the Manitoba-Ontario border, is the most researched group of polar bears in the world, according to Polar Bears International . There are roughly 800 bears living in the territory today, representing a 30 per cent population decline over the last 46 years due to shrinking sea ice caused by climate change, Evan Richardson, a polar bear research scientist with Environment and Climate Change Canada, says. “This is one of the most southern polar bear populations in the world, and it was among the first to show impacts of reduced sea ice availability on individual body condition, growth, reproduction and survival,” Richardson says. Polar bears make their living on the ice, using the frozen platforms to hunt for seals. Open water makes the speedy prey increasingly harder to catch. The Hudson Bay population is experiencing an era of relative stability thanks to several good ice seasons, Richardson says. While this gives current generations of bears a positive start, the survival of the species is dependent on the long-term health of their environment. “Polar bears don’t occur anywhere where there’s not persistent annual sea ice, and so as the habitat melts, it threatens the bears’ existence,” he says. Climate change is further straining the coexistence of bears and humans in northern Manitoba. “It’s a bit of a perfect storm,” York says. “Less ice means the area is more accessible to more human activity. At the same time, more bears are spending more time on shore.” As the ice-free season grows longer, Hudson Bay is seeing more traffic, whether it be freight, tourism or research. In Manitoba, the provincial and federal governments are keen to expand operations at the Port of Churchill to include year-round shipping, an all-weather road, an upgraded rail line and a liquefied natural gas terminal — all of which will bring more people and disturbance to the region. To ease the pressure on residents — bears and humans alike — York believes the governments should focus on shoring up local infrastructure, including Churchill’s garbage facility, before embarking on major national projects in remote northern communities. “Take a quick step back and say, ‘Hey, what’s needed here today for the people who are there now?’ ” he says. “This waste management need has been acute, and we haven’t had the best luck getting the attention we think it merits, from the human-health side, but also the environmental-health and wildlife-health side.” There have been 159 bear sightings and encounters reported so far this year in Churchill to the province’s Polar Bear Alert Program — a 24-hour hotline designed to minimize dangerous interactions while the animals move ashore from mid-July to mid-November. If a bear is reported near the town or dump, Manitoba Conservation officers will chase them away with non-lethal scaring devices, such as noisemakers or flares. “Problem bears” that return repeatedly or refuse to leave the area are placed in the province’s polar bear holding facility near the Churchill airport and relocated more remotely via helicopter. Seven bears have been flown out of town this year. The holding facility, colloquially known as polar bear jail , is also where orphaned cubs begin their journey to Winnipeg. representative.title: L.A. homeless agency meeting canceled after voter turnout surge - Los Angeles Times
representative.author: Doug Smith

snapshot.title: Bass-led turnout surge crashes meeting to replace L.A. homeless outreach agency
snapshot.evidenceText: It's not unusual for a public meeting to be canceled for lack of a quorum. But there isn't even a word for what happened Friday when a once-obscure board canceled a meeting to decide the future of homeless services in Los Angeles because too many people came to vote. More than 1,500 potential voters signed up for a meeting of the Los Angeles Continuum of Care board to pick a replacement for the core duties of the beleaguered Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority. Under the board's unusual charter, they all were eligible to vote merely because of their interest in homelessness. The onslaught was organized by Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who sent out a blast message through her communications networks urging people to join the meeting via Zoom to vote down the board's recommendation that Los Angeles County assume those duties. The response was overwhelming, but it didn't work. Over cries of foul from those who came in person, the board's attorney Shayla Myers announced the meeting was canceled because the Zoom channel had a capacity of only 1,000. Later, the board issued a formal statement saying, "The vote had to be continued today to ensure that all LA CoC members would be able to participate, given an unexpectedly high number of individuals who joined the online meeting." Bass and four City Council members then put out a statement lambasting the board for a failure that disenfranchised members. "Without collaboration and transparency, management of this complex issue will continue to falter, and worse, our unhoused neighbors will continue to suffer," the statement said. The cancellation deepens a crisis over the region's federally mandated homelessness functions. At stake is control over the annual homelessness count, the database that tracks every interaction with homeless people, the matching system that determines who receives housing and the responsibility for submitting applications for federal funding on behalf of dozens of local agencies. The Trump administration touched off the crisis in June when it suspended LAHSA as the agency performing those functions, citing a history of mismanagement and possible fraud. The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development said local homeless service providers would have to apply directly to it for funding. LAHSA contested the move in federal court. U.S. District Judge David O. Carter temporarily stayed the suspension, keeping LAHSA in place for now but allowing 60 days to choose a replacement to assume its duties. That decision, upheld on appeal, put the onus on the Continuum of Care, an amorphous entity with a board and open membership that had long functioned as an appendage of LAHSA but actually had the statutory power to hire or fire the agency. Carter ordered the CoC, as it is commonly called, to report on its recommendations Tuesday and set Oct. 27 as the date to name the new agency. The CoC board, which includes representatives of homeless services contractors, hired outside consultants to set up an emergency bidding process and score the applicants. The City of Los Angeles applied for two of LAHSA's functions, the homeless database and the matching system, but scored below Los Angeles County in both. The county applied for all four functions and won the recommendation. The final step was a vote of the membership on Friday. The meltdown was foreseeable. A member of LAHSA's governing commission predicted it in an August LinkedIn post. Noting that membership “consists of persons and entities interested in collaborative, solution-oriented planning to address homelessness in LA County,” Justin Szlasa concluded, "that could arguably include tens or even hundreds of thousands of people. No comprehensive list of general members currently exists," and it would be almost impossible to compile one. "As the LA CoC takes on more authority and moves out of the orbit of LAHSA, effort should be made to broaden and deepen engagement with stakeholders in our homeless response system ... who are all, by definition, members of the LA CoC," Szlasa wrote. Bass turned that advice into a crash course. As enrollment in Friday's Zoom passed the 1,000 mark, Myers, the CoC attorney, told those present in the downtown meeting room that "because we have reached capacity on Zoom and CoC members are not able to participate, we have to continue this." The board is now working to upgrade its Zoom account and has yet to set a new date. Bass and the council members blamed the CoC for not planning adequately for a large audience. "Angelenos want a voice in the future of homelessness services, and they were silenced today. The current proposal for County-only administration, recommended by the LA CoC Board, leaves no room for those voices to be heard," the statement said. Ben Kay, chair of the CoC board, countered that it could not have anticipated the mayor and City Council using their "immense communications infrastructure to push public turnout" to defeat the recommendation. "Suggesting the board was unprepared for the city's unprecedented actions plays directly into the hands of HUD, which started all of this by saying the L.A. region shouldn't be allowed to make its own decisions about homeless services," Kay said. In a statement Saturday, Supervisor Lindsey Horvath said that, "failing to hold yesterday’s meeting is unacceptable and erodes public trust." Horvath said the county is prepared to partner with every city in the county to "listen to their concerns, and work toward solutions that address them." The county has committed that the City of Los Angeles would "at a minimum" maintain its access to the database and matching system, Horvath said. Times staff writer David Zahniser contributed to this report.

snapshot.title: Turtles found buried in metres of mud returned to rejuvenated wetland
snapshot.evidenceText: Paul Keyte releasing turtles into the Gingham Wetlands. ( Supplied DCCEEW ) The first turtles rescued from a dried-out Gingham Waterhole in the Gwydir Wetlands near Moree are back in the wild. Taronga Western Plains Zoo in Dubbo helped rehabilitate the rescued turtles and is now incubating more than 250 eggs laid by the reptiles. The remaining adult turtles will be progressively released, while hatchlings are expected to be returned to the wild by the end of next year. The first turtles rescued from a dried-out wetland in north-west NSW are back in their natural habitat, with a new generation of turtle hatchlings expected to join them later this year. Ten broad-shelled turtles and three Murray River turtles were released at Gingham Waterhole in the Gwydir Wetlands in September by the NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW). They were among 39 rescued from the waterhole after it dried out in April, and taken to Taronga Western Plains Zoo in Dubbo for rehabilitation. Turtles covered in mud, saved from the Gwydir Wetlands by UNE ecologists in April 2026 ( Supplied: Debbie Bower ) Senior keeper James Witcombe said seeing the first reptiles return to a refilled wetland after months in care was a significant moment. "It's the kind of moment that we as zookeepers and conservationists live for, to see something that's a pretty devastating reality turn into a much better future," he said. "To see that first group of 13 returning to their wetland and seeing photos of the wetland full of beautiful water and invertebrates returning to that space, it really is a special moment." The 13 turtles were returned to Gingham Waterhole as part of a staged release in September. ( Supplied: DCCEEW ) The turtles were found burrowed deep in the mud, after Water NSW temporarily suspended environmental water flows to the wetlands earlier this year. Mr Witcombe said the 39 reptiles arrived in Dubbo covered in thick mud and underwent comprehensive health assessments, while keepers quickly adapted the purpose-built platypus conservation centre to accommodate them. "They were all covered in dense, filthy mud, so we set up a bit of a production line to get them all cleaned off and identified," he said. Keepers and veterinarians monitored the turtles' recovery, regularly weighing them and providing plenty of food to improve their condition after they experienced stress in the drying wetland. Once the turtles were healthy enough, keepers lowered the water temperature to mimic winter conditions and provided UV lamps and basking areas to give the light they needed. The rescued turtles spent several months in care at Taronga Western Plains Zoo in Dubbo. ( Supplied: DCCEEW ) The initial health checks also revealed 14 female broad-shelled turtles were carrying eggs. Because broad-shelled turtles usually lay their eggs during rainy conditions, keepers instead induced egg-laying. Now more than 250 turtle eggs are sitting in an incubator at the Dubbo zoo. Most of the female broad-shelled turtles arrived at the zoo carrying eggs. ( Supplied: DCCEEW ) "We will still see a very large percentage of those make it to hatching stage," Mr Witcombe said. The hatchlings could provide an important boost to the population, with foxes and other feral pests known to dig up the subterranean turtle nests at the Gingham Waterhole. The young turtles are expected to be released into the wild by the end of next year. Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Environmental flows resumed in late May and refilled Gingham Waterhole, allowing the staged return of the turtles to begin. DCCEEW executive director of conservation programs Ingrid Emery said the reptiles were being selectively released. "They are being returned progressively over the coming months as the conditions allow and as they're healthy enough to do so," she said. "We are seeing the ecosystem recover out there," she said. Environmental water deliveries had been suspended earlier this year amid concerns about inundation of neighbouring private property. Wildlife specialists rescued the turtles as Gingham Waterhole dried out earlier this year. ( Supplied: DCCEEW ) Ms Emery said the department was working with landholders and an environmental water advisory group to plan future water deliveries. "We're planning to use our environmental water to maintain refuge habitat, because we know we are going into a dry period," she said. The released turtles will not be individually tracked, but Ms Emery said ongoing ecological monitoring would help the department assess the health of the wetland and plan future water management. representative.title: Naidiri village, Fiji: 18,000 corals and a no fishing zone since 2009
representative.author: Nicole McMahon

snapshot.title: Naidiri village, Fiji: 18,000 corals and a no fishing zone since 2009
snapshot.evidenceText: Naidiri is 32 households on Fiji's Coral Coast. Since 2009 it has kept a stretch of its own sea closed to fishing, and in one year planted 18,000 corals and 10,000 mangroves. Now its youth group wants the protected line pushed further out. Drive the Queens Road along the south coast of Viti Levu and you pass Naidiri without noticing it: a village of fewer than 150 people in Nadroga, with the reef flat right there beyond the beach. Sixteen years ago that reef was in trouble. "We saw overfishing, and we were restoring fish," says Manoa Duwai, who co founded what is now the Naidiri Biodiversity Park. "There was no coral and no juvenile fish. We thought, if this is the case, what will our children ever have? That was when we came up with the idea of a marine protected area." In 2009 the village declared a tabu, a traditional no fishing zone, along about 3.6 kilometres of its shoreline, and left it alone. Two years later its young people formed a youth group to look after it, the first of its kind among the 22 villages of Nadroga. In 2023 alone the community planted 18,000 corals on frames in the lagoon and 10,000 mangroves along the shore. Last year the park took first prize in its category at the OceanLove Innovation Awards in Barcelona, chosen from 260 entries from 64 countries. Waisea Nasokia of the Fiji Sun visited this week and found the fish back, the frames full, and the young people asking for more. Read the full story: Naidiri youths protect ocean for next generation, by Waisea Nasokia, Fiji Sun . More, in Naidiri, means further. Joseva Kungado, the village youth leader, told the Fiji Sun that the tabu must continue and its boundary should be extended out to sea, because the pressure on the reef has not gone away. Storm surges have smashed coral frames and the cages where giant clams are grown, and each time the youth group has rebuilt them. "We don't want our future generation to say our parents and our forefathers did not give something to us," Kungado said. "We want to leave something for them." On Monday a group of visitors planted coral with them at Naidiri Bay, among them Brianna Fruean, the Samoan Pacific leader, and Kal Glanznig, a young Australian ocean champion, who said it was "fascinating to see such incredible work by the youths of Naidiri." It is the simplest conservation there is, and it is the kind that works best close to shore, where the people who gave the water its rest can wade out and watch it heal. Our short take: the full story is by Waisea Nasokia for the Fiji Sun (6 October 2026). Enjoyed this? Every new edition is free, straight to your inbox. Subscribe free In Tla-o-qui-aht waters off Tofino, guardians, scientists and a kelp grower are raising baby kelp on four long lines under the sea and planting it out so young salmon and herring have a forest again. About 1,500 sea otters, back after the fur trade, are helping. At Long Nanny on the Northumberland coast, National Trust rangers kept watch over the dunes day and night all summer, and 126 pairs of little terns nested there, more than double the 1994 record. At Blakeney Point, a thousand pairs of sandwich terns came back after two years away. Voting is open in the ABC's Australian Insect of the Year, a tortoise shelled ladybird is in the final six, and the reigning champion is a dragonfly with painted wings. Good news for a living planet. representative.title: Resident who won’t tidy lawn files human rights complaints against city - MPulse
representative.author: Leslie McMillan

snapshot.title: Resident who won’t tidy lawn files human rights complaints against city - MPulse
snapshot.evidenceText: The City of Mississauga previously lost a court case against a resident who didn’t want to cut his grass Featured image: AI-generated editorial illustration; not a photograph of the reported event. Yard maintenance is once again a human rights issue in Mississauga. An unnamed local man has launched a human rights complaint against the city, alleging discrimination on the basis of disability because neighbours want him to keep his yard tidy. Mpulse first learned about this case when Mississauga resident George Batsakis and his daughter Tina appeared before Mississauga city council on September 9. Batsakis told council about the problems he has with his neighbour’s yard, telling the committee the neighbour, “has not cut it [the grass] in 2 years.” Batsakis, 79, an avid gardener himself, told council that as a result, he has to contend with “rats parading in the backyard,” eating his produce, damaging his plants and “now there’s even snakes.” Batsakis told council that after 2 years with no resolution, he felt his only recourse was to appeal to council for a reduction on his property tax bill. While that appeal was denied, city councillors were sympathetic to his plight. City Solicitor Graham Walsh told council that while the city is working to resolve the issue, the human rights complaint the resident has filed has “complicated onerous enforcement action.” He said the city has offered solutions, such as removing the grass and replacing it with something that would not need to be cut, but that the case is still before the tribunal and nothing has been decided. According to the current by-law, tall grass violations come with a $305 fine and a requirement to comply within 7 days. A failure to comply could lead to greater fines and the city showing up to cut the grass and then adding the bill to the resident’s property taxes. This current human rights case is not the first time a Mississauga resident has challenged the city’s tall grass by-law. Earlier this year, Mississauga man Wolf Ruck won his case in Ontario Superior Court when the court ruled that the Mississauga by-law infringed on his Charter right to freedom of expression. Ruck’s “naturalized garden” had in the past been cut down by the city. In response to the ruling, the city introduced and passed a new “Turfgrass and Prohibited Plant Species by-law” this spring. While it still requires owners or occupiers of a property to ensure that the height of their traditional turfgrass does not exceed 20cm, there are exemptions for naturalized gardens. Depending on the outcome of the current case before the Human Rights Tribunal, there could be more changes to come for the by-law. In the meantime, Walsh told Batsakis that “the law of neighbourly conduct” still applies and “the human rights matter does not stop [Batsakis]] from taking action against his neighbour civilly.” Save my name, email, and website in this browser for the next time I comment.

representative.title: These women are bringing Darwin’s rheas back to Chilean Patagonia
representative.author: Sam Lee

snapshot.title: These women are bringing Darwin’s rheas back to Chilean Patagonia
snapshot.evidenceText: If you liked this story, share it with other people. PATAGONIA NATIONAL PARK — Chile. Mongabay traveled to Chile’s Patagonia National Park to follow a women-led team on a mission to bring 13 Darwin’s rheas back to the wild in April 2026. Working with Rewilding Chile Foundation , these dedicated rangers care for the birds around the clock, facing harsh weather, predators like pumas, illegal livestock grazing, and other threats to the park’s fragile ecosystem. For more than a century, the Chacabuco Valley, where the park is located, was dominated by sheep and cattle ranching. Fences fragmented the vast Patagonian steppes and rheas (Rhea pennata) nearly disappeared. But one of South America’s most ambitious rewilding efforts is helping to turn the tide. Tompkins Conservation, the organization behind Rewilding Chile, acquired former ranchlands and began removing thousands of kilometers of fencing, allowing native wildlife to reclaim the landscape. Now, the team is preparing for another milestone: Releasing 13 Darwin’s rheas into the wild. Mongabay followed the rangers in the days leading up to the release, documenting their preparations, the challenges they faced, and their determination to give these birds the best possible chance of survival. representative.title: How a retired Navajo Nation doctor earned a MacArthur 'genius' grant for public art : NPR
representative.author: Adam Burke

snapshot.title: How a retired Navajo Nation doctor earned a MacArthur 'genius' grant for public art
snapshot.evidenceText: Chip Thomas, a retired physician on the Navajo Reservation, is well known for his large photograhpic murals. Now, he's been recognized with a MacArthur "genius" grant. SCOTT SIMON, HOST: Think of street art and what might come to mind is city buildings with giant murals, subway cars tagged with spray paint or stenciled sidewalks. Well, Chip Thomas creates street art in rural places - large-scale photographs on abandoned buildings across the Navajo Nation. This year, the MacArthur Foundation gave Chip Thomas what's known as a genius grant. KSUT's Adam Burke has this profile. ADAM BURKE, BYLINE: North of Flagstaff, Arizona, the ribbon of highway disappears into a sea of sagebrush and yellow grasses. Chip Thomas steers his hatchback off the road to an abandoned cinder-block building. CHIP THOMAS: This is the natural evolution of a piece on the desert. It's breaking down. BURKE: Lean, bearded, dreadlocks tucked inside a canvas cap, Thomas approaches the tiny structure, which might have been a storage shed at one time. The roof and the door are gone now. THOMAS: This is part of a sight-and-sound installation. Looks like the sound may have stopped. BURKE: Inside, a 10-foot-wide black-and-white image covers the back wall. It's an art piece, spotlighting the devastating health effects of uranium mining among Navajo workers during the Cold War. THOMAS: My images of Kee John, who died at a young age from a cancer related to his work in a uranium mine. BURKE: In the photo, a young Navajo man wears a hard hat with a headlamp and operates uranium mining equipment, but the image is fading. Pieces of the installation are peeling off the walls. (SOUNDBITE OF GEIGER COUNTER) THOMAS: Oh, here we go. The sound loop is working. BURKE: Then suddenly a solar-powered speaker kicks on, and we hear the garbled sounds of a Geiger counter. This is what's left of the installation's audio. THOMAS: This is on its last leg (laughter). But it's impressive. It's been running 3 1/2 years now nonstop. BURKE: Since 2009, Chip Thomas has been putting up artwork in places like this across the Navajo Nation, working against the unrelenting wind and sand. THOMAS: The work is ephemeral, you know, is paper versus the elements, and the elements - Mother Nature always wins. BURKE: On a landscape of disorienting scale and inscrutable distances, his black-and-white installations offer outsized visions of daily life on the rez - men on horseback, grandmothers herding sheep, the delighted faces of children playing. And for Thomas, any building is a canvas - deserted gas stations, old trailers, water tanks. THOMAS: Structures that are close enough to the road that are big enough where I can put an interesting, hopefully engaging piece. BURKE: Twenty-five minutes down the highway, we stop at a roadside stand where vendors are selling table loads of turquoise and silver jewelry. TORREY CHARLEY: Good to see you, friend. THOMAS: Yeah. You too. CHARLEY: Nice to see you. BURKE: Torrey Charley (ph) is working one of the stands. She's 29 and first started seeing Thomas' artwork as a teenager. CHARLEY: I was like, oh, wow, you know, there's somebody that's interested in livestock and kids or, you know, the elders within the community. BURKE: Charley is Navajo, or Dine, as Navajo people call themselves. CHARLEY: I think, as a teenager, I was like, dang, I wonder who this is. THOMAS: I had thought because of the isolation, I would just be there initially for two years, but my two years turned into 36. THOMAS: There was, you know, a degree of trust, and I could stick a camera not literally in someone's face, but I could get closer physically than a stranger could and tell a more intimate story. THOMAS: It was like, oh, my God, this is it. This person has figured out how to take a documentary black-and-white photograph, blow it up to scale and to use it as street art. My mind was blown. representative.title: Mississauga election 2026: Mayoral candidates talk redeveloping Living Arts Centre, platform policy planks
representative.author: Nick Westoll

snapshot.title: Mississauga mayoral candidates talk redeveloping Living Arts Centre, platform policy planks
snapshot.evidenceText: With two-and-a-half weeks to go until Mississauga election day, talk about potentially redeveloping a notable chunk of the city’s downtown entered into the campaign on Thursday as mayoral candidates put forward various policy ideas and focuses. While unveiling the remaining parts of her campaign platform, Bonnie Crombie said she wants to put a stop to studying the potential demolition of the Living Arts Centre as part of a massive redevelopment project. “I will cancel Carolyn Parrish’s proposed redevelopment of the Living Arts Centre and surrounding civic lands, a $2.5-billion vanity project at a time when residents are struggling with everyday bills; this is the wrong priority,” she told reporters, arguing any potential municipal funding should be redirected to other priorities and initiatives. The Living Arts Centre, located just north of Mississauga city hall and west of Square One, opened in 1997. It has a 1,300-seat main auditorium along with various meeting rooms and exhibition spaces. Earlier in 2026, Mississauga city council voted to begin a study and consultation process that could ultimately result in a downtown transformation. The major part of the planning centres around potentially replacing the Living Arts Centre and a nearby park, which totals around 12 acres, with a new convention centre, hotel, music hub, offices, apartments and retail spaces. It is not clear when a possible vote on whether or not to proceed with that vision could be held. While making an announcement on providing additional infrastructure and supports for Ridgeway Plaza as part of a broader small business plan, Alvin Tedjo rejected the idea of proceeding with the potential massive redevelopment. “The mayor’s plan to build a $2.5-billion convention centre is a terrible idea; no one is asking for this. They’re also going to be taking out the parkland and the parking in the area. That green space is so valued for the residents who live in that area,” he said, adding he wants residents to help determine the future for the area and is open to potentially renovating the Living Arts Centre. Dipika Damerla also rejected the idea, saying she wants to proceed with a vision for downtown Mississauga that is focused on a health care innovation district. “[It] will bring young talent and make Mississauga the Silicon Valley of commercializing health care innovation,” she said, pointing to existing and upcoming hospital and education infrastructure in the city and region. Speaking with CityNews ahead of an apartment groundbreaking in Port Credit Thursday afternoon, Parrish said she backs the proposed redevelopment concept. She said a majority of the required funding would come from the private sector and noted there would be an elevated park for residents to use. “I think it’s a fabulous job creator. I think it’s a wonderful way to increase our income and taxes at the City and to enliven our city centre, it’s perfect,” she said. “We’re a modern city and we’re looking at modern ideas.” Parrish said if the plan proceeded, the Living Arts Centre would not be torn down until a new building gets erected. She also said the convention centre could be as big as 300,000 square feet and added she would like to see a five-star hotel opened to support the redevelopment. As advance voting continues in Mississauga until the end of Sunday , the leading Mississauga mayoral candidates continue to put forward policy ideas and focuses. During her announcement Thursday afternoon, Crombie touted various policy proposals on a variety of areas. “I will put the priorities of Mississaugans first and they’re clear: To bring taxes under control, protect jobs, attract investment, get Mississauga moving again and make our neighbourhoods safer,” she said. Damerla told CityNews she plans to keep campaigning and promoting the key themes of her campaign. “Here [are] the highlights of my plan: Freeze property taxes in 2027 and thereafter keep them at or below inflation, stop the waste at city hall (and) hire an independent auditor general, stop the $100 million that we’re bleeding every year to Brampton by fixing the unfair policing formula, (and) allowing ‘six-plexes’ as of right on certain arterial roads to make housing more affordable and realistic for young families,” she said Thursday afternoon. When asked what she wanted to accomplish if she gets elected for a full term, Parrish said she was focused on two areas. “Housing, I want to keep that up. I was at a topping-off ceremony yesterday for three towers on the other side of Port Credit. This is a ground-breaker, and it’s all because of the incentive that we brought in as a council,” she said Thursday afternoon, adding the changes have resulted in support from developers. “We’ve got to work on the taxes, that’s a big one. Step one was getting the road maintenance moved down from the region so we don’t have to subsidize Caledon $30 million next year, another $18 million or so on waste that we’ve moved down from the region. “Of course I’m working on the police budget, which is a 38 (per cent)-62 (per cent) split (with Brampton) and I do have a commitment from the premier that he is going to do it (addressing the funding disparity between the two cities).” Tedjo, speaking outside of Ridgeway Plaza Thursday morning, talked about his small business policy plank, which is part of his broader overall campaign platform. He said initiatives include a new 100-day guarantee for “qualified small-business permits,” small business hubs with “more affordable commercial space,” and expanded youth opportunities. He also said he would pursue bringing a Peel Regional Police substation to the plaza, which has seen crackdowns by officers amid concerns over nuisance gatherings , and extra parking at a nearby site to support the plaza. “Local entrepreneurs are spending too much time navigating city hall, small businesses are struggling to stay afloat and younger people are having a harder time getting a foot in the door. My plan will transform the City of Mississauga from a barrier into a partner,” Tedjo said. Click here for a list of all 14 candidates running for mayor. Election day in Mississauga and all of Ontario’s municipalities is on Oct. 26. representative.title: Eskasoni, efuel company create joint venture to make jet fuel from seawater | CBC News
representative.author: Tom Ayers

snapshot.title: Eskasoni, efuel company create joint venture to make jet fuel from seawater | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: A Mi'kmaw community in Cape Breton is placing a big bet on new technology that it says can turn seawater into environmentally friendly jet fuel. Eskasoni First Nation has invested $1.5 million and is the majority owner in a joint venture called eFuels Mi'kmaq Limited that plans to build a pilot project on band-owned land in Cape Breton Regional Municipality's industrial park in Sydney harbour. Bertram Bernard, a band councillor and chair of Eskasoni Corporate Services, said the investment will create local jobs for band members and is an important step in taking a meaningful role in a growing industry. "For us, this is about creating long-term economic opportunities, while continuing to be responsible stewards of our land and waters," he said during an announcement Thursday at the Sarah Denny Cultural Centre in Eskasoni. The newly formed eFuels Mi'kmaq plans to extract hydrogen from seawater and draw carbon dioxide from the air to create what is known as drop-in fuel, meaning it can be burned like any other fuel without any engine modifications. The process is expected to be powered by wind energy from onshore and offshore sources as they become available. Eskasoni band councillor Bertram Bernard says the joint venture will create lasting economic benefits while ensuring stewardship of resources. (Tom Ayers/CBC) The joint venture is with Aeon Blue, a company that started in the United States but moved to Sydney to take advantage of federal government incentives and the research facilities at the Verschuren Centre on Cape Breton University's campus. Lark Meadow, a co-founder and CEO of Aeon Blue, said it was important to her and her brother, co-founder Deois Ua Cearnaigh, to have Indigenous participation. "We are partnering all the way from piloting to commercialization, so we are going to grow our partnership and the facilities together," she said. Ua Cearnaigh, who is an electrochemist, said the technology to separate hydrogen from seawater and combine it with carbon dioxide to make all kinds of fuels has been around for decades. Aeon Blue CEO Lark Meadow says although the process can produce a wide range of fuel types, jet fuel was chosen because of growing demand. (Tom Ayers/CBC) But he said his patented process improves on the technology and makes it economical on a commercial scale. "It's kind of like saying the cart, four-wheeled vehicles, are thousands of years old, but the car only came around in the 1910s," he said. It also draws more carbon from the air than it uses, with the excess carbon dioxide being sequestered. Meadow said that may be in the ground or in other ways that have yet to be decided. Although the process can produce a wide range of fuel types, Meadow said jet fuel was chosen because there's a growing demand for green fuel in air travel. Officials say the joint venture is expected to produce 12 jobs next year and up to 80 when the efuel process reaches full commercialization. (Tom Ayers/CBC) Ua Cearnaigh said the move from their home in Texas not only made sense because of the government's financial incentives, but he said the Verschuren Centre's laboratories are superior to others and the geography means all of the components needed for the process are readily available. "Cape Breton has sort of this magical location where it is as close to the southern extent of winter sea ice as you can go and still have ice-free ports in the winter, and yet also the wind howls like nobody's business," he said. "It really is an X marks the spot. If you were going to do an efuels project, doesn't matter who you are, you would pick this island." Meadow said a pilot project will be located on Eskasoni's land in Sydport and is expected to start making fuel next year. It is expected to scale up the following year, with full commercialization to follow by 2030. eFuels Mi'kmaq Ltd. plans to build a pilot project on Eskasoni land in Sydport industrial park to make jet fuel from seawater. (Tom Ayers/CBC) Meadow said large-scale commercialization will require more land, but the manufacturing site will still be located along the coast of Cape Breton. The joint venture is expected to start training up to 12 Eskasoni band members in engineering, operations and management next year, and could create up to 80 full-time jobs when full commercialization is achieved. Steve Parsons, CEO of Eskasoni's corporate division, said the deal has been in the works for about 18 months. "We're very excited," he said. "This is a great opportunity for the community." representative.title: Eskasoni, efuel company create joint venture to make jet fuel from seawater | CBC News
representative.author: Tom Ayers

snapshot.title: Eskasoni, efuel company create joint venture to make jet fuel from seawater | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: A Mi'kmaw community in Cape Breton is placing a big bet on new technology that it says can turn seawater into environmentally friendly jet fuel. Eskasoni First Nation has invested $1.5 million and is the majority owner in a joint venture called eFuels Mi'kmaq Limited that plans to build a pilot project on band-owned land in Cape Breton Regional Municipality's industrial park in Sydney harbour. Bertram Bernard, a band councillor and chair of Eskasoni Corporate Services, said the investment will create local jobs for band members and is an important step in taking a meaningful role in a growing industry. "For us, this is about creating long-term economic opportunities, while continuing to be responsible stewards of our land and waters," he said during an announcement Thursday at the Sarah Denny Cultural Centre in Eskasoni. The newly formed eFuels Mi'kmaq plans to extract hydrogen from seawater and draw carbon dioxide from the air to create what is known as drop-in fuel, meaning it can be burned like any other fuel without any engine modifications. The process is expected to be powered by wind energy from onshore and offshore sources as they become available. Eskasoni band councillor Bertram Bernard says the joint venture will create lasting economic benefits while ensuring stewardship of resources. (Tom Ayers/CBC) The joint venture is with Aeon Blue, a company that started in the United States but moved to Sydney to take advantage of federal government incentives and the research facilities at the Verschuren Centre on Cape Breton University's campus. Lark Meadow, a co-founder and CEO of Aeon Blue, said it was important to her and her brother, co-founder Deois Ua Cearnaigh, to have Indigenous participation. "We are partnering all the way from piloting to commercialization, so we are going to grow our partnership and the facilities together," she said. Ua Cearnaigh, who is an electrochemist, said the technology to separate hydrogen from seawater and combine it with carbon dioxide to make all kinds of fuels has been around for decades. Aeon Blue CEO Lark Meadow says although the process can produce a wide range of fuel types, jet fuel was chosen because of growing demand. (Tom Ayers/CBC) But he said his patented process improves on the technology and makes it economical on a commercial scale. "It's kind of like saying the cart, four-wheeled vehicles, are thousands of years old, but the car only came around in the 1910s," he said. It also draws more carbon from the air than it uses, with the excess carbon dioxide being sequestered. Meadow said that may be in the ground or in other ways that have yet to be decided. Although the process can produce a wide range of fuel types, Meadow said jet fuel was chosen because there's a growing demand for green fuel in air travel. Officials say the joint venture is expected to produce 12 jobs next year and up to 80 when the efuel process reaches full commercialization. (Tom Ayers/CBC) Ua Cearnaigh said the move from their home in Texas not only made sense because of the government's financial incentives, but he said the Verschuren Centre's laboratories are superior to others and the geography means all of the components needed for the process are readily available. "Cape Breton has sort of this magical location where it is as close to the southern extent of winter sea ice as you can go and still have ice-free ports in the winter, and yet also the wind howls like nobody's business," he said. "It really is an X marks the spot. If you were going to do an efuels project, doesn't matter who you are, you would pick this island." Meadow said a pilot project will be located on Eskasoni's land in Sydport and is expected to start making fuel next year. It is expected to scale up the following year, with full commercialization to follow by 2030. eFuels Mi'kmaq Ltd. plans to build a pilot project on Eskasoni land in Sydport industrial park to make jet fuel from seawater. (Tom Ayers/CBC) Meadow said large-scale commercialization will require more land, but the manufacturing site will still be located along the coast of Cape Breton. The joint venture is expected to start training up to 12 Eskasoni band members in engineering, operations and management next year, and could create up to 80 full-time jobs when full commercialization is achieved. Steve Parsons, CEO of Eskasoni's corporate division, said the deal has been in the works for about 18 months. "We're very excited," he said. "This is a great opportunity for the community." representative.title: Greenpeace calls for ban on “dead waste” textile imports into Ghana  | Ghana News Agency
representative.author: GNA

snapshot.title: Greenpeace calls for ban on “dead waste” textile imports into Ghana | Ghana News Agency
snapshot.evidenceText: Ghana's preferred news source: Accurate, Credible, Objective, Timely Accra, Oct. 8, GNA – Greenpeace Africa, an independent environmental campaigning organisation, has called on the Government to ban the importation of what it calls “dead waste” textiles into the country, describing them as clothing that cannot be reused, repurposed or resold. The call follows a brand audit of some 201 discarded garments collected from James Town Beach, Kantamanto Market and Agbogbloshie in Accra, which identified labels of global fashion brands including H&M, Primark, Marks & Spencer (M&S) and Next, as major contributors to Ghana’s textile waste. The organisation said the growing volume of discarded clothing in Accra highlighted the need for action both at the source of production and at Ghana’s borders. Presenting the audit findings on Wednesday in Accra, as part of its campaign on “waste colonialism” and the environmental and economic effects of the global fast-fashion industry, Ms Hellen Kahaso Dena, Project Lead for the Plastics Project and Fast Fashion at Greenpeace Africa, said the organisation’s investigations across Accra showed that textile waste was accumulating at several locations, including Kantamanto Market, James Town Beach and Agbogbloshie. She said the problem needed to be addressed by reducing excessive production by global fashion companies and ensuring that only clothing capable of being reused entered Ghana. “We want to tackle this problem at the source, and the source of this problem is the overproduction,” Ms Dena said. She said traders at Kantamanto estimated that about 40 per cent of clothing entering the market was waste, meaning it could not be effectively reused or resold. Ms Dena explained that while Greenpeace was not calling for a complete ban on second-hand clothing imports as the trade provided livelihoods for many Ghanaians, it could also not be left unchecked. “What we do not want is for fashion brands in the global North to actually use that loophole to continue dumping,” she said. She urged the Government to establish standards to ensure that imported second-hand clothing was of sufficient quality for reuse, while supporting Ghana’s local textile and fashion industries, artisans and other workers in the sector. Mr Sam Quashie-Idun, Head of Investigations at Greenpeace Africa, said the audit formed part of wider investigations into the environmental effects of discarded clothing in Ghana. He said the team collected garments and engaged traders and other stakeholders involved in the second-hand clothing trade at the three locations. He explained that the presence of labels from H&M, Primark, M&S and Next demonstrated the international nature of the clothing waste entering Ghana. He also expressed concern about plastic and microplastic pollution arising from synthetic fibres used in many garments. Mr Quashie-Idun cited Greenpeace’s 2024 report, “Fast Fashion, Slow Poison”, which found that 89 per cent of 164 discarded garments tested at three dumpsites in the Greater Accra Region contained synthetic fibres. He said an earlier investigation into the burning of textile waste as fuel at three public washhouses in Old Fadama also detected benzene, a known carcinogen, in samples collected in 2023. Greenpeace also unveiled a six-metre installation, “Fast Fashion, Lasting Damage”, created from discarded garments by The Revival, an upcycling collective based at Kantamanto Market. The installation depicts a model wearing a dress whose large skirt extends onto the ground and merges with hundreds of discarded garments. As part of the campaign, Greenpeace and its partners presented a petition signed by more than 25,000 people to the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry. The petition called for a ban on unusable textile waste, transparent grading and trading practices, stronger producer responsibility mechanisms, investment in Ghana’s textile industry and support for traditional craftsmanship, repair and reuse. It also called for stronger Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) regulations requiring fashion companies to contribute to managing the environmental impact of their products throughout their life cycle. Isabelle McAllister, a Greenpeace spokesperson from Sweden, called on fashion companies to remain responsible for their products even after they left their original markets. “We don’t want to see a total ban on import here. The quality needs to be better and we have to stop the overproduction,” she said. Head Office Location Opp. Registrar General's Department Dodoo Lane, Ministries, Accra Digital Address: GA–144–5449

representative.title: First Digital Face of 315,000-Year-Old Homo sapiens Revealed — SciBeat
representative.author: Priya Raman

snapshot.title: First Digital Face of 315,000-Year-Old Homo sapiens Revealed
snapshot.evidenceText: Researchers digitally reconstructed the face of a 315,000-year-old Homo sapiens from fossils at Jebel Irhoud, Morocco. The composite skull shows a brain volume within the modern male range. By Priya Raman October 10, 2026 3 min read 591 words Scientists have produced the first digital facial reconstruction of a 315,000-year-old Homo sapiens, using fossil fragments unearthed decades ago at Jebel Irhoud, Morocco. The composite 3D skull, published in Heritage by Cicero Moraes and colleagues, has an estimated brain volume of 1,230 cubic centimeters—within the typical range for modern human males. The work draws on bones first discovered in the 1960s, when a miner at a Moroccan mineral extraction site stumbled on a skull with distinctly humanlike features. Archaeologists who followed up excavated more remains and initially dated them to about 40,000 years. They identified the main specimen, Irhoud 1, as an African Neanderthal. That timeline collapsed in 2017, when a separate research team re-dated the fossils to roughly 315,000 years and reclassified them as Homo sapiens. The Jebel Irhoud site now offers the oldest known remains of our species anywhere in the world. The latest study does not change that date. Instead, it gives those bones a face—digitally. The team combined the main Irhoud 1 skull fragment with jaw and tooth pieces from other specimens found in the same archaeological layer. Together, these fragments formed a composite 3D skull. The researchers built this digital skull mostly with open-source software. They started from open-access videos and images released by the Max Planck Institute. They also used a CT scan of a modern adult human skull as a reference model. Using a technique called anatomical deformation, the team digitally stretched and adjusted the modern reference skull until its contours matched the ancient fossil. This approach gave them a complete digital skull in regions where the actual bones had eroded or never survived. With the digital skull finished, the researchers turned to the brain. They fitted their reconstruction inside the skull cavity and extracted a virtual endocast—a 3D model of the impression left by the brain on the inner bone surface. That endocast measured 1,364 milliliters in volume. Converting that figure to standard brain volume gave 1,230 cubic centimeters. That number sits comfortably within the normal range for modern human males, suggesting early Homo sapiens at Jebel Irhoud already possessed brains roughly the size of ours. The reconstruction came in two distinct forms: The team stressed that the lifelike additions—especially hair and skin pigmentation—were artistic interpretations. Those traits do not survive in the fossil record, so the researchers relied on anthropological conventions for ancient North African populations to guide their choices. The reconstruction carries the usual limits of fossil-based facial work. No complete face survived at Jebel Irhoud, and the team assembled the composite skull from fragments of multiple individuals rather than one person. The resulting portraits show a plausible early Homo sapiens rather than an exact likeness of a single real individual. Even so, the open-access pipeline could travel well beyond this one face. The authors argue that other researchers can use similar methods to reconstruct incomplete ancient fossils elsewhere. Digital facial reconstruction may soon become a standard tool in many more paleoanthropology labs. The findings appear in Heritage (DOI: 10.3390/heritage9090369). Senior reporter covering industry trends and analytics at SciBeat.

representative.title: Verity - Study: Gene Therapy Restores Some Sight in Blind Patients
representative.author: Health

snapshot.title: Verity - Study: Gene Therapy Restores Some Sight in Blind Patients
snapshot.evidenceText: Optogenetics has transformed neuroscience by turning neural circuits from theoretical maps into experimentally testable systems. Its emerging clinical applications, including efforts to restore vision, demonstrate how fundamental discoveries can translate into therapies while opening new possibilities for treating complex brain diseases. Optogenetics may represent a remarkable scientific breakthrough, but its therapeutic promise remains unproven. Early findings do not yet establish that these approaches can safely deliver consistent, meaningful benefits for patients. Significant research is still required to determine whether experimental results can completely treat blindness.

representative.title: In backroom ‘sewing’ classes, Afghan women stitch together an education in secret - CSMonitor.com
representative.author: Mark Sappenfield

snapshot.title: In backroom ‘sewing’ classes, Afghan women stitch together an education in secret
snapshot.evidenceText: Our name is about honesty. The Monitor is owned by The First Church of Christ, Scientist, and we’ve always been transparent about that. The church publishes the Monitor because it sees good journalism as vital to progress in the world. Since 1908, we’ve aimed “to injure no man, but to bless all mankind,” as our founder, Mary Baker Eddy, put it. Here, you’ll find award-winning journalism not driven by commercial influences – a news organization that takes seriously its mission to uplift the world by seeking solutions and finding reasons for credible hope. Get unlimited access to global news that cuts through the noise and brings perspectives you won’t get anywhere else. It has been five years since the Taliban outlawed women’s education beyond sixth grade, forcing English and math lessons underground. Across Afghanistan, in basements and storefronts promising sewing classes, a hidden rebellion is taking place. Five years after the Taliban swept back into power, the ban on girls’ education past sixth grade remains perhaps the movement’s most visible act of repression. Afghanistan is the only country in the world where girls are legally prohibited from continuing their education beyond primary school. Yet in secret, women are educating themselves, their schoolbooks hidden inside sewing bags as they listen closely for an unexpected knock at the door. The backroom courses in English, math, or nursing are no substitute for those shut down by the government. Women remember with heartache the day those closures took effect, but they have not yielded. In Afghanistan, courageous teachers and students are finding ways to educate girls right under the Taliban’s nose. These underground networks reflect Afghans’ hopes for a better future. Some 40% of Afghan women “still imagine a future where change and equality are possible,” according to a 2025 survey by UN Women . The underground education networks across the country are a testament to that hope. At 23 years old, Arghawan says she should be finishing medical school right now. (As with all women interviewed for this article, her name has been changed and her location withheld to protect her from retaliation.) Instead, she’s taking clandestine classes in the basement of a vocational center. It’s a dark, sparse, and bitterly cold space once winter sets in, lit by weak solar lamps whenever the power cuts out. If someone spots the morality police approaching, English lessons are wiped from the whiteboard in seconds, and notebooks are replaced with needlework. But when she’s there, the memory of the life she once had – and she hopes to have once again – flickers into view. “I feel as though I am back in my school classroom,” she says. “I feel as though I am alive again.” Polls are clear. Afghans overwhelmingly want to educate their girls and young women. The UN Women report found that 92% of respondents in a national door-to-door survey said it was “‘important’ for girls to continue their schooling.” Support was no lower than 87% among both men and women, in both rural and urban areas. The Taliban banned women from secondary education in 2021 and college education in 2022. Those moments remain seared into the collective consciousness of women nationwide. Arghawan was 17 then, in the 11th grade, with plans to become a doctor or a prosecutor. She remembers the morning being sunny and the market a little quieter than normal. She had no idea the walk to school that day would be her last. Taliban vehicles were already blocking the gate when she arrived. When she asked why, a man who called himself a qari – a Quran reciter – told her and her classmates they were “stupid and irrational,” and asked whether girls like them were supposed to be the ones who built the nation. Once through the door, she says, she found her classmates and gripped their hands tightly. It felt as if letting go might mean losing each other forever. “Unfortunately, our school has been closed,” a teacher said, turning to the blackboard so the girls wouldn’t see her wipe her face. “It was truly like a funeral,” says Arghawan. The Taliban ordered everyone out. Students who resisted were beaten back with sticks. At another school nearby, girls were lined up in the schoolyard and told that anyone above sixth grade could no longer come to class. Some teachers tried to record the moment on their cellphones, but within the hour, the Ministry of Education called the principal and warned that anyone caught filming would be detained. The teachers deleted their videos in front of their students and the Taliban fighters standing at the gate. “We kissed the girls on their faces and sent them home,” says Fazilah, a former math teacher and administrator at the school, “all of them in tears.” Five years later, however, Fazilah is still teaching as best she can. Eleven girls, all former students, now come to her basement to learn English, math, chemistry, and physics. If anyone asks, they are there to learn sewing. Fazilah charges next to nothing, just enough to cover supplies. “I love teaching,” she says. “I believe teaching girls is my right.” She knows the risks. An earlier class she ran – better equipped and teaching English and computer skills more openly – lasted four months before the Taliban found it. She was interrogated and warned that a second offense meant prison. She also knows the threat is real. A colleague was once arrested and released only after community elders intervened, forced to sign a pledge never to teach again. Rana had a year of engineering left when the Taliban closed her college. By the end, there were signs of what was coming. One professor routinely exhorted the class to give up and get married, saying none of them would ever be permitted to work in their chosen field anyway. Today, she teaches at a vocational center where the front door advertises sewing. In the back rooms, Rana teaches mathematics for free, alongside women running secret lessons in English and computer skills under cover of sewing and beadwork. The center has already been raided once, on a tip, Rana says. Staff hid the books and the handful of computers, leaving only sewing patterns chalked on the board. She suspects some of the center’s staff might be informants. She also knows girls whose relatives work for the government, quietly attending the secret classes without disclosing it, and has learned not to say an ill word about the Taliban. But not all encounters with Taliban officials have been catastrophic. Arghawan recalls the time officers walked straight into her classroom without warning. “It was one of the most frightening moments of my life,” she says. “I thought they were going to take us to prison.” They said that they had only come “to advise these women,” she recounts, then delivered a lecture on hijab, prayer, never leaving home without a male guardian, obeying husbands and in-laws, and marrying because it was “God’s command.” Then, they thanked the women in the room for their time and left. Arghawan had tried to stay at home in the years after her high school was closed, but she says she felt “like a prisoner,” unable to move freely even to go to the market. Research by UN Women suggests that fewer than half of Afghan women (41%) leave their homes at least once a day, compared with 88% of men. Some 14% of women leave their homes only once a week. Arghawan waited a year for the closure to lift. It didn’t. An online English class filled seven months until it, too, fell apart. Arghawan says she slid into a depression severe enough that she eventually saw a mental health professional, who told her to hold onto small routines: study, family time, a walk outside when she could manage it. Today, when she leaves for her classes, Arghawan tells her family she’s going to study the Quran. She must wear a black hijab, gloves, and a niqab, leaving only her eyes showing. On one scorching afternoon, she began to collapse from heat exhaustion and was rushed to a hospital. Rana, the former engineering student, carries nothing but a pen and a scrap of paper to her lessons. She has heard what happens to women caught by the morality police on similar pretexts: arrests, days in custody, mistreatment, and in some cases, assault. “I keep my eyes on the road, so that no one pays attention to me.” she says. “But inside, I am afraid.” Afghanistan has been here before. When the Taliban first took Kabul in the mid-1990s, they enacted a similar ban on women’s education, which has since been blamed for many of the country’s problems, including its high maternal mortality rates. Back then, Fazilah’s family fled to neighboring Pakistan, returning only after the Taliban were ousted in 2001. Now she’s thinking ahead to a future where Afghanistan realizes, once again, that it needs female doctors, judges, and engineers. And as a former administrator, she has a clear sense of what young women need to prepare for these roles. They need money for informal schooling, sent through channels that won’t let it be skimmed off along the way. They also need curriculums for compressed, internationally recognized degrees, to make up the time they have lost. And they need scholarships abroad, on the condition that they return home once they’re qualified. Deepen your worldview with Monitor Highlights. snapshot.title: A Laboratory Made of Bottles - shikshalokam.org
snapshot.evidenceText: A plastic bottle, a balloon, a pinch of turmeric, half a lemon. In most schools, these would be rubbish or kitchen scraps. In Shobha Singh’s classroom in Jamui, they are laboratory equipment. The school had no laboratory, and before Shobha arrived, it had never had a science teacher. The bottles were the answer to a simple refusal: the missing laboratory would not be allowed to mean missing science. Shobha grew up in Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, in a home shaped by a father in the Police Department and by discipline, responsibility and service. The love of science came from a science teacher at school, who taught not just the subject but how to observe, and how to ask why things happen. That teacher is the reason Shobha chose science, and then chose to teach it. On 3 June 2013, Shobha joined the government middle school at Malaypur, in the Barhat block of Jamui district, Bihar. It is an area long affected by Naxal violence, and few people there expected much from school. Not many children were interested in studying. The school had very little to teach science with. There was no laboratory and no science teacher had ever worked there. For most children, science was something to read and memorise from a textbook, a list of answers with no questions behind them. They had almost no chance to watch something happen, to try something out, to ask why and find out for themselves. Shobha could have waited for equipment to arrive. Instead, the work started with what was already lying around. Used bottles, balloons, tetra packs, paper, straws, lemons, turmeric, vinegar, salt, sugar and matchsticks became the tools of the science class. Over the years, Shobha built more than forty hands-on activities out of materials like these, all without a conventional laboratory. With them, children explored light and reflection, air and water pressure, how heat travels, electricity, photosynthesis, osmosis and chromatography. They tested food for adulteration and watched seeds germinate. They took a science class to the river to study its ecosystem. In one photograph from Shobha’s classroom, a red laser beam zigzags between mirrors across a darkened room. The point was never to hand children the answer. In Shobha’s class, they were asked to look first, then guess what would happen, then test it, argue about it, and reach their own conclusion. When there was no microscope, Foldscopes, folding paper microscopes that cost very little, let children look at the microscopic world for the first time. When the children first saw the stomata on a leaf, one of them said, “Wow! Leaves also have mouths like us!” Another, looking at a single drop of pond water crowded with living things, asked, “Aree, koi jeev itna chhota bhi ho sakta hai?” Can anything alive really be that small? Shobha also designed a Low-Cost Science Kit so that several concepts could be taught with simple materials, in any classroom. Shobha wanted learning to leave the classroom, too. So the school started a Learning Farm, and it became a living laboratory. Children grew crops side by side with organic and chemical methods, made compost and vermicompost, and watched what each choice did to the soil, the plants and the environment around them. They observed, compared, looked things up and argued over what they saw. More than 250 students have learned this way. Slowly, the habit of asking questions turned into a habit of solving problems. That habit shows up in what the children now build. Priyanshu Kumar, a Class 8 student, knew someone who died when a bike crashed into a roadside tree at night. Priyanshu’s answer was a Green Tree Safety Reflector: reflective strips fixed to tree trunks so that headlights pick them up from a distance. Another student, Sanskar, was tired of watching the family unclog the sink at home, and designed a removable mesh drain guard to stop it from happening. Every year, students from the school are selected for the INSPIRE Award MANAK, a national programme for school students’ innovations, and for the Medha Scholarship. One of them, Ayush Kumar Singh, reached the national level of INSPIRE MANAK with a Bike Towing Tool of Ayush’s own invention. Her students from the school have also represented Bihar at the Eastern India Science Fair. More than 80% of students consistently pass in the first division. Parents noticed. Their children were more curious, more confident, and more willing to ask questions and try new things. More than 50 children have moved from private schools to this government school. The laboratory at Malaypur is still not a room. It is a shelf of bottles and balloons, a farm behind the school, a river bank, but a class full of children who have learned to ask why before they are told. After thirteen years in the classroom, Shobha teaches science and mathematics and works as a master trainer for other teachers at the district and state levels. In 2025, Bihar’s SCERT selected Shobha to represent Jamui district at a state science seminar in Patna. A dreamer at heart, Sonal finds solace in the fictional realms of a book, often preferring them over the real world. A designer and illustrator by instinct, she is driven by the desire to make the world more aesthetic, vibrant, and meaningful than she found it. Currently, managing communications at ShikshaLokam, she is on a journey to become a storyteller- one who bridges emotion, purpose, and design to inspire change. With over 12 years of experience in teaching, she brings the depth of an education enthusiast who believes deeply in the transformative power of knowledge, the right opportunities, and the quiet magic of hard work.
