representative.author: Ophelia Keating

snapshot.title: A Body Encased in Salt: Forensic Scientists Report First Modern Case of
snapshot.evidenceText: When forensic pathologists in southern France were called to examine a male body discovered encrusted in a thick, crystalline crust of salt, they knew they were looking at something extraordinary. The body was not wrapped, treated, or deliberately preserved. Instead, the environment itself had done the work of an embalmer, coating the remains in a layer of halite roughly four centimeters thick and transforming the tissue into a dry, leathery shell. According to a case report published in the International Journal of Legal Medicine by Clémence Delteil of Marseille University Hospital and her colleagues, this is the first modern forensic case of natural salt mummification ever described, and it offers a rare glimpse into how extreme chemistry can rewrite the rules of human decomposition. Mummification is usually associated with deliberate ritual practice, from the embalmers of ancient Egypt to the salt-packing techniques documented in historical funerary customs. But nature occasionally produces the same result on its own. Salt works as a preservative through two complementary mechanisms. First, it is strongly hygroscopic, drawing water out of tissue by osmosis and creating a desiccated state in which the chemical reactions of decay slow dramatically. Second, high salinity is antimicrobial: most of the bacteria that drive putrefaction cannot tolerate concentrated brine, so the microbial ecosystem that normally dismantles a corpse simply collapses. Deprived of both moisture and microbes, soft tissue can survive for months, years, or even millennia. The archaeological record is full of proof. The most famous examples are the salt men of Chehrābād in northwestern Iran, miners who perished in collapses at the Douzlākh salt mine as early as the fourth century BC and were preserved so completely that ancient DNA, isotopic signatures of their diet, and even the fibers of their clothing have been recovered. Previous laboratory work, including experiments in which human tissue was deliberately mummified in salt, has confirmed how rapidly salt halts both microbial growth and DNA degradation. Yet despite this rich archaeological literature, no forensic scientist had ever documented a naturally salt-mummified body in a contemporary medico-legal context, until now. The French case is unusual not only because it happened at all, but because of where it happened. Unlike the Iranian salt men, who were entombed in a dry, cool salt mine, this body was found in a warm, humid, anthropogenic saline environment, a human-made salt production setting in the Mediterranean south of France. The region has a seventy-year history of managed coastal salinas, shallow basins where seawater is evaporated to harvest salt, and abandoned sites where hypersaline water pools and crystallizes under the intense Provençal sun. Local geochemical studies of nearby lagoons such as Lavalduc have documented active precipitation of halite, the mineral form of sodium chloride, in and around these basins. It was in this evaporative, salt-saturated setting that the body lay undisturbed long enough for a crystalline shell to grow around it. External examination revealed a completely desiccated body, brown and leathery in appearance, with the facial features and the morphology of the limbs and extremities remarkably preserved. That degree of anatomical integrity is forensically valuable: it allowed the team to attempt a biological profile of the deceased, the standard assessment of sex, age, and body characteristics that forms the first step toward identification. In many decomposed or skeletonized bodies, such profiling is severely compromised by tissue loss. Here, the salt had effectively frozen the external anatomy in place, demonstrating that natural mummification can paradoxically make a body more identifiable, not less. Autopsy, however, told a more complicated story. Inside the leathery exterior, the researchers found extensive tissue desiccation consistent with prolonged exposure to a highly saline environment, but the preservation was strikingly uneven. Some regions showed classic mummified changes, while others displayed focal putrefactive alteration, including complete liquefaction of the brain. This hybrid pattern, in which desiccation and decay coexist in the same body, had not previously been described in the modern forensic literature. The authors attribute it to the specific dynamics of the anthropogenic saline setting: fluctuations in salinity, intermittent moisture, and ambient heat likely allowed pockets of decomposition to proceed before full desiccation took hold, producing a mosaic of preservation that contrasts with the uniform mummification seen in mine contexts. The case also illustrates the hard limits of forensic science when preservation is this unusual. Toxicological analyses of visceral samples came back negative for drugs and toxic substances, ruling out chemical causes of death detectable in the preserved tissue. DNA analysis and fingerprint examination were both performed, but neither produced an identification. The failure is instructive. Even when tissue appears well preserved, the same osmotic and chemical stresses that stop decay can fragment genetic material in ways that defeat standard amplification, and desiccated skin often cannot yield usable friction ridge prints. For the identification effort, the team had to fall back on contextual and morphological evidence rather than laboratory confirmation. Perhaps the most innovative part of the investigation was environmental. Rather than relying solely on the body itself, the researchers reconstructed the salinity dynamics, evaporation rates, and local climate conditions of the site, and used that reconstruction to support a tentative hypothesis about the post-mortem interval, the elapsed time since death. The logic is analogous to entomological dating, where insect development stages clock the interval, but here the clock is geochemical: the thickness of the salt crust, the rate at which brine evaporates under the regional climate, and the seasonal behavior of the saline basin together constrain how long the body must have lain there. The authors emphasize that this estimate is tentative, but the approach itself is a proof of concept for reading time from the environment in cases where conventional markers are absent. The report arrives amid growing attention to what forensic scientists call complex bodies, remains whose preservation state falls outside the familiar categories of fresh, decomposed, skeletonized, burned, or water-immersed. Recent systematic reviews and procedural proposals have argued that such cases demand a multidisciplinary response, combining pathology, anthropology, radiology, genetics, toxicology, entomology, botany, and environmental science, guided by standardized on-site inspection protocols such as those developed by the European Council of Legal Medicine. The salt mummy of southern France is a textbook argument for that approach: no single discipline could have interpreted the body, but the combined evidence of morphology, chemistry, and environmental reconstruction extracted real forensic information from an apparently intractable case. For the wider forensic community, the implications are twofold. First, investigators encountering desiccated remains in or near saline environments, from abandoned salinas to industrial brine facilities, should now consider natural salt mummification as a genuine possibility rather than a curiosity confined to archaeology. Second, the case expands the known range of environments capable of natural preservation into warm, humid, human-modified settings, which means the global geography of potential salt mummies is far larger than the arid mines and deserts of the archaeological record. As the authors conclude, environmental analysis and multidisciplinary investigation are essential tools for identification and post-mortem interval estimation in complex bodies, and this unique case, a man sealed in salt under the Mediterranean sun, may be only the first of its kind to surface. representative.title: K. Star: Attempts to stir tensions in Hasakah, Our people must remain vigilant -ANHA

snapshot.title: K. Star: Attempts to stir tensions in Hasakah, Our people must remain vigilant
snapshot.evidenceText: Martyrs of 12 March stadium prepares to host Syrian premier league matches after renovation Jil Agha residents: community solidarity is key to foiling attempts to incite discord Hawar News Agency Plan – October 11, 2026 Child killed, two injured while crossing into Lebanon New Israeli incursion into Quneitra countryside YPJ’s Roxan Mohammed: Targeting women values threatens coexistence, stability Derbasiyah Youth and Students: Kurdish language is our existence Loud explosion reported at Riyadh Airport Armed attack targets Rojava Radio team in Hasakah Hassan Kalash’s body identified after found burned in Tel Koçer Alawite religious shrine vandalized in Tartus countryside Condition of three brothers injured in Hasakah, currently stable Protest in Derik condemns international conspiracy Jazira Intellectuals’ Union calls for accountability over Hasakah events Kongra Star has warned against attempts to stir discord in Hasakah, saying that internal and external actors are seeking to fuel conflict in Syria amid tensions that have gripped the city over the past two days. In a statement issued in Kurdish on Saturday and translated into Arabic by ANHA agency, Kongra Star said developments in Hasakah coinciding with the anniversary of the October 9 international conspiracy point to deliberate attempts to provoke tensions, stressing that the timing is no coincidence. The statement said escalating tensions, interference affecting civilians and attempts to target Kurdish neighborhoods threaten peaceful coexistence and regional security. It also warned of the consequences of armed groups moving toward Hasakah from al-Shaddadi, Deir ez-Zor and Raqqa, saying that failure to stop their movements increases the risk of conflict between the region’s communities. Kongra Star stressed Hasakah’s strategic and historical importance as a city home to Kurds, Arabs and other communities, noting that its residents had previously suffered under Arabization policies. It also recalled the city’s role in the fight against ISIS mercenaries, particularly on the fronts of Hasakah, Raqqa, Deir ez-Zor and al-Shaddadi. The statement said the current developments target the forces and political parties that contributed to defeating ISIS mercenaries and seek to undermine relations among the region’s communities. It stressed that the situation in Hasakah cannot be viewed as merely a local crisis, but is linked to policies pursued by internal and external actors seeking to expand their influence in the region. It warned against attempts to revive Baathist policies based on dismantling social cohesion and fueling divisions among peoples through armed groups and social unrest. Kongra Star called on the various communities in Hasakah to adopt a united position against provocations and continue democratic and organized activities. It stressed that preventing armed conflict is not the responsibility of Kurds or Arabs alone, but of all the region’s communities. Kongra Star also called on Syrian officials to fulfill their responsibilities in maintaining security, protecting civilians and controlling the movements of armed groups. It urged them to investigate how armed groups from al-Shaddadi and Deir ez-Zor reached Hasakah, identify those who allowed them to move and explain why they were not prevented from advancing toward Kurdish neighborhoods. Concluding its statement, Kongra Star called on the peoples of Rojava, democratic forces in Syria, women’s organizations and civil society organizations to act responsibly against attempts to incite discord and hostility, and to work to prevent any potential conflict in Hasakah from escalating or spreading to other parts of Syria. representative.title: The unlikely rise of India’s Gen Z rebels – The Irish Times
representative.author: Somini Sengupta, Pragati K.B.

snapshot.title: The unlikely rise of India’s Gen Z rebels
snapshot.evidenceText: H e uncorked a generation’s anger at a broken college entrance exam system. Now the Gen Z movement that Abhijeet Dipke birthed five months ago and called the Cockroach Janta Party has become a formidable finger in the eye of the Indian government. The cockroaches’ latest aim is the resignation of the country’s chief election commissioner, over what they say is a politically motivated purge of 130 million voters from the election rolls. On Saturday, in perhaps their biggest challenge to prime minister Narendra Modi ’s administration, supporters defied a police ban and staged a mass protest in New Delhi over they they said was a politically motivated revision of the nation’s voter roll. Thousands of demonstrators met walls of security forces as they tried to protest. Leaders of the Cockroach party were detained when their flight landed in Delhi shortly before 11 am local time on Saturday. “This is dictatorship,” said Abhijeet Dipke (31), as police officers approached him and the two other leaders before they could disembark, according to a video he shared on social media. Police officers were heard telling him that their protest had been refused permission. In central Delhi, protesters were rounded up by the dozens starting early on Saturday morning and led, sometimes forcefully, into detention buses. They were defying extraordinary measures taken by the authorities to prevent them from reaching the protest site, called Jantar Mantar. The demonstration comes after a week of nationwide protests demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the head of India’s election commission, a body that has recently come under intense public criticism because of the voter roll revision. In fact, India ’s youth have many more grievances: failing schools, insufficient jobs, violence against women, a lack of government accountability. Their frustrations have been boiling for years. There are so many of them – 367 million people between ages 15 and 29, the world’s largest Gen Z cohort. Dipke said in advance of Saturday’s demonstrations that he felt intense pressure. “It’s like someone has dropped a baby at my doorstep,” he said on a recent road trip to highlight the problem with state schools in the countryside. “It actually scares me, to be very honest. “People have too many expectations, too many hopes,” he went on. “It’s like people are expecting me to resolve everything at once.” Modi has not commented on the cockroach protests, though criticism has come from senior politicians of his Bharatiya Janata Party, including the chief minister of Maharashtra state, Devendra Fadnavis, who said their “fake narrative” over the voter roll revision would not succeed. For Dipke – and the cockroaches – the risks are enormously high. In a country where space for dissent has shrunk, they could be crushed as quickly as they appeared. Delhi police have detained hundreds of people who defied the ban and protested in Delhi this week. The cockroaches’ four leaders are all younger than 32, with no political experience. Signs of friction have appeared with the main opposition party, the Indian National Congress. Its leader, Rahul Gandhi, is holding another rally across the country, in Chennai, on Saturday. The cockroaches already have one win under their belt: the rare ouster of a government minister in connection to the entrance exams. They seem to have emboldened many more Indians to speak out against the government. Over the last week, a range of groups, from left-wing student activists to conservative regional politicians, have rallied in several cities. “We are just frustrated by everything. Everything,” said Aayushi Gaikwad (18), who travelled three hours by train to attend a cockroach protest in Mumbai last Friday. It was her first time at a protest. Around her, thousands of people waved Indian flags. As evening fell, Dipke led the crowd in singing the national anthem. Ram Guha, a historian and outspoken critic of Modi, credited the cockroach leaders for puncturing the “invincibility of the Modi government”. Not long after they forced the resignation of the education minister in July, the cockroaches turned to India’s rural schools. A range of Instagram-worthy horrors awaited them. Clogged toilets. Broken water taps. Overheated tin sheds for classrooms. Rotten onions in a school kitchen. Children wading through floodwaters to reach school. Dipke visited a remote district in western Maharashtra state, called Nandurbar, where he had spent the first five years of his childhood before his family moved to a city. [ How India’s young ‘cockroach’ movement has posed the biggest challenge to Modi in years Opens in new window ] He was born to a Dalit family, seen as low on the Hindu caste ladder, in Nandurbar, a remote district in western Maharashtra. He attended private schools. But his cousins, whose parents were not as educated as his, attended rural government schools, and the contrast was obvious to him, even as a child. He sat at a desk; they sat on the floor. He drank filtered water; they sometimes had no water. He went on to Boston University for a master’s degree; they repaired cars or worked in construction. “That has been one of the most neglected things since independence. Government schools have never been given the attention they need,” he said. At a residential girls’ school in a village called Sari, he learned there was no running water in the fourth-floor bathrooms. The girls hauled buckets of water up four flights of stairs. At a primary school, he met the one teacher who taught a class of first through fourth graders. There was no electricity, and the girls had to fetch water for their bathroom from across a field. The boys had no toilet at all. Vishwas Thakarey, the teacher, said he, like many teachers, had been diverted from the classroom because he had been told to work on the voter roll revision. (Teachers are often pulled away on other government duties.) Education experts say they hope the cockroaches will continue their campaign on schools to shine a light on an issue politicians had long ignored. [ India protests ‘could become lightning rod’ for disillusionment with Modi’s leadership Opens in new window ] “The kind of attention they’ve been able to bring to schools, no one I can think of has been able to do that for 20 years,” said Reetika Khera, an economist at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi who has researched rural schools for decades. This article originally appeared in The New York Times . Dipke said in advance of Saturday’s demonstrations that he felt intense pressure. “It’s like someone has dropped a baby at my doorstep,” he said on a recent road trip to highlight the problem with state schools in the countryside. “It actually scares me, to be very honest. “People have too many expectations, too many hopes,” he went on. “It’s like people are expecting me to resolve everything at once.” Modi has not commented on the cockroach protests, though criticism has come from senior politicians of his Bharatiya Janata Party, including the chief minister of Maharashtra state, Devendra Fadnavis, who said their “fake narrative” over the voter roll revision would not succeed. For Dipke – and the cockroaches – the risks are enormously high. In a country where space for dissent has shrunk, they could be crushed as quickly as they appeared. Delhi police have detained hundreds of people who defied the ban and protested in Delhi this week. The cockroaches’ four leaders are all younger than 32, with no political experience. Signs of friction have appeared with the main opposition party, the Indian National Congress. Its leader, Rahul Gandhi, is holding another rally across the country, in Chennai, on Saturday. The cockroaches already have one win under their belt: the rare ouster of a government minister in connection to the entrance exams. They seem to have emboldened many more Indians to speak out against the government. Over the last week, a range of groups, from left-wing student activists to conservative regional politicians, have rallied in several cities. “We are just frustrated by everything. Everything,” said Aayushi Gaikwad (18), who travelled three hours by train to attend a cockroach protest in Mumbai last Friday. It was her first time at a protest. Around her, thousands of people waved Indian flags. As evening fell, Dipke led the crowd in singing the national anthem. Ram Guha, a historian and outspoken critic of Modi, credited the cockroach leaders for puncturing the “invincibility of the Modi government”. Not long after they forced the resignation of the education minister in July, the cockroaches turned to India’s rural schools. A range of Instagram-worthy horrors awaited them. Clogged toilets. Broken water taps. Overheated tin sheds for classrooms. Rotten onions in a school kitchen. Children wading through floodwaters to reach school. Dipke visited a remote district in western Maharashtra state, called Nandurbar, where he had spent the first five years of his childhood before his family moved to a city. [ How India’s young ‘cockroach’ movement has posed the biggest challenge to Modi in years Opens in new window ] He was born to a Dalit family, seen as low on the Hindu caste ladder, in Nandurbar, a remote district in western Maharashtra. He attended private schools. But his cousins, whose parents were not as educated as his, attended rural government schools, and the contrast was obvious to him, even as a child. He sat at a desk; they sat on the floor. He drank filtered water; they sometimes had no water. He went on to Boston University for a master’s degree; they repaired cars or worked in construction. “That has been one of the most neglected things since independence. Government schools have never been given the attention they need,” he said. At a residential girls’ school in a village called Sari, he learned there was no running water in the fourth-floor bathrooms. The girls hauled buckets of water up four flights of stairs. At a primary school, he met the one teacher who taught a class of first through fourth graders. There was no electricity, and the girls had to fetch water for their bathroom from across a field. The boys had no toilet at all. Vishwas Thakarey, the teacher, said he, like many teachers, had been diverted from the classroom because he had been told to work on the voter roll revision. (Teachers are often pulled away on other government duties.) Education experts say they hope the cockroaches will continue their campaign on schools to shine a light on an issue politicians had long ignored. [ India protests ‘could become lightning rod’ for disillusionment with Modi’s leadership Opens in new window ] “The kind of attention they’ve been able to bring to schools, no one I can think of has been able to do that for 20 years,” said Reetika Khera, an economist at the Indian Institute of Technology Delhi who has researched rural schools for decades. representative.title: Victoria's machete bins collect more than 12,000 weapons, including butter knives - ABC News
representative.author: Rachel Eddie

snapshot.title: Butter knives, kitchen scissors among items surrendered to machete bins
snapshot.evidenceText: The machete amnesty bins were rolled out as the Victorian government moved to ban the weapons last year. ( Supplied/ABC News: Cordelia Brown ) Victoria's machete bins collected more than 12,000 machetes and "other knives" after a statewide ban on the weapons was instituted. The bins were manufactured at a South Australian prison before being installed at police stations around the state. The government says the machete amnesty program came in at half the projected total cost, but has not revealed where the money was spent. Machete bins manufactured by South Australian prisoners were trucked off to Victoria in three batches over two weeks last year, before butter knives were counted among the weapons dumped inside them. The bins were rolled out to dozens of police stations when machetes were banned in September 2025, so that Victorians could safely surrender the blades while the government attempted to crack down on violent knife crime. But the government was widely criticised for being opaque with the details of its $13 million program, with the opposition making wild claims about its cost and usefulness despite having called for the ban. The ABC has confirmed the amnesty actually came in at half the projected total cost, at $6.55 million. Documents released to the ABC under Freedom of Information laws colour in further details, revealing inmates at the privately run Mount Gambier Prison, operated by G4S, constructed the 75 blue bins at the facility's metal fabrication workshop. The government paid G4S $925,000 to manufacture the bins and install them outside police stations. The contract also covered collecting, transporting, cataloguing and destroying the surrendered weapons. The bins were manufactured at a South Australian prison before being shipped to Victoria. ( Supplied: Victorian government ) A sample catalogue of items disposed in the bins shows that butter knives were among the dumped items, along with "anomalous content" like kitchen scissors. Guns and axes were also surrendered, images and records released to the ABC show. The Department of Justice and Community Safety (DJCS) said 12,357 machetes and "other knives" — including butter knives — were surrendered to the bins. Retailers handed in another 5,674 machetes after being prohibited from selling them , taking the haul to 18,031 weapons. The 75 bins were made in three batches over 30 days, departmental documents show, and trucked over to Melbourne in lots. G4S had expected to place the bins at 58 stations, but this was reduced to 45. Surplus bins were swapped in and out once they were damaged or full. Under pressure for not being forthcoming with the details, the government has previously put the cost of each bin at $2,400. An early breakdown of estimated costs — buried among the documents — said manufacturing the bins would cost a total of $139,000, including a one-off charge for other "non-technical equipment". This would have amounted to $1,854 per bin, but the ABC has been told design changes and GST pushed the cost up. The machete disposal bins were placed at dozens of police stations across Victoria. ( AAP: Joel Carett ) G4S further expected it would need to spend $600,000 in labour, $260,000 for an operations manager, and $240,000 for vehicle costs including hiring two vehicles. The contractor's proposal estimated the total cost of its work would be between $865,500 and $1.2 million, depending on whether work could be stepped up or down. Another $884,000 contract went towards "creative services" for "editorial and design and graphic and fine art services". Market research to support public messaging cost another $123,000, according to public tenders. The government has not previously explained how the remaining budget was spent, however it included a multilingual public awareness campaign to ensure machetes were handed in. A DJCS spokesperson said the amnesty was delivered on time and under budget, "with the remaining unspent funds redirected to additional police and Protective Services Officers (PSO) in shopping centres to keep Victorians safe". Victoria Police had advised the government that if its machete ban included an amnesty, infrastructure such as surrender bins had to be installed. "Surrender bins prevent individuals walking into police station reception areas with machetes and other edged weapons, which creates significant safety risk and public alarm," a Victoria Police spokesperson said. "The machete surrender bins allow for proactive disposal of these blades by members of the community in a safe and controlled way." Victoria will ban the sale of machetes from today. ( ABC News: Nicole Asher ) Victoria Police said its officers had since seized more than 11,200 knives, machetes and other illegal blades so far in 2026. Despite criticising the government's machete ban, the opposition itself had previously called for it. Premier Ben Carroll has since introduced further anti-knife crime measures, including by borrowing another Coalition commitment to give police greater search powers. It is a sign that knife crime continues to haunt the government heading into the state election, and that it was not resolved by the machete bins. representative.title: Namhae bamboo weirs elevate Korea’s anchovies to premium delicacy - CHOSUNBIZ
representative.author: Yun Hee-hun

snapshot.title: Namhae bamboo weirs elevate Korea’s anchovies to premium delicacy
snapshot.evidenceText: Anchovies are indispensable when boiling soup and making kimchi. They are a common ingredient on Korean tables, but the top grade can sell for hundreds of thousands of won per kilogram at department stores during the holidays. This is the story of "jukbang anchovies" caught in the Jizok Strait in Namhae, South Gyeongsang. The secret to their higher price, despite being the same anchovies, lies in how they are caught. Instead of hauling them up in nets all at once, they are taken using the powerful current and bamboo weirs, a 500-year-old fishing method. Jukbang anchovies are those caught by the "jukbangryeom" method in the Jizok Strait between Samdong-myeon and Changseon-myeon in Namhae County, South Gyeongsang. Jukbangryeom is a traditional fish trap made by driving oak stakes about 10 meters long into the seabed and weaving bamboo screens between them to form a V shape. Instead of chasing fish with nets, it traps fish that ride the current in. The Jizok Strait is narrow and its currents are so strong they reach 13–15 kilometers per hour. Anchovies moving along the swift flow gather in the "baltong," a cylindrical space at the tip of the V-shaped weir. Once inside, they cannot easily escape. Fisherfolk lift the anchovies from the baltong in time with the tides. Large anchovies grown in the rough current are considered to have firm flesh and less of a fishy smell. Operations take place twice a day in time with the tides. They head out by boat at ebb tide, open the baltong gate, go in, and first remove trash, starfish, and jellyfish. Then they carefully scoop up the anchovies with dip nets and nets. If they miss the tide, the trapped fish can die, so timing is crucial. It is a very different scene from typical operations that shake out large nets at the port to pour out anchovies. This lifting method leads to a difference in quality. Ordinary anchovies easily get injured and lose scales as they snag in nets or tangle with other fish. In contrast, jukbang anchovies are scooped with dip nets, so they suffer relatively fewer injuries and keep their scales intact. With their clean appearance and higher marketability, they trade at higher prices than regular anchovies. Top-grade gifts for holidays, in particular, sell at high prices. Jukbang anchovy operations start in spring and continue through the end of Oct. In winter, the facilities are taken down. Names and uses vary by season and size. The small anchovy caught in early spring, "jireumchi," is mainly used for jeotgal. The following "silchi" and "siregi" are popular for stir-frying. Anchovies that grow for about another month are called "baejaengi," and around Chuseok, "jungsari" appear. Among these, jungsari are treated as top grade for their gloss and flavor. After Aug., anchovies grow larger and fattier. They taste good but are relatively cheaper. Even jukbang anchovies from the same sea differ in use and price depending on when they were caught and how much they grew. Anchovies are caught along many parts of Korea's coast, and fishing methods vary by region. In Gijang, Busan, anchovies are caught in spring with gillnets, and Tongyeong, South Gyeongsang, is regarded as the center of anchovy fishing and production, to the point that it is the only place in the country with an Anchovy Pair Trawl Fisheries Cooperative. While those regions use nets to catch anchovies, the Jizok Strait in Namhae is distinctive for using bamboo weirs and the natural current. The value of jukbangryeom is not only in taste and quality. As a traditional fishing method that has continued for more than 500 years, it is also recognized as a cultural heritage. The jukbangryeom area in the Jizok Strait was designated National Scenic Site No. 71 in 2010, and in 2015 it was listed as National Important Fisheries Heritage No. 3. In Jul. last year, it was inscribed as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations. It has been recognized as a heritage where traditional fishing methods, the lives of local residents, and the natural environment come together. The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries selected anchovies as this Oct.'s seafood of the month. Anchovies are rich in omega-3 fatty acids, which help maintain brain and cardiovascular health, and they are high in calcium, which is good for bone health. Because the tiny bones are eaten whole, various nutrients can be consumed together. They are versatile for stir-fries and broth, as well as jeotgal, jjigae, and hoe-muchim.

representative.title: In Odisha, Chandua applique artisans keep a temple tradition alive, but struggle to earn  - The Week
representative.author: Shubhangi Shah

snapshot.title: In Odisha, Chandua applique artisans keep a temple tradition alive, but struggle to earn
snapshot.evidenceText: About 40 kilometres from Puri, Pipili is a village where almost every shop seems to sell the same thing – Chandua, Odisha’s applique craft. Brightly coloured fabrics, black, blue, yellow and red, are cut into geometric shapes and stitched together into canopies, umbrellas and wall hangings. The craft has a deep connection with the Jagannath Temple in Puri, where Chandua canopies are traditionally used to cover the deity. It “is the most valued aesthetic offering made to Jagannath in the Odia cultural imagination,” writes researcher Madhulika S Naidu in ‘Chandua: Canopies of Labour’, a bilingual book documenting Odisha’s living appliqué traditions, launched in Bhubaneswar last month, and published by Odisha Craft Odyssey (OCO). A craft for generations In Pipili, Chandua isn’t the work of a handful of artisans. Almost all the families are involved. Some members cut the fabric, others create and stitch the motifs, while others sell the finished product. For Athar Ali, the craft has been a livelihood since 1982. Over the years, it has taken him far beyond Pipili. “I’ve travelled across India, from Delhi to Andaman & Nicobar, because of this craft,” he says.  Chandua is deeply rooted in the traditions of the Jagannath Temple, and that connection is visible in the craft itself. Its colours and motifs draw from the temple’s visual traditions. Yet the craft is not confined to one community. Artisans from different religious backgrounds, including Muslims, have practised Chandua for generations.  Challenges ahead For all its visibility in Pipili, Chandua does not necessarily translate into a sustainable livelihood for its makers. “It can take up to 10 days to make Chandua. However, we get as little as Rs 500 for it,” says Sharif, an artisan.  The problem, artisans say, is not their ability to make more. It is finding buyers. “We can increase production. But for sales, we require marketing, which doesn’t exist,” says Ali.  The market is not the only concern. Das, one of the two fellows at the OCO Fellowship Programme 2025-26, points to changes in the craft itself. Traditionally, Chandua was colourful but not glittery, she says. Increasingly, artisans are using shiny materials that are cheaper and less durable. The material used has also deteriorated – from handmade cloth to now velvet. “Chandua used to last 15-20 years earlier, but nowadays it gets wasted in a year or two,” she says. Covid, too, was a major jolt, forcing several artisans to take up other trades such as selling vegetables, working at construction sites, or migrating to other states for work. Even before Covid, the relationship between Pipili and tourists had begun to change. The construction of a bypass road to Puri diverted visitors who would earlier pass through the village, says archivist Raj Maurya, a fellow at the OCO Fellowship Programme 2025-26. Today, he says, most visitors to Pipili are those who already know about Chandua.  The Odisha government has meanwhile announced plans to establish an ‘Applique and Handicrafts Hub’ in Puri, aimed at providing a dedicated space for the craft. Whether such initiatives can translate into a larger and more sustainable market for Pipili's artisans remains to be seen.

representative.title: Drone-sprayed bear repellent undergoes testing in northeastern Japan city  - The Mainichi

snapshot.title: Drone-sprayed bear repellent undergoes testing in northeastern Japan city - The Mainichi
snapshot.evidenceText: Please view the main text area of the page by skipping the main menu. The page may not be displayed properly if the JavaScript is deactivated on your browser. KITAAKITA, Akita -- A nonprofit group has started spraying a bear repellent by drone in this northeastern Japan city as part of a demonstration experiment set to continue until around the time bears enter hibernation. The Center of Historical Materials for Science in Akita, a nonprofit group based in Odate, Akita Prefecture, developed the repellent using wood vinegar. The organization, known as Kemusa, works to promote a deeper understanding of the region's natural environment. On Oct. 2, the repellent was sprayed from the air over an apple orchard in Kitaakita as more than 40 students from the neighboring Takanosu campus of Akita Prefectural Hinai special needs school, along with other people involved, looked on. "By adding repellent spraying to bear countermeasures, we may be able to achieve even greater effectiveness," said Kazuhiro Sato, 72, chairperson of the organization. The wood vinegar contained in the repellent is a naturally derived liquid collected by cooling smoke produced during charcoal production. It gives off a distinctive smell that bears avoid. In 2021, the Osarube Shizen no Kai, a residents' group in Kitaakita, revived Akita's traditional Yoshida-style white charcoal kiln under the slogan, "Asian black bears belong deep in the mountains." Kemusa explored ways to use the wood vinegar produced by the kiln as a bear countermeasure. With the cooperation of the Osarube group and students in the chemistry club at Akita Prefectural Odate Homei High School, Kemusa members filtered the wood vinegar. They then added water and capsaicin derived from chili peppers to make a prototype bear repellent. The apple orchard was chosen as the demonstration test site because three bears including cubs were seen roaming around the site from mid- to late October 2025. A welfare facility is also adjacent to the orchard, raising concerns about possible human injuries if bears appear there. The repellent will therefore be sprayed by drone over a distance of more than 300 meters to test its effectiveness. The test uses an agricultural drone made by Toko Tekko Co., an ironworks and machinery manufacturer in Odate, and is supported by a prefectural subsidy. In recent years, bears have been spotted near homes in urban areas and mountain communities in Kitaakita, as well as in fields along roadsides, with crop damage and human injuries occurring one after another. representative.title: Seaweed Farming on a Madagascar Island Balances Livelihoods and Lagoon
representative.author: Gavin Prescott

snapshot.title: Seaweed Farming on a Madagascar Island Balances Livelihoods and Lagoon
snapshot.evidenceText: On the small island of Nosy Boraha, off Madagascar's northeastern coast, an unusual agricultural boom is unfolding beneath the surface of a shallow turquoise lagoon. Farmers wade through water barely five meters deep, tying fragments of a reddish seaweed known locally as cottonii to lines anchored in the sand. The crop, Kappaphycus alvarezii, is prized worldwide as a source of carrageenan, a gelling agent that ends up in everything from ice cream to toothpaste. As wild fish stocks around the island decline, seaweed farming has emerged as a vital supplementary income for villagers such as those of Ilampy, and it has been folded into Madagascar's national blue economy strategy as a flagship of sustainable coastal development. Yet a new interdisciplinary study published in PLOS Sustainability and Transformation suggests that the story of this booming aquaculture is far more intricate than a simple success narrative, weaving together ecology, anthropology, and environmental law in a single portrait of a lagoon under change. The research, led by Isabel Urbina-Barreto of the IRD and colleagues including Rindra Razandriarison, Aline Tribollet, and a team spanning French and Malagasy institutions, set out in 2024 to answer questions that most single-discipline studies leave unasked. What does seaweed cultivation actually do to the benthic habitats of a tropical lagoon? How do the farmers themselves experience this new livelihood? And which rules, formal or customary, govern who may farm where? The team combined marine ecological surveys, remote sensing from satellites and drones, nutrient chemistry, anthropological fieldwork, and legal analysis into one integrated assessment. This kind of triangulation is rare in aquaculture research, where environmental monitoring and social science often proceed on separate tracks, and it allowed the researchers to see connections that would otherwise remain invisible. The physical stage for this activity is the north reef lagoon of Nosy Boraha, an environment the team mapped in detail using satellite and drone imagery. They estimated its extent at roughly 600 hectares, a shallow basin sheltered by a coral reef crest and floored predominantly by sandy substrates colonized by macrophytes. Within the zones used for seaweed cultivation, the ecologists identified four genera of seagrass and three genera of macroalgae, while coral communities, made up of approximately four genera, were found mainly concentrated near the reef crest, at some distance from the main farming areas. This spatial arrangement matters: the corals that give the reef its structural complexity and its role as a fish nursery occupy a distinct band of the lagoon, and understanding whether farming activities encroach on them is central to judging the sustainability of the industry. The scale of cultivation is more modest than the headline numbers might suggest. The company Nosy Boraha Seaweed holds rights to operate across about 300 hectares of the lagoon, an area that sounds enormous until one learns that the actual cultivation plots cover only 8.3 percent of that concession. The rest remains, for now, untouched lagoon bottom. This gap between leased area and farmed area is a crucial detail for managers, because it means the ecological footprint of the industry today is far smaller than its legal footprint, but also that there is substantial room for expansion within existing permits. Whether that expansion proceeds without degrading the lagoon will depend on the environmental safeguards that accompany it, a question the study addresses directly. To probe those safeguards, the researchers measured nutrients in the water, comparing dissolved inorganic nitrogen and phosphate levels inside farming zones with control areas where no seaweed was grown. The results were nuanced. Nutrient uptake was detected both within the cultivation areas and in the control zones, a pattern that complicates any simple claim that the seaweed farms are either cleaning or polluting the lagoon. Seaweeds are known to absorb dissolved nutrients as they grow, which is one reason aquaculture is often promoted as environmentally benign, but the presence of uptake signals outside the farms indicates that other processes, from seagrass metabolism to water exchange with the open ocean, also shape the lagoon's nutrient budget. The finding underscores how much basic biogeochemical monitoring is still needed before broad ecological verdicts can be rendered. On the social side, the anthropological component of the study painted a picture of opportunity shadowed by hardship. For residents of Ilampy and neighboring villages, seaweed farming provides an important supplementary livelihood at a time when fisheries resources are declining, offering cash income in a region where alternatives are scarce. But farmers reported challenging working conditions, and many expressed concerns about the potential impacts of the farms on coral reefs and on traditional fishing grounds. These worries are not abstract. In a coastal community, the same lagoon that hosts seaweed lines also sustains the gillnets and hand lines that have fed families for generations, and any perceived competition for space or perceived degradation of habitat strikes at the heart of local food security. The researchers found that these anxieties coexist with genuine enthusiasm for the income the crop brings, producing a community negotiating its own relationship with a new industry in real time. Perhaps the most distinctive contribution of the study lies in its legal analysis, which examined not only national legislation but also the local customary law known as Dina. In Nosy Boraha, the Dina is grounded in the Fihavanana principle, a deeply rooted Malagasy ethic of solidarity and reciprocity that governs relationships within and between communities. The researchers found that the Dina plays a central role in managing marine resources on the island, operating alongside formal governance structures led by local fisheries committees and by Madagascar's Ministry of Environment and Ministry of Fisheries and the Blue Economy. This layered system means that the fate of the lagoon is not decided solely in ministries in Antananarivo, but also in village assemblies where customary norms carry real weight. For conservation planners, the message is clear: any sustainable management scheme for seaweed aquaculture must engage the Dina, not merely the statute books. The interplay between customary and formal law is particularly significant because Madagascar's blue economy strategy envisions seaweed farming as a growth sector, and pressure to expand concessions is likely to increase. The study's findings suggest both promise and caution. The industry's current physical footprint is small, the farmed plots sit largely away from the coral-rich reef crest, and the crop requires no feed, no fertilizer, and no freshwater, making it inherently less burdensome than many forms of aquaculture. At the same time, the nutrient signals detected across the lagoon, the farmers' own concerns, and the sensitivity of coral communities near the crest all argue for careful spatial planning, continued monitoring, and genuine community participation before the cultivated area grows toward the full 300-hectare concession. What makes the Nosy Boraha case resonate far beyond Madagascar is the method itself. By bringing ecologists, anthropologists, and legal scholars to the same lagoon at the same time, the research produced a picture in which satellite maps, nutrient measurements, farmers' testimonies, and customary rules each illuminate the others. A purely ecological study might have concluded that the farms pose limited risk to corals; a purely social study might have celebrated a welcome new livelihood; a purely legal study might have catalogued the statutes without noticing that the Dina does much of the real governing. Only together do these lenses reveal the true texture of a coastal transformation in progress, with all its tensions and trade-offs intact. As global demand for carrageenan continues to rise and tropical nations search for blue economy opportunities, Nosy Boraha offers an early and instructive test case. The island's farmers, its reef, and its customary institutions are together writing the rules of an industry that could either support coastal communities for decades or erode the very resources they depend upon. The study by Urbina-Barreto and colleagues does not deliver a final verdict, and it is candid that key questions, from long-term nutrient dynamics to the cumulative effects of expansion, remain open. But it demonstrates something equally valuable: that sustainable aquaculture in places like Nosy Boraha will be built not from a single scientific discipline or a single legal instrument, but from the patient integration of ecology, livelihood, and law, anchored in the principle of Fihavanana that has long held the island's communities together. representative.title: In UP SIR, ECI Software Auto-generated 85,854 Forms to Delete Voters Without a Reason
representative.author: Sumedha Mittal, Ayushi Kar, Shubhangi Derhgawen, Edited by : Furquan Ameen

snapshot.title: In UP SIR, ECI Software Auto-generated 85,854 Forms to Delete Voters Without a Reason
snapshot.evidenceText: New Delhi: The Election Commission of India (ECI) forced officers in Uttar Pradesh to sign deletion forms for 85,854 voters without giving any reason during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in the state. All these deletion forms were submitted after the legally mandated deadline. The deletion requests came en masse from election officers during the claims and objections period of the SIR in Uttar Pradesh (UP), between January 6, 2026, when the draft voter list was published, and April 10, when the final voter list was released. The Uttar Pradesh chief electoral officer (UP CEO) displayed all the deletion forms, officially called Form 7 objection requests, on its website. More than 4.3 lakh such forms were submitted. Working with a team of data analysts, The Reporters’ Collective scraped all the Form 7 disclosures from the UP CEO’s website. We found that 20 percent of these removal requests were submitted directly by the ECI’s own assembly-level officers. But the officers did not fill the forms. The ECI’s own software, ERONET automatically generated these forms, when officials deleted voters during the SIR hearings. The auto-generated forms came loaded with the officers’ digital signatures and were sent up for approval by their seniors. The job of these election officers is to adjudicate such claims of deletion. But in these cases they were acting as both the prosecutor and the judge. Under the law, citizens filing objections are required to put down specific reasons for requesting the deletion of voters. The ECI rules are clear on this. Applicants submitting Form 7 to seek deletions are required to select one of the justifications mentioned in the form. The reasons can be: the person is dead, underage, absent/permanently shifted, already enrolled or not an Indian citizen. In our investigation, we also found that a total of 1,10,476 voter deletion requests were submitted by individuals and accepted by the ECI after the legally mandated deadline. Out of 4.3 lakh Form 7 applications, in two assembly constituencies in UP, people with the same name filed hundreds of requests almost exclusively against Muslim voters. In Tarabganj and Pilibhit assembly constituencies, 90 percent of the deletion requests filed were against Muslims. In Tarabganj, 188 objections were raised under one name ‘Reshma’. When we dug further we found that all were filed on the same date against people from the same booth. The pattern repeats across the state. However, the ECI data does not provide identity details, beyond the name, of those who have proposed the deletions. Therefore citizens cannot independently verify or identify them. We sent detailed questions to UP Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa as well as to the ECI in Delhi. They had not replied by the time of publication. We analysed the scraped data and spoke to four election officials at the assembly level. We learnt that the Form 7 requests were automatically generated when officers removed voters during the SIR hearings they conducted. All the forms already had the official’s digital signature, leaving them no choice but to send them up the chain for approval. While 3.43 lakh individual objectors followed the process and specified the reasons for seeking a voter's removal, election officers failed to provide any reasons. We know that the ECI was auto-generating Form 7 requests through its software earlier during the enumeration process, as well. These were being submitted by booth-level officers (BLOs) who found voters to be absent, shifted, dead, or duplicate (ASDD) during enumeration. The BLOs had to specify one of the six reasons while filing deletions that would later be determined by election officers in each assembly, the electoral registration officers (EROs) and assistant electoral registration officers (AEROs), before they were put on the ASDD list. But we have now found that the ECI’s software compelled EROs and AEROs, who have quasi-judicial powers under the Representation of People Act, 1950 to both file and approve the deletion of voters after the SIR hearings were over. This goes against the ECI’s rules for SIR hearings. They explicitly state that a reason must be given or put on record for the voter to be removed. This change in procedure violates the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. The rules say that election authorities must outright reject any claim or objection that is not submitted in the prescribed manner, including specifying a clear reason. But, changes in the software forced election officers to sign off on unlawful forms anyway. UP was one of the 12 states and union territories to conduct the second round of the SIR exercise. It ran in three broad phases. In the first phase, starting November 4 , 2025, BLOs were tasked with distributing and collecting enumeration forms from every voter listed in the state electoral roll as of October 2025. Voters whose forms could not be collected were placed on the ASDD list for deletion. For this step, the ECI’s central software, ERONET, automatically generated a Form 7 that the BLO was required to sign with a specified reason. Of the 15.44 crore voters originally registered in UP, 2.89 crore names were placed on the ASDD list. On January 6, the state CEO published its draft electoral roll. In the following claims and objections phase, hearings were conducted for voters who were flagged as doubtful by the ECI algorithm but placed on the draft list. The ECI marked 3.26 crore electors as doubtful due to ‘logical discrepancies’ or for being ‘unmapped’. Assembly-level officers, including EROs and AEROs, summoned these flagged voters for hearings to prove their identity. If officers failed to verify them, they were struck off the final rolls. On April 10, UP published the final voter roll with 13.4 crore electors. At the press conference , UP CEO Navdeep Rinwa did not specify the number of voters removed during these SIR hearings. But we spoke to four EROs about the en masse Form 7 deletions our investigation found. They claimed the forms were submitted to delete unverified voters during the SIR hearings. The ECI rules for the SIR define the window between the publication of the draft and final rolls – the claims and objections phase – as the period for receiving addition and deletion requests from voters. Draft rolls allow citizens to first inspect who has been wrongfully included or marked under ASDD so that they can submit Form 7 deletion or Form 6 addition requests. The fact that a significant portion of the deletion requests at the time, more than 20%, were filed by election officers raises suspicion. Our analysis of the data scraped from the ECI’s website shows that 85,854 (98.5 percent) of the 87,127 requests filed by EROs and AEROs have no reason mentioned for deletion. For 62 of those, only letters such as ‘A, N, H, E’ had been mentioned as the reason. In 1,211 forms, “absent/shifted” is mentioned as the reason for deletion. All the 87,127 requests by EROs and AEROs were filed within 19 days, between March 15 and April 2, 2026. The four EROs we spoke to claimed these deletion requests were initiated for voters flagged for logical discrepancies or for being unmapped. “As an ERO, whenever we did not approve a voter during a hearing, the system automatically generated a Form 7 on our behalf,” one ERO told The Collective . He clarified that since the mechanism for approving voters in the app was accessible only through their credentials, “it was bound to bear my signature.” We reviewed the ECI’s rules for SIR hearings, which were circulated only to officials and were never made public. They require that, after issuing a suo motu notice, officers put down an explanation for why a person is being removed from the roll. However, UP’s electoral officials claimed the ECI’s software had been tweaked in such a manner that they were left with no option but to become signatories to the deletion of thousands across the state. The EROs suggested the process had been turned on its head in the SIR. Hearings were held first and notices for the deletion of voters were generated next. Sumedha Mittal is an independent journalist based in New Delhi. She is drawn to stories about Indian elections and the functioning of the Election Commission of India. Even in her free time, you will find her chasing stories. Ayushi leads data investigations into India’s political economy for The Reporters Collective. She previously worked as a tech and telecom reporter for The Hindu BusinessLine. She studied at the University College London and writes fiction in her free time. Shubhangi Derhgawen is a freelance investigative journalist who reports on governance, and public policy with a focus on how state decisions shape people’s lives. She was previously with Deutsche Welle and NDTV India. Furquan is a journalist and the managing editor for The Reporters' Collective. He has written at the intersections of politics, identity, conflict and social exclusion for prime Indian and global news outlets such as The Telegraph , IndiaSpend, Hindustan Times, The Caravan and Al Jazeera. His last stint was with Land Conflict Watch, where he led the editorial and product initiatives. Furquan has also worked as a researcher with the International Center for Journalists and been a fellow at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, University of Oxford. He has presented his research at several academic conferences including the International Journalism Festival in Italy, at the UNESCO Press Freedom Day celebration in Ethiopia and at the Kabul University. snapshot.evidenceText: New Delhi: The Election Commission of India (ECI) forced officers in Uttar Pradesh to sign deletion forms for 85,854 voters without giving any reason during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in the state. All these deletion forms were submitted after the legally mandated deadline. The deletion requests came en masse from election officers during the claims and objections period of the SIR in Uttar Pradesh (UP), between January 6, 2026, when the draft voter list was published, and April 10, when the final voter list was released. The Uttar Pradesh chief electoral officer (UP CEO) displayed all the deletion forms, officially called Form 7 objection requests, on its website. More than 4.3 lakh such forms were submitted. Working with a team of data analysts, The Reporters’ Collective scraped all the Form 7 disclosures from the UP CEO’s website. We found that 20 percent of these removal requests were submitted directly by the ECI’s own assembly-level officers. But the officers did not fill the forms. The ECI’s own software, ERONET automatically generated these forms, when officials deleted voters during the SIR hearings. The auto-generated forms came loaded with the officers’ digital signatures and were sent up for approval by their seniors. The job of these election officers is to adjudicate such claims of deletion. But in these cases they were acting as both the prosecutor and the judge. Under the law, citizens filing objections are required to put down specific reasons for requesting the deletion of voters. The ECI rules are clear on this. Applicants submitting Form 7 to seek deletions are required to select one of the justifications mentioned in the form. The reasons can be: the person is dead, underage, absent/permanently shifted, already enrolled or not an Indian citizen. In our investigation, we also found that a total of 1,10,476 voter deletion requests were submitted by individuals and accepted by the ECI after the legally mandated deadline. Out of 4.3 lakh Form 7 applications, in two assembly constituencies in UP, people with the same name filed hundreds of requests almost exclusively against Muslim voters. In Tarabganj and Pilibhit assembly constituencies, 90 percent of the deletion requests filed were against Muslims. In Tarabganj, 188 objections were raised under one name ‘Reshma’. When we dug further we found that all were filed on the same date against people from the same booth. The pattern repeats across the state. However, the ECI data does not provide identity details, beyond the name, of those who have proposed the deletions. Therefore citizens cannot independently verify or identify them. We sent detailed questions to UP Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa as well as to the ECI in Delhi. They had not replied by the time of publication. We analysed the scraped data and spoke to four election officials at the assembly level. We learnt that the Form 7 requests were automatically generated when officers removed voters during the SIR hearings they conducted. All the forms already had the official’s digital signature, leaving them no choice but to send them up the chain for approval. While 3.43 lakh individual objectors followed the process and specified the reasons for seeking a voter's removal, election officers failed to provide any reasons. We know that the ECI was auto-generating Form 7 requests through its software earlier during the enumeration process, as well. These were being submitted by booth-level officers (BLOs) who found voters to be absent, shifted, dead, or duplicate (ASDD) during enumeration. The BLOs had to specify one of the six reasons while filing deletions that would later be determined by election officers in each assembly, the electoral registration officers (EROs) and assistant electoral registration officers (AEROs), before they were put on the ASDD list. But we have now found that the ECI’s software compelled EROs and AEROs, who have quasi-judicial powers under the Representation of People Act, 1950 to both file and approve the deletion of voters after the SIR hearings were over. This goes against the ECI’s rules for SIR hearings. They explicitly state that a reason must be given or put on record for the voter to be removed. This change in procedure violates the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. The rules say that election authorities must outright reject any claim or objection that is not submitted in the prescribed manner, including specifying a clear reason. But, changes in the software forced election officers to sign off on unlawful forms anyway. UP was one of the 12 states and union territories to conduct the second round of the SIR exercise. It ran in three broad phases. In the first phase, starting November 4 , 2025, BLOs were tasked with distributing and collecting enumeration forms from every voter listed in the state electoral roll as of October 2025. Voters whose forms could not be collected were placed on the ASDD list for deletion. For this step, the ECI’s central software, ERONET, automatically generated a Form 7 that the BLO was required to sign with a specified reason. Of the 15.44 crore voters originally registered in UP, 2.89 crore names were placed on the ASDD list. On January 6, the state CEO published its draft electoral roll. In the following claims and objections phase, hearings were conducted for voters who were flagged as doubtful by the ECI algorithm but placed on the draft list. The ECI marked 3.26 crore electors as doubtful due to ‘logical discrepancies’ or for being ‘unmapped’. Assembly-level officers, including EROs and AEROs, summoned these flagged voters for hearings to prove their identity. If officers failed to verify them, they were struck off the final rolls. On April 10, UP published the final voter roll with 13.4 crore electors. At the press conference , UP CEO Navdeep Rinwa did not specify the number of voters removed during these SIR hearings. But we spoke to four EROs about the en masse Form 7 deletions our investigation found. They claimed the forms were submitted to delete unverified voters during the SIR hearings. The ECI rules for the SIR define the window between the publication of the draft and final rolls – the claims and objections phase – as the period for receiving addition and deletion requests from voters. Draft rolls allow citizens to first inspect who has been wrongfully included or marked under ASDD so that they can submit Form 7 deletion or Form 6 addition requests. The fact that a significant portion of the deletion requests at the time, more than 20%, were filed by election officers raises suspicion. Our analysis of the data scraped from the ECI’s website shows that 85,854 (98.5 percent) of the 87,127 requests filed by EROs and AEROs have no reason mentioned for deletion. For 62 of those, only letters such as ‘A, N, H, E’ had been mentioned as the reason. In 1,211 forms, “absent/shifted” is mentioned as the reason for deletion. All the 87,127 requests by EROs and AEROs were filed within 19 days, between March 15 and April 2, 2026. The four EROs we spoke to claimed these deletion requests were initiated for voters flagged for logical discrepancies or for being unmapped. “As an ERO, whenever we did not approve a voter during a hearing, the system automatically generated a Form 7 on our behalf,” one ERO told The Collective . He clarified that since the mechanism for approving voters in the app was accessible only through their credentials, “it was bound to bear my signature.” We reviewed the ECI’s rules for SIR hearings, which were circulated only to officials and were never made public. They require that, after issuing a suo motu notice, officers put down an explanation for why a person is being removed from the roll. However, UP’s electoral officials claimed the ECI’s software had been tweaked in such a manner that they were left with no option but to become signatories to the deletion of thousands across the state. The EROs suggested the process had been turned on its head in the SIR. Hearings were held first and notices for the deletion of voters were generated next. Sumedha Mittal is an independent journalist based in New Delhi. She is drawn to stories about Indian elections and the functioning of the Election Commission of India. Even in her free time, you will find her chasing stories. Ayushi leads data investigations into India’s political economy for The Reporters Collective. She previously worked as a tech and telecom reporter for The Hindu BusinessLine. She studied at the University College London and writes fiction in her free time. Shubhangi Derhgawen is a freelance investigative journalist who reports on governance, and public policy with a focus on how state decisions shape people’s lives. She was previously with Deutsche Welle and NDTV India. Furquan is a journalist and the managing editor for The Reporters' Collective. He has written at the intersections of politics, identity, conflict and social exclusion for prime Indian and global news outlets such as The Telegraph , IndiaSpend, Hindustan Times, The Caravan and Al Jazeera. His last stint was with Land Conflict Watch, where he led the editorial and product initiatives. Furquan has also worked as a researcher with the International Center for Journalists and been a fellow at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, University of Oxford. He has presented his research at several academic conferences including the International Journalism Festival in Italy, at the UNESCO Press Freedom Day celebration in Ethiopia and at the Kabul University. The Reporters’ Collective collaboratively produces investigative journalism. In many languages and mediums. We report truthfully and bring out facts that the powerful prefer to keep hidden from citizens. Besides courage and integrity, such reporting requires resources. We need your support. We need citizens to donate to keep us going and keep our work free to read for those who can’t afford to pay. Your donations will help us remain independent and work without fear. These deletion forms were signed off by ECI officials. The law mandates that people should know the reason for their deletion. The tax authorities have revoked our non-profit status claiming our journalism does not benefit the society. The order has severely choked the funds we need to carry out investigative journalism. If you believe the government and the powerful in the country need to be held accountable to citizens. If you believe our journalism does so, please donate to keep the Collective alive. Now more than ever we need your support. The Reporters' Collective 1/22, Asaf Ali Road New Delhi 110002

representative.title: Last call? Not for this 103-year-old bartender. | The Seattle Times
representative.author: Sophia Solano

snapshot.title: Last call? Not for this 103-year-old bartender.
snapshot.evidenceText: Irvin E. Koch, at 103, has been perfecting his one-liners for decades. He deals them out quickly, with a half smile that reveals the four remaining teeth on his top gums and a flash of mischief in his clear blue eyes. After 63 years tending bar, he has his setup-pause-punch line down to a science. When a patron on a recent evening asks him whether he is the oldest bartender in the world, he doesn’t miss a beat. “Don’t ask me,” he says. “I haven’t been around the world yet.” By many unofficial accounts, Irv (as he is widely known) is indeed the world’s oldest bartender. And since 1963, he has been bartending at Club Sunset Knoll, a dive in a Baltimore suburb that is better known as Irv’s Basement Bar because, well, it’s in Irv’s basement. The waterfront house that Irv bought when John F. Kennedy was president sits at the end of a gravel driveway in Pasadena, Maryland. It has plastic-wrapped windows and a sliver of red above the gray exterior siding, as if the painter went off to fetch a ladder and never came back. When we, two Post reporters, pull into a small, otherwise empty lot on a September afternoon, Irv’s stepgrandson Jason Cook walks outside and ushers us down a concrete staircase. We step through a nondescript door. Irv’s Basement Bar looks today as it has for decades: a retro redoubt from the rest of the world above. The drinks are cheap, the lights are dim, and the jukebox is playing. Scrawled messages cover every surface at Irv’s, from its cracked bathroom walls to its tiled ceilings to its leathery chairs. (“Raise Hell, Praise Irv” reads one note not far from a haphazardly inked phallus. But mostly, people just write their names.) The bar’s round card tables are scuffed. Underneath one, a stray cheetah-print slipper lies forgotten. There are nude Polaroid photos hung next to police department patches from across the country. The pool table takes quarters, and the Smith Corona cash register is about as old as Irv himself. A large banner with his smiling face on it lords above his subterranean kingdom: “Drinking where the sun don’t shine,” it reads. The bar’s most notable feature, however, is the ever-growing collection of bras — padded, underwire, lace — that hang from the ceiling tiles like a tree canopy. They’re mostly graffitied, too, with the names of the women who left them there. The first of them, decades ago, was named Amy. “She did it, I didn’t do it,” Irv says. “Most of the girls want to do it. You probably want to do it yourself.” Cook, who is sitting nearby, has come to expect these sorts of comments. “He don’t hold back anything,” Cook, 43, says later. “That’s for sure.” Nothing here is formal, and the bar only operates on Irv time. “The hours are very simple,” he tells us later. “When the first one gets here, that’s when it opens up.” He closes whenever patrons leave, or when he gets tired. Over a few hours at Irv’s, we learn about many of his dislikes: tattoos, bar covers, the church, babies, naps (“wasting your life away”), cities (“too many people”) and credit cards (“the government can trace everything you do”). He hasn’t had a dog since he was a kid and never bought a cellphone. Irv’s penchant for “telling everybody what he thinks,” Cook says, is one of two qualities that generations of regulars appreciate most about him. The other, according to Cook, is that Irv is a genuinely kind man. When Cook was a toddler, he says, his mother became unable to care for him, and Irv and his wife took him in. Cook recently moved back to the house (with his wife and four children) to care for Irv. Born in 1923, Irv grew up poor in a south Baltimore neighborhood, largely during the Great Depression. As a teenager, he joined the Navy and served in the Philippines during World War II. His younger brother Harry followed him into the armed forces. After the war, Irv worked as a builder for Sears and as a plumber with Harry. Going into the bar business just sort of happened. The house he now lives in was built in 1912 as a summer home for a prominent Baltimore meatpacking family, and later became an inn before Irv bought it in 1963. “This was up for sale,” Irv says unsentimentally. “We needed a house, so we bought the house — and guess what? The bar came with it.” Not everyone who discovers that their new digs come with a fully functioning tavern would opt to leave their career for bartending. Irv did. “Well, I was gifted it, so I took it,” he says. “When I was born and all, everything was pennies, nickels and dimes. Now it’s twenties, fifties, hundreds. So that’s why I opened up the bar. For the money!” He says this line with a well-rehearsed flourish that shows he has delivered it countless times. Cook doubts its veracity. For one, the cash-only bar makes just enough for Irv to live off. He’s pretty sure Irv doesn’t just do it for the profit. “He loves the interaction, socializing with people,” Cook says. “He likes the attention, too. It definitely seems to keep him alive.” Around 6 p.m., people begin trickling in, a lone regular here, a group of four police officers there. They order bottles of Coors Light from Irv and flip through the jukebox offerings: Buddy Holly, Dean Martin, Billboard’s Top Country Hits of 1960. People used to come to Irv’s just for its cold beer and low prices. Many now come to reach back in time to before the digital age. When patrons line up for photos with Irv, their cellphones look out of place. Kathleen Hooper, 48, is there celebrating her 17th wedding anniversary with her husband, Robert. “It’s almost like Ripley’s Believe It or Not meets ‘Coyote Ugly’ meets your neighbor,” she remarks about the space. She has lived in the area for years but never before made the trip. “This is a thing that people put on their bucket list,” she says. “We just felt like we had to do it before we didn’t have the chance. … Once it’s gone, it’s gone.” Hooper was nervous before her visit because of the lack of information available about Irv’s. No website, no phone number, no firm business hours. But the adventure, the not knowing, is the fun of it, she says. She grabs a Sharpie and scrawls on a doorframe “Love! Rob + Katie 4evah,” leaving her small mark on this storied place the same scribbling way thousands of others have before. Since starting his bar, Irv has never worked another job and has never thought about quitting his basement tavern. And after Irv’s wife and brother died, “he never stopped,” Cook says. “He is very good at taking emotions and feelings and somehow either getting rid of them or just pushing them down and hiding them away.” Like his bar, Irv is a product of a different era. He doesn’t spend much time thinking about the past, and second-guessing isn’t in his makeup. “If I could go backwards?” He considers the question. “There ain’t too much I would change.” Once a party ends, Irv is looking to the next one, he says. Right now, he’s excited for his 104th birthday party in August. “Who knows if this place will exist once he goes?” Cook says. “But everybody should come on down and check us out while they still can. And meet the famous Irv.” Stay secure and make sure you have the best reading experience possible by upgrading your browser!
