representative.title: A 75-Year-Old Nalanda Cobbler, Who Mended Shoes All His Life To Help His Children Stitch A Bright Future
representative.author: ETV Bharat English Team

snapshot.title: A 75-Year-Old Nalanda Cobbler, Who Mended Shoes All His Life To Help His Children Stitch A Bright Future
snapshot.evidenceText: Nalanda: Once upon a time, Kedar Mochi was repairing shoes on the pavement near JP Market on Ranchi Road. It was that spot which remained the only constant in his life, and the only means to earn a living, that helped him pay for his children s education and upbringing. Now past 75, Kedar has left behind his mud house and lives in Sabanhua Dihpar tola in Ward 5 of Harnaut Nagar Panchayat in Bihar’s Nalanda district, in a single-storey pucca house, that his children built for him and the family. Bringing up six children was not easy for Kedar but he ensured their education never took a back seat. Today, he proudly says that his elder son Sanjar Ravidas, also known as Manoj Kumar, is a school headmaster, younger son a rozgar sevak under MGNREGA and and two of his four daughters work in community healthcare."I am happy to see that my hard work paid off. All my children are doing well in life. The only reason of worry for me is my old-age pension which I have not received since last four months, says Kedar.Between mending shoes and polishing a few, Kedar reminisces, how he would take time out to read the newspaper. He also remembers how the discussions between customers influenced him and helped him develop a broad outlook. Politicians and educated people who stopped at my pavement shop there often stayed to talk. For me those conversations opened a world beyond daily earnings. I started questioning why poor families were denied ration, why students did not receive scholarships and what could be done about it, explains Kedar, who had completed matriculation level education.He began taking those grievances to the block office. He also understood how important is education for the children. With my limited earning I grew aware that apart from the worries of the next meal, my children s education should be the immediate priority, he says.His younger son, Ranjan Ravidas, recalls how old customers later on came not only have their shoes repaired or polished, but also to meet his father. The shop became a meeting point of old friends and acquaintances. "My father stitched shoes on the pavement but he also fought against injustice. If a ration dealer refused someone their ration, or anyone was denied their rights, he openly opposed it and confronted the officials," Ranjan says, recalling his father’s dealings with block development and circle officers.Poor students waiting for scholarships and families struggling to obtain ration found someone willing to accompany them and argue their case. Such encounters sharpened Kedar’s understanding of politics and made him a familiar figure among local residents.Although he never contested an election himself, he encouraged his wife, Kesari Devi, who had received no formal education, to enter public life. She was elected a ward member twice from Sabanhua panchayat. In 2006, Ranjan became a ward member, while Kesari served as a panch in the gram kachahri, the village-level dispute resolution body."We helped get work done for people in the village and educated our children, Kesari recalls on how she entered politics. At home, however, there was little money to spare. Kesari remembers the mud house and days when arranging two meals was difficult. Kedar continued to put the children’s education ahead of his own needs."We earlier had a mud house to live in, and at times even two meals a day were a struggle. But he never bothered about his own needs. He spent every rupee he earned on educating our two sons and four daughters," she says.Sanjar completed master’s degrees in sociology and English, along with a BEd, and became a teacher in 2007. In 2025, he cleared the Bihar Public Service Commission selection process for headmasters. He now serves in Triveniganj in Supaul district.Ranjan completed a master’s degree in history and joined MGNREGA as a rozgar sevak in 2008. He is currently posted in Hajipur.Kedar also ensured that all four daughters studied up to Class 10. All are now married and two work as ASHA and Mamta workers under the health department. His daughter Mamta Kumari, an ASHA worker in Khabra panchayat in Muzaffarpur, remembers how different their circumstances once were."Papa repaired shoes by the roadside but it was his hard work that ensured that our circumstances change. We all studied and that improved our condition later," she said.Kedar’s encouragement to participate in public life extended to his daughters-in-law. Pooja Devi, Sanjar’s wife and a graduate, contested the district council election from Harnaut in 2011 though she lost by just 200 votes."My father-in-law was involved in politics and he encouraged me to contest. He would go to the block office to help people get their ration and I was motivated with his way of dealing with people s issues. I therefore contested the district council election from Harnaut," Pooja says.His younger daughter-in-law, Shobha Devi, also contested a municipal election in Harnaut in 2023. The family said she received 5,500 votes but lost. Shobha said contesting elections required money that the family did not have. Her hopes now centre on the children’s education - she wants them to become doctors and engineers.Kedar s house now has a kitchen and a toilet and the uncertainty that once surrounded their daily meals has eased. Age and ill health have, however, confined Kedar largely to the house. I fought for people s issues but I have been deprived of my own old age pension since months. Occasionally even obtaining ration becomes difficult, rues Kedar.His children’s livelihoods offer some comfort, but those complaints remain unresolved. For a man who spent years arguing that poor families should receive what was due to them, the wait has become too personal now. But I am hopeful things will change and I will get my due. I have always taken up the cudgels for others, so, I believe, my concerns will be addressed, says Kedar with a faint smile.Also Read:After Laying Down Arms, Bastar s Arjun Clears Class X In First Division, Sets Target To Become An Education Ambassador 5 Doctors In The Making: This Poor Tribal Family From Kandhamal Village In Odisha Has All Children Studying Medicine

The only reason of worry for me is my old-age pension which I have not received since last four months, says Kedar.Between mending shoes and polishing a few, Kedar reminisces, how he would take time out to read the newspaper. He also remembers how the discussions between customers influenced him and helped him develop a broad outlook. Politicians and educated people who stopped at my pavement shop there often stayed to talk. For me those conversations opened a world beyond daily earnings. I started questioning why poor families were denied ration, why students did not receive scholarships and what could be done about it, explains Kedar, who had completed matriculation level education.He began taking those grievances to the block office. He also understood how important is education for the children. With my limited earning I grew aware that apart from the worries of the next meal, my children s education should be the immediate priority, he says.His younger son, Ranjan Ravidas, recalls how old customers later on came not only have their shoes repaired or polished, but also to meet his father. The shop became a meeting point of old friends and acquaintances. "My father stitched shoes on the pavement but he also fought against injustice. If a ration dealer refused someone their ration, or anyone was denied their rights, he openly opposed it and confronted the officials," Ranjan says, recalling his father’s dealings with block development and circle officers.Poor students waiting for scholarships and families struggling to obtain ration found someone willing to accompany them and argue their case. Such encounters sharpened Kedar’s understanding of politics and made him a familiar figure among local residents.Although he never contested an election himself, he encouraged his wife, Kesari Devi, who had received no formal education, to enter public life. She was elected a ward member twice from Sabanhua panchayat. In 2006, Ranjan became a ward member, while Kesari served as a panch in the gram kachahri, the village-level dispute resolution body."We helped get work done for people in the village and educated our children, Kesari recalls on how she entered politics. At home, however, there was little money to spare. Kesari remembers the mud house and days when arranging two meals was difficult. Kedar continued to put the children’s education ahead of his own needs."We earlier had a mud house to live in, and at times even two meals a day were a struggle. But he never bothered about his own needs. He spent every rupee he earned on educating our two sons and four daughters," she says.Sanjar completed master’s degrees in sociology and English, along with a BEd, and became a teacher in 2007. In 2025, he cleared the Bihar Public Service Commission selection process for headmasters. He now serves in Triveniganj in Supaul district.Ranjan completed a master’s degree in history and joined MGNREGA as a rozgar sevak in 2008. He is currently posted in Hajipur.Kedar also ensured that all four daughters studied up to Class 10. All are now married and two work as ASHA and Mamta workers under the health department. His daughter Mamta Kumari, an ASHA worker in Khabra panchayat in Muzaffarpur, remembers how different their circumstances once were."Papa repaired shoes by the roadside but it was his hard work that ensured that our circumstances change. We all studied and that improved our condition later," she said.Kedar’s encouragement to participate in public life extended to his daughters-in-law. He would go to the block office to help people get their ration and I was motivated with his way of dealing with people s issues. I therefore contested the district council election from Harnaut," Pooja says.His younger daughter-in-law, Shobha Devi, also contested a municipal election in Harnaut in 2023. The family said she received 5,500 votes but lost. Shobha said contesting elections required money that the family did not have. Her hopes now centre on the children’s education - she wants them to become doctors and engineers.Kedar s house now has a kitchen and a toilet and the uncertainty that once surrounded their daily meals has eased. I have always taken up the cudgels for others, so, I believe, my concerns will be addressed, says Kedar with a faint smile.Also Read:After Laying Down Arms, Bastar s Arjun Clears Class X In First Division, Sets Target To Become An Education Ambassador 5 Doctors In The Making: This Poor Tribal Family From Kandhamal Village In Odisha Has All Children Studying Medicine

representative.title: Inside Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine’s push to recapture Donetsk Oblast territory
representative.author: Diana Delyurman

snapshot.title: Inside Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine’s push to recapture Donetsk Oblast territory
snapshot.evidenceText: Tsyhan and Kalash, combat wing operators of the Darts crew of the NAFO, the 66th Mechanized Brigade, set the drone up for launch in the Lyman sector, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 11, 2026. (Diana Delyurman / The Kyiv Independent) DONETSK OBLAST — On a screen, live footage from a reconnaissance drone shows two men in Ukrainian pixel camouflage dashing in short bursts through the ruins of apartment buildings. Then they vanish into a basement. It is late summer, and the 3rd Army Corps and attached units are fully engaged in a counteroffensive in the Lyman sector called Operation Vivaldi . Russian forces are trying to recapture Lyman, a city in Donetsk Oblast that Russian officials have claimed their forces control. Ukrainian infantry on the ground tell a different story. For weeks, the operation ran under a news blackout until 3rd Army Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi made it public on Sept. 15 . By late September, the corps said it had retaken 176 square kilometers using closely coordinated infantry, air defense, electronic warfare, aerial drone units, and unmanned ground vehicles. Watching the video feed are drone operators from the 66th Mechanized Brigade, subordinate to the 3rd Army Corps. They are waiting for a batch of Darts, fixed-wing strike drones, to join the fight for Lyman . Their commander, call sign Deputat, is rushing to bring the drones. His car races down a road beneath tunnels of anti-drone netting, pine forests on either side, a landscape typical of northern Donetsk Oblast. Out of the darkness, a roadside coffee stand appears, glowing faintly. The car speeds past, then turns off onto rough ground. "Turn on the electronic warfare device," Deputat orders a soldier in the car. After some time, Deputat stops, quickly unloads the cargo, shakes hands with the soldiers, and drives off. The crew carries the drones into the dugout. They moved into this position only recently, after pushing closer to the front line. The gray zone is less than 10 kilometers away. Four men live, sleep, and work in the cramped shelter. Crews usually rotate every couple of weeks, but heavy Russian shelling near the positions can delay a rotation. In one corner is a workstation: a desk with several screens, one showing a video call with other units, another a live map of Donetsk Oblast. The areas marked gray or occupied are different from the picture Russian commanders paint. The soldiers listen to the call as they prepare to join a combined strike. For hours, units attached to the 3rd Army Corps have been striking a Russian artillery position with HIMARS rockets and drones. According to the 3rd Army Corps, such missions play a crucial role in the operation by pushing Russian mortar and artillery crews out of the area and clearing the way for the infantry. On the call, someone says, "If I were in their shoes, I'd hop on a motorcycle and get the hell out of there." The soldiers in the dugout laugh. The Ukrainians say the Russian crew won't abandon its howitzer because its soldiers are more afraid of their own commanders. The strike is delayed. As the wait drags on, the young men grow restless and step out into the dugout's corridor to smoke. Kalash, a soldier with light stubble, is the oldest in the crew. The others jokingly call him Mom. As he cooks breakfast on a camping stove, the smell of scrambled eggs and sausage fills the damp air. Finally, the duty officer on the call says, "Let's start the mission." "This is the NAFO crew. We want to join the strike on the howitzer," replies a soldier with the call sign Intelihent, who is piloting today. Every member of the crew can do every job: assemble the drone, prepare it for launch, navigate for the pilot, and fly the strike. Tsyhan, tall and tanned, assembles a Dart. It reminds him of building Lego as a kid, he says. He and Kalash carry the drone out into the field, set it up for launch, and talk over the radio with the men in the dugout. "Get out of there," comes the voice over the radio. The drone must fly several dozen kilometers. Intelihent works the controls while Bratok, a dark-haired soldier, helps him navigate. Back in the dugout, all four stare at the screen, fidgeting nervously on the wooden bench. The drone strikes. Direct hit. The men cheer and clink cans of energy drink. On the reconnaissance drone's feed, a stand of trees bursts into flames. Russian soldiers run out of a dugout and try to put out the fire. Then the feed cuts out. Pleased, the men post screenshots to the platoon's group chat. But someone on the call reports that the smoke is clearing and the target has survived. They must strike again. "Don't worry, we've got plenty of planes," Kalash tells the others. But the threat of retaliatory strikes looms over the dugout. Drone operators are among Russia's top targets. "I think it'll be a few days before they come after us," Tsyhan says. Eventually, several Ukrainian units working together destroy the Russian artillery position. The 3rd Army Corps said coordination between neighboring units played a key role in the operation. The men finish the breakfast Kalash made. Some stretch out on camping mats on the wooden benches and sleep fully dressed. Another strike request could come at any moment. Bratok is on duty, keeping an eye on the screens. To pass the time, he flips through live feeds from reconnaissance drones and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs). On the screens, the war plays out in real time across the Lyman sector. The video feed from a ground robot catches his eye: a dirt road, and in the corner a tiny call sign that reads Kuzya. Elsewhere in the Lyman sector, Kuzya himself is watching the same feed. The young redhead was one of the first UGV operators in the 66th Brigade's tank battalion. He used to be a driver, risking his life to bring food, medicine, and ammunition to the infantry. He still delivers supplies, but at far less risk. His UGVs can carry half a metric ton of cargo and keep going even after hitting a mine. The battalion began building up its UGV capabilities in early 2026. They learned how to use ground drones from the 3rd Army Corps. Now, the 66th Brigade ranks among the top five units for UGV use, according to the Delta system's June 2026 rating. According to the team, its 20 operators now cover most of the battalion's logistics, running 100 to 150 missions a month and rarely taking a day off. At first, the battalion's commanders were skeptical of the robots, until a heavily mined road left them unable to resupply a group of Mavic operators. Today, UGVs play an important role in Operation Vivaldi. The 96th Separate Support Battalion’s robots move ahead of the infantry and clear mines. Some are carried behind Russian lines by drones and launch an assault. But less visible work, logistics, matters just as much. "Soldiers win battles, but logistics wins wars," says Aibolit, a burly man whose long beard gives him a Viking look. At the UGV hub, he decides which cargo goes on which vehicle. The increased use of UGVs for logistics in the 3rd Army Corps and its attached units means infantry can reach the front line in armored vehicles or on foot, carrying only light backpacks. Reliable logistics also lets support teams deliver small comforts to the front, lifting the morale of infantrymen who may hold the same position for a month. Orders come in every day. A soldier can order something in the morning and be drinking a soda in the gray zone by midnight. "It's like ordering pizza," Aibolit says. As evening falls, the men prepare two vehicles, open platforms on massive wheels, for a mission. They load packs of bottled water, fuel canisters, a generator, and sealed boxes of food the soldiers ordered. It takes them only minutes. "Is the sky clear?" Aibolit asks over the radio. A drone icon flashes on their screens. It seems to be heading straight for the hub. "Maybe it'll come here, maybe somewhere else," one of them says, and shrugs. The soldiers play it down, saying their town is quiet, yet not a day goes by without a Russian strike. To disrupt Ukrainian logistics, Russian forces freely use guided bombs, including against targets with no apparent military value. Once the threat has passed, the men drive the vehicles out into the yard. A few minutes later, the robots roll off into the darkness. Kuzya usually takes the vehicles into the gray zone, where the ground is heavily mined. He knows every pothole and bush on the route. His screen is almost entirely black, except for a stretch of cratered road lit by the robot's headlight. Along the way, he passes wrecked cars marked with a white "Z." Stray dogs run up and bark at the strange visitor. Before long, they get used to it and trot alongside until they lose interest. Kuzya smiles. Eventually, the robot stops. Soldiers in camouflage appear on the black-and-white screen and quickly unload the cargo. One walks up to the camera and gives Kuzya a thumbs-up before they disappear into the woods. Kuzya turns the robot around to reload for the next mission. On a narrow dirt road, it meets another robot, and the two little vehicles circle each other as if they were dancing. That evening, Deputat drives back from another delivery to his soldiers, beneath the netting, stars peeking through the mesh. A burned-out SUV, recently hit by a Russian Lancet, lies by the roadside. "When you're coming back from the positions and you see the coffee stand, you know you're safe," he says. Diana Deliurman is a Ukrainian independent journalist and photographer. Born in Odesa, Ukraine, in 2000, she earned a degree in History of Art from Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv. During her studies, she began her journalism career, taking part in various training programs and fellowships, including an internship at the Kyiv bureau of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. Since then, her reporting and photography have been published by outlets including The Kyiv Independent, The Telegraph, The Conversationalist, Frontliner, and LB.ua. She is also a contributor to Getty Images. This story exists because readers chose to back it. Behind it is a newsroom that will not look away — and a community of people who make that possible. representative.title: Flydubai investigation: 7 findings that change what we know about attempted terror attack | Khaleej Times
representative.author: Sahim Salim

snapshot.title: Flydubai investigation: 7 findings that change what we know about attempted terror attack
snapshot.evidenceText: Sun, Oct 11, 2026 | Rabi al-Thani 29, 1448 | Fajr 04:58 | DXB 30.1 °C An attempted suicide attack targeting an airport terminal, two earlier flights used for reconnaissance and a pilot whose suspicions helped thwart the plot: The UAE's latest investigation into flydubai flight FZ1073 has revealed significant new details about the September 30 incident that nearly ended in disaster. The findings, announced by UAE Attorney-General Dr Hamad Saif Al Shamsi on Friday, October 9, establish what the 29-year-old Omani co-pilot allegedly intended to do, how he prepared for the attack and how those aboard the aircraft prevented it. Here are seven key findings and how they change what was previously known. In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the co-pilot was accused of attempting to crash the aircraft. Early reports suggested he intended to use the plane as a weapon against a target in Israel, with Ben Gurion Airport and a high-rise building in Tel Aviv mentioned as possible targets. The UAE investigation has now identified a specific intended target: the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport. According to prosecutors, the co-pilot planned to seize control of the aircraft and carry out a suicide attack designed to cause the "greatest possible loss of life". The suspect's motives were among the biggest unanswered questions in the initial days of the investigation. Early reports raised different possibilities, including terrorism and mental health issues, while later accounts pointed to extremist beliefs and radical online activity. The UAE investigation now traces the first signs of his radicalisation to 2017, when he was studying in Australia. Prosecutors said he was influenced by takfiri ideology through extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks. The investigation adds a significant new detail: the suspect admitted drawing inspiration from the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States. The findings establish a much longer history of alleged radicalisation and planning than was previously known. Earlier reports suggested the co-pilot had planned a similar attack in July but abandoned it at the last moment. Some accounts claimed he changed his mind because someone he knew was aboard. The UAE investigation found that he used two earlier flights to Tel Aviv specifically to familiarise himself with the route and Ben Gurion Airport as part of his preparations for the terrorist plot. The findings establish that the earlier journeys were used for reconnaissance, but neither confirm nor reject claims that he had planned an earlier attack and abandoned it because he knew someone aboard. Earlier reports suggested Oman Air had removed the suspect from flying duties over concerns about his beliefs and assigned him to an administrative role. According to UAE prosecutors, he worked for Oman Air between 2020 and 2024, followed by a period at Royal Air Maroc in 2025, before joining flydubai in January 2026. Investigators examined flydubai's recruitment procedures and found that the suspect had met the professional and security requirements for employment. These included holding a pilot's licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks. None of these procedures revealed his extremist beliefs or intentions, prosecutors said. The nature of the assault was initially unclear, with early witness accounts describing a stabbing and raising questions about whether a knife or another weapon had been used. The UAE subsequently established on October 3 that the co-pilot had attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with an emergency axe. The latest investigation adds forensic evidence to that finding. According to prosecutors, the captain's injuries were concentrated on his head, a vital area where such injuries could have been fatal. The forensic findings were consistent with the accounts of the suspect, the injured captain and witnesses. Who actually landed flydubai flight FZ1073 after its captain was seriously injured in the cockpit? The question sparked conflicting accounts, with some early reports suggesting that an Israeli plumber with no flying experience had helped bring the aircraft down safely. The UAE investigation has now clarified the roles of professional pilots aboard the aircraft, whose actions were crucial to stopping the attacker and bringing the plane safely to the ground. According to prosecutors, a pilot assigned to operate the aircraft's return flight was near the cockpit when he noticed its door opening and closing repeatedly. Suspecting something was wrong, he approached and attempted to enter using the access code. After gaining entry, he witnessed the co-pilot attacking Captain Machchhar with an emergency axe. He immediately intervened, assisted by a cabin crew member and several passengers, who together rescued the injured captain and restrained the attacker. The captain assigned to the return flight and his co-pilot then regained control of the aircraft, diverted it to Saudi Arabia and landed safely at Tabuk Airport. The investigation establishes their crucial role in saving the aircraft and those aboard, although the two pilots have not been publicly identified. In the days after the attack, questions emerged about whether the co-pilot had acted independently or had connections to terrorist organisations or foreign actors. Earlier investigations had not established links to an organised terrorist group, although speculation about outside involvement continued. The UAE Public Prosecution has now obtained a detailed confession from the suspect in the presence of his lawyer and with the required legal safeguards. Prosecutors said he admitted acting alone, without the involvement of others. However, investigators have not treated that claim as conclusive. The Public Prosecution is continuing to examine evidence, investigate possible accomplices and other connections, and review recordings and technical reports. As Associate Editor, Sahim Salim helps tell the UAE story like no one else does — and leads a team of reporters that asks the questions to get news and headlines that matter. Prosecutors said he was influenced by takfiri ideology through extremist literature and online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks. The investigation adds a significant new detail: the suspect admitted drawing inspiration from the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States. The findings establish a much longer history of alleged radicalisation and planning than was previously known. Earlier reports suggested the co-pilot had planned a similar attack in July but abandoned it at the last moment. Some accounts claimed he changed his mind because someone he knew was aboard. The UAE investigation found that he used two earlier flights to Tel Aviv specifically to familiarise himself with the route and Ben Gurion Airport as part of his preparations for the terrorist plot. The findings establish that the earlier journeys were used for reconnaissance, but neither confirm nor reject claims that he had planned an earlier attack and abandoned it because he knew someone aboard. Earlier reports suggested Oman Air had removed the suspect from flying duties over concerns about his beliefs and assigned him to an administrative role. According to UAE prosecutors, he worked for Oman Air between 2020 and 2024, followed by a period at Royal Air Maroc in 2025, before joining flydubai in January 2026. Investigators examined flydubai's recruitment procedures and found that the suspect had met the professional and security requirements for employment. These included holding a pilot's licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks. None of these procedures revealed his extremist beliefs or intentions, prosecutors said. The nature of the assault was initially unclear, with early witness accounts describing a stabbing and raising questions about whether a knife or another weapon had been used. The UAE subsequently established on October 3 that the co-pilot had attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with an emergency axe. The latest investigation adds forensic evidence to that finding. According to prosecutors, the captain's injuries were concentrated on his head, a vital area where such injuries could have been fatal. The forensic findings were consistent with the accounts of the suspect, the injured captain and witnesses. Who actually landed flydubai flight FZ1073 after its captain was seriously injured in the cockpit? The question sparked conflicting accounts, with some early reports suggesting that an Israeli plumber with no flying experience had helped bring the aircraft down safely. The UAE investigation has now clarified the roles of professional pilots aboard the aircraft, whose actions were crucial to stopping the attacker and bringing the plane safely to the ground. According to prosecutors, a pilot assigned to operate the aircraft's return flight was near the cockpit when he noticed its door opening and closing repeatedly. Suspecting something was wrong, he approached and attempted to enter using the access code. After gaining entry, he witnessed the co-pilot attacking Captain Machchhar with an emergency axe. He immediately intervened, assisted by a cabin crew member and several passengers, who together rescued the injured captain and restrained the attacker. The captain assigned to the return flight and his co-pilot then regained control of the aircraft, diverted it to Saudi Arabia and landed safely at Tabuk Airport. The investigation establishes their crucial role in saving the aircraft and those aboard, although the two pilots have not been publicly identified. In the days after the attack, questions emerged about whether the co-pilot had acted independently or had connections to terrorist organisations or foreign actors. Earlier investigations had not established links to an organised terrorist group, although speculation about outside involvement continued. The UAE Public Prosecution has now obtained a detailed confession from the suspect in the presence of his lawyer and with the required legal safeguards. Prosecutors said he admitted acting alone, without the involvement of others. However, investigators have not treated that claim as conclusive. The Public Prosecution is continuing to examine evidence, investigate possible accomplices and other connections, and review recordings and technical reports. snapshot.title: A century after it was taken, ancestral tipi cover returns to Kawacatoose First Nation
snapshot.evidenceText: Cree community in Saskatchewan brings home their Ancestor sîpiskwêsîkan’s painted fabric from Smithsonian in ‘Washington, D.C.’ Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter Those were okimâw (Chief) Cory Dustyhorn’s words when he first touched the tipi cover connected to his great-great-great-grandfather, sîpiskwêsîkan. After a century away from Kawacatoose First Nation , the ancestral item has returned to the Cree community. Community and family members gathered around the tipi cover after it was brought back from the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of the American Indian in “Washington, D.C.” “When I first touched it, I just felt so emotional,” Dustyhorn said. “I was thinking of all those that are gone on before me.” He thought about his parents, grandparents and ancestors — who preserved the history of the item through generations. He prayed for them to be present as the community finally brought home a piece of their history. “I told all of them, ‘Come with us, come and attend with us,” Dustyhorn recalled. “I know they were in between all of us — and they were here, too.” The tipi cover remained in the community for four nights before being temporarily housed at the Royal Saskatchewan Museum in oskana kâ-asastêki (Regina). Until the First Nation can build a permanent museum or cultural centre to house it safely, they plan to bring it home each year. The return followed a reparation process that lasted almost three years. Andrew Miller, an associate professor at the First Nations University of Canada, helped the Dustyhorn family locate the item and communicate with the Smithsonian. Miller described the tipi cover’s return as a meaningful example of reconciliation in action. “One of my friends from the Royal Saskatchewan Museum said, ‘Congratulations, you’ve just realized reconciliation,’” Miller said. “That’s what this is.” But for Miller, reconciliation means more than merely acknowledging past injustices. It also requires returning ancestral belongings and supporting communities as they restore cultural teachings. Dustyhorn said the return also highlights the need for stronger support from governments and museums — for all Indigenous communities hoping to recover what was taken away from them. “They talk about truth and reconciliation,” he said. “They splash that all over the news for a few years. “But where’s their help? How can we get the stuff back that was taken from us, too?” Miller and Dustyhorn said the tipi cover was taken during an era when museums and governments declared that Indigenous cultures were disappearing and needed to be archived. That view justified an urgent push to collect ceremonial belongings and other ancestral items from Indigenous communities worldwide. “They were wanting to capture the disappearing Indian,” Dustyhorn said. Miller said museums particularly sought items connected to regalia, ceremonies, and other cultural practices as part of that colonial narrative. “They were targets,” Miller said, describing sacred belongings as part of the “vanishing Indian culture” narrative. But, Dustyhorn emphasized, “We’re still here.” Miller first learned about the tipi cover from a former student, Andrea Dustyhorn. Years later, while researching ethno-ornithology — the relationships between people and birds — he found the tipi cover in the Smithsonian’s catalogue. “You should see this,” he told the chief. “What do you want to do?” Together they began an arduous process to bring the cover home. Dustyhorn’s family provided genealogical information and oral histories connecting it to his great-great-great-grandfather. During one meeting, he recounted Smithsonian representatives asking how he knew the tipi cover actually belonged to his community. Their question, he said, reflected what he called a big difference between written museum records and Cree ways of preserving history: through oral stories, saved for generations. “Everything is handed down orally,” Dustyhorn told them. “Let me tell you a story.” Dustyhorn began sharing the history passed down through his family about the tipi cover — and the person who took it. As he described the collector’s journey from Alaska through Saskatchewan, the Smithsonian representatives recognized details that matched their own written archival records. “They said, ‘Did you know he started in Alaska?’” Dustyhorn recalled them asking about information he already knew. “And I’m like, ‘Really?!’” The exchange connected the community’s oral history with the Smithsonian’s documentation, which to the museum established the family’s claim to the cover. According to archival records, the item was taken in Saskatchewan in 1926. Although the National Museum of the American Indian has since deleted its record of the tipi cover, an archived version of its webpage states it was obtained by museum staffperson Donald Cadzow — who it notes was a “non-Indian.” “Collected from Dusty Horn (sîpiskwêsîkan, Plains Cree, b. ca. 1863),” the record states. Cadzow was hired seven years before he took sîpiskwêsîkan’s painted fabric, promising payment the community says never came. “He made four field trips north,” the Smithsonian Institution states, “and collected over 2,000 objects from northern Athapaskan and Plains peoples.” It was later transported through Winnipeg, “Toronto” and “New York City”— before finally reaching “Washington, D.C.” A century later, last June, the Smithsonian notified the family it had deemed the cover was ready to return. At the time he was travelling to “Regina” when he got the email. “I just started pumping my fist,” he remembered. “Yeah, it’s the tipi,” he replied. “It’s ready to come home.“ In August, a group from Kawacatoose First Nation finally travelled to “Washington, D.C.” to repatriate the tipi cover. On the journey back, Dustyhorn said the weather changed as they approached the border. Rain, hail and lightning surrounded the vehicle. “It started raining really hard,” Dustyhorn said. “It was raining and lightning happening all around us… it started hailing.” He saw the weather as a sign that the tipi cover was leaving behind the painful history connected to its removal. “It’s washing the negativity — the 100 years of negativity that it is carrying … leaving it in the States,” he said. Miller also remembered that storm — but also the clear skies that emerged soon after they crossed into “Canada.” The travelers placed tobacco down, seeing the brightening weather as a meaningful part of the tipi cover’s return journey home. Yolanda Dustyhorn, the community’s cultural co-ordinator, described the item’s return as an emotional and historic moment. “Words can’t describe,” she said. “It’s very touching to have it come [back home]. She also spoke about the item’s condition after so many decades away. “The way it’s preserved, it’s 100 years old … yet we were able to still erect it,” she said. “It’s amazing.” She hopes having the tipi cover available in Saskatchewan will help younger generations learn about their history, culture and traditional teachings. “We gotta bring our culture back,” she said. “I want them to see this and to realize we gotta bring our culture back.” She plans to incorporate the returned tipi cover into programs for Youth. Her work includes teaching traditional medicines, ribbon skirts, belts and other cultural practices. “I’m targeting the Youth and the children,” she said. “We are gonna start bringing culture back.“ Miller said the loss of cultural belongings continues to impact many Indigenous communities a century later. “It impacts the present generation to this day.” He said the removal of ceremonial belongings like the tipi cover significantly disrupted cultural education, language and traditional practices. “This was involved in ceremony,” Miller said. But there are countless more ancestral belongings from Indigenous Peoples still held in museums and archives around the world. “There’s a lot out there,” he said. “Pipes, rattles, regalia, medicine bundles.” Reflecting on his correspondence with the Smithsonian, Dustyhorn said he felt there were unnecessary delays throughout the repatriation process. “We’d wait months for a reply,” he said, and they kept setting up more and more meetings. Although they were ultimately successful, Miller argued that museums should be willing to participate more proactively in repatriating communities’ cultural belongings — “to give back the things that are requested,” he said. For Kawacatoose’s leader, despite the hurdles he had to jump through, the return of his great-great-great-grandfather’s tipi cover proved what communities can accomplish when they keep fighting for their belongings. He encouraged other First Nations hoping to recover ancestral belongings to be persistent. “Start the process and finish the process,” Dustyhorn recommended. “Keep going forward — one foot in front of the other everyday — until they get it home. “I want all the other communities to get their stuff, to bring pride back to their Nations.” His First Nation is now working to bring home additional belongings, he said, estimating that about 900 artifacts connected to the community are held at the Glenbow Museum in otôskwanihk (Calgary). The community is also preparing for the return of objects from the Field Museum in “Chicago.” Miller said that collection could include roughly 60 items. For the Nation and the Dustyhorn family, the return of sîpiskwêsîkan’s tipi cover is both a homecoming — and a renewal of their profound cultural pride. “I want all our kids to be proud,” the chief said. “Walk with your head held high.” Brittany Boschman, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter Brittany Boschman is of Swampy Cree-German heritage, born and raised in Brandon, Manitoba, with strong ties to her home community of Pimicikamak Cree Nation. Brittany holds a Bachelor of Arts in Indigenous Studies and Indigenous Communications Arts (INCA) from the First Nations University of Canada, with minors in Cree and Kinesiology. snapshot.title: Deputy mayor’s pals given huge DEI payday by city hall | Toronto Sun
snapshot.evidenceText: I\u2019m a page editor but I also regularly report on Toronto City Hall, especially the kind of stories that require a little extra digging. I\u2019ve been editing for the Toronto Sun since April 2018 and have been with Postmedia since 2011. Before joining the company, I worked a few years at the Fort McMurray Today. That was shortly after I graduated from the journalism program at what was then called Humber College. I\u2019ve been called an \u201caward-winning journalist\u201d but as far as I know that\u2019s only true in that I was on the winning team of the Postmedia Editorial Services spelling bee one year. I try to travel whenever I can. I love baseball! I\u2019m always looking for city hall story tips! You can email me at jholmes@postmedia.com. See more Toronto Sun on Google — save as a Preferred Source Toronto city hall has given hundreds of thousands of dollars to a DEI consulting firm with long, personal ties to both Olivia Chow’s most trusted staffer and one of her deputy mayors, the Toronto Sun has learned. Contracts, invoices and other documents, some obtained via freedom of information and some publicly available, show more than $500,000 in taxpayer money has been paid to Monumental Projects Inc. since 2022. In the fall of that year, Ausma Malik was elected the councillor for Spadina-Fort York. Malik has personal relationships going back years with Monumental’s founders, Zahra Ebrahim and Kofi Hope. Ebrahim and Hope are also listed as founding advisers by the political organization Progress Toronto. Despite that, Progress Toronto founder Michal Hay appears to have personally signed a Monumental Projects expense on behalf of Chow, while serving as chief of staff to the mayor in 2023. In a series of statements, city hall confirmed its contracts with Monumental “on two separate projects” in 2022, but did not acknowledge invoices dated from 2023 to 2025, when Chow and Malik were in power. “The city’s procurement processes include conflict-of-interest requirements for both suppliers and staff,” Genevieve Sharkey, the city’s chief procurement officer, said in a statement. “Suppliers are required to disclose potential conflicts, and staff involved in procurement activities must comply with the city’s procurement policies, ethical standards and applicable bylaws.” Nora Cole, who works with Malik’s re-election campaign, said in a brief statement that none of Monumental’s work was for the councillor’s office and pointed to the city’s procurement protocols. In a written statement, Monumental defended its work but did not address questions about the founders’ ties to Malik and Chow. “We are proud that since 2020, Monumental has been delivering the highest quality work to a range of clients across Canada,” the statement said. “We approach every bid with the highest standards of integrity. For each tender we consider, we follow the qualification requirements, instructions and procurement processes established by our clients.” Representatives for Chow did not respond to a request for comment, nor did Progress Toronto. Monumental was paid for DEI-related consulting work, including training, speaking and public engagement, involving a range of departments at city hall, from the parks division to housing and planning all the way to the mayor’s office. Many of the contracts and invoices were provided to the Sun by the political advocacy group Integrity TO, which obtained them in a pair of freedom-of-information requests. That group was founded by Daniel Tate, a vocal critic of Chow and her allies on city council, who is running for council in a downtown ward next to Malik’s. representative.title: ‘A culture of corruption’: One voter card, many polling options; Brampton candidates question how City Hall plans to stop duplicate voting | The Pointer
representative.author: Adrian Peries

snapshot.title: ‘A culture of corruption’: One voter card, many polling options; Brampton candidates question how City Hall plans to stop duplicate voting
snapshot.evidenceText: Brampton residents hoping to vote in the October 26 municipal election should have received their voter cards detailing their respective polling locations. This is nothing out of the ordinary, as elections allow voters to cast a ballot ahead of time, should they not be able to make it on election day. This year, a rarely used system has prompted Brampton residents to voice concerns over the glaring holes in the widely criticized way the city’s officials have chosen to run the voting process. On their polling cards, there is a list of multiple locations, in some cases more than a dozen, where eligible residents can turn up and vote within their ward. People, including candidates, are asking, how would the City know if one resident votes multiple times? “Confidence in the integrity of the election has to come first,” says candidate Monica Singh Soares. “These are not accusations…they’re basic election integrity questions.” Wards 7 and 8 councillor candidate Monica Singh Soares says confidence in the election is key. (Submitted) Prabh Gill is running to be the next mayor of Brampton and recently sent a letter to City Hall that he shared with The Pointer. “Dear City Clerk, I am a registered candidate for Mayor in the 2026 Brampton municipal election. I am writing to ask for information about the voting and vote-counting equipment that will be used in this election. I want to be clear that I am not alleging wrongdoing by the City, its staff or any supplier. My purpose is to make sure residents and all candidates have the same clear information before voting begins.” Gill is seeking clarification about the process that was used to acquire the electronic voting machines that are being used, and what accountability is in place to ensure the integrity of the system. “The City's Bids and Tenders page for NRFP2025-347, Lease of Election Tabulation System and Electronic Voting System, lists the bid as awarded on January 9, 2026. The same page shows no awarded vendor and no contract value.” Brampton mayoral candidate Prabh Gill has questions about the integrity of the electronic vote counting machines being used in the election. (Supplied) The Pointer also sent questions to City staff about steps that are being taken to ensure voting integrity and what can be done if any irregularities crop up. There was no response. The City of Brampton website reports that the municipal Voters' List identifies people who are eligible to vote in the municipal election, by name, qualifying address, school support and residency.” “The Voters' List is live and when a voter attends a voting location, they are marked as having voted. This information is updated immediately and all other voting locations will see the same information.” There is very little information on the voting page that explains what safeguards are in place to ensure voting integrity. “Our online tool will allow you to confirm or provisionally update or add your information to the Voters' List. Soares said she was told by City officials that a live voters’ list will record each vote and all other polling locations will be able to see it. The Pointer asked how such safeguards would actually work and what protocols are in place to ensure the integrity of the live voters list. It’s unclear how a volunteer or worker at one voting station would know that someone who appears to cast a ballot has already voted somewhere else. City staff did not explain why the usual system that has been in place in Brampton, restricting voters to one designated polling station where they are registered to cast a ballot, was not used this year, and why the city is not doing what other municipalities across the country do. Many residents, including candidates, think a live voters list is not enough to ensure fair elections, and are questioning why the City changed the usual system used in Brampton and across the country, which tells voters which specific nearby polling station they have to show up at to cast one single ballot, after scrutineers cross them off the list for that specific location, the only one they are able to vote at. Soares, a candidate for councillor hoping to represent Brampton’s Wards 7 and 8, is not accusing anyone of cheating; she is concerned about safeguards and the loss of trust in the system that residents are raising. She said voters have no idea what safeguards are in place to prevent someone from voting up to a dozen times. The City’s position effectively relies on the honour system, putting the onus on voters not to break the rules. Soares says a live voters list allows someone to be marked as having voted at a site once they cast a ballot. But what happens if they do the same at another polling station? She wants to know how a duplicate vote is flagged, and how it would be reconciled afterward. “The government should be going above and beyond what they can, not simply saying ‘trust us’”. She is especially concerned about the choice to move away from the usual system after years of controversy at City Hall, which she described as having a “culture of corruption.” “There’s a culture of corruption,” she said. “And people are nervous. And I think that’s what may be an elephant in the room that people are not talking about.” One of the voter cards in Brampton, for the 2026 municipal election, with multiple listed locations a resident can choose to vote at in their ward, instead of the usual system across the country that gives voters only one location where they are registered to cast their ballot. Candidates are worried about fraud. (Submitted) Soares said being outside of City Hall’s politics, she calls out potential corruption when she sees it. Soares also raised concerns over the identification that can be used. “A voter notice itself is also not identification,” she said. A publicly-sourced review of ballot counting machines in Brampton, or EVMs (electronic voting machines) dated October 5 has been spreading across the internet, raising concerns about who controls the vote counting process. It is a closed system in Brampton, with City Hall entirely in charge of taking the voting data from the machines and recording the results. It is possible that in the hands of unethical City Hall leaders those responsible for the voting machines could easily manipulate the results to favour certain candidates. Only a complaint under provincial rules could trigger an external review, and even then it’s not clear how a sophisticated vote rigging scheme could be exposed. The document claims that the American company ES&S was the 2022 election supplier for voting tabulator machines . The City of Brampton leased DS200 tabulators and 15 ExpressVote accessible units. A 2026 staff report says the old contract had expired, and a Request for Proposals (RFP) was being developed. The public document also raises serious issues over ten years. For example, in 2023, a coding error on ExpressVote XL machines in Northampton County, Pennsylvania, made printed summaries appear to flip judicial retention votes, and ES&S acknowledged fault. On the City of Brampton’s voter FAQ page, the use of voter machines is addressed. “The City has established procedures and safeguards governing the use of voting and vote-counting equipment to protect the accuracy, security and integrity of the election. Each piece of voting equipment undergoes rigorous testing ahead of an election. The technology does not eliminate a paper ballot. All votes processed by vote tabulators have a corresponding paper ballot. The use of voting and vote-counting equipment is permitted under Ontario's Municipal Elections Act and is commonly used by municipalities across Ontario.” There is no information about independent, external oversight of City Hall staff. Mayor Patrick Brown was asked about concerns regarding the change to allow multiple voting locations and if there is an independent, external auditor monitoring the use of voting machines so no manipulation takes place. He did not respond. Gill sent ten questions to Brampton’s City Clerk regarding the integrity and transparency of the voting system: 1. Who is the final awarded supplier for NRFP2025-347, and what legal entity signed the agreement? 2. What is the total contract value, including lease, software, support, licensing, training, ballot services, accessibility units, maintenance, peripherals, optional work and taxes? 3. Who submitted bids, and what was the final scoring matrix? 4. Why does the public tender page say Awarded but also show No Awarded Vendors? 5. Does Brampton use any modem, cellular, wireless, VPN, remote support or internet based transmission for election night results? If yes, when is it active and what safeguards exist? 6. Are final official results physically uploaded and cross checked with printed tapes and paper ballots before certification? 7. What independent testing, logic and accuracy testing, cybersecurity testing, vulnerability scanning, DGSI compliance review and accessibility review will be completed before advance voting? 8. Will candidates be allowed to observe equipment demonstration, testing, sealing and post election tabulation certification? 9. Have all conflict of interest declarations been signed by vendors, evaluators, staff, consultants and elected officials where applicable? 10. Will the Clerk publish an incident reporting protocol for tabulators and accessible voting devices before Election Day? Soares said, “Technology isn’t inherently the problem, transparency is the issue.” The Pointer also sent questions to the City Clerk’s office and elections coordinator Roger Wilson, asking if the system being used this year is open to fraud, and what the City is doing to protect the voting machine process and the ballot casting process from fraud, including the possible hiring of an independent external oversight auditor. snapshot.title: Update: China issues guidelines on developing new quality productive forces
snapshot.evidenceText: BEIJING, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- The Communist Party of China Central Committee and the State Council have issued a set of guidelines aimed at accelerating the development of new quality productive forces to bolster high-quality development. These guidelines outline 19 key measures in five areas, namely advancing scientific and technological innovation, deepening the integration of sci-tech and industrial innovation, innovating development approaches, promoting institutional and mechanism innovation, and improving mechanisms for talent development. Noting that developing new quality productive forces is an intrinsic requirement and an important focus of promoting high-quality development, these guidelines stress the importance of innovation-driven development, reform and measures tailored to local conditions, and following the approach of "establishing the new before abolishing the old." The guidelines call for pursuing high technology, high efficiency and high quality, properly handling the relationships between the government and the market, between the qualitative nature of productive forces and the forms they take in industry and business, between reform and development, and between self-reliance and opening up, while coordinating development and security. "The new round of scientific and technological revolution and industrial transformation has opened up broad prospects for developing new quality productive forces. Seizing this historic opportunity requires moving faster to achieve greater self-reliance and strength in science and technology and raising innovation capacity across the board to maintain strategic initiative," said Wang Shengxiao, a researcher with the Party School of the Communist Party of China Central Committee. The guidelines call for stronger original and transformative sci-tech innovation, with major sci-tech projects to focus on strategic, landmark and leading products, targeting the cutting-edge of global science and technology and serving major areas of economic development, major national needs, and people's health. They stress the need for faster breakthroughs in key core technologies, including efforts to promote the high-quality development of key manufacturing industrial chains and implement industrial innovation projects in priority areas. The guidelines emphasize coordinated efforts to strengthen national strategic sci-tech capabilities, giving full play to national laboratories in organizing major national sci-tech projects and building major innovation platforms. The guidelines also urge optimizing the roles and distribution of national sci-tech research institutions, high-level research universities and leading sci-tech enterprises. The guidelines underline the principal role of enterprises in sci-tech innovation, encouraging technology-based small and medium-sized enterprises to increase research and development investment and supporting capable private enterprises in taking the lead in major national technological breakthrough tasks. To speed up the transformation of sci-tech achievements into real productive forces, the guidelines call for leveraging the advantages of China's vast market to better connect technology with the market and advance the development of new quality productive forces on a larger scale. The guidelines also urge upgrading traditional industries through the application of digital, intelligent and green technologies. The country should seek to advance producer services toward greater specialization and the higher end of the value chain, while improving the quality, diversity and convenience of consumer services, according to the guidelines. For emerging industries, the guidelines emphasize efforts to foster their growth and develop new pillar industries. The guidelines encourage greater cross-industry and cross-regional integration, measures to avoid "involution-style" competition, and support eastern regions to help central, western and northeastern regions develop emerging industries in line with local conditions. The guidelines call for forward-looking planning for future industries and emphasize the need to make full use of existing fiscal policies to support their development and guide social capital to steadily increase investment. The guidelines also urge promoting the deep integration of the digital economy and the real economy, optimizing the layout, construction and operation of national data infrastructure, advancing the digital transformation of the manufacturing sector, and building digital industrial clusters with international competitiveness. The guidelines call for fully implementing the "AI Plus" initiative, using artificial intelligence (AI) to transform traditional industries, accelerating innovation in AI and other digital and intelligent technologies, and promoting the widespread application of AI across industries. Efforts are also needed to establish systems for technology monitoring, early risk warning and emergency response to ensure that AI is safe, reliable and controllable, the guidelines note. These guidelines further propose building a green, low-carbon and circular economic system by strengthening green manufacturing, developing green services, expanding the green energy industry, and driving the supply of green products via green consumption. Efforts should be made to optimize the policy toolbox for green development and implement fiscal, financial, investment, pricing, technological and environmental policies that promote green and low-carbon development, according to the guidelines. The country will actively advance the energy revolution and accelerate the green transition of energy use in production and daily life across society, the guidelines add. The guidelines call for deepening reform to promote close integration of science and technology with the economy, saying that efforts should be made to build an open, shared and secure nationally integrated data market. The guidelines also stress the need to improve the market regulation system and increase the supply of innovative financial products. The guidelines pledge to allocate advanced production factors globally by expanding high-standard opening up and actively building a global innovation cooperation network, and encouraging foreign venture capital institutions, international standards organizations and others to develop in China. The guidelines urge cultivating talent urgently needed for the development of new quality productive forces, adding that policies on the use and flow of talent should be improved. "New quality productive forces are primarily driven by transformational technological breakthroughs, which bring profound changes to how innovation is organized, industries evolve and resources are allocated," said Liu Zhenzhong, a researcher at the Institute of Industrial and Technological Economics of the National Development and Reform Commission. "These changes require deeper reforms to reshape institutional frameworks and remove obstacles to development." The outline of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) identifies the development of new quality productive forces as a key strategic task and sets out 28 major projects related to this goal, accounting for 25.7 percent of the 109 major projects outlined in the plan. The projects focus on four priorities: strengthening industrial capabilities and competitiveness, fostering emerging industries, pursuing breakthroughs in cutting-edge technologies, and enhancing innovation capabilities. At an international seminar held in Beijing in September, Chinese experts said China's development of new quality productive forces could provide fresh momentum for global economic growth and create new opportunities for countries at different stages of modernization. Abdulrahman Bello Dambazau, Nigeria's ambassador to China, noted that the emphasis on talent development, scientific research and industrial upgrading could offer useful reference for developing countries. China's development of high-tech, green and intelligent industries is also creating more opportunities for cross-border investment and industrial cooperation. At the China International Fair for Investment and Trade in September, representatives from European countries explored cooperation with China in areas such as clean energy, AI, smart manufacturing, biomedicine and the digital economy. ■

representative.title: Ebola spreads in eastern DRC as Kenya confirms imported case | News | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Prosper Heri Ngorora

snapshot.title: Ebola spreads in eastern DRC as Kenya confirms imported case
snapshot.evidenceText: New cases in eastern DRC and a fatal imported infection in Kenya highlight the challenges of containing Ebola. Beni, Democratic Republic of Congo – The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has spread to another health zone in the east, while a fatal imported case in Kenya has underscored the risk of cross-border transmission. The World Health Organization (WHO) said in an October 8 update that Alimbongo health zone in North Kivu province had reported cases for the first time. As of October 6, four confirmed cases, including two deaths, had been recorded there. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a species of Ebola virus. According to the WHO, cases had been reported in 64 health zones across seven provinces in the DRC. Ituri remained the worst-affected province in cumulative cases, while North Kivu was accounting for a growing share of newly confirmed infections. As of October 6, the WHO had recorded 8,728 confirmed cases and 4,205 confirmed deaths in the DRC. A further 2,269 people had recovered, and the crude case fatality ratio stood at 48.2 percent. Kenya confirmed its first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease on October 6, according to the WHO. The patient, a Kenyan citizen who had been living in the DRC, fell ill there and received treatment at several health facilities before travelling to Kenya through Uganda. The patient travelled by road to Kampala, Uganda, before flying to Nairobi, arriving on October 3. The patient was isolated in hospital and tested positive for the virus. Despite supportive treatment, the patient died on October 5, the WHO said. Kenyan authorities identified 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers. The WHO also reported efforts to trace passengers and crew members from the flight to Nairobi. Public health measures have been initiated in Kenya and Uganda, including contact tracing and enhanced surveillance. On October 8, preliminary laboratory results for a suspected Ebola case in Kenya’s Wajir County came back negative, according to the county governor. The result eased concerns about a possible second case, although monitoring continued. The imported infection has underscored the importance of surveillance and coordination between neighbouring countries. Identifying exposed people and monitoring them for symptoms are central to detecting infections early and interrupting further transmission. In the DRC, the response is facing mounting pressure from limited treatment capacity, insecurity and difficulties securing cooperation from some communities. Daniel Makasi Levergénois, founder of Watoto Radio, said insecurity and misinformation were undermining efforts to contain the outbreak. In Beni and Butembo, both in North Kivu, rumours and misconceptions about Ebola had contributed to reluctance among some residents to cooperate with response teams, he said. In an October 5 update, medical charity Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said North Kivu accounted for nearly 40 percent of newly confirmed cases nationwide, up from 24 percent at the end of August. MSF also reported that, as of September 28, 34 percent of confirmed Ebola patients were being treated in non-specialised health facilities. Dedicated treatment centres lacked sufficient beds, while delays in diagnosis meant some patients were being treated outside facilities equipped to manage Ebola. The organisation warned that many of these facilities lacked the resources and expertise needed to manage the disease, increasing the risk of transmission among patients and healthcare workers. “For weeks, treatment capacity has stretched to its limit,” said Stephanie Hoffmann, coordinator of MSF’s Ebola treatment centre in Butembo. “Because there are not enough beds available, we are sometimes forced to refer confirmed Ebola patients elsewhere, despite the significant risk this poses to the wider community. In addition, standards of care in some peripheral facilities do not always meet the requirements for Ebola treatment. This is extremely concerning.” Alberto Lusenge, a community leader in Beni, said the failure to stop transmission early in Ituri province, followed by new cases and attacks on response workers in Beni and Butembo, had deepened public concern. Lusenge warned that mistrust could discourage residents from reporting symptoms or cooperating with health workers. He said North Kivu could become a greater focus of the outbreak if authorities failed to secure stronger cooperation from local communities. The WHO said response teams were following up 23,741 of the 29,535 identified contacts as of October 4, equivalent to 80.4 percent – below the response target of at least 85 percent. Contact tracing allows health authorities to identify people who may have been exposed, monitor them for symptoms and detect infections early. Gaps in follow-up can make it harder to identify and interrupt chains of transmission. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for a community-centred response, including active case finding, systematic contact tracing, daily follow-up of exposed people and sustained engagement with local communities. The DRC’s 2018–2020 Ebola outbreak, caused by a different virus species, killed nearly 2,300 people. The current outbreak presents distinct challenges: According to the WHO, there are no approved vaccines or specific treatments for Bundibugyo virus disease. Early detection, supportive care and infection prevention therefore remain central to the response. But as infections spread into additional health zones and treatment facilities struggle to accommodate patients, health authorities face the dual challenge of containing transmission and maintaining public trust. Jean Kaseya, director-general of Africa CDC, has stressed the importance of rapidly identifying and monitoring people exposed to the virus. “To bring this outbreak under control, we need to know where every contact is, track them and quickly identify anyone showing symptoms before they pass the virus on to their family, their community or across borders. We will only bring this outbreak under control once the last chain of transmission has been broken,” Kaseya said in a news release seen by Al Jazeera.
snapshot.imageAlt: Ebola spreads in eastern DRC as Kenya confirms imported case

representative.title: Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government | Humanitarian Crises News | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Al Jazeera Staff

snapshot.title: Taiz hospitals near collapse as Houthis tighten siege: Yemen government
snapshot.evidenceText: Medical services in Taiz risk shutting down as fuel, medicines, and supplies run alarmingly low under Houthi blockade. Yemen’s internationally recognised government has warned of an “imminent health and humanitarian catastrophe” in the besieged city of Taiz, in the country’s southwest, as the Houthis continue their siege and “obstruct essential supplies”. Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health and Population said in a statement on Saturday that medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies and fuel at the city’s health facilities were “nearing depletion”. It said emergency care, surgery, intensive care, dialysis and neonatal services could be forced to stop if the situation continued, putting patients, injured people, pregnant women and newborns “at immediate risk”. Fuel shortages also threaten electricity generators, ambulances and the cold chains that keep medicines and vaccines usable, which could cause “severe complications and preventable deaths”, the ministry said. It demanded the siege be lifted immediately, and supply routes reopened, with safe passage for patients, ambulances, health workers and aid. It called on the United Nations and humanitarian organisations to “deliver medicines, intravenous fluids, medical supplies, oxygen and fuel” to the city’s health facilities. “Every delay increases the risk of service interruption and loss of life,” the ministry said. The Houthis, an armed group backed by Iran and also known as Ansar Allah, seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, by force in 2014 and later imposed their own government. They control the country’s north and northeast. Taiz endured a devastating Houthi siege between 2015 and 2016, when Yemeni government forces were confined to an enclave in the city centre. The siege was broken in 2016, though the Houthis kept a partial blockade through other access points. In 2024, they agreed to reopen a route from the east, but it has been closed after fighting resumed. The renewed siege took shape in early October. The Houthis launched an offensive along the Red Sea coast of the Taiz governorate in September, capturing the port city of Mocha, and by October 4 had taken the town of At Turbah, cutting the last main road between Taiz city and other government-held areas. Yemeni government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, began a counteroffensive in early October. Nabil Jamil, director-general of the Yemeni government’s planning and development office in the Taiz governorate, told Al Jazeera the current siege is “more comprehensive and its impact more severe than in 2015”. He said about 2.8 million people live in government-held areas of the governorate, along with 200,000 who have recently been displaced. Fuel has become scarce, and on the black market, the price of a 20-litre (5.2-gallon) container of petrol has risen from 30,000 Yemeni riyals ($19) to 90,000 ($58). “We are still waiting for a response or intervention on the ground,” Jamil said. The UN refugee agency and the World Health Organization have warned that the fighting is putting Yemen’s fragile health system in peril. “Civilians must never be turned into a means of exerting pressure in any conflict,” said Nabil Sharyan, a lawyer and head of the Justice for Rights and Development Organization.

representative.title: Where the Power Comes From Could Decide the Carbon Cost of Your Concrete
representative.author: Sloane Callahan

snapshot.title: Where the Power Comes From Could Decide the Carbon Cost of Your Concrete
snapshot.evidenceText: Concrete is everywhere, and so are its emissions. The construction industry is one of the largest carbon emitters on the planet, and in China the production of building materials alone accounts for 24.4 percent of the nation's energy-related carbon emissions, roughly 2.6 billion tons of carbon dioxide. For decades, researchers have tried to shrink that footprint by tweaking cement chemistry, swapping in industrial by-products, and optimizing structural designs. But a new study published in Case Studies in Construction Materials suggests that one of the most powerful levers for cutting the carbon cost of advanced concrete has been hiding in plain sight: the electrical grid that powers the factories making the materials. The research, led by Yuanyuan Yang, Tengfei Xu, Tong Guo, Dapeng Mei, Bo-Tao Huang, and Tianyu Xie, focuses on steel fiber-reinforced concrete and ultra-high-performance concrete, two advanced materials prized for their exceptional toughness, tensile strength, and crack resistance. Unlike conventional concrete, whose carbon emissions are dominated by cement production, these fiber-reinforced composites introduce a second major emission source: the steel fibers themselves. Steel fibers are manufactured through an electric arc furnace short-process route followed by extensive wire drawing, and this production chain is extraordinarily electricity-hungry. Around 58.4 percent of the total energy consumed in making steel fibers is used during the wire drawing phase alone, which stretches hot-rolled wire down to fibers as thin as 0.15 millimeters. That electricity dependence is what makes the new findings so striking. While the carbon emissions of cement are largely locked in by the chemistry of clinker calcination, a process that accounts for roughly 90 percent of cement's footprint and is essentially independent of where it is made, the emissions of steel fibers swing wildly depending on the carbon intensity of the regional grid supplying the factory. Across the 31 provinces of mainland China, grid carbon emission factors range from 0.04 to 0.97 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent per kilowatt-hour, a nearly 24-fold difference. The consequence is dramatic: the carbon emission factor for a kilogram of steel fiber can range from 0.72 to 4.35 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent, purely because of where it was produced. The study's authors built a spatiotemporally explicit life cycle assessment framework that replaces the single, static national average emission factor used in most conventional carbon accounting with province-level and season-level values. They compiled provincial power generation mixes for 2022 and 2024, calculated fuel-specific emission factors for thermal power including upstream fuel emissions, accounted for inter-provincial electricity transfers and transmission losses, and then applied these refined factors to the cradle-to-gate emissions of concrete mixes spanning strength grades from C30 to C180. The results expose how badly national averages distort the picture. Using a unified national average overestimates emissions in clean-energy provinces by up to 177.5 percent while underestimating them by 25.5 percent in coal-dependent regions. The geography of China's power system explains the pattern.
