representative.title: Off Gulf coast of Florida, giant concrete domes were dropped more than 200 feet underwater to help restore corals and sea life. All corals outplanted in 2025 survived and even grew - The Economic Times
representative.author: Shawn Dass

snapshot.title: Off Gulf coast of Florida, giant concrete domes were dropped more than 200 feet underwater to help restore corals and sea life. All corals outplanted in 2025 survived and even grew
snapshot.evidenceText: What looks like an unusual underwater construction project is actually part of a long-term attempt to bring damaged coral habitats back to life. Off Florida’s northern Gulf coast, scientists have been placing specially designed concrete domes more than 200 feet below the surface, creating new foundations where corals and other marine life can settle. The experiment is already showing encouraging results. In a 2026 follow-up mission, researchers found that all of the corals outplanted at one Gulf site in 2025 had survived and even grown.Why are scientists putting concrete domes on the seafloor?The project targets mesophotic corals, which live in the ocean’s “twilight zone”, where sunlight becomes increasingly limited. These deep-water communities were among the habitats affected by the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill. NOAA says the spill injured more than 770 square miles of seafloor habitat in the Gulf. The restoration programme is now testing ways to help these ecosystems recover.In June 2025, scientists aboard the RV Point Sur deployed six custom-made concrete domes off Florida’s northern Gulf coast. Each dome weighed about 60 pounds and was lowered to the seafloor at a depth of approximately 65 metres (213 feet). A remotely operated vehicle then guided each structure into position near naturally occurring coral colonies.The domes are designed to become new marine homesThe dome structures were designed to resemble rocky terrain and contain small spaces that can provide shelter for animals living around coral. They also have pre-drilled holes where coral fragments can later be attached. Stainless-steel hardware allows the structures to be lifted and repositioned, while temporary 3D-printed plugs cover the attachment points until divers are ready to use them. NOAA said concrete was selected because it is an “accessible, low-cost, and versatile substrate” with potential for coral propagation. That could be important if scientists eventually determine that artificial structures can be deployed more widely without harming surrounding habitats.134790781Scientists get an encouraging sign from 2025 coral outplantsThe biggest breakthrough came not from the domes alone, but from monitoring corals that had already been returned to the seafloor. In 2025, researchers outplanted 24 coral colonies from a laboratory in Galveston, Texas. The team returned in 2026 to check how the colonies were doing. At a site north of Geyer Bank, the results were particularly promising: every coral placed there in 2025 survived and grew. The finding is significant because mesophotic corals are slow-growing organisms and restoring them in their deep-water environment presents major logistical challenges.How scientists get corals more than 200 feet below the surfaceWorking at these depths requires specialised equipment and carefully planned dives. During the 2026 restoration work, NOAA and its partners used remotely operated vehicles, technical divers and a specially designed “coral elevator” to transport coral fragments to the seafloor. NOAA Fisheries reported that the 2026 mission successfully placed 26 mesophotic corals on artificial domes at 66 metres, while 16 additional coral fragments were relocated to start new colonies. Scientists also collected sediment and biological samples and mapped more than 14 square nautical miles of seafloor. The work involves NOAA, the U.S. Geological Survey, the University of Rhode Island and Marine Applied Research and Exploration.Long-term attempt to rebuild gulf’s hidden ecosystemsThe successful coral survival is encouraging, but scientists are not presenting it as proof that the restoration challenge has been solved. The teams plan to keep returning to the sites to measure coral growth and monitor how artificial structures interact with the surrounding ecosystem. Researchers are also testing different substrates, depths and coral species to determine which approaches work best. The broader restoration programme began after the Deepwater Horizon disaster and is funded through the settlement reached between BP and the federal government and Gulf states.For an ecosystem damaged more than a decade ago, the sight of laboratory-raised corals surviving and growing back on the Gulf seafloor offers a rare piece of good news. The concrete domes may be small compared with the scale of the ocean but scientists hope they can become the starting points for much larger underwater communities.

snapshot.title: Syrian President calls for Israeli forces to withdraw from Syrian territory
snapshot.evidenceText: Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa said Wednesday that his country was entering a new phase of reconstruction and international engagement after years of war, while calling for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Syrian territory. Addressing the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, al-Sharaa said Syria was rebuilding diplomatic relations, seeking economic recovery and establishing new international partnerships while maintaining its sovereignty and independent decision-making. “Today, Syria is rising again, united once more,” al-Sharaa said, recalling his appearance at the U.N. General Assembly a year earlier. Al-Sharaa said nearly 100 countries had established channels of communication with Syria since what he described as the country's liberation, through thousands of meetings and diplomatic contacts. He said nearly 60 diplomatic missions were now operating in Damascus as foreign delegations returned to the country. The Syrian president also pointed to the repeal of the Caesar Act, the easing of European and British sanctions and the restoration of Syria's cooperation agreement with the European Union as evidence of a broader shift in the country's international relations. He said the removal of Syria's designation as a state sponsor of terrorism had also brought an end to what he described as decades of international isolation. Al-Sharaa linked the diplomatic opening to developments inside Syria, saying more than 3.5 million refugees and internally displaced Syrians had voluntarily returned to their homes. “Syria is transforming from a crisis into an opportunity for progress around which the international community can unite,” he said. The Syrian government has sought to present reconstruction, economic recovery and the return of displaced people as central elements of its postwar strategy. Earlier this week, al-Sharaa arrived in New York with a delegation including Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani to participate in the U.N. General Assembly. Al-Sharaa also highlighted Syria's cooperation with international organizations on chemical weapons and nuclear-related issues. He said 42 chemical bombs had been destroyed through an initiative involving Syria and seven other countries, while Damascus had restored its rights at the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. He added that Syria was cooperating with the International Atomic Energy Agency with what he described as the “utmost transparency.” The president also outlined efforts against organized crime and drug trafficking, saying Syrian authorities had seized approximately 700 million Captagon pills through more than 1,500 operations and dismantled 90 international criminal networks. He said the authorities were also working to combat human trafficking and other forms of organized crime. A major part of al-Sharaa's address focused on Israel and the Golan Heights. The Syrian president reaffirmed Damascus' position that the Golan Heights are Syrian territory and rejected measures aimed at changing its status. He cited U.N. Security Council Resolution 497, adopted in 1981, which declared Israel's decision to impose its laws, jurisdiction and administration on the occupied Syrian Golan “null and void” and without international legal effect. Al-Sharaa accused Israel of carrying out nearly 500 air and artillery strikes against Syria, more than 1,200 incursions and the detention of nearly 300 Syrians. He said the actions threatened Syria's stability and contradicted international efforts to support the country's recovery. “Our stated position remains unchanged,” al-Sharaa said, reaffirming Syria's commitment to the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement and calling for Israeli forces to withdraw to the lines of Dec. 8, 2024. The U.N. has continued to treat the Golan as occupied Syrian territory, while Security Council Resolution 497 remains a central international reference concerning Israel's 1981 annexation move. Al-Sharaa said Syria's priorities remained centered on state sovereignty, the rule of law and international law. He said attempts to impose new realities on the ground would not alter the authority of the Syrian state, while reconstruction and improving living conditions would remain at the heart of his government's approach. His remarks came as Damascus seeks to strengthen relations with foreign governments and international institutions while encouraging the return of Syrians displaced during years of conflict. Al-Sharaa said Syria's emerging international partnerships could help transform the country from a source of regional instability into a partner in economic recovery, development and regional cooperation. snapshot.title: Iraq to truck crude to Syria's Mediterranean coast from mid-October
snapshot.evidenceText: Iraqi crude is set to move overland to a Mediterranean port by lorry starting in mid-October, under a route Syria has agreed to provide, Bloomberg reported Friday. Yousef Qiblawy, chief executive of state-owned Syrian Petroleum, said the agreement between Baghdad and Damascus is almost complete and that exports should begin as soon as possible. Trucking crude is slower and costlier than tanker shipping, so the mid-October convoys read less as a commercial upgrade than as insurance: Iraq is building a second outlet for a revenue stream that is 90 per cent of the budget and almost entirely routed through one strait. The Baniyas fuel oil and petrol flows show the corridor already works in both directions. Watch whether the first truck convoys reach Syria by mid-October and whether Baghdad and Damascus formally sign the agreement. Also watch Kpler’s Gulf export averages and any move by the Iraqi Oil Tankers Company to purchase its own tankers. The day's top news and analysis, in your inbox every evening. You can unsubscribe at any time from any email.

snapshot.title: Iraq asks Syria to help export oil via its territory, bypassing Strait of Hormuz
snapshot.evidenceText: Fuel tankers carrying Iraqi oil arrive at the coastal storage facilities of the Baniyas Oil Terminal in Tartus province, Syria, on September 13, 2026. [Hasan Belal – Anadolu Agency] Iraq has directly asked Syria to help with oil exports, Bloomberg reported wednesday, citing sources. Syria is preparing to provide a secure route for Iraqi crude oil exports to avoid the Strait of Hormuz, “with a stream of trucks being lined up to haul oil overland to a port on the Mediterranean Sea,” the report said. The Iraqi government has asked Syria to help export crude oil as well as fuel, Syrian Petroleum Company CEO Yousef Qablawi told Bloomberg in an interview. “I expect the export of Iraqi crude via Syria by trucks to start as soon as possible as the deal between both governments is almost done,” Qiblawy said. “So, hopefully, by mid-October the first chain of trucks with crude will come to Syria,” he added. READ: Pro-Iran Iraqi factions say they are ‘not bound by any timeline or agreement’ on weapons Iraq already uses a fleet of trucks to transport some fuel to Syria’s Mediterranean port of Baniyas, where the shipments are transferred to tankers for onward export. Qablawi said about 1,000 trucks transport fuel each day, with each load carrying up to about 220 barrels. He expects the number of trucks used to transport crude oil to be similar or higher, given the large volume of Iraqi crude. The Syrian Petroleum Company plans to provide storage tanks for Iraqi crude at Baniyas port, allowing the shipments transported by road to be received and prepared for export. However, the quantities that can be transported by truck through Syria will remain limited compared with Iraq’s total crude exports, which averaged about 2.7 million barrels per day last month, according to Iraqi government data. representative.title: Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’? | Houthis News | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Al Jazeera Staff

snapshot.title: Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’?
snapshot.evidenceText: Fighting is intensifying between the Yemeni government forces and the rebel Houthi group. Fighting continues to intensify in Yemen as the internationally recognised government forces push a military offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, which controls part of the country. Speaking at the United Nations Security Council on Friday, the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, said the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”. Government forces are particularly looking to retake the important Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital trading chokepoint that has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks have all but halted shipping. At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations. More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in September, the UN’s migration agency (IOM), said. Fierce battles across several fronts have prompted concerns from rights groups that Yemen has essentially returned to civil war after the relative quiet brought by a 2022 ceasefire that followed a lengthy civil war which first erupted in 2014. Amid the US-Iran war, Yemen’s worst fighting in years threatens to destabilise the region further, experts say. Here’s what we know: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are advancing on the Houthis in a bid to recapture areas around the Bab al-Mandeb, a critical trade route for global shipping into and out of the Red Sea. Riyadh has increasingly relied on it for oil exports amid the US-Iran war, which has closed the Strait of Hormuz. On Sunday, the Yemeni government announced the start of the operation “Dawn of Yemen”, which aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa. On Saturday, it said it had conducted more than 2,750 precision strikes during military operations over the previous 24 hours, resulting in the “neutralisation” of more than 1,400 Houthi fighters. The spokesperson for the armed forces, Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, said in a statement carried by Saba news agency that the operations also targeted high-value military assets deep within Houthi-held territory. He added that ground forces “successfully” breached Houthi defences, recaptured operationally significant positions, secured their field gains and continued to advance the offensive according to operational plans. The Bab al-Mandeb strait emerged as yet another front in the US-Israel war on Iran when the Houthis declared a blockade on ships linked to Saudi Arabia in July. While the Houthis said that was in retaliation for ongoing Saudi blockades on Yemen, analysts viewed the move as calculated to provide more leverage for Iran amid on-and-off negotiations with the US – a close ally of Riyadh. Battles are now raging around the strategic southern cities of Mocha and Dubhab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of Bab al-Mandeb. The Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014, seized the area in September, effectively taking control of the strait, although both sides currently claim control of the shipping lanes. The Houthis, who have developed sophisticated weapons systems, including ballistic missiles, have also targeted Saudi Arabia with missile and drone attacks. On Friday, Saudi Arabia’s aviation authorities said three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, had been killed and several others wounded in Houthi strikes on the international airport in Riyadh – the first such deaths in the kingdom since fighting resumed. Several airlines suspended flights. The coalition forces also heavily bombarded Sanaa, on Friday, with several injuries reported, including a child. Both sides are also fighting to control Taiz. Civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis took control of Sanaa and imposed their own government in the capital. The seizure came amid dissatisfaction with the ruling government and following a revolution three years earlier. A coalition of armed forces and local armed groups backed by Saudi Arabia launched military operations and restored the internationally recognised government in Aden. Fighting resulted in the deaths of between 150,000 and 227,000 people, while millions were displaced. While the Houthis controlled much of the north, the Yemeni government controlled the southern regions. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 saw a lull in fighting and allowed aid to reach the deprived population, which has faced famine since 2016. In 2023, the Houthis, who form part of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” alliance of proxy armed groups, began disrupting shipping in the Red Sea in response to Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip. In March this year, the Houthis fired missiles at Israel amid the war on Iran, officially entering the US-Israel war with Iran which began in February. Tensions escalated when the group declared a naval blockade of Saudi ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July, shattering the relative calm in the country since 2022. It followed the announcement with a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back Yemeni coalition forces from the strategic port city. In September, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait. On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, leader of the Yemeni government’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced a military offensive to “restore state authority”. Analysts say the scale of fighting means Yemen has fallen back into civil war as both sides come under scrutiny for targeting civilians. As the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, declared that the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”, civilians, including women and children, are the ones bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”. The envoy stressed the need for the UNSC to support urgent mediation once more, although analysts have pointed out that recent gains by Yemeni government forces could mean they are more determined to push through the ongoing offensive, rather than agree to a settlement. But “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now”, Grundberg warned. Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, said: “It is beginning to resemble the 2015 Saudi-led coalition war on Yemen, when Sanaa and various other provinces were attacked relentlessly around the clock.” A number of sites in Sanaa have been targeted, he said, including Sanaa International Airport. Several industrial facilities, including a chips factory in the north and a sponge factory in the south, have also been hit. At least four telecommunications infrastructure sites have been struck in the capital and throughout areas controlled by the Houthi movement. Mount Attan in Sanaa was also hit by 10 air raids. Mawry reported that, according to Saudi coalition officials, strikes have destroyed 136 military targets in areas under Houthi control, including military sites, launch pads and radars belonging to the Houthi group. “Meanwhile, the Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of targeting public infrastructure and telecommunications facilities, warning that the campaign risks plunging the country back into a humanitarian crisis similar to the one experienced from 2015 to 2022,” Mawry said. The US, which has previously indicated that it does not want to get involved in the Yemen conflict, nevertheless on Friday called on the Houthis to stop attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, while demanding that Iran end its support for the group. Speaking at a UN Security Council meeting on Yemen, Jeff Bartos, the US ambassador to the UN for Management and Reform, said Washington was “gravely concerned” by the Houthis’ recent escalation, including attacks on civilian infrastructure and airports. “The pattern remains unmistakable. The Houthis act as instruments of Tehran to threaten freedom of navigation, undermine regional stability, and terrorise innocent civilians,” Bartos said. “We demand that the Houthis cease their attacks against the legitimate governments of Yemen and Saudi Arabia and we demand that Iran cease all support to the Houthis,” he added.

representative.title: Iran turns on Pakistan as Saudi defense pact takes effect | Iran International
representative.author: Maryam Sinaiee

snapshot.title: Iran turns on Pakistan as Saudi defense pact takes effect
snapshot.evidenceText: Iran has sharpened its criticism of a Saudi Arabia-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact after it became operational, warning against intervention in Yemen and questioning Pakistan’s role as a mediator between Tehran and Washington. The trilateral pact entered its operational phase on October 5 following an escalation in Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi infrastructure. Turkey and Pakistan said they had begun taking measures to support Saudi Arabia. Under arrangements discussed by the three countries, Pakistani and Turkish forces are expected to provide military, technical and intelligence support to Saudi Arabia, including defensive capabilities inside the kingdom. Officials have said the forces will not take part in offensive operations in Yemen. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, asked on Sunday about reports that tens of thousands of Pakistani troops could be deployed to Saudi Arabia, said: “We have also heard this rumor, and we hope it is not true.” “The countries of the region are well aware that any intervention in the Yemen issue could have undesirable consequences for the region,” he added, expressing hope that pacts such as the Mecca agreement would not be used “against the interests and welfare of the Muslim community.” The Saudi Arabia-Turkey-Pakistan defense pact, signed in August in Mecca, stipulates that an attack on any one of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all three. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, without directly referring to the pact, called on neighboring countries to pursue “self-reliance” and a policy based on “genuine brotherhood.” He also said such agreements would not constrain Iran. Several lawmakers dismissed the pact as largely symbolic. Ahmad Bakhshayesh, a member of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, called it a “paper and political pact.” Sharper criticism came from committee member Ebrahim Rezaei. “The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as years of one-sided milking of the Americans did not bring them security,” he wrote on X. “Correct your policies so that you do not have to beg others for security.” That tone has hardened as the pact has moved into its operational phase. Alaeddin Boroujerdi, a member of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said Thursday that Turkish and Pakistani involvement in the Saudi conflict with Ansarullah, as the Houthis are formally known, would neither weaken the group nor restrict its ability to operate in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. “The entry of Pakistan and Turkey will definitely work to their own detriment,” he told ISNA. “They should learn from history ... Saudi Arabia once had a coalition with a large number of countries, but after seven years of war in Yemen, it was defeated.” Iranian criticism has focused more heavily on Pakistan than Turkey, in large part because of Islamabad’s prominent role in mediating between Tehran and Washington. Lawmaker Ahmad Naderi wrote on X that “Pakistan’s entry alongside Saudi Arabia into the war against the people of Yemen … shows that Pakistan should no longer be considered a mediator but a regional intervenor.” The Tabnak news website went further, saying Iran viewed the deployment of Pakistani forces to Saudi Arabia as a threat to its security and “will not tolerate Pakistan’s military presence for military operations in the Yemen war.” It also warned that Pakistan’s increasingly overt alignment with Saudi Arabia could heighten sectarian tensions at home and bring instability to the Iranian-Pakistani border. Conservative commentator Hassan Hanizadeh similarly accused Saudi Arabia of seeking to create a religious divide, describing a recent meeting in Riyadh involving Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials as a sign of “the formation of a Shiite-Sunni polarization in the region.” Boroujerdi pointed to potential domestic opposition in Pakistan, saying its people were “revolutionary, Muslim and highly sensitive to such issues” and that Islamabad would not have an easy path if it entered the war. Iranian state media have adopted a more confrontational tone as the pact has become operational, while giving extensive coverage to warnings from Houthi officials directed at Turkey and Pakistan. Tasnim described the development as “Turkey and Pakistan join the Saudi war against the Yemeni people,” while Nour News, which is close to Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, asked: “Mecca alliance or alliance against the oppressed people of Yemen?!” In a Thursday commentary, Tasnim warned that if Ankara and Islamabad participate in attacks on Yemen, “they may be directly harmed through attacks on their ships, interests and perhaps even their own territory.” At least five Iranian military and police personnel were killed and several others wounded in four armed attacks across southeastern Iran within 24 hours, local rights group Haalvsh reported, as violence targeting security forces continued across the area. Haalvsh, which covers developments in Sistan and Baluchestan , said more than 12 personnel were killed or wounded overall between Wednesday evening and Thursday evening in Nikshahr, Nosratabad, Faryab and Jaleq, but cautioned that the final toll could be higher because some casualties had not yet been identified. The People's Fighters Front took responsibility for the attacks in Nikshahr, Nosratabad and Jaleq, according to Haalvsh. The alliance, announced in late 2025, includes several Baluch armed groups, among them Jaish al-Adl. The group had not taken responsibility for the killing in Faryab. In the Nikshahr area, Haalvsh said two vehicles carrying military personnel were attacked. Mohammadreza Okati was killed and five others were wounded, according to the outlet, which identified the wounded as Ali Najafi, Mohammadreza Hosseini, Mojtaba Mir and two others identified by the surnames Keikha and Iranmanesh. Haalvsh said those casualties were taken to Mohammad Rasoulallah Hospital in Nikshahr, while other wounded personnel were evacuated by helicopter to medical facilities in Chabahar, Konarak and Iranshahr. It said it had not established their number or identities. Iran's army separately confirmed on Thursday that Okati was killed when personnel from its 88th Armored Division came under fire while traveling for a shift change, but said three people were wounded. In the Nosratabad area near Zahedan, Haalvsh said at least three security personnel were killed and two wounded when gunmen attacked a police commando patrol on the Lakhshak road. It identified two of those reported killed as Vahid Enayat and Abbas Aghaei. Iranian police had earlier confirmed only Enayat's death, saying officers returned fire and that several attackers were wounded before fleeing. In Faryab, Haalvsh reported that Major Mehdi Jamshidi was shot dead while traveling in a private vehicle in the center of the county. The outlet said Jamshidi was struck by seven bullets. It also cited reports that he had been among police personnel present during a confrontation involving women and other protesters in the village of Pashmuki in June. The People's Fighters Front had not issued a statement taking responsibility for Jamshidi's killing, Haalvsh said. The fourth attack targeted the police command headquarters in Jaleq, the administrative center of Golshan County, on Wednesday evening. Haalvsh said the People's Fighters Front announced that its fighters had used a mine, rocket-propelled grenades and other weapons in the attack and said six police personnel were hit. Videos obtained by Haalvsh showed heavy gunfire around the facility and at least one support vehicle being targeted, according to the outlet. Haalvsh said it had not independently established the final number or identities of those killed or wounded. IranWire also reported an explosion and gunfire around the police facility. The latest incidents follow a series of attacks on Iranian security forces in the southeast. Earlier this week, gunmen attacked two military vehicles in Bampur, while last week a roadside attack near Zahedan and clashes in Rask and other areas produced further casualties. Official Iranian accounts and reports from Haalvsh have repeatedly differed over casualty numbers in recent attacks. Haalvsh said the toll from the four latest incidents should therefore be treated as provisional, particularly because some wounded personnel were transferred to hospitals outside the areas where the attacks occurred. Iraq has created a specialized unit within the Popular Mobilization Forces to take control of drones held by armed factions as part of Prime Minister Ali Faleh al-Zaidi’s plan to bring weapons under state authority, Erem News reported on Friday, citing an Iraqi security source. The source said three of the five factions covered by the plan had completed agreed handovers, but had not surrendered their entire arsenals. The process instead focused on heavy and specialized weapons and dismantling separate military headquarters. The Popular Mobilization Forces, which the report said formally operates under Iraq’s commander-in-chief, had received the weapons and military headquarters covered by the agreements. It had also begun integrating faction members and severing their previous political and administrative affiliations, according to the source. The new drone unit is intended to absorb the factions’ unmanned-aircraft capabilities into official state structures rather than leave them under independently run organizations, the source told Erem News. But the source stressed that the agreements “do not mean complete disarmament.” Instead, they involve transferring specialized weapons and reorganizing armed formations within the PMF. Erem News said effective control over those military capabilities would depend on completing the integration process and establishing the chain of command responsible for authorizing their use. The report did not identify the three factions that had completed the handover. A political source close to Iraq’s Coordination Framework told Erem News that the government was also seeking amendments to the law governing the PMF, including limiting the term of its chairman to two years and bringing professional officers from the regular military into senior posts. The proposal would directly affect the position of current PMF chairman Falih al-Fayyadh, according to the report. The source said the plan faced opposition within the Coordination Framework, particularly from Nouri al-Maliki’s State of Law coalition, which wanted any changes tied to a broader political agreement. Erem News said Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba remained opposed to surrendering their weapons, while other factions had accepted the principle of integration into state security institutions. Zaidi has set June 30, 2027, as the deadline for completing the weapons-control plan and has said decisions on war and peace belong exclusively to Iraq’s constitutional authorities. According to the political source, he has also told Coordination Framework leaders that he intends to continue implementing the plan even if political agreement on some of its details stalls. The source said Zaidi warned that failure by groups with armed wings to meet agreed commitments could expose Iraq to security, economic and political consequences, including additional sanctions or pressure, while adding that the prime minister still favored negotiations over a direct military confrontation with factions resisting the plan. US President Donald Trump said Thursday the United States would not attack Iran before the November 3 midterm elections and that "productive" talks were underway, after reports of US preparations for possible large-scale strikes. Trump said on Truth Social that Washington was having “productive discussions” with Iran and would not attack the country before the November 3 elections. He said, however, that the US blockade of Iranian ports would remain in place. Trump had made similar remarks ahead of previous military action against Iran. In June 2025, he said he would decide within two weeks whether the United States would join Israel’s war against Iran, citing a “substantial chance” of negotiations. US forces struck Iranian nuclear sites days later. Also days before the 2026 war, Trump said he preferred a diplomatic solution with Iran while also laying out the case for possible military action. The remarks offered the clearest timeline yet for a pause in renewed US strikes, while leaving open the possibility of military action after the elections. On the Iranian side, President Masoud Pezeshkian said during a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Tehran had not left the negotiating table and was working on its response to the latest US proposal. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi provided further detail Thursday, saying Iran had received Washington’s response to Tehran’s “seven-day plan” and was reviewing it. Araghchi said Tehran would deliver its response within the next few days and that messages continued to pass between Iran and the United States through mediators. The talks are continuing as Washington prepares for the possibility of renewed military action. Senior US officials told Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir earlier this week that the White House and Pentagon had instructed US forces to prepare for a possible large-scale attack on Iran within the next three weeks, Israel’s Channel 12 reported Thursday. The network cited a senior US official and another source briefed on the conversation. Zamir warned that an attack within that timeframe could lead to the postponement of Israel’s October 27 election, based on an assessment that Iran would respond with heavy missile fire against Israel. Trump’s pledge not to strike Iran before the US midterms appears to rule out that timeline, but does not remove the prospect of renewed military action after the November 3 vote. snapshot.title: Iran turns on Pakistan as Saudi defense pact takes effect
snapshot.evidenceText: Iran has sharpened its criticism of a Saudi Arabia-Pakistan-Turkey defense pact after it became operational, warning against intervention in Yemen and questioning Pakistan’s role as a mediator between Tehran and Washington. The trilateral pact entered its operational phase on October 5 following an escalation in Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi infrastructure. Turkey and Pakistan said they had begun taking measures to support Saudi Arabia. Under arrangements discussed by the three countries, Pakistani and Turkish forces are expected to provide military, technical and intelligence support to Saudi Arabia, including defensive capabilities inside the kingdom. Officials have said the forces will not take part in offensive operations in Yemen. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, asked on Sunday about reports that tens of thousands of Pakistani troops could be deployed to Saudi Arabia, said: “We have also heard this rumor, and we hope it is not true.” “The countries of the region are well aware that any intervention in the Yemen issue could have undesirable consequences for the region,” he added, expressing hope that pacts such as the Mecca agreement would not be used “against the interests and welfare of the Muslim community.” The Saudi Arabia-Turkey-Pakistan defense pact, signed in August in Mecca, stipulates that an attack on any one of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all three. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, without directly referring to the pact, called on neighboring countries to pursue “self-reliance” and a policy based on “genuine brotherhood.” He also said such agreements would not constrain Iran. Several lawmakers dismissed the pact as largely symbolic. Ahmad Bakhshayesh, a member of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Commission, called it a “paper and political pact.” Sharper criticism came from committee member Ebrahim Rezaei. “The Saudis should know that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as years of one-sided milking of the Americans did not bring them security,” he wrote on X. “Correct your policies so that you do not have to beg others for security.” That tone has hardened as the pact has moved into its operational phase. Alaeddin Boroujerdi, a member of parliament’s National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said Thursday that Turkish and Pakistani involvement in the Saudi conflict with Ansarullah, as the Houthis are formally known, would neither weaken the group nor restrict its ability to operate in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. “The entry of Pakistan and Turkey will definitely work to their own detriment,” he told ISNA. “They should learn from history ... Saudi Arabia once had a coalition with a large number of countries, but after seven years of war in Yemen, it was defeated.” Iranian criticism has focused more heavily on Pakistan than Turkey, in large part because of Islamabad’s prominent role in mediating between Tehran and Washington. Lawmaker Ahmad Naderi wrote on X that “Pakistan’s entry alongside Saudi Arabia into the war against the people of Yemen … shows that Pakistan should no longer be considered a mediator but a regional intervenor.” The Tabnak news website went further, saying Iran viewed the deployment of Pakistani forces to Saudi Arabia as a threat to its security and “will not tolerate Pakistan’s military presence for military operations in the Yemen war.” It also warned that Pakistan’s increasingly overt alignment with Saudi Arabia could heighten sectarian tensions at home and bring instability to the Iranian-Pakistani border. Conservative commentator Hassan Hanizadeh similarly accused Saudi Arabia of seeking to create a religious divide, describing a recent meeting in Riyadh involving Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish officials as a sign of “the formation of a Shiite-Sunni polarization in the region.” Boroujerdi pointed to potential domestic opposition in Pakistan, saying its people were “revolutionary, Muslim and highly sensitive to such issues” and that Islamabad would not have an easy path if it entered the war. Iranian state media have adopted a more confrontational tone as the pact has become operational, while giving extensive coverage to warnings from Houthi officials directed at Turkey and Pakistan. The People's Fighters Front took responsibility for the attacks in Nikshahr, Nosratabad and Jaleq, according to Haalvsh. The alliance, announced in late 2025, includes several Baluch armed groups, among them Jaish al-Adl. The group had not taken responsibility for the killing in Faryab. In the Nikshahr area, Haalvsh said two vehicles carrying military personnel were attacked. Mohammadreza Okati was killed and five others were wounded, according to the outlet, which identified the wounded as Ali Najafi, Mohammadreza Hosseini, Mojtaba Mir and two others identified by the surnames Keikha and Iranmanesh. Haalvsh said those casualties were taken to Mohammad Rasoulallah Hospital in Nikshahr, while other wounded personnel were evacuated by helicopter to medical facilities in Chabahar, Konarak and Iranshahr. It said it had not established their number or identities. Iran's army separately confirmed on Thursday that Okati was killed when personnel from its 88th Armored Division came under fire while traveling for a shift change, but said three people were wounded. In the Nosratabad area near Zahedan, Haalvsh said at least three security personnel were killed and two wounded when gunmen attacked a police commando patrol on the Lakhshak road. It identified two of those reported killed as Vahid Enayat and Abbas Aghaei. representative.title: The FE - Credible account of banks' undercapitalisation, fuel excise duty bind new lending
representative.author: Doulot Akter Mala

snapshot.title: Credible account of banks' undercapitalisation, fuel excise duty bind new lending
snapshot.evidenceText: Published by Syed Nasim Manzur for International Publications Limited from Tropicana Tower (4th ﬂoor), 45, Topkhana Road, GPO Box : 2526 Dhaka- 1000 and printed by him from The Transcraft Limited, 229, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dhaka-1208 PABX : 02223389780 (Hunting) | Mobile: 01917231083 | Fax : 880-2-02223387049 © 2026 - All Rights with The Financial Express About Us Contact Us Terms of Service Privacy Policy A new International Monetary Fund (IMF) lending programme for Bangladesh is set to be bound by strings like introducing excise duty on fuel and establishing credible estimates of banks' undercapitalisation. Officials have said preliminary discussions between the IMF and the Bangladesh government have identified several new conditions for the proposed US$4.5-billion loan programme spanning three years. A delegation led by Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury will attend the seven-day IMF-World Bank annual meetings beginning Monday in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, when a decisive discussion is likely to take place on the sidelines. The proposed conditionalities were recently shared with the Ministry of Finance, following several virtual meetings based on the IMF staff's visit in July, its January Article IV staff report and discussions during the spring meetings. Detailed discussions on the new loan programme will be held with IMF representatives in Bangkok. Senior officials from the Finance Division, Financial Institutions Division, Bangladesh Bank and the National Board of Revenue (NBR) will join the meetings. Officials familiar with the developments and involved in the process of reviewing observations from the last scoping missions in July said the IMF was serious about conducting a system-wide assessment of banks and preparing bank-specific resolution plans. The multilateral lender has asked Bangladesh not to rely primarily on the recovery of non-performing loans (NPLs) as a source of funding for bank resolution. It has also sought clarification on the scope and modalities of fiscal support and burden-sharing, subsidy reductions, and the phased withdrawal of all tax exemptions. Bangladesh needs to provide a realistic, time-bound implementation plan for the reforms recommended by the IMF, the officials said. A major emphasis under the proposed credit programme is on conducting a time-bound Asset Quality Review (AQR) of banks, they added. The IMF has sought AQR findings as the primary basis for determining recapitalisation needs and bank-resolution costs. Its staff has requested Bangladesh to complete a comprehensive triage of all banks and share the results with the Fund. The IMF has proposed classifying banks into three categories based on their viability: viable banks without solvency concerns, viable but undercapitalised banks, and non-viable or insolvent banks. For all weak and non-viable banks, the IMF has sought bank-specific resolution strategies based on the least-cost principle. These would determine the appropriate allocation of losses, recapitalisation needs, fiscal -support requirements and implementation timelines for each bank. It has also sought a detailed assessment of merged banks, including how they will restore capital adequacy, absorb losses and ultimately eliminate their reliance on central-bank support. On fiscal measures, the IMF's recent technical assistance (TA) recommendations include overhauling the existing tax system to broaden the tax base, modernising excise duties on tobacco and introducing excise duty on fuel. Similar to the previous loan programme, which the present government decided not to continue, the IMF has recommended repealing statutory regulatory orders (SROs) providing tax and VAT exemptions, market-based exchange rate, increasing tax-to-GDP ratio and introducing a standard 15-percent VAT rate. The IMF has also reiterated the need to continue the automatic fuel-pricing mechanism, cut fertiliser subsidies and reduce excessive reliance on withholding taxes for revenue mobilisation. Earlier, on January 30, 2023, the IMF approved a $4.7-billion loan arrangement for Bangladesh. The then Awami League government had sought the assistance through a letter sent in July 2022. Of the seven instalments under that arrangement, $3.64 billion had been disbursed in five instalments. During the interim government, the size of the loan programme was increased by $800 million to $5.5 billion in June 2025. However, the current government was not interested in continuing with the programme because of changing economic challenges and stringent conditions. It informed the IMF of its position during the IMF-World Bank spring meetings in April this year. On June 3, the government formally sent a letter seeking a new loan programme. The IMF subsequently welcomed the move in a press release. Zahid Hussain, former lead economist at the World Bank's Dhaka office, told the FE that the government had not continued the automatic fuel-pricing mechanism and other reform measures recommended by the IMF. He thinks the conditionalities under the new programme would remain largely similar, focusing on revenue mobilisation and banking-sector reforms. *Regarding energy subsidies, Bangladesh might be able to convince the IMF to consider the country's current circumstances," he said, adding that banking-sector reform would be the main point of discussion. He has noted that the AQR process had made little progress and should be conducted by reputed audit firms. Under the previous lending package, Bangladesh was supposed to receive the full $5.5 billion in instalments by 2027. The IMF had also set deadlines for completing specific reforms as conditions for releasing the instalments. However, many of the reforms missed completion timelines.

snapshot.title: Bangladesh to do feasibility study on its own
snapshot.evidenceText: FHM HUMAYAN KABIR | October 10, 2026 00:00:00 Bangladesh is set to conduct feasibility study on the long-stalled Teesta river-management project on its own to avoid any external meddling and get a better way of managing the cross-border water basin, officials said. Since the proposed Teesta project is a geopolitically sensitive one, the Bangladesh government wants to conduct the feasibility study with its own funds for finding out viability and justification for the water-management project, they added. "There some geopolitical issues involved in the Teesta river-management project. This time, the government itself wants to go for the feasibility," a senior official of the Ministry of Water Resources told The Financial Express. Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB) has recently undertaken a Tk 233.40-million project for feasibility study and sent to the Planning Commission (PC) for approval. "We have undertaken the feasibility-study project before going to develop the water-management system and river-restoration programme in the Teesta basin," said a senior BWDB official. The proposed project for development of the river waters will cover five northern districts--Nilphamari, Lalmonirhat, Rangpur, Kurigram and Gaibandha. Bangladesh has a stretch of 120-km water flow out of the total 315 kilometres in the Bangladesh-India cross-border Teesta River. The river originated in Sikkim, India. The project is among the most closely watched infrastructure initiatives in the country, and it has drawn interest from major regional and global powers. The past interim government last year sent a Preliminary Development Project Proposal (PDPP) to Chinese seeking necessary funds for the 1st phase of the "Teesta River Comprehensive Management and Restoration Project (TRCMRP)". The government wanted to start project works in January next and complete the first phase within four years. It ultimately didn't proceed and the current BNP-led government now prepared the feasibility-study project for a better start-off. Meanwhile, during Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's visit to China in June last, the two countries advanced cooperation on the Teesta project, including a new feasibility-study effort. Besides, nearly a decade ago in September 2016, a memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed between BWDB and China's state-owned Power Construction Corporation (Power China). But that project didn't advance either due to "shifting geopolitical circumstances". Water resources ministry officials have said the fresh study would be crucial to taking the plan toward implementation, and that it would determine the precise locations and scope of the proposed works. They stress that this is not the end of the planning stage. Environmental-impact assessment, final design, government approval, financing and field-level implementation would have to be done after the feasibility study. According to the feasibility-study project proposal, the BWDB would conduct the study between October 2026 and March 2028. Under the component-1 of the study project, the Board will analyse river erosion, flood, sedimentation and water-scarcity problem, and will develop "adaptive, integrated and sustainable plan". In the componenent-2, the water development board will develop high-quality and scaled physical model representing the Teesta River focusing area under realistic hydrodynamics and sediment-transport condition, and prepare detailed data-sheet to support calibration, validation and performance evaluation of the models. The Teesta originates in the Himalayas, flows through Sikkim and West Bengal and enters northern Bangladesh before falling into the Jamuna River. Bangladesh's section of the river supports irrigation, agriculture, fisheries and the livelihoods of communities in the Rangpur region. The proposed TRCMRP aims to manage the river as a basin-wide infrastructure and restoration project, with several objectives like reducing riverbank erosion and monsoon flooding, dredging sediment and improving river-channel management, storing and managing water to help address dry-season shortages. Also, the project aims to reclaim land for agriculture and other economic activities; improve embankments, transport links and river access, restore the river ecosystem, and support communities along its banks. The Teesta plan comes as the government commits heavily to water infrastructure. It recently approved the first phase of the Padma Barrage project, worth over Tk 330 billion. Bangladesh and India have negotiated a proposed interim water-sharing agreement for years. A draft was finalised in 2011, but it was not signed. India's federal and state-level political considerations, including the position of West Bengal, have been major obstacles to reaching agreement. In their September 2022 joint statement, the two countries reiterated the need to work towards a Teesta water-sharing agreement. India's official position has also referred to reaching an equitable agreement acceptable to all stakeholders. The central issue is seasonal water availability. Bangladesh needs sufficient dry-season flow for irrigation and livelihoods, while farmers and water users in India's West Bengal also depend on the river. representative.title: Govt in talks with Singapore's PSA to operate more Ctg Port terminals: Minister | The Business Standard
representative.author: TBS Report

snapshot.title: Govt in talks with Singapore's PSA to operate more Ctg Port terminals: Minister
snapshot.evidenceText: The government is in talks with more leading global port operators, including Singapore-based PSA International, to operate container terminals at Chattogram Port as part of efforts to modernise port management and increase handling capacity, Shipping Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam has said. "The government has already taken steps to bring APM Terminals into the operation of the Laldia Terminal, while discussions with PSA and other leading operators are ongoing," the minister said at a press conference following the signing of an agreement with Dubai-based global port operator DP World to operate and manage the New Mooring Container Terminal (NCT) at Chattogram Port. The signing ceremony was held at Invest Bangladesh's office in Dhaka's Agargaon. "Chattogram Port has several terminals. We have already been able to bring APM Terminals into the Laldia Terminal project. APM is one of the world's top five container terminal operators. DP World is also among the top five. Betterminal and Singapore's PSA are also among the leading five operators. Discussions with them are ongoing. We hope to reach agreements with them as soon as possible," he added. The minister also said, "Of the world's top five companies, we have been able to bring three into the operation of different container terminals at Chattogram Port. This means Bangladesh's port management and container handling are becoming modern and moving closer to international standards. This is a major achievement." According to its website, PSA Singapore is one of the flagship terminals of PSA International, a leading port group with a global network spanning 179 locations across 45 countries. 15-year agreement, investment of over Tk1,000 crore Under the agreement, DP World will operate and manage NCT for 15 years. However, ownership and control of the terminal's land and infrastructure will remain with the Chittagong Port Authority (CPA), the minister said. DP World will pay an upfront fee of around Tk600 crore at the beginning of the contract. The company has also committed to investing more than Tk1,000 crore in the terminal's modernisation, equipment and technology during the first 10 years, he added. The agreement includes financial penalties if the company fails to meet its targets. The CPA will receive a share of the terminal's operating revenue as well as a fixed annual fee. According to the minister, DP World will pay the CPA 67% of the revenue from container handling per twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU). Container dwell time targeted to fall to 3-4 days The government plans to introduce paperless operations at Chattogram Port to improve efficiency and reduce delays, the minister said. The average container dwell time at the port is currently around 9.4 days. The government aims to reduce it to three to four days. "Modern terminals can clear containers within one to three days. Bangladesh will also move towards that standard. If we can bring dwell time down from 9.4 days to three or four days, our trade and commerce will expand significantly," he said. The minister added that a ship currently takes around two and a half to three days to unload its containers and leave the port. The government expects this turnaround time to fall further following the agreement with DP World. Chattogram Port handles 92% of Bangladesh's trade Highlighting the port's importance to the national economy, Shaikh Rabiul Alam said around 92% of Bangladesh's imports and exports pass through Chattogram Port. "Considering the national interest, we are working to make the port more modern and expand its capacity to support economic prosperity. That is why we have taken the initiative to hand over responsibility for modernising NCT's operations and management to DP World through this agreement," he said. Explaining the decision to select DP World, the minister said the company is one of the world's top five container terminal operators and operates around 80 container terminals in nearly 70 countries. Asked when DP World would begin operations, he said the company would take over responsibility as soon as possible. "The terminal will require some modernisation and upgrades in both its digital and manual management systems. I believe these tasks can be completed within six months, allowing the company to begin operations according to its own system. We expect it to operate at full capacity within one to two years," he said. The government has set an annual container-handling target of 1.23 million TEUs for the terminal. With improvements in DP World's operational capacity, the figure could rise to 1.6 million to 1.8 million TEUs, significantly increasing government revenue, he added. Asked whether Bangladeshi laws would apply under the agreement, the minister said all relevant laws would remain in force. "All laws of Bangladesh will apply. The laws governing ports will remain effective. If any deviation or irregularity occurs, the port authority and the government will be able to take the necessary decisions," he said. Minister acknowledges concerns over agreement Responding to concerns raised by different groups over the agreement, the minister described the debate as part of democracy. "This is part of the beauty of democracy. Those who attended the event included various port stakeholders, and we have held discussions with them. Some may be concerned about losing their jobs or their authority and control. We respect their views, and the government takes their opinions into account," he said. He claimed that around 250 container terminals worldwide are operated by four major companies, with international operators managing approximately 80% of them. "This does not mean that the countries concerned lose ownership or overall authority. Rather, it increases competition and operational efficiency," he said. Asked whether paperless operations would reduce harassment by customs officials, the minister said automation would limit manual intervention in container handling. "Customs is responsible for collecting taxes and completing the related procedures. Once container operations become automated, there will be fewer opportunities for customs officials to hold up containers or intervene manually," he said. Bangladesh targets $10bn trade with UAE by 2030 The minister also highlighted Bangladesh's plans to strengthen economic ties with the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Bangladesh receives around $4.5 billion in remittances annually from the UAE, while bilateral trade between the two countries stands at approximately $2 billion, he said. "Our goal is to increase bilateral trade to $10 billion by 2030," he added. Describing the DP World agreement as an important step towards economic progress, Shaikh Rabiul Alam said the signing marked the beginning of further improvements in the country's economic management. "Today marks the beginning of a good day. We have completed an important step in our journey towards ensuring a better economic framework for the country," he said. Addressing the business community, he urged stakeholders to trust the government's efforts. "Have confidence in the work being done by the state and the government. We are working to fulfil the aspirations and expectations of the business community," he said. CPA Chairman Rear Admiral Mohammad Moniruzzaman signed the agreement on behalf of the port authority, while Essa Kazim, chairman of DP World's board of directors, signed on behalf of the company. Shipping State Minister Md Rajib Ahsan, UAE Ambassador to Bangladesh Abdullah Ali Al Hamoudi and Invest Bangladesh Chairman Chowdhury Ashik Mahmud Bin Harun, among others, attended the ceremony. representative.title: Jubilee, ENI Partners Pledge $3.5bn for Ghana Oil Sector
representative.author: Kwame Darko

snapshot.title: Jubilee, ENI Partners Pledge $3.5bn for Ghana Oil Sector
snapshot.evidenceText: Jubilee and ENI partners have pledged a combined $3.5 billion to Ghana's offshore oil fields, including funding for 20 new wells, in what officials describe as the strongest sign yet of renewed investor confidence. Ghana's upstream oil industry has received a major financial vote of confidence, with international partners operating the Jubilee and ENI fields announcing combined investment commitments of $3.5 billion. The figure was disclosed by Simon Madjie, Chief Executive Officer of the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority (GIPA), during an appearance on Joy News' PM Express Business Edition, according to MyJoyOnline. Of the total, the Jubilee partners — operating through Cosmos and Co. — have committed $2 billion to drill 20 new wells in the Jubilee field, one of Ghana's flagship offshore oil developments. Separately, ENI and its partners announced a $1.5 billion investment, though Madjie did not disclose specific details of what that funding would cover. Madjie pointed to the announcements as proof of growing activity in a sector that has grappled with underinvestment in recent years, with Ghana's crude oil production having declined from peak levels recorded in earlier years. He also cited other signs of renewed interest, including a memorandum of understanding signed by Chevron and Shell at Africa Oil Week to explore opportunities in the Eastern Keta Basin, and reported interest from Brazilian firm Petrobras in available Ghanaian oil blocks and acreages. When asked about ExxonMobil's potential return to Ghana's oil sector, Madjie confirmed that discussions had taken place but declined to provide further details, saying such disclosures were best left to the Minister of Energy and Petroleum Commission. He similarly directed questions about the technical scope of the Jubilee and ENI investments to the Petroleum Commission and the Ministry of Energy, saying those bodies were better placed to provide further specifics. The fresh investment pledges come against the backdrop of years of legal and fiscal disputes in Ghana's oil industry. Among them was a tax arbitration case involving Tullow Ghana, which was settled in the government's favour in September 2026. That dispute, along with broader declines in output from Ghana's major oil fields, had raised concerns about the attractiveness of the country's upstream sector to international investors. For ordinary Ghanaians, renewed drilling activity in the Jubilee field and fresh commitments from ENI could translate into more jobs in the oil and gas supply chain, increased drilling and support-vessel activity offshore, and potentially higher government revenue through royalties and taxes once new wells come online. Ghana's petroleum revenues have historically funded parts of the national budget, including infrastructure and social programmes, making any boost to production relevant to public finances. The sources did not provide a timeline for when drilling on the 20 new Jubilee wells would begin or when ENI's $1.5 billion investment would be deployed. Madjie referred further technical and scheduling questions to the Petroleum Commission and the Ministry of Energy and Petroleum, neither of which has yet issued a public statement detailing project timelines, according to the available reporting. The Ghana Investment Promotion Authority (GIPA) is the government agency responsible for promoting and facilitating both domestic and foreign investment into Ghana. The Jubilee field is one of Ghana's largest offshore oil discoveries, located in the deepwater Tano Basin, and has been a cornerstone of the country's oil production since it began producing in 2010. ENI is an Italian multinational energy company that operates the Sankofa oil and gas fields off Ghana's coast. At seven feet tall, Ephraim Saawa gets stopped for photos on the streets of Amanfro and Kasoa. He wants Ghanaians to one day stop him for a different reason — wearing the national basketball jersey. representative.title: US seeks changes to rejected $109m health compact with Ghana - Mahama - MyJoyOnline
representative.author: Emma Ankrah

snapshot.title: US seeks changes to rejected $109m health compact with Ghana - Mahama - MyJoyOnline
snapshot.evidenceText: The United States is seeking to revise its proposed $109 million health compact with Ghana, including amending or removing clauses that led to its rejection by Cabinet, President John Mahama has disclosed. Speaking at a citizens’ engagement in Goaso in the Ahafo Region, the President said the US government has requested further discussions on the agreement “The health compact the Americans brought to us, I have talked about it when I was in New York, so everyone knows about it. Later, they came back and said they wanted us to sit down and discuss the clauses we object to in the compact, with a view to either amending or removing them. We will sit down with them and discuss,” he said Ghana rejected the proposed agreement after raising concerns about provisions relating to sensitive health information, national sovereignty, counterpart funding and the regulatory authority of the Food and Drugs Authority (FDA). The proposed compact was intended to provide approximately $109 million in US health assistance over five years, replacing some funding previously received through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). At a dialogue hosted by the Council on Foreign Relations in New York on September 25, 2026, President Mahama explained why Cabinet rejected the proposed compact. He said Ghana had followed its established procedures, with the Ministry of Health reviewing the document and submitting an information paper to Cabinet. The review identified provisions the government considered problematic. One major concern was a requirement for Ghana to provide the United States with its pathogen profile, which contains information about disease-causing organisms circulating in the country. The President also objected to provisions he said required Ghana to share medical records. “It states that we shall give the United States our pathogen profile. I’m sure there are medical experts who understand that better than me. And it also says we should give our medical records. I mean, who takes another country’s medical records?” he asked. President Mahama further said the agreement required Ghana to commit its own funds to the programme while restricting the FDA’s authority to inspect medicines and other medical products brought into the country under the arrangement. Describing the conditions, he said, “I mean, it was humiliating.” He added that Cabinet rejected the agreement with government deciding it would not proceed with it under the proposed terms.

representative.title: BRICS Or Balance? What Ghana’s bid really means - MyJoyOnline
representative.author: Emmanuel Tetteh

snapshot.title: BRICS Or Balance? What Ghana’s bid really means - MyJoyOnline
snapshot.evidenceText: Ghana’s decision to apply to join BRICS is not a diplomatic footnote; it is a strategic signal. On October 6, 2026, Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa announced that Cabinet had decided to pursue membership, saying the objective was to diversify partnerships, widen economic opportunities and deepen cooperation with the Global South. .India, whose foreign minister was visiting Accra, has been approached to help Ghana navigate the application. The World Bank puts Ghana’s 2025 GDP at $114.2 billion, with 6.0 percent growth, while its population stands at 35.1 million. Ghana is not a great power seeking to rewrite the international system or dictate the rules of global commerce. It is a middle-sized African state seeking more room to manoeuvre within it. BRICS has grown considerably beyond the original Brazil-Russia-India-China grouping. Its current membership comprises 11 states, representing about 49 percent of the world’s population, 39 percent of global GDP and 23 percent of international trade. Its expanding economic and geopolitical weight offers Accra a platform for trade, investment and diplomatic coalition-building. Membership could provide another channel for engaging major emerging economies, reducing excessive dependence on traditional Western partners and broadening Ghana’s strategic options. The attraction is not ideological alignment with every member, but the opportunity to operate in a wider economic and diplomatic ecosystem as global power becomes more dispersed. Membership, however, is not automatic. Ghana has announced a bid, not secured a seat. BRICS says accession moves from formal interest to potential membership and then full membership, with Sherpas, foreign ministers and ultimately leaders deciding by consensus. Accra must demonstrate that its application can win political support from members. The bid is therefore the opening move in a consequential geopolitical negotiation, not a guaranteed victory. The test is whether Ghana can convert its interest into gains without damaging longstanding relationships with the United States, European Union and other Western partners. Ghana already trades heavily with BRICS economies, China and India. Ghana-China trade reached a record $14.1 billion in 2025, up 19.3 percent. In 2024, China supplied 45.9 percent of Ghana’s imports from Asia, while India supplied 13.7 percent. This concentration creates opportunity and vulnerability. A formal BRICS relationship could help Ghana move beyond buying manufactured goods and exporting raw commodities, supporting investment in processing, infrastructure, digital technology, energy and transport. The New Development Bank makes the prospect relevant. It has $52.7 billion in paid-in capital and supports development projects across member countries. For a country seeking infrastructure and industrial financing, engagement with the BRICS ecosystem could open additional channels of capital and development cooperation. But BRICS cannot substitute for economic reform. Ghana’s debt problems, currency risks, productivity constraints and dependence on commodities will not disappear because Accra sits at the table. Diplomatic access is not guaranteed investment, and every proposed project must still meet Ghana’s needs, affordability tests and transparency standards. Ghana could use closer ties with China, India, Brazil, the Gulf and other emerging economies to negotiate from a broader base with Western partners. The objective should not be to replace one sphere of dependence with another, but to expand Ghana’s room for manoeuvre. Membership can strengthen that position if Accra treats it as an instrument of diversification and strategic autonomy. BRICS is not a military alliance and offers no Article 5-style collective-defence commitment. Its significance is political: it provides a forum for coordinating positions on global governance, sanctions, development and the international order. Joining would not give Ghana a BRICS security guarantee against jihadist violence spilling south from the Sahel, maritime insecurity in the Gulf of Guinea or cyber threats. Ghana’s existing Western security relationships remain substantial. In August 2026, the Defence Ministry said US cooperation included joint exercises, intelligence sharing, counter-terrorism support, maritime security and plans involving drone-based intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. In September, Ghana reaffirmed its defence and security partnership with Washington, including logistics, institutional development, peacekeeping, cyber defence and maritime security. Strategic balance is essential. Accra should not allow BRICS membership to undermine interoperability with the United States, European partners or African security institutions. The objective should be diversification rather than substitution: add partnerships, markets and diplomatic options without trading one dependency for another. The deeper consequence is diplomatic. Ghana’s bid would place it more visibly in the debate over whether the international system should remain predominantly Western-led or become more plural and representative. BRICS says it seeks stronger Global South participation and reform of global governance. A stronger voice within Global South coalitions could reinforce its calls to reform institutions whose voting structures often lag behind economic realities. But autonomy has a cost. BRICS includes China and Russia, whose relations with the United States and its allies are marked by strategic rivalry and, in Russia’s case, war-related sanctions. Ghana may face pressure to clarify positions on sanctions, conflicts, technology standards and contested international norms. BRICS criteria emphasize good relations among members, support for governance reform and, for partners, avoiding unilateral sanctions not authorized by the UN Security Council. Accra must be disciplined. Ghana should join only if it can preserve what has made its foreign policy effective: flexibility, credibility and the ability to work across competing blocs. The objective is strategic autonomy, not bloc politics. The smartest policy is conditional engagement. Ghana should seek market access, investment, technology, development finance and diplomatic leverage from BRICS while maintaining US and European security partnerships, ECOWAS commitments and wider African obligations. The test is simple: does membership expand Ghana’s choices? If yes, the bid is strategically sound. If it merely replaces one external dependence with another, it is not diversification; it is dependency under a different flag. Ghana’s geopolitical asset is not allegiance, but room to manoeuvre as rival powers compete for influence. It is trying to ensure that, in an increasingly fractured world, it has enough partners to choose for itself. — The writer is a lecturer in journalism and media studies and the CEO of The International Lens (theinternationallens.com).

representative.title: Prime Minister Carney announces landmark investment to retrofit one million homes, cutting energy costs and emissions - Canada.ca
representative.author: Environment, Climate Change Canada

snapshot.title: Prime Minister Carney announces landmark investment to retrofit one million homes, cutting energy costs and emissions - Canada.ca
snapshot.evidenceText: The Government of Canada is investing $2 billion over eight years to deliver one million home retrofits to lower energy costs for Canadians and reduce emissions. The Government of Canada is investing $2 billion over eight years to deliver one million home retrofits to lower energy costs for Canadians and reduce emissions. At the same time, we are doubling our grid, giving Canadians access to more affordable, reliable, and cleaner electricity than ever before. This $2 billion investment, over eight years, will provide easy-to-access rebates to up to 820,000 homeowners installing eligible electric cold climate air source heat pumps. Homeowners can apply quickly for the Rebate when their existing heating system breaks down and they decide to replace it with a new heat pump system. They can also apply as their existing heating system approaches end of life, and they want to make the transition before a breakdown occurs. The Government of Canada will work with HVAC installers on the rollout of this program to maximize its effectiveness and reach as many eligible Canadians as possible. Consultations with industry will begin immediately following the program announcement. The government will engage key industry partners regarding program details and ensure installers are equipped to act as champions for this program. The government will also work with technical colleges and industry associations on certifications, and support upskilling and growth of the workforce. The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) will help rental housing providers access private financing from approved lenders on more favourable terms to undertake energy-efficiency retrofits in existing rental buildings. These investments can improve building quality and energy performance for tenants while reducing energy use. Operating through CMHC’s existing mortgage loan insurance framework, the initiative will leverage private capital, rather than relying on new direct government spending. CMHC receives insurance premiums and fees for the coverage, typically paid by borrowers, such that the product is delivered at no cost to taxpayers. Through this initiative, CMHC is expected to support retrofits in up to 250,000 rental housing units over the next eight years. This Canada Infrastructure Bank (CIB) initiative will target up to an additional 30,000 residential units in Multi-Unit Residential Buildings (MURBs), by mobilizing more private sector investment in building retrofits. The CIB will leverage its existing government allocation, meaning no new funding is required from the federal government. The Government of Canada will invest nearly $110 million over three years starting in 2027-28 to renew the Deep Retrofit Accelerator Initiative. This initiative funds third-party accelerators that help building owners tackle complex retrofits by guiding them from planning through to implementation. These accelerators also help build a knowledgeable and innovative retrofit sector, through training activities, to meet growing demand and to maximize energy and cost savings for building residents. The Deep Retrofit Accelerator Initiative builds a pipeline of projects for new retrofit financing, including through the Canada Infrastructure Bank and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and ensures that investment dollars go as far as they can go.
