representative.title: In parched Hungary, volunteers build their own dams to hold onto vanishing water
representative.author: Marton Monus, Krisztina Than

snapshot.title: In parched Hungary, volunteers build their own dams to hold onto vanishing water
snapshot.evidenceText: LADANY-VOLGY, Hungary – In a bone-dry valley in Hungary, forest workers and volunteers piled up terraces of logs and deadwood, hoping to catch any trickles of water that make it down the hillside when the rains finally come. In other areas, groups fanned out, building barriers across streams and small creeks – their own man-made “beaver dams” designed to pool water and prepare the landscape for an even hotter, drier future. As of this week, they were still waiting for that rain after a drought-hit summer that brought river levels to record lows, disrupting everything from cargo barges to the country’s Paks nuclear plant, which relies on flows of cooling water from the Danube. But the teams working under the banner of the grassroots, volunteer “Water Guardians Movement” kept on building, getting ready. “The wells (on my farm) have practically run dry,” said Bence Bardos, a forest engineer leading the team building terraces in the Ladany valley in eastern Hungary near the border with Slovakia. “This is the impact from climate change and our special geography in the Carpathian basin.” There was little locals could do about that, he said. “But we can improve the situation by small steps, by reversing the water runoff and drainage,” the 36-year-old added. The volunteers are turning out in the hundreds to help the country build structures to retain rainwater and restore wetlands – techniques that mark a sharp turnaround from the past, when programs focused on managing floods, not droughts. Nearly a quarter of the country lies on floodplains, and experts spent decades draining wetlands and building canals to channel water away from the fields and open up more land for agriculture. “We have regulated our rivers, cutting their bends, which means the rivers flow faster, which drains ground water nearby,” Diana Ürge-Vorsatz, a professor at the Central European University in Vienna, said. Much of that now needed to go into reverse. The important thing now was to “restore the original natural conditions as much as possible, to allow rivers to flow on longer routes and thus slower, and retain ground water in the winter-spring,” Ürge-Vorsatz added. The government announced a new strategy in August which prioritized “natural water retention methods” and, far from draining fields, said some farmland should be deliberately flooded. Agriculture, one of the planks of Hungary’s economy, has borne the brunt of the drier conditions. Many farmers have given up on maize and shifted to alternatives, as researchers work on drought-resistant varieties. This was the first year when the harvested area of maize in Hungary fell below the area planted with sunflowers, said Zoltan Kende, associate professor at the Institute of Agronomy at the MATE University. But even sunflowers have suffered from the drought. “We have shown that dry weather alters the fatty acid composition of sunflowers, resulting in a change in oil quality,” Kende added. Researchers could not “perform a rain dance” but there were recommendations they could make on cultivation and other methods to help adaptation, he said. “For each cultivated plant species, we investigate the optimal factors as for temperature, moisture … that result in the fastest germination. This approach helps enhance resilience against drought damage.” Hungary’s central bank has said the drought damage to agriculture would cut economic growth by 0.4 percentage points in 2026. representative.title: In parched Hungary, volunteers build their own dams to hold onto vanishing water
representative.author: Marton Monus, Krisztina Than

snapshot.title: In parched Hungary, volunteers build their own dams to hold onto vanishing water
snapshot.evidenceText: LADANY-VOLGY, Hungary – In a bone-dry valley in Hungary, forest workers and volunteers piled up terraces of logs and deadwood, hoping to catch any trickles of water that make it down the hillside when the rains finally come. In other areas, groups fanned out, building barriers across streams and small creeks – their own man-made “beaver dams” designed to pool water and prepare the landscape for an even hotter, drier future. As of this week, they were still waiting for that rain after a drought-hit summer that brought river levels to record lows, disrupting everything from cargo barges to the country’s Paks nuclear plant, which relies on flows of cooling water from the Danube. But the teams working under the banner of the grassroots, volunteer “Water Guardians Movement” kept on building, getting ready. “The wells (on my farm) have practically run dry,” said Bence Bardos, a forest engineer leading the team building terraces in the Ladany valley in eastern Hungary near the border with Slovakia. “This is the impact from climate change and our special geography in the Carpathian basin.” There was little locals could do about that, he said. “But we can improve the situation by small steps, by reversing the water runoff and drainage,” the 36-year-old added. The volunteers are turning out in the hundreds to help the country build structures to retain rainwater and restore wetlands – techniques that mark a sharp turnaround from the past, when programs focused on managing floods, not droughts. Nearly a quarter of the country lies on floodplains, and experts spent decades draining wetlands and building canals to channel water away from the fields and open up more land for agriculture. “We have regulated our rivers, cutting their bends, which means the rivers flow faster, which drains ground water nearby,” Diana Ürge-Vorsatz, a professor at the Central European University in Vienna, said. Much of that now needed to go into reverse. The important thing now was to “restore the original natural conditions as much as possible, to allow rivers to flow on longer routes and thus slower, and retain ground water in the winter-spring,” Ürge-Vorsatz added. The government announced a new strategy in August which prioritized “natural water retention methods” and, far from draining fields, said some farmland should be deliberately flooded. Agriculture, one of the planks of Hungary’s economy, has borne the brunt of the drier conditions. Many farmers have given up on maize and shifted to alternatives, as researchers work on drought-resistant varieties. This was the first year when the harvested area of maize in Hungary fell below the area planted with sunflowers, said Zoltan Kende, associate professor at the Institute of Agronomy at the MATE University. But even sunflowers have suffered from the drought. “We have shown that dry weather alters the fatty acid composition of sunflowers, resulting in a change in oil quality,” Kende added. Researchers could not “perform a rain dance” but there were recommendations they could make on cultivation and other methods to help adaptation, he said. “For each cultivated plant species, we investigate the optimal factors as for temperature, moisture … that result in the fastest germination. This approach helps enhance resilience against drought damage.” Hungary’s central bank has said the drought damage to agriculture would cut economic growth by 0.4 percentage points in 2026. The challenges were already there to see as the volunteers worked on the slopes of Ladany valley. Borbala Kanizsay, who was there with her husband, said the creek that ran past their nearby house ran dry in May for the first time she could remember. Most of her parched trees shed their leaves in July. A “terrible sight,” the 41-year-old added. “We must adapt to this situation that our climate has changed, and we must strive to keep Hungary a livable place.” Give directly to The Spokesman-Review's Northwest Passages community forum series -- which helps to boost local journalism -- by using the easy options below. representative.title: Hittite royal archive with 184 tablets unearthed in central Türkiye | Daily Sabah

snapshot.title: Hittite royal archive with 184 tablets unearthed in central Türkiye
snapshot.evidenceText: A royal archive unearthed at the ancient Hittite settlement of Samuha, in present-day Sivas in central Türkiye, has shed new light on the Hittite Empire , revealing records of a deadly epidemic, military threats and royal life dating back about 3,400 years. Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced that archaeologists uncovered 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments during the 2026 excavations at Kayalıpınar in Sivas’ Yıldızeli district. Together with 53 tablets and fragments found at the site last year, the number of discoveries has reached 184. The documents, dating to the reign of King Tudhaliya II, are considered the most extensive Hittite-language archive discovered in the 21st century, according to the excavation team. The ancient settlement is known as Samuha in Assyrian and Hittite sources. The tablets, written in Hittite and Hurrian, provide firsthand records of state administration, military affairs, religious practices and the experiences of the royal family. “The royal archive at Kayalıpınar has taken its place in history as the most comprehensive Hittite-language archive uncovered in the 21st century,” Ersoy said in a statement shared on social media. Among the most striking documents are records concerning a high-fever epidemic that spread from city to city and appears to have particularly affected children and infants. The tablets show that the health of young princes and princesses, as well as children of high-ranking Hittite officials, was monitored through divination rituals during the outbreak. The records also reflect the concern caused by the disease within the royal family. One document describes a baby princess who was still being breastfed and whose health was being closely monitored. Diviners sought to determine her future through omens. Another tablet records her death and the funeral rites performed for her. A separate tablet sent to the king by a diviner indicates that the princess fell ill in Ziulila, a city whose location has not yet been identified. The archive also contains evidence of the military pressures facing the Hittite state. In a letter sent by Hittite generals in western Anatolia to the king at Samuha, the commanders warned that the Hittite territory was surrounded by enemies. They requested soldiers, horses and chariots to confront the threat. The generals warned that the Hittite army could be destroyed if the requested reinforcements failed to arrive. They also told the king that they would not accept responsibility for the consequences if the necessary support was not provided. The newly discovered texts also offer insight into Hittite divination practices, particularly the use of birds to interpret omens. One tablet records the journeys of bird diviners who left Samuha and traveled through different regions. Their routes, the cities where they stayed and the birds they observed were recorded in a format resembling a diary. The documents also provide previously unknown information about how bird omens were observed, evaluated and interpreted by the Hittites. The archive includes texts covering divination, correspondence, rituals and prayers, offering researchers new material for studying Hittite religious practices as well as the development of the Hittite language and scribal culture. The 53 cuneiform tablets and fragments discovered in 2025 are believed to have belonged to the same royal archive. With the 131 new finds from this year's excavations, the collection now comprises 184 tablets and fragments. The texts are dated to the reign of Tudhaliya II and are expected to provide new information on Hittite political and military history, religious practices, language and administrative culture. Excavations at Kayalıpınar have been conducted since 2021 with the permission of the Culture and Tourism Ministry under the direction of associate professor Çiğdem Maner of the Department of Archaeology and History of Art at Koç University.

representative.title: Kodungallur fisherfolk forced to fight seaweed, plastic waste for survival | Kerala News in English | Onmanorama
representative.author: Vaishnavi M Nair

snapshot.title: Kodungallur fisherfolk forced to fight seaweed, plastic waste for survival
snapshot.evidenceText: For the past 20 years, 60-year-old Selvan of Anapuzha has set out to fish at 6.30 pm, returning only at dawn after a long night on the Karupadanna River. But the hours he spends casting his drift nets are no longer yielding enough to sustain his family. Choked by invasive seaweed and plastic waste, the river that once provided him with a livelihood has become a source of mounting losses. "Long gone are the days when we could sustain ourselves and our families through fishing," Selvan told Onmanorama. Selvan now has to wade through thick mats of African seaweed, which, he said, are either discarded by commercial farmers clearing their fields using backhoe loaders or washed into the river from nearby farms. "The seaweed sinks in the water and decomposes, reducing the oxygen levels needed for fish to thrive," he said. Drift net fishing involves suspending vertical walls of net in the water, held up by surface floats and weighed down by leads at the bottom. The nets then drift freely with the wind and the water. "For drift nets, we use plastic or nylon lines, locally known as 'tonguese', with a mesh size of 65 mm. The nets need to be lowered three metres into the water," Selvan said. "One net costs 30,000. When seaweed or waste gets trapped in it and damages it, repairs cost around 5,000 to 10,000 and take two to three days. Having to repair the net two or three times a year is a huge loss for us," Selvan said. "Yet another issue is the plastic waste that has accumulated in the water, either thrown in by passersby or washed in from elsewhere. After just a day of fishing, our boats get so dirty that we have to clean them thoroughly before heading out again," he said. Selvan is not alone in facing these challenges. Fisherfolk across Kodungallur, including those who use stake nets and Chinese fishing nets, are grappling with a crisis that threatens their livelihoods, pushes families into financial distress and drives younger generations away from the traditional occupation. Kodungallur Taluk AITUC secretary Sajeevan P K, who practises stake net fishing, said the pollution posed a serious threat to aquatic life. "People dump plastic waste and chicken waste from slaughterhouses into the water. This reduces oxygen levels, making it difficult for fish to survive and reducing fish stocks," he told Onmanorama. "Neighbouring farms overrun by seaweed and other invasive plants dump the vegetation directly into the river," Sajeevan said. The decline in fish stocks has severely affected the incomes of households dependent on the sector. "Previously, we used to get fish for at least 10 months a year. Now, we barely get a good catch for 100 days. If a fisherman used to earn 1,000 earlier, he now gets just 200, Sajeevan said. Fisherfolk have also raised concerns about illegal night fishing using torchlights, a practice they said is banned by the government. "People who come to fish illegally using torchlight either do it from boats or from the shore. They do not know which fish to catch and which to leave behind, thereby damaging the ecosystem. They are the main reason why green chromide, or karimeen, is declining and has become almost nonexistent in this area," Selvan said. Varghese, 70, from Pantheerampala in Pullut, who operates a Chinese fishing net, said that weeds, rather than fish, often get caught in the net. The crisis extends far beyond those who cast the nets. Fishing supports an entire chain of workers, from those who sort the catch to those who transport it to markets and sell it. With smaller catches, these workers, too, are losing their incomes. Selvan recalled a time when drift net fishing could comfortably sustain a household. "We used to get 10 to 15 kg of fish a day. My wife and I raised our two children on my wages alone and even built a small house. But now, that is unimaginable. We barely get 5 kg, and that too only on a good day. Otherwise, the catch is just 2 to 3 kg. I will never let my children enter this profession," he said. Sajeevan said his own experience had shaped his son's decision to pursue a different career. "My son, who now works in a bank, has not shown any interest in fishing, seeing how much I have struggled and how much this sector has declined, he said.

representative.title: Fresh Face of Frisby: How a community transformed a school’s outdoor spaces – Another Way: Join us in shaping the world

snapshot.title: Fresh Face of Frisby: How a community transformed a school’s outdoor spaces – Another Way: Join us in shaping the world
snapshot.evidenceText: In this month’s Community Spotlight, we are in in Frisby-on-the-Wreake, Leicestershire. Flor Ferreira tells us how the local primary school spent the summer holidays transforming unloved space into a forest school and wildlife sanctuary. It all started when the school realised that the school pond and surrounding areas had been left unmaintained and pupils could no longer make use of them. They saw the potential to create purposeful spaces where children could explore and experience activities that can be difficult to recreate in a classroom. “Outdoor learning is incredibly valuable because it gives children the chance to get hands-on with the world around them. They can learn about biodiversity by seeing it for themselves, understand where food comes from by growing it, develop practical skills through gardening and begin to understand why caring for our environment matters,” said Mrs Charmaine Ainge, Headteacher at Frisby CofE Primary School. That led to the idea of The Fresh Face of Frisby , bringing around 20 people together over the summer to create a foundation that pupils and staff could continue developing. The school reached out to parents, carers and the wider local community, with social media helping to spread the word… Once the summer holidays started, the project could begin in earnest. As you can imagine, restoring a pond and woodland involved a lot of physical labour – and as we know, this year was the hottest on record. Working in the thirty degree heat, the Frisby team realised that they may have slightly underestimated the scale of work… and how long it would take. But the start of school waits for no-one. Undeterred, the volunteers took on extra days of work to make sure everything was ready for the pupils’ return. As the team explained, as people could see what the project could achieve for the children, there was a real sense of teamwork and generosity, with everyone motivated by the opportunity to create something that the children could benefit from for years to come. So, sun hats on, the work continued. By the time September arrived, the area had been transformed and was ready to welcome both school students and new wildlife residents. The restored pond and surrounding outdoor areas will now support Forest School activities, as well as science and wider environmental education. Pupils will be able to learn first-hand about plants, wildlife, habitats, ecosystems and biodiversity rather than only reading about them in a book. There are also opportunities to develop practical life skills through gardening, planting and caring for the environment. The school hopes these spaces could allow pupils to produce some of their own products and develop a small pupil-led enterprise around what they grow and produce. This could teach children about food production, healthy eating, sustainability and the journey from growing something to creating a finished product. “The really exciting part is that this is only the beginning,” said Mrs Ainge. “Our Eco Club is already taking responsibility for the spaces, and we have plans for further planting and a beehive with support from a local beekeeper. We want our pupils to have a real sense of ownership and to see that even small actions can make a positive difference to the environment and their community.” What began as an effort to restore an overlooked part of the school grounds has become so much more. You don’t need a huge amount of money or resources to make a positive impact for the planet; a lot can be achieved with a dedicated and determined group of people and a supportive community. Another Way is a registered charity (No. 1181438)

representative.title: After US Intervention, Crime Still Controls Venezuelan Mines (Part I) – CONVEN.ORG | HOME

snapshot.title: After US Intervention, Crime Still Controls Venezuelan Mines (Part I) – CONVEN.ORG | HOME
snapshot.evidenceText: This is an abridged version of the original story in Spanish , the second part of award-winning investigative journalism project Dorada Opacidad . We will publish the second (and last) part of this investigation tomorrow. When they pass through the streets of the Las Claritas–Kilómetro 88 mining corridor in Bolívar state, southern Venezuela, a thick, yellowish cloud of dust blankets them like a veil. The sound is unmistakable: a convoy of 15, 20, or 25 motorcycles riding together. Aboard are soldiers from the Orinoco Mining Arc Protection Group (GPAMO)—a unit conceived and activated in 2022 under the command of the Strategic Operational Command of the Bolivarian National Armed Forces (CEOFANB) to safeguard the deposits. They had never been there before June 9, 2026, when three rockets, shot by a US aircraft, shook the area’s flimsy houses. Now, GPAMO is the law. Although some cover their faces, Rafael knows them well. He owns one of the gold mills operating at the El Mecatico mine—one of many in an area that holds the world’s fourth-largest gold deposit, according to a 2018 certification by Canadian mining company Gold Reserve. Standing beneath the tin roof that shelters his business, he explained that he would soon have to pay the GPAMO 20 grams of gold (roughly 2,000 US dollars) in exchange for a registration form that in theory is free. He is also required to make monthly payments to remain on the site. For Rafael and the residents of Las Claritas, everything changed on the morning of June 9, when they woke up to find the area occupied by the military. In the early hours, dozens of vehicles transported hundreds of troops from various branches of the Bolivarian National Armed Forces (FANB)—such as the Special Affairs Directorate (DAE) of the General Directorate of Military Counterintelligence (DGCIM)—who patrolled the streets alongside unidentified men dressed in black and carrying long guns. Meanwhile, a pair of military aviation Cougar helicopters flew just above the rooftops of the houses. The objective of that mobilization was to dismantle “The System.” That was the name given to the criminal alliance between Juan Gabriel Rivas Núñez—known as “Negro Juancho”—and Yohan José Romero (nicknamed “Johan Petrica” ​​or “El Viejo”), one of the leaders of the “mega-gang” born in the Tocorón prison: the Tren de Aragua. For over a decade, this criminal alliance had dominated the territory containing one of the world’s largest gold mining complexes—Las Brisas-Las Cristinas—and had subjugated the local population through torture, mutilation, and murder. All signs pointed to a “change of government”—a term used in the Venezuelan criminal underworld to describe one criminal group replacing another in a territory. The residents were so terrified that they remained locked themselves in their homes for days. Published - October 10, 2026 12:53 pm IST - HYDERABAD Dr. Koyyala Ruth John Paul from Hyderabad has become the first transgender person in India to complete a postgraduate medical course, after clearing all subjects in the recently announced MD/MS examination results. Photo: Special Arrangement There were days when Dr. Koyyala Ruth John Paul struggled to find food. Estranged from her family after coming out as a transgender woman, she spent years trying to make ends meet, searching for jobs while refusing to give up on her dream of becoming a doctor. When the path to postgraduate medical education was blocked by the absence of clear admission procedures for transgender candidates, she turned to the courts. On Saturday (October 10, 2026) her perseverance culminated in a milestone. Dr. Ruth John Paul cleared all subjects in the recently announced MD/MS examination results, completing her postgraduate degree in Emergency Medicine at the ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar, Hyderabad, where she studied during the 2023-26 academic session. She has become the first transgender person in India to complete a postgraduate medical course. “I am feeling very happy. It is a matter of pride for me and my community. It is a great achievement in my life,” she said. The youngest of three siblings, Dr. Ruth John Paul hails from Khammam district and grew up in a family with limited financial means. She lost her father when she was eight years old and was raised by her mother. She completed her schooling and intermediate education in her native district before clearing the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test (NEET) and pursuing undergraduate medical education. She came out as a transgender woman during her undergraduate years. This led to her family rejecting her, leaving her separated from them for nearly six years. The period that followed was marked by financial insecurity and the struggle to survive independently. “There were times when I did not even have food. I struggled to survive and looked for jobs,” she said. In 2021, she found part-time work at Mitr Clinic (now Sabrang Clinic), which is India’s first transgender clinic. She worked there for around two years while continuing to prepare for postgraduate medical entrance examinations. Clearing the entrance examination was not the end of her struggle. Dr. Ruth John Paul said she encountered difficulties during postgraduate medical counselling because there were no clear protocols for accommodating transgender candidates. With the assistance of transgender rights activist Vyjayanti Vasanta Mogli, she approached the Telangana High Court seeking relief. The legal proceedings continued for nearly two years. An interim order from the High Court eventually enabled her to proceed with admission. In 2023, she secured a seat in Emergency Medicine at ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Sanathnagar. Her admission marked a turning point, but the challenges did not end there. She said she continued to encounter stigma and apprehension from people who were unfamiliar with transgender individuals. Working in a clinical environment brought its own challenges. As an emergency medicine trainee, she had to interact with patients during some of their most vulnerable moments, while also navigating the prejudices that transgender people can face. She recalled how some people were initially hesitant or uncomfortable around her. “Initially, some people were scared and did not know how to respond. But when I interacted with patients and treated them with care, they began to appreciate me. People who were initially apprehensive have now become comfortable with me,” she said. Now that she has completed her postgraduate course, Dr. Ruth John Paul wants to use her medical training to help people in need, particularly transgender individuals who require emergency and critical care. “I want to serve everyone, especially transgender people who face critical medical emergencies. I want to provide care without discrimination based on gender identity or sexuality,” she said. Terms & conditions | Institutional Subscriber Comments have to be in English, and in full sentences. representative.title: The outlaw bear that captured Asheville • Asheville Watchdog
representative.author: JACK EVANS

snapshot.title: The outlaw bear that captured Asheville • Asheville Watchdog
snapshot.evidenceText: She knew the name might annoy people — that it could strike them as gimmicky, craven, even exploitative. The first time she mentioned it to a friend, he told her: That’s a terrible idea. But it had come to her almost involuntarily, and now she couldn’t stop thinking about it. Was it so unusual? Neighborhood bears are named all the time. They pick up monikers like they do ticks or briars. One bear might have a different name from each house on the street. This bear, though, was unusual. Everyone was talking about her. She was wanted by the state. She had developed a taste for cat food, which she realized could be found inside houses; had several times broken into homes in a north Asheville neighborhood; and, on Aug. 18, had injured the occupant of one of those homes as she tried to escape. Wildlife officials planned to capture her, euthanize her, and relocate her cubs. Depending on who you asked, the bear was either a menace to public safety or a victim of human negligence. Hannah Furgiuele was not the only person — and certainly not the only person in Beaverdam Valley — with strong feelings about the bear’s apparent fate, but she would become the neighbor with the most sway over it. The name was an inflection point. Some of Furgiuele’s less sympathetic neighbors called the bear “Baddie Patty,” but another idea had been kicking around Furgiuele’s head. America’s most beloved country singer had just died, and Furgiuele had been reading about her conservation advocacy, her love of her mountain home. It felt right, not just because of the pun embedded in the name but also because of how it turned the story on its head — what if the villain of the story could be seen in the light of someone who, everyone agreed, was a saint? Soon there were signs all around the neighborhood, a website, a petition. Thousands of people signed it, then tens of thousands. There was a new rallying cry: Pardon Dolly. All of this was possible because the story didn’t have an ending. Dolly, as so many people suddenly knew her, didn’t disappear. She didn’t even stop trying to break into houses. But she also didn’t get caught. Beaverdam Valley is the kind of neighborhood that would look good on an Asheville real estate brochure. In a city unceasingly described as being nestled among the Blue Ridge Mountains, the valley really is suspended between two worlds: A few minutes in one direction stand the restaurants and supermarkets lining Merrimon Avenue; in the other, the Craggy Mountains and Blue Ridge Parkway. One might, beginning a quick jaunt to Trader Joe’s, have to stop their car to let a herd of deer or a flock of wild turkeys cross the street. This liminal, pastoral quality casts a sense of serenity over the community. It’s not unusual for neighbors to leave their windows open and doors unlocked. The same features have also made Beaverdam Valley a site of frequent meetings between human and ursine residents. Sometimes, these encounters reify the neighborhood’s splendor. “If you are around a mother bear and her cubs, you will fall in love,” Reb Haizlip, a retired children’s-museum architect who lives there, said, “It’s impossible not to see the beauty and playfulness in those animals — the love that exists between a mother and her cubs, the way they play and work together.” The human-animal relationships can also be more frictive. Bears’ lives center on finding food; they’ll take it wherever they can get it, and once they locate a reliable source, they’ll go back for more. Chris Todd, the president of the Beaverdam Valley Neighborhood Association, said that the bear-resistant trash can he acquired through a city program worked well for a while, until the bears figured out that tossing it in the air and letting it crash repeatedly would do the trick. Now he has bear-proofing straps on his bear-proof can. Between May and September of this year, the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission received more than 800 bear-related reports from Buncombe County — nearly half the statewide total. Seventy-one of them involved a break-in. And no community had more than Beaverdam Valley. One evening in August, a houseguest returned to the home where she was staying on Spooks Branch Road — one of many streets named for the area’s streams and coves — to find a mother black bear and her cubs playing in the twilit back yard. The homeowner and her guests usually entered through the back door. But so did the bears: Multiple times this summer, the mother had let herself in and absconded with bags of cat food. The entries had left the back door broken. The visitor gave them a wide berth, went through the front door, then came back out to clean up some lawn clippings. When she turned around, she saw the cubs playing on the front porch but no sign of the mother. Then she realized the front door was open. Inside, the homeowner woke to the sound of her guest banging on her bedroom window. She exited her room, saw the bear, and tried to shield herself behind her front door. The bear swatted at the homeowner, walked out of the house, and departed with her cubs. Within the hour, Ashley Hobbs, a biologist with the Wildlife Resources Commission, was en route to Mission Hospital, where the injured woman was taken by ambulance. Hobbs found her alert and talkative, with a pair of gashes along the upper right side of her face — “relatively speaking, in terms of bear attacks, pretty minor,” Hobbs said. (This account of the attack is drawn from a WRC incident report; the victim declined to be interviewed for this story.) Hobbs spends much of her time talking to homeowners and government officials in and around Asheville, trying to convince them to adopt habits and policies to keep people and bears safe from each other — stowing food and locking doors, issuing bear-resistant trash cans and developing ordinances to punish intentional feeding. She’s also the person who responds when a particular bear becomes a nuisance or, worse, a threat. That nobody else in the wildlife agency has a job like Hobbs’ one-place-one-animal gig is one of many indications that Asheville is a crucible of human-bear relations. Plenty of residents live harmoniously with the creatures. But Asheville is also full of tourists and transplants who have never seen bears; of residents who fail to secure their dog food or bird seed; of people who have either never heard the adage that “a fed bear is a dead bear” or who are foolish enough to think it doesn’t apply to them; and of trash cans and dumpsters and garage fridges not designed for a world full of hungry, persistent, 400-pound animals who want what they have. Of the 18 injuries caused by bears statewide since 2017, 11 have taken place in Buncombe. That night in the hospital, the victim told Hobbs everything that had happened: the pattern of cat food theft, the unlocked doors, how just that morning the same mother bear and her cubs had gotten into her trash. They would talk again in the morning; for now, she told Hobbs, she didn’t want the bear killed. What happened next would not be so uncomplicated. Most of the 9,000 or so black bears in western North Carolina’s mountains don’t become nuisances, and even most bears that do — the kind that can often be found feasting on the contents of overturned trash bins — don’t become so dangerous that they leave wildlife managers only one option. But by the morning after the Beaverdam Valley incident, it had become clear to state wildlife officials that this bear had crossed the threshold. She unlocked her phone and started typing. “This bear has young cubs,” she wrote. “Euthanizing her doesn’t help people learn to coexist in bear country.” Furgiuele first lived in Beaverdam Valley in her 20s. Bears were a regular presence then, too; her cat, Puma, had a knack for befriending cubs who visited her yard. snapshot.title: The outlaw bear that captured Asheville • Asheville Watchdog

representative.title: Dixcove Fishermen Reject Offshore Gold Exploration
representative.author: Kwame Darko

snapshot.title: Dixcove Fishermen Reject Offshore Gold Exploration
snapshot.evidenceText: Fishermen at Dixcove have rejected GoldCoast Resource Corporation's bid to explore for gold offshore, saying the ocean that sustains their families cannot be handed over without their consent. For generations, the waters off Dixcove in the Ahanta West Municipality have put food on tables and paid school fees for families along Ghana's Western Region coastline. Now, fishermen there say that lifeline is under threat from a proposed offshore gold exploration project they were never properly consulted about. Fishermen in the coastal town have rejected plans by GoldCoast Resource Corporation to explore for gold offshore, arguing the venture could endanger their livelihoods and damage the marine environment, according to the Ghanaian Times . The fishermen insist the ocean remains their traditional source of food and income, and that any decision affecting its use must involve the communities whose survival depends on it. Their position emerged on Tuesday during an engagement organised by Friends of the Nation (FON), a civil society organisation that works on coastal and marine conservation issues, the Ghanaian Times reports. The meeting brought together stakeholders at Dixcove to discuss the proposed exploration and examine its possible effects on fishing grounds, marine ecosystems and the wider coastal economy. representative.title: 'Home' documentary from 'Degrassi' co-creator explores complexities of Ontario encampment
representative.author: News Staff

snapshot.title: 'Home' documentary from 'Degrassi' co-creator explores complexities of Ontario encampment
snapshot.evidenceText: TORONTO — When tents started popping up on the lawn in front of a sprawling provincial property in Cobourg, Ont., television producer Linda Schuyler wondered who the people living in the encampment were. “I started to go in and get to know them,” said Schuyler, a filmmaker and producer who is best known as the co-creator of the “Degrassi” television series. “As Torontonians, we have been very aware of the homeless crisis for a long period of time. And I always felt kind of helpless about it. It seemed like such a big problem. I didn’t know what I could do to help,” said Schuyler, who splits her time between Toronto and a community near the southern Ontario lakeside town. She teamed up with filmmaker Will Bowes to explore the inner workings of the encampment and the complex individual circumstances of its residents. The result is a new documentary, titled “Home,” set to premiere on TVO on Saturday, coinciding with World Homeless Day. The film introduces audiences to several unhoused people who settled at Brookside, a vacant property owned by the province that had previously been home to Cobourg’s elite and later became a youth detention centre. It details the myriad reasons how someone can end up without a home, from executives and business owners losing their livelihoods, to those who faced abusive partners, the death of loved ones and the challenges of addiction and mental health. The filmmakers said they first entered without filming equipment and simply listened to people’s stories. Once they formed relationships, the filmmakers asked if people were comfortable speaking on camera. If they did, they’d receive a Tim Hortons gift card to acknowledge their time. Schuyler said they’d also ask people if they would give them a tour of their tents or structures. “And without a doubt, they would all say, ‘Oh, just a minute. Let me tidy up a bit,” she said. “They really took pride in building little gardens and little pathways to get to their homes,” Bowes added. “It was remarkable what they were able to accomplish.” Along with highlighting the people inside the encampment, the film, which collected around 60 hours of footage over about a year, also shared the perspectives of people in the local community. That included the town’s mayor as well as social workers, community advocates and concerned citizens who had reservations about the proximity of the encampment to local schools. “Even though we wanted to get to know the people in the encampment, we did want to be fair to the community and give some of the local people an opportunity to talk about it from their perspective,” Schuyler said. The documentary does not, however, include any narration, a deliberate choice because “narration can be leading and it can be judgmental,” Schuyler said. “It’s a principle that we had way back in ‘Degrassi.’ We really wanted to give our young people an authentic voice and we really wanted to look at whatever issue we were dealing with from multiple sides. And that approach spilled over into this documentary,” Schuyler said. “Without getting too political about it, we wanted to just show that it’s a multi-faceted story,” she said. Bowes said the experience of making the documentary forced him to acknowledge the biases he had formed around homeless people. “I also felt like if you end up in an encampment, that is a result of years, if not decades of bad decisions (and) definite substance abuse,” Bowes said. “But that couldn’t be farther from the truth. Many people are there because they had a really terrible time during COVID.” Making this film also showed him how the journey of homelessness is not linear. For example, at one point, the documentary follows a few people who moved into a motel after the encampment was dismantled following the sale of Brookside. However, their motel stay was temporary and soon after they arrived, they had to leave. “Sometimes you’re getting ahead and then the rug gets pulled out from under you, and that was really frustrating for us obviously as filmmakers, who are trying to put together a narrative, and you want the narrative to progress and get better and see someone start thriving or at least start taking the steps to,” Bowes said. “But unfortunately that just wasn’t possible,” he said. The filmmakers said the goal isn’t for the documentary to provide a clearcut answer for how to solve the issue but rather for audiences to walk away having to mull it over for themselves. “We are so rich with resources, both land and otherwise, I find it embarrassing as a Canadian that we cannot treat our unhoused better,” Schuyler said. “I hope that that sentiment somehow will arouse in people who watch the documentary.” Bowes said he also hopes the film leads to more empathy for homeless people. “A little bit more understanding for the human being that you might have otherwise walked past or put a label on,” he said. representative.title: UNICEF Warns Impending El Niño Threatens Education, Health, and Safety for Millions | Inter Press Service
representative.author: Oritro Karim

snapshot.title: UNICEF Warns Impending El Niño Threatens Education, Health, and Safety for Millions
snapshot.evidenceText: A mother and her child stand in the wreckage of their destroyed home in Toamasina, Madagascar, following a devastating cyclone. Credit: UNICEF/Tsiory Ny Aina Andriantsoarana UNITED NATIONS, Oct 9 2026 (IPS) - New figures from the United Nations Children’s Fund ( UNICEF ) project that the impending 2026-2027 El Niño cycle could be one of the strongest on record. Marked by unusually wet and dry conditions, this cycle is forecast to trigger a host of extreme weather events, threatening the health, security, education, and development of over 347 million children worldwide. “For children, El Niño is far more than a weather pattern. It can mean increased displacement, malnutrition, water shortages, and disease outbreaks. Children are also at risk of schools closing, while families could experience added financial hardship,” said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell, emphasizing that anticipatory action is critical in protecting communities from climate shocks in the coming months. Nearly half of the world’s children—roughly 1.1 billion—are already exposed to at least three overlapping climate hazards, including droughts, extreme heat, and floods. The impending El Niño cycle could affect children and communities across nearly 100 countries and territories between October and December 2026. Rohini Sampoornam Swaminathan, UNICEF Statistics and Monitoring Manager, tells IPS that children are uniquely vulnerable because of their early developmental stage and dependence on essential services and caregivers. This significantly limits their ability to withstand climate shocks, especially as basic services begin to disappear when extreme weather hits. “Communities may not have fully recovered from one shock before another one strikes, causing the impacts to compound over time,” she said. The Asia-Pacific region is projected to face the heaviest toll, with roughly 190 million children estimated to be at risk. Substantial populations are also critically vulnerable across East and Southern Africa, with 41 million children vulnerable to climate shocks, alongside another 41 million in Latin America and the Caribbean. Approximately 22 million children are similarly vulnerable in Europe and Central Asia, followed by 20 million in the Middle East and North Africa, and 20 million in West and Central Africa. El Niño’s regional impacts are expected to vary significantly and could compound pre-existing humanitarian crises. Swaminathan underscored that climate shocks that are manageable in some areas can become pronounced humanitarian crises in others. Tropical nations—such as Colombia, Papua New Guinea, Fiji, and the Philippines—are forecast to face unusually dry conditions, driving weaker agricultural outputs and severe water scarcity. This, in turn, could elevate rates of acute malnutrition and adverse health outcomes among children. Conversely, communities in the Greater Horn of Africa could face alarmingly high levels of rainfall, particularly in Somalia, where there is a greater risk of riverine and flash flooding. Children in this region are especially vulnerable to outbreaks of water-borne diseases. Between 2016 and 2023, weather-related disasters displaced more than 20,000 children daily. Swaminathan stressed to IPS that regions facing wetter climates could experience exacerbated displacement as floods push more communities far from their homes and into crowded, temporary shelters, which amplifies protection risks. In protracted conflict or crisis zones such as Chad and Afghanistan, El Niño poses a direct threat to survival for children. Already bearing the burdens of extreme hunger, displacement, and an overwhelming lack of access to essential services such as protection, these children have no safety net when climate shocks ravage their communities, as they are already on the brink of collapse. Beyond physical hazards, UNICEF’s findings highlight that disruptions to schooling are among the most alarming consequences of the impending cycle. Severe droughts and floods threaten widespread school closures, declining attendance, and rising dropout rates. In 2025 alone, extreme weather patterns interrupted education for an estimated 171 million students globally. Swaminathan warned that climate-induced disruptions to schooling carry profound risks for children’s safety, exposing them to heightened risks of violence, exploitation, and child marriage. Girls bear the brunt of these impacts, often taking on family caregiving roles that can lead to compromised health and nutrition, as well as limited access to essential services. “When girls leave school, they are often less likely than boys to return,” she noted. UNICEF estimates show that every US $1 invested in disaster risk reduction and prevention efforts can yield up to $15 in saved recovery costs. Yet less than 1 percent of humanitarian funding is allocated for anticipatory action, even with months of warning and massive projected losses. The agency continues to call on governments, donors, and partners to invest in lifesaving anticipatory intervention before peak impacts hit vulnerable communities. UNICEF highlights building climate resilience, securing essential services, and guaranteeing humanitarian access as key priorities in its response. Swaminathan underscored that children with disabilities, who already face persistent barriers in education, healthcare, and nutrition, must be considered in disaster preparedness. She emphasized that inclusive planning is essential in addressing structural inequalities and ensuring every region is adequately prepared. “Despite efforts to plan for disasters, most resources are mobilized only after the damage occurs, and the focus is often on the immediate response phase of a crisis,” said Swaminathan. “With forecasts providing months of warning, UNICEF is urging governments, donors, and partners to act before needs escalate by investing early and before impacts peak. Building resilience is not only about infrastructure and early warning systems, but also about strengthening the services and institutions children rely on and addressing the inequalities that make some communities far more vulnerable to climate shocks than others.”

snapshot.title: Canada marks Royal Assent of legislation for Self-Government Treaty with the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got’įnę
snapshot.evidenceText: From: Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada Today, the Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations, the Honourable Rebecca Alty, announced that Bill C-27 has received Royal Assent. This Self-Government Treaty will support the community to make decisions that best support their people, strengthen their culture, and grow their economy. It provides the formal basis for a new government-to-government relationship between us and the Government of Canada, and a government-to-government relation between us and the Government of the Northwest Territories. It is our generation’s legacy to our children and future generations. We will do our best to use it to preserve, protect, exercise, and advance the inherent and treaty rights of the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got’įnę for the benefit of all our people living in Canada, here today. But our youth are the future, and this agreement provides our youth with the foundations to do the same when they take on the task of preserving, protecting, exercising and advancing our rights. Use this Self-Government Agreement, learn from the mistakes we may make and take us into the future—secure as Sahtu Dene/Metis people within the larger Canadian mosaic.” Sherry Hodgson President of Tlegohli Got’ine Government Inc. “Reconciliation requires action. We welcome Canada’s decision to move forward with legislation to give legal force to the Final Self-Government Agreement for the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got’įnę, establishing it as a Self-Government Treaty. Collaborative governance is a cornerstone of our mandate, and this step reflects a shared commitment to recognising Indigenous rights and building a stronger future in partnership across the Northwest Territories.” R.J. Simpson Premier of the Northwest Territories “At its core, this legislation recognises an enduring truth: that the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got’įnę have an inherent right to govern themselves, as they have since long before Canada existed. Today, we celebrate the renewal of Canada’s relationship with the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got’įnę and the new opportunities that self-government will bring. I extend my heartfelt congratulations to the leadership, Elders, negotiators, and community members whose dedication and hard work over more than two decades made this milestone achievement possible.” The Honourable Rebecca Alty Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations and Member of Parliament for the Northwest Territories On September 18, 2025, after 20 years of negotiations, the Tlegohli Got’ine Government Inc., the Government of Canada and the Government of Northwest Territories signed the Final Self-Government Agreement for the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got’įnę. Bill C-27 makes the Final Self-Government Agreement legally binding, formally recognising the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got’įnę’s inherent right of self-government. When the Final Self-Government Agreement comes into effect on a date set by an Order in Council, the Tłegǫ́hłı̨ Got’įnę Government will be the governing body that represents the Sahtu Dene and Metis of Norman Wells, one of five Indigenous communities in the Sahtu Region of the Northwest Territories. Amendments to the Mackenzie Valley Resource Management Act and related laws reflect the recognition, status, and power of the new government. Bill C-27 is aligned with the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and respects the rights in the 1994 Sahtu Dene and Metis Comprehensive Land Claim Agreement , which is protected by Canada’s Constitution. representative.title: Could Quebec's new government derail plans for Alto's high-speed train project? | CBC News
representative.author: Chloë Ranaldi

snapshot.title: Could Quebec's new government derail plans for Alto's high-speed train project? | CBC News
snapshot.evidenceText: The Crown corporation responsible for a proposed high-speed rail line connecting Toronto to Quebec City says it plans to deliver on the project, despite opposition from the newly elected Parti Québécois (PQ) government. During the election campaign, the Parti Québécois (PQ) said it would withdraw from Alto’s proposed train project if it came into power. PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon argues the money intended for the project should instead go toward maintaining the province’s aging infrastructure, such as its hospitals, roads and public transit. A recent report from the Parliamentary Budget Office suggests building the proposed high-speed rail project could cost between $75 billion and $113 billion, an amount higher than initially estimated. St-Pierre Plamondon says if there are billions of dollars to invest in infrastructure, building the high-speed rail isn’t among the top priorities for Quebecers. Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has said the Alto high-speed rail line connecting Quebec City to Toronto, and stopping in five other cities along the way, is not among Quebecers' priorities. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press) In a public meeting on Wednesday afternoon, Alto said the project from its inception to completion will last around 15 years and there will be many governments they will work with. Their objective is to begin construction by 2029. "The issue of government relations between the government of Canada and the government of Quebec, the government of Ontario — that's for the governments. That's not our jobs, that's above our pay grade," said J. Robert S. Prichard, chair of the board of directors at Alto. "Our job is to laser focus on preparation and being ready to deliver this project on time, consistent with the budget, consistent with the expectations of our mandate. That's the job we have," he said. Alto says it does not want to divide or separate communities, and that it does not intend to sever federal or provincial highways – building over and underpasses when possible. (Alto) When asked about the PQ's opposition to the project, the office of the federal minister of transport, Steven MacKinnon, says the Canadian government believes in co-operative federalism, and is ready to work with the Quebec government on this project. “Alto is a project of exceptional scale that will benefit Quebecers for generations to come,” a statement from the office reads. “It will transform the way people travel between major centres in Quebec and Ontario, with tangible benefits for their work, education and social lives.” What to expect from a Parti Québécois government Alto high-speed rail project could cost more than originally thought: budget watchdog But André Lecours, a professor in the school of political studies at the University of Ottawa, doesn’t believe the project is viable without the support of the Quebec government. "I think it's dead,” said Lecours. "I don't think that the federal government would go ahead against the wishes of the PQ. "I think it's in the interest of the government of Canada to minimize tensions with the Quebec government at this point." Lecours added that it seems unlikely that opposition parties will put their efforts into supporting this project and attempting to influence the PQ to support it. The Conservative Party of Quebec, which won a historic 19 seats in the general election , has also spoken out against the project. Jérémie Letellier, president of the Fédération de l'UPA de la Montérégie, says the high-speed rail line would be catastrophic for agricultural communities. (Chloë Ranaldi/CBC) Jérémie Letellier, president of the Fédération de l'UPA de la Montérégie, a regional branch of Quebec's largest agricultural federation, says the rail project would be catastrophic for farming communities in Ontario and Quebec. "In the end, the decision goes to the federal government, so it's clearly a political issue right now," he said. "We will do whatever we can to stop this project. There's nothing good for farmers in this.” He says compensation offered to farmers will not be enough, since the train would severely affect operations by cutting through farmland. Alto high-speed train would be ‘catastrophic’ for Quebec farmers, federation says During the public meeting, Alto wanted to reassure farmers. "There will never be a break in a numbered highway, a federal highway, a provincial highway or a major highway," said Alto's CEO, Martin Imbleau. Alto says a more detailed route for the network's initial section between Ottawa and Montreal is expected in the fall. Construction of the first segment of the train line is planned for 2029. Chloë Ranaldi is a journalist covering Montreal's off-island communities like Vaudreuil-Dorion, Hudson and Saint-Lazare. Chloë has an office space in Hudson. Audience Relations, CBC P.O. representative.title: 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals the landscape that sustained early humans in the Levant | Archaeology News Online Magazine
representative.author: Dario Radley

snapshot.title: 700,000-year-old elephant tooth reveals the landscape that sustained early humans in the Levant | Archaeology News Online Magazine
snapshot.evidenceText: A well-preserved elephant tooth from northern Israel has given researchers a picture of the land where early humans lived 700,000 years ago. The tooth came from Gesher Benot Ya’aqov, a prehistoric site in the Jordan Rift Valley, south of today’s Hula Valley. Early humans made stone tools there. Hannah Farrell, a PhD candidate at the University of Haifa, led the study. Her team published the results in Quaternary Science Reviews. Prof. Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai University excavated the site. The elephant remains, a molar and tusk fragments, lay next to basalt handaxes and cleavers. Those tools belong to the Acheulian tradition, one of the earliest and most widespread stone-tool technologies in human history. The animal was a Palaeoloxodon antiquus , the straight-tusked elephant . This species ranked among the largest land mammals of the Pleistocene. Farrell’s team didn’t study the elephant alone. They treated the tooth as a record of the whole ecosystem, one shared by big animals and human toolmakers . The researchers used CT scanning, 3D reconstruction, microscopic wear analysis, isotope chemistry, and pollen studies. Micro-CT scans identified the tooth as a lower third molar. Carbon and oxygen isotopes in the enamel showed the elephant lived in a well-watered place. Wear marks on the chewing surface pointed to a mixed diet of tree leaves and grasses. The animal fed in woodlands and along rivers, likely in the Jordan Valley. The tooth sat close to the stone tools, so the findings tie directly to human activity at the site. Pollen from the sediments under the tooth backed this up. Samples held pollen from Mediterranean trees and open grassland. They also held plants from riverbanks and water, including reeds, sedges, willow, tamarisk, and aquatic species. Together, the evidence points to a lasting landscape of woodlands, grasslands, marshes, rivers, and shallow water. The Hula Valley sat inside the Levantine Corridor, a land bridge linking Africa and Eurasia. Early humans and animals moved along this route. Scientists have long known the corridor mattered, but little was clear about its plants and climate during the Acheulian period. The new work fills part of that gap. The valley looks like a stable refuge, with steady water and food for wildlife and for people passing through. Sharon says water, plants, and animals decided where humans and wildlife could survive. Learning how both groups responded to environmental change hundreds of thousands of years ago helps explain what shaped our species. He describes the wetlands, rivers, and woodlands of the Hula Valley as a support for life along one of the world’s earliest migration corridors. Cheryl Makarewicz led the isotope work, and Nimrod Marom handled the archaeozoology. Minji Jin and Dafna Langgut of Tel Aviv University studied the pollen. The results add to knowledge of elephant and early human interaction in the Levant during the Early Pleistocene . representative.title: Nepal floods damage 1,800 hectares of crops and kill thousands of livestock

snapshot.title: Nepal floods damage 1,800 hectares of crops and kill thousands of livestock
snapshot.evidenceText: In this interview, Beth Bechdol, FAO Deputy Director-General, outlines the impact of the floods on rural communities and the urgent path towards agricultural recovery Rome – The devastating flash floods that swept through Nepal’s Bhote Koshi–Trishuli river corridor on 26 August 2026 have taken a heavy toll on communities, killing over 1000 people, forcing many to flee their homes and causing extensive damage to agriculture and rural livelihoods. Preliminary assessments indicate that around 1,800 hectares of crops—mostly paddy—were damaged, while thousands of livestock were killed. Farmland, fisheries, food stocks and agricultural infrastructure were also affected, threatening the food security and incomes of farming families well beyond the immediate emergency. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) is supporting the Government of Nepal’s response, including through emergency veterinary support and assessments of damage to agriculture and rural livelihoods. In this interview, FAO Deputy Director-General Beth Bechdol discusses the impact of the floods on farmers and livestock producers, the most urgent agricultural needs and why restoring production ahead of the next planting season will be critical to recovery. Q1. What has been the impact of the floods on people’s livelihoods? BB: First of all, the human toll of the recent floods has been devastating. More than 1,000 people have lost their lives, thousands more remain unaccounted for, and entire communities have been affected. But this disaster has also washed away the means by which many families feed themselves and earn an income. Crops have been buried under mud and sediment. Fishponds have been swept away, and roads, bridges and markets have been damaged, disrupting the movement of food, animal feed, milk and other agricultural inputs. FAO’s preliminary assessment indicates that around 1,800 hectares of crops have been damaged, mostly paddy fields, with production losses approaching 7,700 tonnes. For farming families, these losses are about much more than the current harvest. Losing a crop can mean losing next season’s production and next month’s income. Q2. How have the floods affected livestock and poultry? BB: This is also an important livestock-producing area. Across 11 affected municipalities, there were more than 350,000 head of cattle, buffalo, sheep and goats, as well as 1.6 million poultry. Thousands of animals have now been reported lost, and we estimate that 5 to 10 percent of the livestock and poultry population in these communities may have been completely lost. For a farming family, losing an animal is not only about losing food today. It can also mean losing an important source of income and future production. That is why agricultural recovery needs to be considered as part of the response, and it has to begin early. Q3. What are the most urgent needs for farmers and livestock producers? BB: Farmers will need seeds, while livestock will need feed and veterinary care. There is also an increased risk of animal disease following flooding like this. So vaccination, treatment and disease surveillance will also be important. representative.title: How October 7 redrew the map of the Middle East | US-Israel war on Iran News | Al Jazeera
representative.author: Simon Speakman Cordall

snapshot.title: October 7 redrew the map of the Middle East, opening new faultlines
snapshot.evidenceText: Three years of war have upended alliances, weakened US influence and reshaped the region’s power balance. In the past three years, following the October 7 attacks and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the wider region has been marked by conflict, economic turmoil, and a shattering of the balance of power. The network of alliances maintained by Iran, long central to its regional power, has been hit hard and severely weakened. Yemen’s Houthi rebels remain one notable exception. Israel has made gains. Many of the leaders of the Lebanese group Hezbollah and the Palestinian group Hamas have been killed, while Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was also assassinated in February. Israel occupies most of Gaza, where it has also killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and reduced much of the enclave to rubble. Its military aggression has come at a cost, isolating it from its traditional allies and making it globally unpopular, including in the United States. The potential for more normalisation deals with Arab countries seems unlikely, at least in the short term. Instead, Israel continues to launch attacks across the region, crossing previously held red lines – such as the 2025 attack on Doha, Qatar – and making many governments around the world view it as the primary source of unrest in the Middle East. “Before October 7, the US’s entire policy in the Middle East rested on normalising Israel’s presence in the region through its so-called Abraham Accords,” HA Hellyer of the Royal United Services Institute said, referring to the normalisation deals with several Arab states, including the United Arab Emirates. “Israel’s response to the October 7 attack ended that.” Instead, rather than a stable Middle East with Israel at its centre, the US entered into a war with Iran this year, and has since looked on as Tehran targeted US allies across the Gulf, shattering the perceived security of the US security umbrella. Drones and missiles hit Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas hub and started fires near Dubai airport and at Fujairah’s oil zone. In September, the Houthis surged down Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking the port of Mocha and nearby islands. Their gains tightened their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, threatening a key route for global trade and energy supplies that had become even more important amid disruption in the Strait of Hormuz. “There’s been a loss of faith in the US as a singularly sufficient security guarantor,” Hellyer continued. “This is why you’re seeing many in the region talk to other external actors, in addition to continuing, and in some cases deepening their US ties, as well as initiatives such as the Mecca security pact as states in the region look elsewhere for ways to safeguard their security,” he said, referring to the defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, signed in August, agreeing that an attack on one was to be regarded as an attack on all. Alongside the loss of confidence in the US as a security guarantor has come a dramatic reordering of alliances and rivalries. Much of Iran’s network – most notably Hezbollah, whose reputation had long served as a deterrent against Israeli attack – appeared to buckle under Israeli pressure. That, in turn, emboldened an Israeli military push that saw troops invade Lebanon in October 2024 and again in March 2026 , and seize Syrian territory during the brief power vacuum that followed Bashar al-Assad’s ouster in 2024 . “The Middle East has always been multi-aligned. However, now it’s even more so,” Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, said of the increased leverage given to external actors, such as Turkiye in Syria and China’s involvement in negotiations over the end to war on Iran, as Beijing finds its own energy supplies under threat. “It’s ironic, since October 7, it’s Israel that has emerged as the revisionist power and Iran almost as the status quo power,” she said of the apparent reversal in status of the two belligerents, with Tehran seemingly more focused on regaining the ground it has lost in the last three years rather than advancing beyond them. However, none of this was to overstate Israeli influence, or liken it to a regional superpower, Vakil cautioned. “Israel may currently be the preponderant military power in the Middle East, but real power is typically classed as being able to project stability, which Israel hasn’t shown itself able or willing to do,” she said. While Israel and the US hoped February’s attacks would swiftly topple Iran’s government, they have instead opened a new front. Tehran now wields economic leverage over Israel, the US and their partners through the Strait of Hormuz, which borders Iran and typically carries about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, and through Bab al-Mandeb, which is now threatened by its Houthi allies. Whatever Tehran’s intentions, the economic pain has been uneven. The West, cushioned by emergency reserves, record US oil production and supplies from countries such as Norway, has so far avoided the turmoil of the 1970s oil shocks, when US drivers queued for petrol, even though the current disruption is on a greater scale. In April, the International Monetary Fund trimmed its 2026 global growth forecast only slightly, to 3.1 percent from 3.3 percent. Gulf exporters, in contrast, have fared far worse. The same assessment cut its forecast for Saudi Arabia from 4.5 to 3.1 percent, and turned Qatar’s from growth of 6.1 percent into a contraction of 8.6 percent. “It’s curious, in many ways the West’s reduced need for Gulf oil has increased the degree to which Israel has become a liability for the US,” Israeli political economist Shir Hever told Al Jazeera, referring to a diplomatic alliance between the two states long underpinned by Israel’s strategic position in an oil-rich region central to US interests. “There’s a train of thought in Israel that the current crises may push the Gulf states into allying with it,” he said, while noting the irony that Israel had been the main aggressor in the conflicts that followed October 7. “Though that seems fairly unlikely.”
